(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for Nabatean water bread (K͟hubz al-māʾ al-Nabaṭī):[/b]\nTake 1 makkūk (7½ pounds) good quality samīd͟h flour and sift it in a big wooden bowl (jafna). Mix with it 3 ūqiyyas (3 ounces) yeast, and add 30 dirhams (3 ounces) salt that has been dissolved in water and strained. \n\tKnead the mixture into very firm dough, as firm as stone (ḥajar) and press it well. Continue pressing it while rubbing the bottom of the dough 120 times with water in doses of 5 dirhams (1 tablespoon) each until it develops a consistency which is a little firmer than that of the zalābiya dough. Cover the dough and let it ferment. With the help of some oil of hulled sesame seeds (s͟hayraj muqas͟hs͟har) divide dough into portions and shape them like farānī. \n\tLight the tannūr and wait until the fire starts to smolder gently. Wipe clean the inside of the oven with a piece of cloth. Rub each portion of the dough with 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) sesame oil or zayt anfāq (olive oil extracted from unripe olives) then flatten it by hand and stick it to the inside of the smoldering oven (tannūr hādiʾ). This recipe will make 15 pieces of bread. \n\tWhen you are done sticking all the portions in the tannūr, cover it with its lid for a short while. As soon as the breads are set (jamuda), sprinkle them lightly with water, about ½ kūz (½ cup), and return the lid as it was before. Wait for a short while, then remove the cover, and open up the bottom vent hole (ʿayn al-tannūr) to expose the breads to more heat. As soon as they brown (iḥmarra), take them out. Scrape their backs with a knife and wipe them with a small amount of water. Stack the breads, enclose them in a damp piece of cloth, and set them aside for an hour or so. \n\tServe this bread whenever you need it, it will be the best, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for bread called k͟hubz al-qanānī (bottle bread):[/b]\nMake soft dough similar in consistency to zalābiya dough, using as much as needed of good quality, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran-free) and water. \n\tPour a little pure olive oil (zayt naqī) or sesame oil into wide-mouthed heatproof thin bottles and sprinkle the inside with rose water. Pour the batter into the bottles until they are almost full. Place the filled bottles on flat tiles (qarāmīd) spread in the bottom of the tannūr, and let them bake in medium heat (muʿtadila) until done. To test for doneness, insert a toothpick (k͟hilāl) into the baking dough. If it comes out clean, it is done. \n\tWhen you take out the bottles and break them, the breads will come out looking like bottles, God willing. \n\tTo serve, moisten the breads, if you like, with refined sweetened milk perfumed with mastic and rose water, or with milk and honey, or eat it plain, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making k͟hubz maʿrūk (pressed and rubbed bread):[/b]\nTake 1 makkūk (7½ pounds) flour (daqīq) and add to it 3 ūqiyyas (3 ounces) yeast and 20 dirhams (2 ounces) salt and water. Knead the mixture thoroughly into stiff dough and cover it and let it ferment fully well. \n\tSprinkle dough with 30 dirhams (1/3 cup) water in three batches. Divide it into portions and on a slab of smooth marble, press dough pieces in consecutive rubbing movements using olive oil (zayt). Shape portions into flat discs and drape them with a moistened piece of cloth. \n\tLight fire in the tannūr and let it smolder quietly. Sprinkle the bread pieces with a mixture of water and milk and stick them into the oven. Cover the oven with its lid as well as a piece of wet sackcloth (k͟hīs͟h) and let the breads bake. When they are done, open up the bottom vent hole (ʿayn al-tannūr) to let the breads brown (yaḥmarr). As soon as you take them out of the oven, wipe their faces with water to make them look glossy. You can get more gloss if you wipe them while they are still in the oven. \n\tI have recited these lines, Ibn al-Rūmī composed on this variety of bread: \n[i]Nothing surpasses the bread I saw while once by Kark͟h was passing. A show stealer:\nI saw it first in the baker’s hands pressed and kneaded on the board, and like springing pearls bounced back.\nHe took a pearl and faster than fate itself, looking like a shield, he put it back.\nLike an expert in the art of spinning, between his palms he turned the bread.\nThe flattened bread, like the halo of the moon, looked lovely and splendid.\nA glimpse we had of it, white like the full moon, getting into the fire; soon to come out golden like the brightest of suns.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making barāzīd͟haj:[/b]\nTake 1 makkūk (7½ pounds) good quality, pure flour (daqīq naqī jeyyid), and mix with it 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) yeast, and 20 dirhams (2 ounces) salt and būraq (bakers’ borax). Mix them into dough by adding water and knead vigorously. Cover it and let it ferment. \n\tDivide dough into small portions, the weight of each should be 1 Levantine ūqiyya (1½ ounces), brush each portion with 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) zayt al-anfāq, and flatten it on a wooden board to medium thinness. Prick the breads with feathers, but not much, and cover them with a dry piece of cloth. \n\tLight the tannūr. Let it get hot then wipe clean its inner wall and wait for the fire to subside. With the help of a piece of cloth transfer the breads to the tannūr and stick them into the oven. If you like, squirt some water on them before baking. \n\tWhen they are done, take them out of the oven, and drape them with a piece of cloth for an hour or so, God willing. \n\tHere is what a poet said describing barāzīd͟haj: \n[i]In the farthest end of Kark͟h of Baghdad, a baker I saw offering bread, splendidly marvelous.\nFrom purest of essence of wheat contrived. Radiant and absolute, you may see your image reflected, crystal clear.\nBarāzij rounds glowing with lovely whiteness, more playful than gorgeous singing girls,\nThey look like crystal trays, and were they indeed so, they would have served us as plates.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making ruqāq (thin breads):[/b]\nTwo kinds of ruqāq are made: labiq, and jarmāzaj. The first variety is small and neatly shaped into perfect rounds flattened into extreme thinness. Jarmāzaj is larger. \n\tRuqāq is made, kneaded, and cut the same way barāzīd͟haj is done. However, labiq weighs 2 Baghdadi ūqiyyas (2 ounces) and karmāzaj weighs 3 to 4 ūqiyyas (3 to 4 ounces). Moreover, ruqāq breads are not pricked with feathers (bi-lā rīs͟h) and the tannūr is heated before flattening the breads. As soon as one piece is flattened, it is immediately stuck into the tannūr, which is to remain hot all the time. \n\tYou cannot bake more than one bread at a time because they are thin and bake fast. You need to flatten the ruqāqa, stick it into the tannūr, and wait until it is done. It should be wiped with water the moment it is taken out and while it is still at the top of the oven (raʾs al-tannūr). The breads are to be stacked as they bake until the whole batch is finished, God willing. \n\tIbn al-Rūmī composed these verses on ruqāq: \n[i]I remember once a baker by whom I passed, as fast as lightening ruqāq breads was flattening.\nBetween seeing it turning from a ball in his hands to a large full circle like the moon,\nTook only as much time as an ever-growing circle in water takes when a stone into it is thrown.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making bread of Abū Ḥamza:[/b]\nUse as much as needed of fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran-free). This bread is dry. \n\tThe dough is made similar to that of barāzīd͟haj above, except that this bread is a little thinner and smaller, it is pricked a lot with feathers before baking, and neither būraq (bakers’ borax) nor any sweetening ingredients are used in making it. However, you need to knead into it zayt al-anfāq, the amount of which depends on how much oily you want it to be. Moreover, after you stick them to the inside wall of the tannūr and they are fully baked, take them out and stack them at the top of the oven (raʿs al-tannūr). Keep them there until they are completely dry. Store them in wicker baskets and use them as needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for kabk, made for Abū ʿAṭā Sahl bin Salīm al-Kātib:[/b]\nTake 1 kaylaja (2½ pounds) or 1 makkūk (7½ pounds) fine samīth flour (high in starch and bran free). Make it into dough using 100 dirhams (10 ounces) ground sesame seeds that have not been extracted of their oil (i.e. tahini), 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) almond oil, and 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) salt. For each makkūk add 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) white sugar and 3 dirhams (1½ grams) saffron. Knead the mixture with 10 dirhams (1 ounce) yeast and some water. \n\tWhen dough is fully fermented, rub it with a little fat and rose water beaten together. Roll it out on a board into a square and cut it out into small squares. Bake them in the tannūr by sticking them into the inner wall. When done, take them out and leave them at the top of the tannūr for a short while to dry out, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for aqrāṣ fatīt (crumbly crackers), Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī made:[/b]\nTake 1 kaylaja (2½ pounds) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) and take for it ½ raṭl (½ pound) ṭabarzad (white cane sugar) dissolved in 1 raṭl (2 cups) water. Knead vigorously and set dough aside to ferment. \n\tAfter dough has risen, pour on it, 5 Baghdadi ūqiyyas (5 ounces) oil of skinned almonds and knead lightly. \n\tCut out dough into regular even-sized discs using a mold (qālab) and sprinkle them with hulled sesame seeds. Prick the pieces with a feather and bake them in the tannūr until they are golden (yaḥmār). Take them out of the oven and set them aside in the open air for about an hour until they dry out. When eaten they will crumble in the mouth. \n\tIf ṭabarzad sugar is not available, use instead Sulaymānī sugar or red sugar (sukkar aḥmar). The amount used depends on how sweet you want the cookies to be. \n\tOnce Muḥammad al-Amīn had aqrāṣ jāffa (dry cookies) made by Abū Naṣīr al-K͟habbāz (the Baker). He liked them so much that he sent some to Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī (his uncle). In return, Ibrāhīm wrote this poem: \n[i]So kind and generous was it of al-Amīn to send me a gift of k͟hubz al-fatīt, and his affection proved.\nShaped like perfect discs of equal size, each of which the full moon resembles.\nAs luscious as honey they taste and like the breeze sweetly perfumed. Like silver and gold, white and yellow juxtaposed.\nShaped with calculated care. Measure a cookie and you would say ‘tis qubarā.\nKneaded with ṭabarzad pure. As if sugar, honey, and perfume is all they have.\nAdding saffron and mastic to dough bestowed color, taste, and aroma.\nGenerously kneaded with fresh almond oil. They drip with oil when barely touched.\nSesame, almonds, and pine nuts on them are sprinkled in consecutive lines,\nIn rows arranged. Tilt them, and they shimmer as if with nuggets of gold.\nAmīn by God
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making thin sheets for lawzīnaj (almond confection):[/b]\nDissolve starch (nas͟hāstaj) to thick paste and strain it. For each ūqiyya (1 ounce) of starch, add 1 egg white and whisk mixture thoroughly and continuously. \n\tHeat the tābaq and wipe it with a cloth wrapped with pieces of wax and shelled walnut. Ladle out some of the mixture and pour it on the tābaq. When the thin bread is done scrape it out. Wipe the tābaq once more with the cloth and make another piece. \n\tIf you desire to make thicker lawzīnaj pastries then make a thicker batter, shape each portion into a disc (malg͟hama) and stick it onto the tābaq as I have explained, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sawīq made with wheat:[/b]\nPick over wheat grains, wash them briefly, and soak them overnight. The following morning, drain the grains and wash them again. Toast the seeds until they brown then put the pan away from heat. When cool enough, grind and sift them then store them away. When needed, add water to the ground grains. Stir in sugar as much as the drinker desires, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sawīq made with almond:[/b]\nSkin almonds by scalding them in hot water, let them dry in a shaded place then grind them until they resemble k͟hiṭmī (ground marsh mallow root). Pound sukkar ṭabarzad (white cane sugar) and sift it with a piece of silk cloth. \n\tTo make sawīq mix 4 parts sugar, 1 part sawīq Quras͟hī without the fat, and 1 part ground almonds. Sift mixture in a sieve of hair and add 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) saffron, 1 dānaq (½ gram/a pinch) mastic, and 1 dānaq (½ gram /a pinch) camphor. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sawīq Quras͟hī:[/b]\nPick over white wheat grains, wash them very well, bruise them before they get dry, and spread them on mats. Then remove the husk the way you do with wheat of hurās. Wash the grains again and spread them until they are almost dry. \n\tToast the grains in a pan very well. Stir them all the time so that they do not scorch. Take them away from the fire and let them cool down. Next, grind the grains as fine as possible then sift them using a piece of silk cloth. Mix each makkūk (7½ pounds) of this flour with 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) samn ʿArabī (clarified butter of goats and cows). Then sift the mixture using a fine sieve made of hair and store it away, God willing. As for sawīq maṭbūk͟h (cooked), it is prepared like sawīq Quras͟hī but the wheat grains are cooked first, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sawīq made with pomegranate:[/b]\nTake wheat and prepare it the same way you do with the Quras͟hī . Pick over dried pomegranate seeds. For 3 parts of wheat, use 2 parts pomegranate seeds. Mix the two and grind them as fine as flour. Sift mixture using silk cloth if possible. If not, then use a small sieve (munk͟hul). To each part of this mixture, add 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) sukkar Sulaymānī (crushed hard sugar-candy). \n\tKnow that the best and tastiest wheat used for all kinds of sawīq is the white variety. Next in excellence is yellow wheat. \n\tHere is what a poet said describing sawīq: \n[i]On a pilgrimage, a glassful of sawīq is one’s sole brother and friend.\nWhen one with heat is overwhelmed, ‘tis best brother or mate can be.\nMade of barley which after toasting was ground as fine as flour,\nMixed with equal amount of ṭabarzad sugar, also ground but not as fine.\nWhen with drinking water the traveler carefully stirs it in his glass,\nIt satisfies his hunger and cools his heart after being scorched with heat.\nThe sharp-witted after having but one sip would think it cannot but nectar be.\nThe best ever for you to have when on the go, so take heed and make it your amigo.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making vinegar, much more acid than vinegar of ʿunṣul by Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Aḥwal:[/b]\nTake a jar coated with pitch (ināʾ muzaffat) and wash it thoroughly. Pick over grapes, discarding any rotten or over-ripe ones. Fill the container with the grapes and shake it so that the grapes fit in so tightly that not a single grape will have room to stir. Seal the container with gypsum (jaṣ) and put it away for a year. \n\tWhen you open the container at the end of the year, you will find that the grapes have made a net-like formation in the jar. Press the grapes in the jar with a utensil and pour out the vinegar. It will not be much. \n\tStir the remaining pressed grapes with your hand and pour water on them. The amount should equal a quarter of the container’s capacity. Seal it with mud and set it aside for 6 months after which you open it up and press out the liquid. Then pour water into the remaining grape solids, the amount of which should equal half the capacity of the container. Then seal it with mud and set it aside for 3 months. \n\tOpen up the container and take out the resulting liquid again. Add water to the remaining grape solids, the amount of which should equal three quarters of the container’s capacity. Set it aside for one month after which you strain the resulting liquid. To the remaining grape solids add water enough to fill the whole jar and set it aside for one month after which you strain the liquid for the last time. \n\tNothing excels such varieties of vinegar, which are so excellent and so strong that nobody can even bear smell them. When you want to use this vinegar, dilute it with water. For each dirham (½ teaspoon) of vinegar, use 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) water. Indeed, it renders using other kinds such as those made from raisins, dates, or figs, unnecessary, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for vinegar of is͟hturg͟hāz:[/b]\nTake red vinegar made from grapes or wine and strain it. For each 10 parts of vinegar add one part ishturg͟hāz. Keep mixture in a container and seal it with mud until needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Vinegar made white without distilling it (taṣʿīd):[/b]\nAdd wheat bran (nuk͟hāla) to vinegar and mash and press them in a sieve set on a bowl. Do this in small batches until you gather the amount you need of the dripping liquid. Add lime borax (būraq al-jīr) and wait until it becomes clear like water without using an alembic or fire, God willing. \n\tYou can also get clear vinegar by adding to it a mixture of crumbled hot bread and ammonia (nas͟hādir). Stir the mixture and wait until vinegar becomes clear then strain it, God willing. \n\tMoreover, vinegar can be whitened by putting it in a glass bottle (qinnīna) and vigorously whipping an egg in it. Keep the bottle warm by wrapping it in many layers of clothes overnight. It will become clear, God willing. \n\tHere is what a poet said describing vinegar: \n[i]Distilled vinegar from white wine made, lustrously clear, for water it might be taken.\nWere one to have but a sip of it to taste, with his own saliva he would choke on it.\nToo pungent to enjoy if in the pot ‘tis put undiluted.\nI masterly made it in earthen jars with squills suspended on it.\nA full month I kept it under the blasting sun and now it looks as red as ruby.\nCrystal clear when you look at it from above. You might think ‘tis oil of k͟hīrī,\nShimmering with luster when at the table served in a bowl.\nPut to the ‘taste’: some as high as gold rank it but others may barely stand it.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for seasoned salt (milḥ muṭayyab):[/b]\nTake sumac, dried pomegranate seeds, asafetida root (maḥrūt), dried asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), hulled sesame seeds, nigella seeds (habbat al-sawdāʾ), hemp seeds (s͟hahdānaj), flax seeds (bazr al-kattān), cumin, green terebinth berries (habbat al k͟haḍra). Toast each of these separately and add them to the salt while they are still hot, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for delicious (ṭayyib) salt:[/b]\nMacerate for one day and one night dried sour pomegranate seeds in sour wine vinegar along with asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān). Then strain the seeds, toast them, pulverize them until very fine, and sift them. Add them to the salt along with thyme (ṣaʿtar), toasted sesame seeds, toasted hemp seeds (s͟hahdānaj), and pounded (dried) bread, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for K͟hurāsānī salt:[/b]\nPound and sift good quality andarānī salt. Put it in a ṭinjīr (large copper pot) on slow-burning fire. Sprinkle on it sour wine vinegar, bit by bit, and stir it with the fire still burning under it until salt turns black. Put it away from heat and let it cool down. \n\tAdd dried sour pomegranate seeds, sumac, nigella seeds, sesame seeds, hemp seeds (s͟hahdānaj), anjud͟hān sark͟hasī, asafetida root (maḥrūt), and other similar seasonings. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for seasoned salt made for al-Rashīd:[/b]\nTake white pure salt and finely grind it. Grind for it asafetida root (maḥrūt) and asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān) and stir them into the salt. Add nigella seeds (ḥabba sawdāʾ) half the amount of the salt-mix. Let the seeds be whole. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for laxative salt (mushil):[/b]\nIt is good for gout (naqris), hemiphlegia (fālaj), facial paralysis (laqwa), arthritis (awjāʿ al-mafāṣil), diseases caused by cold and humidity, and spleen-related ailments. It also has a purging power (yajlū) \n\tTake 6 ūqiyyas (6 ounces) andarānī salt, and 12 dirhams (12 ounces) black pepper. Also take 4 dirhams (4 ounces) of each of the following: zanjabīl (ginger), dried zūfā (hyssop), anjud͟hān (leaves of asafetida), bazr al-karafs (celery seeds), sād͟haj Hindī (Indian leaf), g͟hārīqūn (agaricum), saqmūnyā (scammony resin), ḥurf (seeds of garden cress), and qurṭum (safflower seeds). \n\tMix, grind, and sift all the ingredients. Store them in a glass jar (ināʾ zujāj) and use as needed. \n\tIbrāhīm bin al-Mahdī has these verses on salt: \n[i]Following decrees of books of medicine, the ingredients I perfectly balanced.\nWith it we begin our meals after the name of God we invoke, Exalting in His Glory.\nOf spices, walnut, sesame, nigella, asafetida root (maḥrūt), and cardamom (hāl),\nCoriander toasted in tābaq, sumac and asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), equal parts.\nAnd toasted hemp seeds (s͟hāhdānaj), thyme, and saffron pure rendered it complete.\nKnow that salt left untoasted will not be savored.\nIt’s only by toasting and seasoning that it will be perfectly flavored.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making bazmāward (rolled up sandwiches), Baghdadi style:[/b]\nPrepare meat by pounding it the way you do with sausages (laqāniq). Add a small amount of kidney fat, onion, fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb), and rue. Add to these, coriander, black pepper, caraway, cumin, spikenard, cloves, nutmeg, ginger, and cassia, all pounded. Break 5 eggs on the meat mixture and add a little chopped garlic and onion. Pound the mixture until it blends very well. \n\tSpread caul fat (t͟harb) of sheep on a soft ruqāqa (thin sheet of bread). Let it cover as much as possible of the bread. Spread the pounded meat mixture on the caul fat. \n\tTake 5 boiled eggs, peel them but leave them whole. Arrange them in a row along the spread meat paste. Tightly roll up the ruqāq bread with what is spread on it, and truss the roll with clean intestines. Put the roll on 4 sticks of k͟hilāf tree (willow) and tie it with a thread so that it stays intact. Lower it into the tannūr and place it on a flat tile (ājur) put directly on the fire. \n\tWhen the roll is done, take it out of the oven and slice it crosswise into bazmāward (slices). Arrange the pieces on a platter (jām) and serve them with Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce) or mustard, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for bazmāward with citron pulp (ḥummāḍ), called al-Maʾmūnī:[/b]\nChop cooked chicken and spread it on ruqāq (thin sheet of bread). Let there be underneath the chicken some skinned walnut, citron pulp (ḥummāḍ al-utruj), naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), tarragon, bat͟harūj (basil), and salt. Roll up the bread with the filling inside. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe made for al-Mutawakkil:[/b]\nUse cold cooked meat of two legs and shoulders of a kid or lamb. Finely shred the meat into thread-like pieces. \n\tChoose whatever you like of leaf vegetables, excluding watercress (jirjīr) and endives (hindibāʾ). Finely chop them until they resemble sesame seeds and mix part of them with the shredded meat. Set mixture aside. \n\tNow choose good quality sharp cheese, scrape it with a knife, and collect the scraped cheese. Coarsely grind walnut and add it with the cheese to the set-aside meatless chopped vegetables. Add as well some chopped herbs (abzār ruṭb) and rue. \n\tA portion of the chopped vegetables should have been set aside unmixed with meat. \n\tNow peel and chop some olives and add them to the meatless chopped vegetable mixture. \n\tSpread a soft (labiq) and large ruqāqa (thin bread), spread it with some of the meatless vegetable mixture and sprinkle it with seasoned salt (milḥ muṭayyab). Next, spread the meat and vegetable mixture to which you should have added some ḥawāyij. Then arrange a layer of eggs sliced lengthwise. \n\tNext, spread another layer of the meat and vegetable mixture followed by a layer of the meatless vegetable mixture. Sprinkle them with pleasant-tasting salt (milḥ ṭayyib) and drizzle them with sweet vinegar (k͟hall ʿad͟hb) and rose water. \n\tTightly roll the ruqāqa bread with the filling and slice it crosswise into rounds. Arrange the pieces on a platter (jām) and pass them around (tufarriquhā), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for wasṭ (filled sandwich) made by Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nChoose a round and thick bread made with fine, bran-free flour (rag͟hīf samik ḥuwwārā). Using a knife, cut it crosswise in half and set it aside. \n\tTake meat of cooled sikbāj (beef stew soured with vinegar) and shred it. Finely chop leaf vegetables (baql). \n\tCover the cut side of one piece of the bread with the chopped vegetables followed by another layer of the prepared meat. Sprinkle the surface with pleasant-tasting salt followed by chopped cheese, chopped olives, and chopped walnuts, almonds, pistachio, and pine nuts. Put another layer of the chopped vegetables and cover the filling with the other half of the bread cut side down. Keep the prepared sandwich pressed using a weight for about an hour. Make as many as you wish of these sandwiches following the same rule. \n\tCut the filled sandwiches into squares and then cut them into triangles (s͟hawābīr). Arrange the pieces on a platter (jām) and serve them, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for open-faced sandwich (wasṭ mas͟hṭūr) made by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nRemove the top crust and edges of a whole bread (rag͟hīf). Spread (yus͟haṭṭar) its face with binn al-sakārij, slather it with walnut oil, and put it on a brazier (kānūn) until it is thoroughly heated. Spread yolk of soft-cooked eggs (nīmbaris͟ht) on top of the binn and eat it. You may sprinkle it with pounded cheese (jubn madqūq), which will make it even more delicious. \n\tIbrāhīm bin al-Mahdī has a poem describing this sandwich: \n[i]What a delicious sandwich on the brazier I made, slathered with binn and walnut oil.\nFragrant and shining, as if the binn I used with ambergris and musk embalmed.\nOf nigella seeds I put what it needed, as for fennel, I did sprinkle some.\nOlive oil I made sure to add, for it gives a luscious coating and a saffroned glow.\nSmeared with egg yolk, with cheese sprinkled, like speckled embroidered silk.\nAs colorful as striped silk it looks, exuding musk and camphor.\nThe taste, luscious as pure honey, for the best aromatic spices I did use.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida taken from the book of al-Maḍamūn:[/b]\nMix vinegar and murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and add to them coriander seeds, cassia, black pepper, fresh and dried thyme, cumin, caraway, cilantro, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), rue, parsley, pulp of small and smooth cucumber (lubb al-k͟hiyār), and crushed rāsan (elecampane). Mix into sauce and pour it all over roasted pullets or any other young fowl. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another bārida from the book of al-Wāthiq:[/b]\nTake a roasted chicken. Disjoint it and arrange the pieces on a platter (jām). Beat together mustard made with good wine vinegar and a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and some sugar so that the sauce tastes sweet and sour (muzz). Add to the mixture, ground walnut and a little anjud͟hān (asafetida leaves). \n\tPour the sauce over the chicken to drench it. Then pour olive oil (zayt) all over. Finally, sprinkle the top with chopped rue and garnish it with pomegranate seeds, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Delicious bārida, called Kisrawiyya:[/b]\nTake about 1 raṭl (1 pint) juice of unripe sour grapes and mix it with finely chopped pulp (lubb) of a small smooth cucumber (k͟hiyāra) as follows: After you discard the peel and the solid part surrounding the pulp, chop it as fine as possible. You need to thinly slash the pulp first then chop it fine with a thin-bladed knife. Avoid using a board on which something else has been chopped lest it should affect the taste of the cucumber. \n\tAdd to sauce a small amount of chopped cilantro. \n\tNow take some plump pullets that have been roasted in the tannūr and taken out while still succulent. While they are still hot, disjoint them and arrange the pieces on a platter (jām). Pour on them the (ṣibāg͟h) you have just prepared along with 2 ūqiyyas (4 tablespoons) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). Scatter on it whole leaves of basil (bād͟harūj) and thyme. Garnish the dish with slices of peeled ribbed cucumber (qit͟ht͟hāʾ) cut like dirham coins (i.e. small discs). \n\tChill the dish with ice and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Green bārida dish (k͟haḍrāʾ):[/b]\nMix about ¼ raṭl (½ cup) fresh cilantro juice, 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) rue juice, 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) purslane juice, and ¼ raṭl (½ cup) vinegar. Add ¼ raṭl (½ cup) water and salt as needed. \n\tAlso take ½ dirham (1½ grams) each, of black pepper, ginger, cassia, and long pepper; and ¼ dirham (¾ gram) galangal , 2 dirhams (6 grams) caraway seeds, and 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) shelled pistachio. Crush all these spices with 5 dirhams (15 grams) ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar) and mix them with the juices to make sauce (sibāg͟h). \n\tArrange hot disjointed pieces of roasted pullets on a platter (jām) and pour the sauce all over them. Set aside for a while until the chicken absorbs the flavor of the sauce. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Yellow bārida dish (ṣafrāʾ):[/b]\nTake ½ dirham (1½ grams) each, of black pepper, cassia, long pepper, and ginger; ¼ dirham (¾ gram) galangal; 1 dānaq (½ gram), each, of spikenard, and cloves; 1 dirham (3 grams) each, of cumin, caraway seeds, chopped rue, and asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān); and 3 dirhams (9 grams) sugar. \n\tAlso take ¼ raṭl (½ cup) wine vinegar, 1 raṭl (2 cups) murrī, and 5 ūqiyyas (2/3 cup) pure water. \n\tBeat all these ingredients together and add to them ½ mit͟hqāl (2¼ grams) saffron. Pour sauce over hot boned pullets. Pour olive oil all over them and set them aside for a while until the meat absorbs the flavor of the sauce. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida dish, tried and true (mujarraba):[/b]\nGrill a chicken or pullet and put it on a platter (jām). Take almonds and skin and finely pound them. Add sugar or sweet jullāb (syrup flavored with rose water). Pour sauce over the chicken and sprinkle on it some chopped rue. Pour sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) over it. \n\tGarnish the dish with boiled egg yolk and pomegranate seeds, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida by Abū Jaʿfar al-Barmakī:[/b]\nTake pullets and grill them. Then disjoint them and put them on a platter (jām). Sprinkle the dish with coriander, black pepper, cumin, and cassia. Pour on them juice of sour unripe grapes and chop on top fresh naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), tarragon, and thyme. \n\tPour sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) on top, and sprinkle some chopped fresh herbs. Garnish the dish by putting chopped k͟hiyār (small and smooth cucumber) all around it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida dish, Um al-Faḍl made for al-Mahdī:[/b]\nGrill pullets to succulence, disjoint them, slice the breasts, and arrange the pieces on a platter (jām). \n\tThoroughly crush 20 skinned almonds. Crush with them ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) white sugar and the pulp of 2 k͟hiyārs (small and smooth cucumbers). Pour on mixture ½ raṭl (1 cup) wine vinegar with 2 dirhams (6 grams) salt. Add to the mixture, 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) olive oil and 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) almond oil. Beat all these ingredients in a bowl (g͟huḍāra) to mix them well. \n\tPour sauce all over the chicken. When after a while sauce is absorbed, drizzle ½ ūqiyya (1 tablespoon) almond oil all over it and garnish it with k͟hiyār, chopped fresh thyme, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), and basil (bād͟harūj). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida with pomegranate juice, prepared two ways (tubmal lawnān):[/b]\nPress out sour pomegranate juice and mix it with some murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and olive oil. Pour it all over roasted pullets then sprinkle on them chopped fresh naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) and small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār). \n\tAlternatively, you may substitute murrī with salt, crush some sprigs of dried naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) between the fingers, add it to the juice, and set it aside so that it absorbs its flavor. Drop in it a bruised clove of garlic (mas͟hdūk͟h) and leave it in the sauce until it absorbs its flavor then take it out. Pour it on the roasted chicken \n\tPour olive oil on the dish, chop on it some k͟hiyār (small and smooth cucumber) and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Dark (daknāʾ) bārida dish:[/b]\nDissolve a lot of salt and a lot of sugar into vinegar. Add these little by little and taste every time you put some until you get a delicious balanced sauce. Then add ground spikenard, enough to flavor and color the sauce. Pour into it some olive oil. \n\tYou have the option of arranging the roasted pullet pieces on the sauce. You may also add qāqulla (black cardamom) to the sauce. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida dish with rak͟hbīn (dried buttermilk), made by Um al-Faḍl, too:[/b]\nChoose plump pullets, wash them, and salt them very well. In a clean bowl, mix 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) rak͟hbīn with some water then strain it in a sieve. Add to the resulting liquid 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Rub the prepared pullets inside and out with the rak͟hbīn mix. Insert them into a skewer (saffūd) and rotate them on the fire (kard͟habāj). Baste the revolving pullets with the remaining rak͟hbīn mix using a feather. Take the pullets off the heat while they are still moist and succulent (ṭarī). Disjoint them, slice the breasts, and arrange the pieces on a platter (jām). \n\tTake 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) shelled and cleaned pistachio and crush them thoroughly with 1 raṭl (1 pound) fine white cane sugar (ṭabarzad). Add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) sour vinegar, 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) extracted juice of pulp of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), and ½ dirham (1½ grams) fine rock salt (andarānī). \n\tPour this sauce all over the pullets. When they absorb the sauce after a while, finely chop the pulp of 2 k͟hiyārs (small and smooth cucumbers) and sprinkle it over the chicken. Pour on it 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), sprinkle it with finely chopped fresh naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) and basil (bād͟harūj), and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for pâté de bārida (maʿjūna):[/b]\nFinely chop a cold roasted chicken. Also, finely chop elecampane (rāsan), fresh cilantro, parsley (karafs), rue, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), tarragon, fresh thyme, small and smooth cucumbers (k͟hiyār), preserved ginger (zanjabīl murabba), and mix them. \n\tCrumble into the mixture some ṭalʿ and boiled egg yolk, and knead ingredients into paste by adding wine vinegar, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and ground coriander seeds, black pepper, caraway seeds, and cassia. Shape paste like furniyya and decorate it with the chopped white head of fresh onion (bayāḍ al-ʿasal), chopped black olives, and cooked turnip fingers (saljam muṣabbaʿ). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Black bārida dish:[/b]\nPound black zabīb (raisins) very well. Stir and mash it (yumras) with a small amount of vinegar. Strain the liquid and add a small amount of cassia, galangal as needed, and a little ginger. Pour over it some olive oil and add a small amount of chopped rue. Pour sauce over roasted pullets. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another bārida dish:[/b]\nDisjoint roasted pullets and arrange pieces on a platter (jām). \n\tGrind together 20 shelled almonds, 5 dirhams (15 grams) fine cane sugar (ṭabarzad), ¼ raṭl (½ cup) wine vinegar, ¼ raṭl (½ cup) pure water, ½ dirham (1½ grams) white rock salt (andarānī), 2 dānaqs (1 gram) ginger, and 1 dānaq (½ gram) ground cassia. \n\tPour sauce over the pullets and chop on them naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), parsley, and a little rue. Next, drizzle the dish with olive oil, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another black bārida dish:[/b]\nTake vinegar, and add salt to it as needed. Mix in sifted ground caraway seeds, as needed, and a little cassia and galangal. \n\tDisjoint the roasted pullets, and put the pieces in the vinegar sauce. Pour a little olive oil on them, and chop for them rue and cucumber (k͟hiyār). \n\tIf you desire, finely chop the roasted meat of the pullets and chicken with a knife and mix it with the sauce. The quantity depends on how much meat you used. After you pour the olive oil, chop on it naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) and parsley. \n\tA poem on Bārida by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī: \n[i]If you ever wish to eat a delicious hurried dish, here is bārida in the summer for you.\nGet two parts almonds and sugar and two parts vinegar and mustard, too.\nMix them in a bowl and with safflower crown them.\nThus, you get sauce enough for a lamb as dip.\nNow fetch herbs and peeled k͟hiyār, qit͟ht͟hāʾ , and faqqūṣ, and pomegranate for garnish.\nChop all the greens but chop them fine then sprinkle them to cover the dish.\nThe cucumbers, chopped, you add to the greens. Next, the oil pour, but sparingly.\nNow get lovely plump pullets to perfection grilled.\nWith a knife disjoint them to goodly pieces, and on the dish align them well.\nGarnish with pomegranate seeds and gemlike almonds and olives scattered.\nThen eat it, may God your guide be, if you ever wish before the meal enjoy a hurried dish.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida dish with pomegranate juice, similar to Abū-Isḥāq’s Jurjāniyya:[/b]\nCrumble stale fine white bread (rag͟hīf samīd bāyit) then take the fine crumbs, and set them aside. \n\tPress out the juice of sour pomegranates by hand and put it in a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra), the amount should be enough to saturate the breadcrumbs. Strain the juice in a fine sieve. To the resulting liquid, add as much as needed of ground andarānī salt, 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) ṭabarzad (white cane sugar), and 2 dānaqs (1 gram) cassia. \n\tPour the juice mix on the bread crumbs in a clean bowl. Set aside until bread absorbs the liquid and then transfer it to a wide shallow bowl (g͟haḍāra mabsūṭa). \n\tFinely chop parsley, rue, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), basil (bād͟harūj), and fresh thyme. Scatter them on the sopped bread. Mix 2 ūqiyyas (4 tablespoons) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) and 2 ūqiyyas (4 tablespoons) almond oil and pour them on the tharīd (sopped bread). Set aside. \n\tGrill to succulence Kaskarī pullets on a rotating spit (kard͟habāj). Disjoint them and arrange the pieces around the prepared tharīd just before serving the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida dish of gizzards and livers (qawāniṣ wa kubūd) served with other cold dishes:[/b]\nGizzards and livers can be made like a baked omelet (bujja mas͟hwiyya) using eggs and green herbs or they can be made as a simple omelet (bujja sād͟haja) with fresh herbs and onion. . Alternatively, they can be fried with olive oil and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). However, they need to be sprinkled with water, enough to make a small amount of sauce in the dish. Next, eggs are cracked on them and left to cook until eggs are set. They can also be cooked the same way, except that all the liquid is allowed to evaporate and crakked eggs are poured all over them. Then the mixture is scrambled until the eggs are set. Finally, enough murrī is drizzled to moisten the dish. They may be cooked with vinegar and caraway only or just murrī and olive oil. \n\tHowever, whichever way you choose to cook them, you need to cut off the tendons on both sides of the gizzards and discard them. \n\tYou may chop the gizzards and livers fine, or just split the livers into two pieces and the gizzards into three pieces after getting rid of the tendons. Additionally, you can lightly boil livers of lamb or kids then slice them and braise them (yuṭajjan) in olive oil, murrī, and a little black pepper then serve the dish, God willing. \n\tHere is a poem by Abū-Isḥāq on bārida: \n[i]To me, of the prepared cold dishes, nothing compares with chicken delicious,\nEaten roasted with sour grape juice. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A basic recipe for muṭajjana:[/b]\nDisjoint plump pullets. Using a knife, cut open— from the inside—the chest and the back all the way down to the tail to be able to flatten the pieces. Wash them and put them in a pot. Pour about 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) olive oil, a similar amount of water, and 1 dirham (3 grams) salt. Let the pot cook until all water evaporates. \n\tAdd to the pot, 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) vinegar. Stir it continuously until meat is browned and vinegar is cooked. Pour ¼ raṭl (½ cup) murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and sprinkle 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) black pepper. Put the pot away from heat until needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muṭajjana of plump pullets (farārīj simān):[/b]\nPut olive oil in a pot, as needed, and let it come to a good boil. Take disjointed pullets, and add them to the pot with a little ground white rock salt (andarānī). When both sides are browned, stir the pot with a ladle (mig͟hrafa) and pour in a little wine vinegar and water, enough to make the dish taste slightly tangy. When vinegar is cooked, drizzle the pot with a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce) add a few sprigs (ṭāqāt) of rue then stir until the rue emits its aroma. Season the pot with black pepper and cumin. \n\tWhen it is ready to serve, add to the pot some breadcrumbs. Remove the rue that is already in the pot and replace it with fresh chopped rue, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muṭajjana by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nDisjoint some young fowl and fry the pieces in washed olive oil (zayt mag͟hsūl). Drizzle a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and vinegar, and sprinkle some black pepper and coriander seeds. Drizzle with some water and sprinkle ground pistachio and sugar on it. \n\tLadle the dish onto a platter and garnish it with chopped rue. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muṭajjana of chicken breasts (ṣadr al-dajāj) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nSlice chicken breasts, chop them into small pieces, and fry them in olive oil. When they are almost done, add to the pot black pepper, fresh cilantro and drizzle it with vinegar and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Sprinkle the dish with ground almond as well, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muṭajjana Wāt͟hiqiyya:[/b]\nTake Kaskarī pullets or two young fowls and discard their bones. Finely chop the meat, shape it into a patty similar to jardaq bread. Put it in a pot along with 1/3 raṭl (5 ounces) chopped onion, and ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) chopped fresh cilantro. Add enough water to cover the ingredients by a double of their height. Also add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb) and salt as needed. Let the pot cook until it comes to a boil. \n\tNow prepare good quality cleaned truffles, an equal amount to the chicken used in the recipe. Chop them into pieces larger than those of the pullets, add them to the pot, and cook until the ingredients are done. \n\tAdd coriander seeds to the pot, put as much as your fingertips put together can hold. Add 1 dirham (3 grams) black pepper, ½ dirham (1½ grams) each of ginger and galangal, and 1 dirham (3 grams) cassia all ground. Stir the pot. \n\tBreak 15 eggs into a bowl and beat them with a little chopped cilantro and naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). Pour egg mixture into the pot, and stir so that eggs scramble a little and mix with the meat patty (jardaq) and the truffles. Wipe clean the sides of the pot and cover it until serving time. \n\tNote: Pour the egg mixture after you put the cooked pot away from the heat and while it is still boiling. [b]Another version, called Ibrāhīmī:[/b]\nIt is cooked as in the previous recipe except that ½ raṭl (1 cup) vinegar mixed with 1 dirham (3 grams) saffron are added. Use only ½ dirham (1½ grams) salt. Besides, let there be in it ¼ raṭl (½ cup) murrī Rāzī. The rest is the same. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muṭajjana by Abū Samīn made for al-Wāthiq:[/b]\nDisjoint two pullets and put them in a pot. Pour on them ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil, a small amount of white rock salt (andarānī), a handful of chickpeas, and enough water to cover all the ingredients. Let the pot boil until almost done and pour into it ½ raṭl (1 cup) wine vinegar. \n\tJust before it is done, add a handful of chopped fresh cilantro, a little coriander seeds, and a bunch (bāqa) of naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). Also add 2 ūqiyyas (4 tablespoons) of maṭbūk͟h wine or good quality aged mus͟hammas wine. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another muṭajjana, which al-Rashīd craved and Masrūr al-‘aghīr’s cook made:[/b]\nChoose 4 tender pullets with plump breasts and 4 fattened young fowls. Sprinkle it with ½ raṭl (1 cup) wine vinegar and keep on stirring until vinegar evaporates. Carry the pot back to the fire and add black pepper and coriander seeds. Sprinkle again with 2 ladlefuls of vinegar and 1 ladleful Nabatean murrī. Add 1 bunch rue, 1 bunch parsley, and chopped pulp of one small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), which has been moistened in maṭbūk͟h (cooked wine). Stir the pot very well. The sauce of this dish is not supposed to be thick. \n\tAbū al-Ḥusayn recited to me a poem on muṭajjana composed by another poet: \n[i]Muṭajjanāt dishes of fabulous chicks fried, in sesame oil submerged.\nFresh rue, as fragrant as musk, does in them make its presence.\nBetween the sliced and the diced, like a beautiful flower it looks in a sprouting bough,\nBrought by the wasp-waisted one clad in qurtaq, like red anemone her cheeks aglow.[/i] \n\tIbn al-Rūmī has a poem on making muṭajjana: \n[i]Ye, lover of scrumptious food, which before wine drinking is offered.\nGet thee some pullets and let them be Kaskarī, and a young turtledove, plump and ʿAskarī.\nAfter you scald them, my pal, join them with duckling meat.\nDisjoint them all, joint by joint, not sparing any.\nIn a stone pot, you put the meat and pour olive oil as you need.\nBut sesame oil you better add. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for stuffed fish (samak maḥs͟hū) from the book of al-Fatḥ bin Khāqān:[/b]\nChoose whatever you like of big fish. Skin it starting with the back but do not slit the belly open. The head, fins, tail, and skin should stay in one whole piece. Now, open up the belly take the meat, discard the gallbladder (marāra) and set aside the entrails (buṭūn). Take additional meat from other fish until you have enough to stuff the prepared fish skin. Discard all bones. \n\tPut the fish meat on a board and pound it very well with a knife. Sprinkle a little salt, and continue pounding until it has the consistency of the brain (damāg͟h). Crack some eggs on it and continue pounding. Add a little sugar or honey and ground spices (afāwīh) as needed such as spikenard, cloves, cassia, ginger, black pepper, cumin, and caraway seeds. Also add māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce) and olive oil. Chop fresh rue and cilantro and add them to the fish. Add as well skinned almonds and sesame seeds. Mix all. \n\tStuff the meat mixture into the fish skin with the head, fins, and tail intact. Let the stuffing be tight no matter how big the fish is. Arrange split canes lengthwise around the filled fish and tie it with the canes using threads at two or three places. \n\tLine the bottom of the tannūr with flat tiles (ājur), enough to accommodate the length of the fish, and press them onto the fire. Place the fish on the bricks and let it bake slowly. \n\tWhen it is done, take it out and serve it along with any of the fish sauces, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for soused fish (halām samak):[/b]\nChoose a big fresh fish and scale it completely. Slit open the belly and discard the inside. Wash the fish thoroughly and cut it into medium pieces. \n\tBoil fish in vinegar and salt until it is done, but avoid overcooking it. Take it out and submerge it in cold water. Take out the pieces and drain them very well then wrap them individually in a coarse linen or woolen cloth and gently press pieces between your hands or between two wooden boards to drain them as much as possible of the moisture. Arrange the fish pieces on a tray made of willow sticks (ṭabaq k͟hilāf) and set it aside until fish is thoroughly drained. \n\tSubmerge fish pieces in wine vinegar and add to them the usual halām spices . Set aside until needed. It will stay delicious in the summer for many days. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for bārida (cold dish):[/b]\nTake a bunch of cleaned watercress (jirjīr), a bunch of cleaned parsley, a bunch of kurrāt͟h Nabaṭī, and a bunch of kurrāt͟h Rūmī, the most tender you can get. Boil the herbs separately. Finely chop them and pound them very well to press out their juices. Then set them aside, separately. \n\tBoil some fish, remove all bones then cut it into pieces as desired. \n\tSet a soapstone pot (burma) on a trivet. Put whichever you wish of the prepared vegetable juices—watercress, parsley, or leeks—in the pot. Add in small amounts: zayt al-anfāq (oil extracted from unripe olives), black pepper, coriander, cumin, caraway, and māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce). Cook the mix and add to it the cut pieces of fish. Stir the ingredients then break 4 or 5 eggs on them and stir until done. Take the pot away from the fire. \n\tYou can get four varieties of cold dishes with four different tastes following the same method by using one kind of the prepared vegetables each time you make it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fried fish (samak maqlū) by Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nTake as many fish as you desire, slit open their bellies, and wash them very well. Set a frying pan on a trivet, and pour excellent quality sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib fāyiq). \n\tTake a little flour and salt sifted together and sprinkle the prepared fish with them. Fry the fish until browned and take them out of the pan. \n\tNow finely chop some onion, set it aside, and wash the frying pan of any traces of oil or fish. \n\tMix and strain ½ sukurruja (¼ cup) of binn (fermented condiment) with 2 sukurrujas (1 cup) wine vinegar set them aside. \n\tReturn the frying pan to the fire and pour into it ½ sukurruja (¼ cup) zayt al-anfāq (oil extracted from unripe olives). Add the chopped onion and fry it until cooked. \n\tAdd a little black pepper and caraway seeds to the binn and wine vinegar mixture, pour it into the frying pan, and mix well. \n\tWhen you get to the step when you know that the onion is cooked, arrange the fried fish on a platter, and it is at this point that you add the binn and wine vinegar mixture to the onion and oil so that you mix them well and pour it immediately over the fish. This will be its sauce. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A fish recipe in which the head is roasted, the middle is poached, and the tail is fried:[/b]\nScale a big fish and take out its entrails. You may stuff the fish as I have already described to you at the beginning of the chapter. After you clean the fish, stuff its mouth, gills, and between the jaws with as much as possible of finely chopped citron leaves, apple peel, salt, thyme, and rue. \n\tUsing a wide strip of thick cloth (ḥās͟hiya) soaked in oil, wrap the middle part of the fish three times, the width of two fists put together, starting at four fingers’ width below the head. Make sure to wrap it three times. Otherwise, the cloth will burn and the whole fish bakes, which will defeat the main design of the recipe. \n\tAs for the lower third of the fish, wrap it with an overlapping bandage-like strip of linen cloth (mus͟hāqqa) drenched in oil. You can secure the wrappings with a thin string made by twisting thin mus͟hāqqa cloth and winding it around the middle cloth and the tail cloth. \n\tLower the fish into a well-heated tannūr. When done, take it out and untie both wrappings. Thus, you will get a fish cooked in three different ways: the head is baked, its middle is poached, and its lower part is fried. \n\tFor each part prepare a sauce that goes with it so that nobody would suspect that the whole fish was actually cooked as one piece, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Roasted Fish by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nChoose a huge live fish and throw it into a basin filled with the juice of red grapes. The basin should be big and wide enough for the fish to dive and swim in. Let the fish drink as much as possible of the juice. Noticeable decrease in the juice level in the basin is an indication it has penetrated into its whole body. Take out the fish then clean it and roast it. Serve it with a sauce made of asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), murrī (liquid fermented sauce), wine vinegar, juice of parsley and naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), and caraway seeds. \n\tThis dish, or any other fish dish for that matter, does not taste good and is not complete without serving it with its appropriate dipping sauce (ṣibāg͟h) because it is only by serving condiments with fish that makes it delicious. \n\tA poet composed verses on a liar. He compared him to a fish dish served without ṣibāg͟h: \n[i]Abū Isḥāq has got no damāg͟h (brain) and his skin is without dibāg͟h (tan).\nHis words are like fresh fish presented without ṣibāg͟h.[/i] Here is Ibn al-Mahdī’s poem on this fish dish: \n[i]On a hot summer day, the cook brought a dish of s͟habbūṭ fish, a golden kid resembled.\nMasterly roasted, with parsley, leeks, olive oil, and thyme stuffed.\nThen its ṣibāg͟h he made of pomegranate juice, sugar, and almond,\nVinegar, murrī, asafetida leaves, black pepper, rikābī olive oil, walnut, and coriander.\nHe brought it in like the sun, a radiant delight, redolent with ʿūd, misk, and amber.\nOnce its skin was stripped off it, dazed we were by essence, light, and loveliness.\nI have never seen a sight more delightful, nor have I tasted more scrumptious dish.\nLike the sun when we first saw it, turned to moon once the skin was peeled off it.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A fish dish made for al-Rashīd, called qarīs (fish aspic):[/b]\nChoose several big fish and cut off their heads. Wash the heads very well and put them in a pot then add wine vinegar, a tied bunch of parsley and rue, a piece of galangal, a piece of cassia, and three whole onions. Add as well, a handful of ground coriander seeds tied in a small bundle of linen cloth. Also added in a tied bundle of cloth are a piece of ginger, spikenard, cloves, black pepper, and long pepper (dār fulful). \n\tLet the pot boil until fish heads are cooked. Steep saffron in a little water and add it to the pot. Add enough to color it radiant red (aḥmar bālig͟h). \n\tTake the heads out of the pot and pull out the lips (mas͟hāfir) and the tongues from the roots. Remove cassia, galangal, spice bundles, bunched herb, and onions from the vinegar. Return the fish tongues and lips to the pot. Let them steep in the vinegar until the liquid gets cold and gels (taqrus), God willing. \n\tIbrāhīm bin al-Mahdī used to eat nothing of the fish but its tongue and the rest of it was usually given to whoever was present with him and his pages. He also used to eat tongues of all other animals. He composed this poem on the dish: \n[i]I have qarīṣ dish of bunnī fish, which our cook perfected and brought to us chilled.\nLike ruby on the platter, set in a pearl. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ṣibāg͟h taken from Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī’s copy:[/b]\nTake mustard sauce (k͟hardal maʿmūl), and add to it caraway seeds, thyme, asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), cassia, and rue. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe from his copy, too:[/b]\nTake a handful of picked over zabīb (raisins) and soak them in vinegar. Crush the raisins, mix them with a small amount of garlic, and beat them with the vinegar in which they were soaked. \n\tTake 1 uskurruja (½ cup) of the raisin mixture and add to it another uskurruja of vinegar mixed with walnut and mustard. Add as well asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), asafetida root (maḥrūt), cassia, caraway, and aniseeds (anīsūn). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṣibāg͟h recipe from al-Maʾmūn’s copy:[/b]\nTake one part maṣl (whey from drained yogurt), one part walnut, and one part garlic. Pound these and put them in a pot. Pour on them 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Light fire under the pot, and let the mixture heat and boil thoroughly. Add murrī (liquid fermented sauce), pour it into a platter (jām), and serve it after you put the roasted fish on it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṣibāg͟h recipe from al-Muʿtamid’s copy:[/b]\nTake fatty fish, boil it, and rinse it in cold water. Put in a ṭābaq (large flat pan), a little vinegar, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), ground coriander seeds, and finely chopped onion. Cook the mixture until done then take it out and while still hot, add a little olive oil and caraway seeds. Pour sauce on the fish while it is still hot. Set it aside until it cools down and the fish picks up the flavor of the sauce, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A ṣibāg͟h recipe by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nTake mustard sauce (k͟hardal maʿmūl). Mix it with strained raisins that have been picked over and macerated in vinegar. Add a pounded clove of garlic, asafetida root (maḥrūt), thyme, galangal, cumin, coriander seeds, and a bit of aniseeds (anīsūn). Mix sauce well and pour it on cooked salted dried fish (samak mamlūḥ). Chop on it some fresh rue and parsley and set it aside until it absorbs the flavor of the sauce, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ṣibāg͟h to use when traveling and at home (al-safar wa ’l-ḥaḍar):[/b]\nPound together two parts pomegranate seeds and one part zabīb (raisins). Add to them black pepper, and cumin. Knead the mixture well and shape it into discs (aqrāṣ) and store them. Whenever needed, dissolve the pomegranate discs in vinegar and have the sauce with fish. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṣibāg͟h for fresh fish:[/b]\nTake wine vinegar, parsley, rue, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), thyme, black pepper, cumin, caraway, cassia, a lump of sugar, and coarse salt (milḥ jarīs͟h). Mix them 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṣibāg͟h Aṣbahānī style:[/b]\nCrush coarse salt with cheese peeled of its rind. Mix them with ground walnut and crumble on them dried asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān) and thyme. Add salt and mix well. Pour into it some vinegar and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tHere is a poem al-Muʿtamid composed on ṣibāg͟h: \n[i]The concept of ṣibāg͟h is so subtle that none other than the smart can fathom.\nWalnut and garlic with yogurt whey (maṣl) are the most you may need for it.\nOr make it with vinegar, maḥrūt, and coriander. But with anjud͟hān it will be even better.\nIf not, then mustard and garlic mixed with anjud͟hān and onion, equal parts, will make your relish.\nOr with just vinegar and onion eat your fish and it will still be a tasty dish.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṣibāg͟h by Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake 2 dirhams (6 grams) black pepper, 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) coriander seeds, 1 dirham (3 grams) each of cassia, cloves, ginger, spikenard, caraway, and Persian thyme (ṣaʿtar Fārisī). Also take 3 dirhams (9 grams) qardamāna (wild caraway). Pound all these abāzīr and sift them. \n\tTake mustard, ground walnut, and a little salt. Stir them into raisin juice (māʾ zabīb) and pomegranate seeds. Add this mixture to the prepared spices and herbs (abāzīr). \n\tAdd to this sauce, disjointed pullets grilled on a rotating spit (farārīj kardanāj), roasted young fowls, or roasted meat, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṣibāg͟h, similar to the above:[/b]\nTake 2 dirhams (6 grams) cassia; 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) each of coriander seeds and caraway; 1 dirham (3 grams) each of black pepper, ginger, cloves, spikenard, and asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān); and ½ dirham (1½ grams) qardamāna (wild caraway). \n\tGrind them all and stir them into a mixture of juice of fresh rue, cilantro, and fūd͟hanaj (wild mint), which you may substitute with naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). Add as well the juice of a whole head of garlic and a head of onion, which have been crushed with wine vinegar and salt then drained. \n\tAdd to this sauce, a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Put in it pullets which you have roasted (mas͟hwiyya), braised (muṭajjana), or grilled on a rotating spit (kardanāj). Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Delicious ṣibāg͟h for poultry grilled on a rotating spit (kardanāj), and roasted (s͟hawī) in the tannūr:[/b]\nBoil fresh radishes then rinse them in cold water. Take some mustard froth (rag͟hwat k͟hardal) and put it on a platter. Add some sugar and asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān) to the mustard. Mix well. \n\tArrange the boiled radishes on the sauce and drizzle them with sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). Serve the radish platter with roasted chicken or pullets. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṣibāg͟h by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nChoose an excellent quality chicken, scald it to remove feathers, gut it, and wash it. \n\tNow take 10 pomegranates, half sweet and half sour. Extract their juice and put it in a container. Stir in 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) aged murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tGive the chicken a rub with olive oil then with pleasant-tasting salt (milḥ ʾad͟hb) and thyme. Grill it on a rotating spit over coals (kardanāj). Add to the pomegranate juice and murrī mix whatever dissolves of the chicken fat while rotating and continue doing this until the chicken is fully grilled. \n\tShell and pound 20 walnuts, stir them into the pomegranate mix, and eat the sauce with the chicken. It is delicious, scrumptious, wonderful, and quite popular (lad͟hīd͟ha, ṭayyiba, ʿajība, mustaʿmala). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for stuffed maṣīr al-dawwāra:[/b]\nFinely chop red meat and chop as much alya (sheep’s tail fat). Finely chop fresh herbs, onion, and rue. Add them to the meat then pound the meat mixture with a knife until it has the consistency of ointment (marham). Add cassia, black pepper, caraway, māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce), a little vinegar, and olive oil. Knead the mixture very well and stuff it into a large intestine with the fat adhering to it (muṣrān g͟halīẓ s͟haḥim). Also stuff with it some small intestines (maṣārīn). Cook them with whatever dishes you prefer, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for laqāniq (sausages of small intestines) by al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nTake as needed meat from the upper thigh, the rump, the shoulders, and kis͟htamāzika (tenderloin). Pound them all very well. \n\tPound together a small amount of onion, cilantro, and rue. Pound coriander seeds, cumin, black pepper, cassia, and ginger that has a pronounced taste. Add these to the meat and pound them together, sprinkling murrī (liquid fermented sauce) as much as needed. \n\tTake the meat paste out of the stone mortar, and put it in a container. For each raṭl (pound) of meat use 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Knead well together. \n\tNow take a length of small intestines (muṣrān), clean it, slick it off, and wash it in water. Do this meticulously and thoroughly until the intestine becomes very thin and free of slime. \n\tFit the sausage feeder (miḥas͟hs͟ha) into the opening of the intestine, then feed the meat mixture into the intestine until you use up all the meat. Tie the sausages with cotton threads, put them aside, and use them as needed. \n\tTo serve, fry as much as needed in a frying pan and offer them with mustard. You may use them to garnish other dishes. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another laqāniq recipe:[/b]\nTake meat from a hot thigh (i.e. freshly slaughtered). Remove the sinews (abṣāb), blood vessels (ʿurūq), and bones. Chop meat into fine pieces and pound it with two mallets (miḍrāb). Wash the stone mortar (ḥajar) with salt and water and wipe it dry. Put the meat in it along with some coarse salt and pound it into paste. Add 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) hard sugar-candy (Sulaymānī), 1 sukurruja (small bowl) honey, ground black pepper, finely chopped fresh cilantro and rue, a small amount of māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid of fermented sauce), cassia, spikenard, and ground cloves. Put more of black pepper than the rest of the spices. Continue pounding then finely chop alya (sheep’s tail fat), add it to the meat mixture, and pound them together very well until all ingredients become one whole mass. \n\tStuff the meat mixture into small intestines (muṣrān). Boil the sausages then fry them in a pan using sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Cut the fried sausages into fingers, arrange them on a platter (jām), sprinkle them with chopped rue, and serve them with mustard, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Laqāniq recipe:[/b]\nTake meat from the thigh and remove the sinews, blood vessels, and bones. Chop the meat, pound it very well and then put it in a stone mortar along with salt and finely chopped onion, cilantro, and rue. Continue pounding. Add the spices I mentioned in the previous recipe to the meat mixture. Also add māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid of fermented sauce), 5 egg whites, and 1 uskurruja (½ cup) zayt al-anfāq (oil extracted from unripe olives). Mix all the ingredients very well until they become one mass. \n\tStuff small intestines (muṣrān) with the meat mixture and boil and fry them as mentioned above. However, do not sprinkle chopped rue on them. Serve them with mustard, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another laqāniq recipe:[/b]\nFinely chop 10 bunches (bāqāt) of kurrāt͟h al-baql (tender-leaf leeks), fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb), and rue. Add pounded cheese, ground nuts, pounded spiced meat, salt, shredded chicken breast, 1 uskurruja (½ cup) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), black pepper, spikenard, cloves, cassia, galangal, coriander, cumin, and ginger. Mix the ingredients by hand and stuff the mixture into maṣīr al-dawwara (one long piece of small intestines). Tie both ends with a thread, and boil it in hot water until cooked. \n\tPour zayt al-anfāq (oil extracted from unripe olives) into a frying pan and add fresh and dried thyme, and peels of citron, apple, and quince. Also add a piece of cassia and a whole piece of galangal. Put the boiled sausage in the frying pan until it is browned. Take it out of the oil, cut it into pieces, and serve it with mustard, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another laqāniq recipe:[/b]\nPrepare the meat and pound it as I mentioned for which muṣrān (small intestines) or mibʿar (large intestines) are used for stuffing. Boil alya (sheep’s tail fat) then chop it and add it to the prepared meat. Take them out and fry them in sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). They will taste marvelously delicious and will stay good for up to a month. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ṭardīn (thin meat patties):[/b]\nTake lean meat (laḥm aḥmar) and meat from the shoulders. Thoroughly pound them in a stone mortar. Throw into the mixture, ground coriander seeds, cumin, black pepper, cassia, ginger, galangal, and aniseeds. Pour in a small amount of murrī (fermented sauce) and a little olive oil. \n\tTake the meat paste out of the mortar, and spread it on a sheet of papyrus (qirṭās) or paper (waraq). Boil water in a pot and put the sheet in it until the meat is done. \n\tTake the sheet out of water and cut meat into triangles (s͟hawābīr). Pour zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) into a frying pan and fry the pieces until browned. Arrange them on a platter (jām), put a small bowl (uskurruja) of mustard in the middle, and serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making sanbūsaj:[/b]\nFor the filling, take meat from the shoulders, the inner thigh, rump, and sheep’s tail fat. Remove the blood vessels and finely pound the meat on a wooden board, using a knife. Add the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), leek leaves (kurrāt͟h al-baql), cilantro, rue, and a little naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). Pound all the ingredients together quite well. \n\tPour as much as needed of Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Add coriander seeds, black pepper, cassia, cloves, as much as you like of aromatic spices (afāwīh al-ʿiṭr), and ginger. Mix the meat with the spices, add some olive oil, and cook it until it is done. Prepared this way, the meat filling is called isfīd͟hbāj (white and plain). \n\tIf you like it to be sour, add to the meat mixture as much as you like of pulverized maṣl (dried yogurt whey). You may use rak͟hbīn (dried buttermilk), sumac juice, or any other sour ingredients, as you wish God willing. \n\tWhen the meat mixture is ready, use it to stuff ruqāq (thin sheets of bread) then roll the pieces into triangles, squares, or rectangles. \n\tIf wished, you may add dried fruits or nuts to the meat stuffing such as walnut, almond, coconut, pistachio, hazelnut, pine nut, or any other fruits. You can also decorate them with eggs the way some people do in banquets (wālāyim) and public feasts (simāṭāt). \n\tAlternatively, you may shape them Bābakī style. Take fermented dough and roll it out very thin. Cut out rounds using a concave wooden mold, similar to a ḥuqq (small bowl). Stuff these rounds with the meat mixture, and seal them by pressing all around the edges with the fingernail. \n\tFry the filled pastries in zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) or sesame oil (s͟hayraj). Take them out when they brown (iḥmarra) and eat them with whatever you prefer of sauces made with vinegar or mustard. This is the way to make all kinds of sanbūsaj excluding the sweet varieties. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making bone marrow (muḥ):[/b]\nTake equal amounts of fresh fat of sheep’s tail and spleen (ṭiḥāl). Pound them in a stone mortar very well and stuff them into a lead tube, which you then put in boiling water or whatever boiling liquid you like. When done, empty the tube stuffing into a bowl and serve it sprinkled with salt and sugar. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making mock bone marrow (muḥ muzawwar):[/b]\nTake 40 walnuts. They may be fresh and tender or newly dried. You may add the egg yolk. \n\tPut the mixture in a glass (qadaḥ zujāj) and put it in a pot that already has water in it. Light fire under the pot and let it boil. The mixture inside the glass will thicken and set. It will be bone marrow that is wonderful, scrumptious, and delicious (ʿajīb, lad͟hīd͟h, ṭayyib). Serve it and eat it, God willing.

(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making mustard:[/b]\nPick over and sift through mustard seeds to get rid of dust, twigs, rotten seeds, and other impurities that might be in it. Pound the seeds thoroughly. If this proves to be difficult, add to the seeds a piece of cotton. This will make pounding them much easier. Once you finish pounding, add to the seeds an equal amount of walnuts, and continue pounding. Then pour as much as you like of vinegar and strain the mixture in a fine sieve. You will get fine mustard that is whiter than sea foam itself (zabad). Take the foam only, and add to it a little salt and serve it, God willing. \n\tMake ṣināb sauce ( ﺏﺎﻨﺻ) with the remaining mix by adding pounded zabīb (raisins) and vinegar, or sugar and vinegar. It will be fabulous, indeed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making laban māst (thick and sour yogurt made with rennet):[/b]\nPut milk in an earthenware jar (jarra) and set it aside from morning till mid-day, or until you notice that it has started to sour. Stir rennet (infaḥa) into the milk after you pound it. For each 10 raṭls (10 pints) of milk, use 1 dirham (3 grams) of rennet. \n\tBeat the mixture by hand and set it aside undisturbed until the following day. It will set (yajmud) and become māst (thick sour yogurt). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making s͟hīrāz (drained yogurt):[/b]\nPut some māst yogurt recipe above in an earthenware jar (jarra). Add salt to it. For every 10 raṭls (10 pints) of māst yogurt, use 3 ūqiyyas (3 ounces) salt. Stir the yogurt, transfer it to a white leather container (ziqq), and place it on a wooden board to allow liquid to drain, leaving behind just the thickened yogurt in the ziq. While draining, keep washing the ziqq from the outside to keep the pores open. This is how to make s͟hīrāz. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making k͟hilāṭ (yogurt infused with herbs):[/b]\nPut laban rāyib in an earthen jar. Discard any whey that comes up until it thickens. \n\tYou may put whatever you like of herbs after you chop them and wilt them under the sun. Stuff the wilted herbs in a white leather container (ziqq) then add the yogurt. For each 10 raṭls (10 pounds) of herbs, use three times as much of yogurt (i.e. 30 pints), and 1 raṭl (1 pound) salt. \n\tFor those who want to have their k͟hilāṭ with its own butter, let them substitute the rāyib with laban ḥalīb bāyit. \n\tThe way to make ḥalīb bāyit is to put milk in an earthenware container from the evening to the following morning until it curdles and thickens and the whey is filtered through the pores then use it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making cheese (jubn):[/b]\nTake fresh milk that has just been drawn, and while it is still warm, mix with it infaḥa (rennet). The proper way to use it is to take the rennet as it is with the skin no need to pound it and stir it into the milk while it is still warm. When the milk curdles (jamuda), put it in molds made of willow wood (k͟hilāf) then press it, sprinkle it with salt, and stow it away. \n\tIf you need to eat it right away, do not salt it. In this case it is called sād͟haj (plain cheese). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making qarīs͟ha (ricotta cheese):[/b]\nTake the drained whey resulting from pressing the cheese, put it in a pot, and let it cook on a gentle fire. Sprinkle milk on it. For each raṭl (1 pint) of whey, add 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) of milk. Put the pot away from the fire, skim the top curds, and discard the remaining liquid. You will get delicious qarīs͟ha. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making jājaq:[/b]\nTake a clean leather container (ziqq) and scent it. Pour yogurt into it and add salt. The outside of the ziqq needs to be salted, too. \n\tStir into the yogurt, chopped onion, whole skinned cloves of garlic, finely chopped parsley, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) tarragon, rue, k͟hiyār (small, smooth cucumbers), and qit͟ht͟hāʾ (ribbed, long cucumber), peeled lettuce stems, and—when in season—some artichoke (ḥars͟haf). Use also fresh and tender green almonds. The best vegetables and herbs added to it are a suitable amount of naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), rue, parsley, onion, and garlic. Besides, you need to keep the leather container clean all the time to allow liquids to drain. When it is ready to eat, serve it with olive oil. \n\tHere is a poem by Maḥmūd bin al-Ḥasan. He describes a selection of bowls of yogurt (sakārij albān) once given to him as a present: \n[i]Bowls of buttermilk (mak͟hīḍ al-laban) has he arranged for us on a tray.\nOne is sour, and the other with yogurt (rāyib) shines.\nFive other bowls were put together of yogurt infused with herbs and tender leaves:\nOne with rue vibrantly green, one with tarragon fresh picked long before noon,\nOne with thyme snipped just in time, one with fragrant basil freshly gathered,\nAnd one with fresh mustard leaves, wonderfully sharp for those who relish.\nAnother bowl he filled with butter, which it did adorn,\nLike the full moon when at dusk it shines.\nDrained yogurt (s͟hīrāz) tempered with milk in a bowl, harmoniously blended,\nDrizzled with olive oil, easily mistaken for a net of gold.\nLibaʾ on a platter put, like a crescent turned to full moon.\nPorous, as if bees have made their home in it.\nGod will surely bless him with joy and lasting ease, as he is most worthy of these.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making būdaj, which is qamn:[/b]\nTake as much as needed of wheat flour or wheat and barley flour in equal amounts. Knead the flour into very dry and stiff dough by adding a little water. Do not use yeast, but add a lot of salt to prevent the dough from breeding worms. \n\tShape dough into small thick discs, which you wrap with fig leaves or cover with their own sifted bran. Bury them in ash or hey for 40 days and take them out. The good ones should be rotted and reddish in hue. Let them dry out completely and use as needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]How to rot bread (taʿfīn al-k͟hubz):[/b]\nUse unleavened bread (k͟hubz faṭīr) for making binn and leavened bread (k͟hubz k͟hamīr) for making kāmak͟h. \n\tIf bread is thick, split it open with your fingers and wipe the surface with water while it is still fresh. Stack the breads in layers in an ijjāna (large tub) or jarra (jar), which you then turn upside down, cover, and set aside for 40 days. When bread completely rots, take it out. \n\tIf you want to use the mold, take hot unleavened bread and break it into pieces. Place a piece between each two of the layered bread mentioned earlier. The bread will mold and rot so well that it will look like sprouting grass. \n\tAfter you take the rotted bread out, dry it, and discard the pieces that look like cobwebs. Dry the rest for a few days, and grind it and use it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making faṭīr (unleavened bread):[/b]\nMake dough with wheat flour, using neither yeast nor salt. Flatten it into discs immediately and bake it in the tannūr. If you prefer, add some oil to the dough. \n\tDry the breads, grind them, and use them as needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A fast method for making binn al-sakārīj:[/b]\nTake one part out of a total of ten parts of ground būdaj that has been sifted in a fine sieve (munk͟hul ṣafīq), and nine parts of sifted rotted bread (k͟hubz ʿafin) recipe above. Put them in a container, mix them well, and add water enough to cover. \n\tAdd nigella and fennel seeds (rāzyānaj). Half of the amounts should be added ground and the other half added whole. Pour 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) olive oil and set the mixture aside overnight. \n\tIn the following morning, stir the mixture by hand very well until it looks like ointment (marham). Add pleasant-tasting salt (milḥ ʿad͟hb), the amount of which depends on how salty you want it to be. In any case, the maximum amount of salt you can add should not exceed one tenth of the total amount of the mixture. \n\tCover the container and set it aside in a shaded place. After a week, you can eat it with some olive oil. It will be truly delicious. \n\tIf you like to keep it longer, add fresh bread, spices, olive oil, salt, and water. It will keep for as long as you wish, unchanged, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for red kāmak͟h from which other varieties can be made:[/b]\nTake 1 part of ground and sifted būdaj recipe above and 4 parts ground and sifted pith of unleavened bread (lubāb al-k͟hubz al-faṭīr) recipe above. Mix these well and add a handful of salt. Add fresh milk (laban ḥalīb) and knead mixture. \n\tPut the dough in a container and set it aside exposed to the hot summer sun. Keep on feeding it with milk whenever it gets dry and stir it twice a day until it looks red. Divide it into portions and make different kinds of kawāmīk͟h with it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h of cloves:[/b]\nGrind and sift 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) cloves and add it to 1 Levantine raṭl (8 pounds) red kāmak͟h recipe above. Put the mixture in a container and set it aside in a sunny place. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h of cassia:[/b]\nMake it exactly the same way as above using the same measurements using cassia. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h of caraway seeds:[/b]\nTake 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) caraway seeds and grind them coarsely (daqqan jarīs͟han). Add them to 1 Levantine raṭl (8 pounds) of this kāmak͟h. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h of rose:[/b]\nTake as much as you wish of roses, dry them, discard their bottoms, and mix them with the kāmak͟h. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making white kāmak͟h:[/b]\nTake milk (laban) and make it into kāmak͟h the way you like, but do not add any fresh greens or herbs. When it matures and develops a tongue-biting sour taste, put it in a new white jar, and for each 10 raṭls (10 pints/20 cups) of it, add 1 raṭl (1 pound) ḥuwwārā (fine bran-free flour).
