Beat mixture with a stick and put the jar in a cool shaded place. For the following 50 days, daily add ½ raṭl (1 cup) or less of milk (ḥalīb). Meanwhile, keep washing the jar from the outside to keep pores open until it develops the desired thickness. \n\tTransfer the kāmak͟h into a green glazed jar and add chopped rue, peel of fresh green citron, and nigella seeds if wished. You may leave it plain. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h with fragrant spices (afāwī):[/b]\nTake spikenard, ginger, and cumin, ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) each. Also take 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) cassia, 1 dirham (3 grams) black pepper, and 4 mit͟hqāls (18 grams) cloves. Grind them all and sift them. \n\tDiscard the seeds from zabīb (raisins) and pound them until they resemble bone marrow (muk͟h) in consistency. Mix all the ingredients, and knead them well with fresh milk, add enough to bind them. Sweeten it with honey and a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making kāmak͟h of capers (kabar):[/b]\nTake as much as you like of newly dried capers. Put them in a green glazed jar and pour on them enough water to submerge them. Put the jar in a sunny place for a day and a half. \n\tDrain the water, submerge the capers in fresh water again, and add to them enough pleasant-tasting salt (milḥ ʿad͟hb). Stir with the hand twice or thrice daily for 6 days. \n\tOn the seventh day strain the capers and transfer the drained liquid to green-glazed tubs. Place them in a sunny place and cover them well. Transfer the liquid from one tub to another daily and discard the sediments that have settled in the bottom of the tub. Do this until the liquid is clear of all sediments and develops an intensely blackish hue. Transfer the liquid into a container and use it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h with thyme (ṣaʿtar):[/b]\nChoose tender thyme sprigs, and pick the tender leaves at the tips of their stems. Add to them as much as they can take of red or white kāmak͟h. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h al-rayḥān (sweet-smelling herbs):[/b]\nPick the tender tips of the herb stems and add to them as much as they can take of kāmak͟h. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h of ajowan (nānjawāh):[/b]\nPound and sift 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) ajowan and add to them as much as they can take of red kāmak͟h. [b]Kāmak͟h of aniseeds (anīsūn):[/b]\nDo the same as above. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Enhancing elecampane (taṭyīb rāsan) from the book of Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nPut elecampane roots in a new earthenware kūz (cup-like container with handles) and wrap it with sackcloth (k͟hīs͟h). Sprinkle the container with water whenever it gets dry for several days. The roots will swell and enlarge, and become lighter in color. They will also lose some of their burning heat. When eaten, they will easily disintegrate in the stomach and get digested much faster. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making chutney (maqra):[/b]\nTake one part turnip, one part quince and Levantine apple combined, and half a part of citron. Finely chop them, put them in a container, and sprinkle them with a handful of salt. \n\tTake some sour yeast of wheat dough and dissolve it in water. Add it to the chopped vegetables. Stir the mixture twice a day. You need to add a handful of whole fennel seeds (rāzyānaj). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Olives (zaytūn) prepared by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake black and green olives, but the black variety is better. Put them in a barniyya (large wide-mouthed jar) and add to them salt and thyme. Submerge them in sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and set the container aside until needed, God willing. \n\tIbn al-Muʿtazz described a tray of kawāmīk͟h bowls: \n[i]Enjoy a wicker basket that comes with rows of platters laden.\nAssorted bowls of all kinds, red, and yellow, finely disposed:\nKāmak͟h of tarragon with its blooms, and red kāmak͟h and capers, too.\nThe noon sun bestowed them a hue, radiant with light from the sun they borrowed.\nSuch a soothing aroma, they smell as though musk was in them crushed.\nKāmak͟h of marjoram is across from cloves, the best one can get.\nKāmak͟h of cassia is there, which neither in taste nor color does rival have,\nAs if it exhales a musky breeze with pungent taste and fabulous aroma.\nKāmak͟h of thyme, fresh and tender, redolent with musk and bay.\nLook at kāmak͟h of garlic and you see perfume enjoining you to eat.\nThe olives, as dark as night, put next to mamqūr, are shining with light.\nLook at the onions and marvel, as if of silver made with fire filled.\nPerfectly round turnips, subtly taste of vinegar, a gift of the generous rains.\nThe white turnips and the red look like silver dirhams overlapping with dīnārs.\nFrom every corner, a star glows like the resplendent light of dawn.\nLike a garden flower juxtaposed with full moon, sun, darkness, and radiant lights.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making rabīt͟hā (relish of crushed shrimp):[/b]\nTake a big jar (qulla) of the small fish (samak) kept in brine. They look like d͟harr (small ants), as big as locusts, and are called rabīt͟hā. Empty these onto a sieve made of rush stems (g͟hirbāl asal) underneath which you put a green-glazed tub (ijjāna k͟had͟hrāʾ) to receive the drained liquid. \n\tWhen the shrimps are fully drained, let them dry in a shaded place, and throw away any twigs, salt grains, and other similar things. Put the shrimps in a stone mortar, and grind them into a fine mush. Add to them, 10 peeled Levantine apples, and 20 dirhams (2 ounces) dried Nabatean thyme, and continue grinding. \n\tAdd to the mix as much as it needs of olive oil and knead it. Pour into it 1 raṭl (2 cups) honey wine (nabīd͟h ʿasal) and stir them well. \n\tDivide the mixture among three big wide-mouthed bowls (barānī). Add into one of them, 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) ground dried anjud͟hān (asafetida leaves); into the second, add 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) ground caraway seeds and ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) ground fennel seeds (rāzyānaj). Leave the third one plain (sād͟haja). \n\tBy doing this you will end up having three kinds of the relish. \n\tYou can do the same thing with ṣiḥnā (salted small fish). Just add to it ḥabbat al-k͟haḍrā (green terebinth berries), thyme, cumin, fennel seeds, Levantine apples, and quince. Then knead the mixture with olive oil and put it aside until needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making ṣiḥnāt (salted and dried small fish):[/b]\nPick over small fish and wash them only once. Add what equals ¼ of the fish’s weight of salt. Put them aside in an airy, warm, and shaded place away from direct sunlight. Add to them dried thyme and dried anjud͟hān sark͟hasī, a handful of each. Store them away, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for making ṣiḥnāt al-jarād (locusts pickled in brine):[/b]\nUse locusts that have just been caught. Discard the dead ones and put the live ones in brine. When they all suffocate and die, strain them, but keep the drained liquid in which they suffocated. \n\tGrind as much as needed of coriander seeds, fennel seeds, and dried leaves of asafetifa (anjud͟hān). \n\tIn a big, wide jar, put a layer of the drained locusts, sprinkle them with the prepared spice mix, and give them a generous sprinkle of salt. Repeat the layers. \n\tAllow the sediments of the drained brine in which the locusts suffocated to settle down. Slowly pour enough of the clean brine all over the layered locusts to submerge them. Completely seal the jar with mud. No air should be allowed to get into the jar, as this will cause the pickled locusts to go bad. \n\tNow be patient and wait for them until they mature and become delicious and eat them. \n\tHere is what Maḥmūd bin al-Ḥusayn said about locusts: \n[i]When the fleeting locusts swarmed in, and their troops our abodes their camps made,\nFerociously greedy as they are you should be. Longevity is the last thing you wish for such despots with shearing and snipping mouths.\nTheir middles so thin, with thighs like lutes.\nTheir tails like daggers, the pupils as big as eyes.\nThese ruthless shielded attackers with spoils of war were rich, but the counter fighters with fury ignited:\nThe hovering ones, exterminated, perished; the flying ones, caught and fallen.\nThus, the tables have turned, and the transgressors have only themselves to blame.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for Levantine kis͟hk:[/b]\nAfter you boil wheat and dry it, crush it coarsely and winnow it to get rid of all bran and finely ground grains (duqāq). \n\tKnead the sifted grains with enough hot water, and a small amount of yeast. Put the dough in a tub (ijjāna) and leave it exposed to the sun. Uncover it during the day and cover it during the night. Do this for six-days or more until it becomes intensely sour. \n\tFinely chop as many kinds of herbs as you like. However, you should avoid endive (hindibāʾ) and watercress (jirjīr) because they are not good with kis͟hk. Use a lot of tender-leaf leeks (kurrāt͟h al-baql), cilantro, and rue. If you prefer to use finely chopped small round onions, do so by all means. You can also add eggplant (bād͟hinjān), gourd (qarʿ), and cabbage (kurunb). All these will make it quite delicious. \n\tNow add k͟hawk͟h al-dubb ( ﺏﺪﻟﺍ ﺥﻮﺧ) which is small and sour plum. Sour grape juice will be good, too. \n\tKnead together all the ingredients very well and leave the dough in a sunny place for five days. Then divide it into portions, which you shape into discs and set aside to dry out. When completely dry, thread them into necklace-like links, and hang them for storage. \n\tIf you like, you can substitute water used in kneading the grains with defatted sour yogurt (laban ḥāmiḍ rāyib). In this case, of all the herbs mentioned above, use only naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) and parsley. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for kis͟hk:[/b]\nTake one kayl of wheat, husk it, par-boil it, dry it, coarsely grind it, and mix it with ground chickpeas. Add yeast and a little salt, then knead mixture into dough with enough water. Keep it in a sunny place for 15 days and whenever it gets dry replenish moisture by adding to it extremely sour yogurt from which butter was extracted. \n\tYou need to add a little salt to it when you knead it. \n\tAfter 15 days finely chop naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), Persian parsley (karafs Fārisī), purslane (baqla ḥamqāʾ), rue, cilantro, and qirṭ which is kurrāt͟h al-baql. Mix the herbs with the wheat dough and shape it into discs. Leave them out in the sun to dry. \n\tIf you like to add garlic, then go ahead and do so. In addition, you also have the option of substituting yogurt with sour grape juice, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ahlām of veal:[/b]\nSlaughter a calf, cut off its head and discard it along with the extremities (aṭrāf). Disjoint the animal and discard the entrails. Cut the meat into smaller pieces with the skin on, and arrange them in a pot so as the sides with skin on are put face to face. Submerge the meat in vinegar and cook it until done. \n\tTake the meat out of the pot and wipe clean the skins with the hand, using cold water. Wrap the meat in pieces of linen cloth (k͟hām) and weigh them down with a stone overnight. \n\tIn the following morning, put the pieces in large, big-mouthed jars (barānī). Pour on them wine vinegar and add chopped root of asafetida (maḥrūt), rue, and parsley. Add as well nigella seeds, coriander seeds and two fistfuls (ḥafna) of sesame seeds, citron leaves, citron peel, peel of Lebanese apples, and quince. \n\tStash the jars away. Whenever needed, take some pieces out and present them on a platter (jām), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ahlām:[/b]\nSlaughter a calf, disjoint it with the skin on, and wash it very well with water. Boil vinegar and cook the disjointed meat in it until done. Transfer the pieces to cold water and take them piece by piece and strip skins clean of hair. Set pieces aside on a plate until they become even in color. \n\tNow take good quality vinegar and pour it into a big wide bowl (jafna). Add galangal (k͟hūlanjān), root of asafetida (maḥrūt), cassia, thyme, parsley, quince, citron, nigella seeds, and salt. Add the meat to this mixture and let it macerate overnight. \n\tIn the following morning, put the meat with the vinegar mixture in large, big-mouthed jars (barānī) or big, green-glazed earthenware jars (g͟haḍār). \n\tWhen you wish to eat it, take some out of the bowl and serve it on a platter (jām) garnished with saffron and nigella seeds. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for hallām of Kid:[/b]\nScald a kid and scrape the skin thoroughly until it is clean of any dirt and hair. Split it open from the breastbone (qaṣṣ) to the hips (wirkayn) to flatten it. Next, slit open the thigh from the inside down to the joints. \n\tPour 10 raṭls (20 cups) wine vinegar that has been whitened with flour. Add water to the vinegar and let it be more than the amount of vinegar used. Put the prepared kid in the liquid, and let it cook until done. \n\tTake the meat out and wash it in cold water and andarānī salt. Spread it on a wide low table (k͟hiwān), putting clean pieces of thick cotton cloth on top and underneath it. Put a heavy weight on it to press it flat. You should remove all the bones before pressing it like this. \n\tYou need to prepare the appropriate sauce (ṣibāg͟h) for it while it is cooking and being pressed using whitened vinegar that has been prepared the night before. To this whitened vinegar add thyme, asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), parsley, and rue. Put the pressed meat in this sauce and add asafetida root (maḥrūt) and citron leaves. \n\tTo serve the meat, you need to prepare small bowls, one filled with cheese, one with olives, another with a dipping sauce (ṣibāg͟h) prepared with sour juice of grapes and one with sauce made with pomegranate seeds mixed with mustard, ginger, black pepper, and salt. In addition to these, a bowl of maḥs͟hī (condiment of dressed eggplant), and another one filled with clean and picked-over thyme. \n\tSpread a big tray with a variety of endive leaves (hindibāʾ), parsley, and buqūl K͟hurāsāniyya of all kinds. Put the prepared meat in the middle. \n\tAlso prepare ten kinds of bazmāward (rolled sandwiches) filled with conserves (murabbā) of walnut, citron, quince, apple, and gourd (qarʿ). Slice them, and arrange the pieces around the meat. \n\tWhen served, this dish will look like an orchard (bustān). Let there be with it s͟harāyiḥ m
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida (cold dish) of roasted rabbit by Yaḥya bin K͟hālid:[/b]\nChop roasted rabbit meat as fine as sesame seeds and put it in a g͟haḍāra (green-glazed bowl). \n\tTake vinegar and murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and mix them using the required amounts to produce a balanced taste. Add 2 dānaqs (1 gram) asafetida root (maḥrūt), 1 dānaq (½ gram) asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān) 1 dirham (3 grams) caraway seeds, 2 dirhams (6 grams) chopped rue, and 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) different spices (abzār). Also add 4 dirhams (12 grams) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil), and 5 dirhams (15 grams) white sugar. \n\tPut two whole onions in the sauce but discard them before serving the dish, God willing. \n\tRabbit meat is the lightest of game meat (laḥm al-waḥs͟h). It has the capacity to rejuvenate semen (taqwiyat al-māʾ). The most delicious part of the rabbit is its lower tenderloin (kis͟htamāzija). It is at its best when cooked as nārbāj (sour pomegranate stew), maḥs͟hī, and s͟harāʾiḥ mubazzara. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another bārida dish made with game meat and kid’s meat:[/b]\nTake 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) of raisin juice obtained by soaking raisins in pomegranate juice then pounding and straining the mix. Add a small amount of garlic that has been crushed with 1 dirham (3 grams) rue. Set this aside as a sauce served with the cold dish \n\tChoose slices of shoulder meat (mutūn), tenderloins (kis͟htamāzaj), and similar cuts of the best of game meat. Put the meat in a pot and pour on it about 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) water, ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil, and 1 dirham (3 grams) salt. Set the pot on a trivet (yunṣab) on the burning coals and cook the meat the way you do with ṭabāhijāt (braised red meat). When meat is done, add about ¼ raṭl (½ cup) murrī (liquid fermented sauce), 1 dirham (3 grams) black pepper, and a similar amount of cassia. \n\tTake the pot away from the fire, and while it is still bubbling, add mustard prepared with zabīb (raisins), pomegranate seeds, and rue. \n\tArrange the meat in a g͟haḍāra (green glazed earthenware bowl), and pour on it the sauce prepared above. You may serve the dish hot or cold, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a dish made for Yaḥya bin K͟hālid:[/b]\nThinly slice chunks of red lean meat and sprinkle them with salt. Put a clean frying pan on the fire without adding any fat to it and let it heat until it becomes red. Spread the meat slices on the pan and flip them frequently until they are cooked. \n\tThis is the way to prepare kabāb k͟hāliṣ (griddled meat, pure and simple). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for beef bārida:[/b]\nTake beef from the thigh but do not use any tallow. Cook the meat in water. When it is done, take it out and put it in lukewarm water (māʾ fātir) and set it aside. \n\tTake 20 shelled walnuts and finely pound them in a mortar and pestle (hāwan). While pounding the walnuts, sprinkle them with a small amount of vinegar and add two sprigs of rue and a little salt. Let the mixture be rather thick in consistency (k͟hāt͟hir) like mustard sauce. \n\tPress dry the cooked beef, and put it in a clean platter (jām). Sprinkle it with māʾ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid of fermented sauce), pour over it the ground walnut mixture, and drizzle it with zayt anfāq (oil pressed from unripe olives). Take boiled eggs, cut them into quarters, and garnish the meat with them. Sprinkle the dish with a little rue, deck it with herbs, and serve it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another beef bārida:[/b]\nTake beef chunks from the shoulders and cook them in water and salt. When the meat is done, slice it into big pieces, and set it aside. \n\tPut 50 whole onions in a soapstone pot (burma) and sprinkle them with a little vinegar and māʾ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid of fermented sauce). Light the tannūr and put the pot in it to roast the onions. Then chop some rue on them and serve them with the prepared meat. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another bārida of gazelle meat (laḥm g͟hazāl) by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nCut meat of gazelle into large chunks taken from shoulders and thighs. Using a knife, make slits in the meat chunks and stuff each slit with skinned almonds and pistachio and if desired, a small amount of garlic. \n\tCook the meat in wine vinegar, salt, parsley, rue, citron leaves, cassia, galangal, coriander seeds, and black pepper. When done take the meat out of the liquid (maraq) and let it cool down. \n\tSprinkle some chopped parsley, rue, and naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) on the meat and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A stuffed dish (maḥs͟hū) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nClean a long piece of large intestines (mibʿar). \n\tBreak 10 eggs into a big bowl (g͟haḍāra), add to them onions cut into wedges (yuqaṭṭaʿ s͟habābīr), cilantro, and rue chopped. Also add sukkar Sulaymānī (hard sugar-candy), the quantity depends on how sweet you like it to be. Beat the egg mixture and pour it into the prepared intestine. Tie both ends with a thread and boil it in hot water until eggs set. Take it out of the pot and fry it in sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Add a piece of cassia, galangal, and fresh or dried thyme. Fry the sausage until it browns then take it out, slice it into darāhim (like coins), and serve it on a platter. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mamqūr (meat soused in vinegar), eaten hot and cold:[/b]\nChoose fatty pieces of lamb from the loins (k͟hāṣira). Clean the meat and start cooking it in vinegar. When it comes to a boil, take the meat out of the pot and pour off the vinegar. Replenish the pot with fresh vinegar and with it add the usual mamqūr spices and herbs , as well as salt. Return the meat to the pot and let it cook until it is done. \n\tLadle the meat out into a big serving bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and slice it lengthwise then crosswise. Spread on it all the spices and herbs cooked with it and garnish it with whatever is available of large and small sausages, ṭardīn, boiled eggs, cheese, olives, and herbs, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Vegetables usually served as ṣalāyiq (boiled):[/b]\nAsparagus (hilyawn), cauliflower (qunnabīṭ), hops (junjul), white soy beans (lūbyā Yamāniyya), leeks (kurrāt͟h), orach (qaṭaf), g͟hūs͟hina (variety of mushroom), chard (silq), cabbage (kurunb), carrot (jazar), turnip (saljam), spinach (isfānāk͟h), fresh fennel (rāzyānaj), chard root (aṣl al-silq), gourd (qarʿ), and eggplant (bād͟hinjān). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Asparagus dish recommended for coitus from the book of Ibn Māsawayh, which al-Maʾmūn and Ibn al-Mahdī used for this purpose:[/b]\nBoil asparagus just until done, do not overcook them. Serve them seasoned with olive oil and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Cook the remaining liquid with some bees’ honey and cilantro and rue bundled together and tied with a string stripped from a date palm leaf (k͟hūṣ). When the herbs are cooked, take them out. Add a bit of aniseed (anīsūn) and black pepper to the pot. Let it boil then set it aside to cool down. Strain the liquid and make a drink with it mixed with honey or cooked wine (ṭilā). \n\tMuḥammad bin al-Ḥusayn once recited a poem to me describing asparagus: \n[i]We have spears with leaning tips, but the rest is straight like ropes firmly twisted.\nGood-looking and free of knots, with heads out of bodies peering.\nBy the Everlasting One made, tender and brittle as arrows standing erect.\nIn green silk clad, draped on glowing garments steeped in red.\nRed as if mixed with the redness of a cheek that a furious palm imprinted,\nThus, the redness of the cheek and hand with it are mingled.\nYou see them on a platter after being cooled,\nLike tiered piles of shields of gold, arrayed.\nLike spread embroidered silken dress, displayed.\nIf only they stay forever like this!\nThey were the gems of rings that the chaste ones wear,\nWith murrī running between ebb and flow,\nDressed as if with a sumptuous gown of oil,\nWhich, once it settles, turns to spread nets of silver or gold.\nTheir sight alone would ravish the devout,\nThe mouths would water and they break the fast.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]ﻑﺍﺮﳋﺍﻭ ﺍﺪﳉﺍ ﻑﺍﺮﻃﺃ ﻦﻣ ﺕﺎﻗﻼﺼﻟﺍ ﺔﻔﺻ:[/b]\nThe first to cook ṣalīqat al-jedī (boiled kid’s meat) was Abū Samīn ʿAbdullāh bin Samīn. Al-Maʾmūn used to choose the fattest of kids for this dish. \n\tHere is how to make it: Take the extremities (aṭrāf) of a kid along with the head and liver. Clean them and put them in a pot. Pour a lot of water on them. When pot comes to a boil, skim froth, add chard, carrot, and salt. When meat is almost done, add 10 eggs. \n\tWhen fully cooked, take the meat out and let it cool down. Next, remove the outer skins on the meat, divide it into small portions, and spread it on a big platter, or a shallow big bowl (ṭayfūriyya mabsūṭa). Put the head in the middle of the plate after you remove the brain. Loosen the bone joints. \n\tPound the liver and color it with saffron, and set it aside. Put the egg yolks on the left cheek of the head. \n\tPound walnut, stir it with some pistachio oil to make it like mustard in consistency, and set it aside. \n\tMake mustard in a big bowl (uskurruja kabīra) and pour it all over the head and meat. Pour also some sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). \n\tNow, spread a layer of the prepared walnut on the meat, top it with a layer of the chard followed by a layer of the prepared liver. Do this until the layers are four fingers’ width high. \n\tYou need to have on hand some chopped rue and liver to scatter as garnish for the top. Then further decorate it with whatever is available such as pomegranate seeds, sumac, and almonds. Drizzle the dish with zayt al-māʾ and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṣilāqa recipe, Byzantine Style (Rūmiyya):[/b]\nHere is the basic way to prepare ṣilāqāt: \n\tTake the head, trotters (akāriʿ), neck (raqaba), and extremities (aṭrāf) of a kid. Put them in a pot, and add salt, a handful of chickpeas, and sprigs of dill (aʿwād s͟habat). Pour oil and water into the pot, and let it cook until done. \n\tPut a lot of mustard sauce in a big deep bowl (qaṣʿa), and ladle the meat with some of the broth into the bowl. Serve it hot or cold, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ṣilāqa, Persian style (Fārisiyya):[/b]\nBoil the head, trotters, and extremities (aṭrāf) of a kid. Rinse them in cold water then put the head in the middle of a platter after you remove the jaws and the tongue. \n\tCut into bite size portions the tongue, cheek meat, and whatever meat there is in the legs and neck. Spread the meat portions around the head along with chard stalks (ʿasālīj silq). \n\tTake the foam of mustard prepared with sour buttermilk (mak͟hīḍ al-laban al-ḥāmiḍ) instead of water. Beat the foam with white cane sugar (ṭabarzad) along with drained sour yogurt (laban t͟hak͟hīn ḥāmiḍ). Pour this sauce all over the meat. Pour on the dish some olive oil, chop on it rue and boiled egg yolk, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṣilāqa recipe:[/b]\nTake 50 skinned almonds, finely grind them, and beat them into a mixture of mustard foam, vinegar, and fine cane sugar (ṭabarzad)). \n\tNow take the boiled meat prepared as described in ṣilāqa Fārisiyya recipe above along with the chard stalks. Pour all over it mustard which has been prepared with vinegar, almonds, and sugar. Pour on the dish some olive oil, spread chopped eggs on it, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for g͟hāmiḍ:[/b]\nBoil the liver lightly in water (ṣalqa k͟hafīfa) and chop it into fine pieces. Add sifted sumac and salt, the amount of salt should be slightly less than sumac. Pour olive oil on the dish and chop on it some fresh herbs. Also, garnish it with chopped boiled eggs. However, you need to separate the whites from the yolks first before chopping them. Mix the chopped egg whites with the fresh herbs when you add them to the dish. You may add boiled and split stalks of chard. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another Persian ṣilāqa:[/b]\nTake the head and trotters of a kid, clean them, and put them in a clean pot. Pour water on them and add salt and skinned chickpeas. Cook the meat until done and add Persian thyme (ṣaʿtar Fārisī). Serve it with mustard, God willing. \n\tA poem by Abū al-Fatḥ al-Kātib: \n[i]I have, may God your guide be, a dish of cold kid, ṣilāqa, and bawārid.\nThe choicest and most tender meat was used, which our slave girls masterly cooked.\nFive pots put together were sent to us, looking as if one pot. The daintiest of dishes comprised.\nThe wine looks rosy in the glass, the dear child in it but the father has long passed.\nHoney k͟habīṣa, which wearied the hands that beat and stirred, is thick and chewy.\nGood morrow to you my friend and our guest be, so to what I witness my witness be.[/i] \n\tHe also recited to me a poem by Ibn-Ṣadaqa: \n[i]We have a suckling kid, well fed and nourished.\nWhich the cook perfectly boiled and excellently grilled, ‘tis dripping with fat.\nCome early and with this kid nourish yourself, and let the best morsels your target be.\nOf the most delicious cuts make your pick, shoulder, breast, and thigh.\nThe wine, I hope, you will not mind since it was made just two months have passed.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Eggplant: A recipe for dressed eggplant (bād͟hinjān maḥs͟hī) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nCook whole eggplants in water until done. Take them out of the hot water and put them in cold water. \n\tPrepare a small pot. Take a small amount of chopped onion and fresh herbs and fry them in the pot with olive oil. Mix vinegar, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), binn (fermented sauce), caraway seeds, and cassia, and add them to the fried onion. \n\tCut off the calyxes of the eggplants, put them in a plate, and pour the vinegar mixture all over them. Drizzle the dish with a small amount of olive oil and eat it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another dressed eggplant (bād͟hinjān maḥs͟hī), also by him:[/b]\nBoil the eggplants and chop them into small pieces. Pound walnuts, put them along with the eggplant in a bowl, and add salt. Knead mixture with some vinegar, make it into a patty, and stick it to a big bowl (ṭayfūriyya). Smoke the eggplant by pouring some olive oil on a burning fire. Scrape the eggplant patty (qurṣ) and flip it to the other side to allow it to smoke. \n\tStir the smoked eggplant with some vinegar and caraway seeds. You may add some onion if you like. Drizzle some olive oil on the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for dressed eggplant (bād͟hinjān maḥs͟hī) by him, too:[/b]\nBoil eggplant and chop it into fine pieces. Take a platter (jām), and pour on it a little vinegar, white sugar, ground almonds, saffron, caraway seeds, cassia, and mix. Spread the chopped eggplant and fried onion all over the sauce. Drizzle some olive oil on the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bād͟hinjān Būrān (eggplant of Būrān):[/b]\nChoose small eggplants, prick them with a knife, remove their calyxes, and put them in salted water. In a small pot, pour olive oil and sesame oil (s͟hayraj), and fry the drained eggplants until cooked. Sprinkle them with some murrī (liquid fermented sauce), black pepper, and caraway seeds. Chop some rue leaves on the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another eggplant recipe similar to the above:[/b]\nTake small eggplants and cut them lengthwise into halves. Let them soak in salted water. \n\tTake a small pot and heat in it a mix of sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and sesame oil (s͟hayraj). Fry the drained eggplant pieces until done. Sprinkle the eggplant with murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and add to the pot cassia and galangal a piece each. Add as well sprigs (ṭāqāt) of rue. \n\tSpread the eggplant on a platter, grind 10 shelled walnuts, and spread them over the eggplant while it is still hot. Cover the plate with a piece of cloth to let the walnuts release their oil. Spread on the dish a small amount of fresh leek (kurrāt͟h raṭb) which has been fried in olive oil along with cilantro and rue. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for soused eggplant (bād͟hinjān mamqūr):[/b]\nAt the end of their season, cut the calyxes of eggplants and cook them in vinegar until done. Take them out, drain them well, and set them aside. \n\tFinely chop some round onions (baṣal mudawwar), along with cilantro, rue, and parsley. Fry them in olive oil until browned. Pour vinegar on them and add some spices (abzār). \n\tArrange the eggplants in wide-mouthed jars (barānī) and pour on them the vinegar which has been seasoned with the herbs and spices. Let it cover the eggplants. \n\tStore away the jars. Prepared like this the eggplant will stay good for a whole year. Whenever you wish to eat it, take some out and put them in a bowl, garnish them with chopped rue, and serve them, God willing. \n\tHere is a poem by Abū al-Fatḥ on eggplant: \n[i] Ignorantly he chides me because in eggplant I revel,\nWhile the doctor himself eating it will never quit.\nI said to him, ‘tis like a lover whose love I won, and like a rival in my way you stand.\nIf ever behind my back you eat it, your ally will the cross be.\nEggplant has a taste like saliva a generous lover freely offers.\nA pearl in a black gown, with an emerald set from which a stem extends.\nIn taste ‘tis like no other, whether hurriedly cooked or well done.\nYearning for this little wonder, the witty in hosts hasten to it.\nOnly fools have no appetite for it. As for the smart, they just love it.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A cold dish (bārida) of dressed carrots (jazar maḥs͟hī):[/b]\nBoil the carrots, cut them crosswise into rings like dirhams (coins), and set them aside. \n\tChop onion, fresh herbs, and rue. Fry them very well in olive oil and pour on them murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and vinegar. Add as well cassia, black pepper, galangal, coriander seeds, caraway seeds, ginger, spikenard, and cloves, all ground. Bring the pot to a good boil, and pour the vinegar mixture all over the carrots, which have been put on a platter. Chop rue on it and serve it, God willing. \n\tMaḥmūd bin al-Ḥusayn composed a poem describing this dish: \n[i]Dīnārs of carnelian and gold in a vessel so delicate, it may almost melt and flow.\nAll radiating with luster like carnelian shimmering on pearls.\nIn the vessel harmoniously combined, here together and there disperse.\nThe spices emitting fragrance like wine mingled with sweet breeze.\nOn top are pearls and silver decked with gems,\nWhich the cook delicately fashioned, a gorgeous dish with flavor and perfume.\nThe scattered rue is flowers of turquoise gems, vibrantly green,\nJiggling with murrī and olive oil, ebbing and flowing with sheen.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for bārida of fava beans (bāqillī) by Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake fresh fava beans, snip off both ends (yuqarraḍ), and boil them. Next, discard the jackets and skin the beans. Put them on a platter and pour on them murrī and vinegar which have been boiled with juice of fresh onion, coriander seeds, cumin seeds, cassia, spikenard, cloves, and caraway. \n\tChop some parsley on the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another bārida of fava beans by Ibn Abī Nūḥ al-Kātib:[/b]\nSnip off both ends of fresh fava beans and boil them. Next, discard the jackets and skin the beans. Pound them in a mortar and pestle (hāwan) along with boiled chard leaves, shelled pistachio, walnuts, and almonds. \n\tTake the mixture out of the mortar and fry it in a pan (miqlā) with olive oil, sesame oil, and the chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). While still in the frying pan, add to the mixture black pepper, cloves, spikenard, cassia, coriander seeds, cumin seeds, and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tSpread the mixture on a platter and arrange skinned almonds on the surface so that they look like scattered stars. Color some almonds yellow with saffron and garnish the dish with them. Serve with mustard foam (zabad al-k͟hardal), God willing. \n\tHere is a poem Abū al-Faraj composed. It is on fava beans and picnicking in a pleasure boat (ḥarrāqa): \n[i]Comely-skinned fava beans, musk of the earth, harvested honey, tender and juicy.\nIts luster beautifies the sorest of eyes; so soothing, grievances of the heartsick it heals.\nThe place, so cool, away from the stone-melting heat, delightfully refreshing from the summer gentle drizzle.\nFava beans, like unthreaded necklace or gems in virgins’ hands,\nOr virgin pearls enclosed within folds of shells of emerald.\nHarvested today, not a single day deferred, nor was it from hand to hand transferred.\nSweeter than slumber after a sleepless night, or a promise of a rendezvous fulfilled.\nSweeter still than when a frightened heart is secure.\nI came early even before the songs of birds,\nAnd the sun like a dagger was still unsheathed,\nI came with a group of promising youths:\nNobles, gluttons, opportunists, heirs to thrones, the smart, and the good-for-nothing.\nWe all swooped like a flock of locusts, handsomely clad and most admirably joined,\nGuided by the fragrance fava bean imparted. God bless it,
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Cold dishes (bawārid) of vegetables prepared with yogurt:[/b]\nThe vegetables used are gourd, roots and stalks and leaves of chard, mallows (g͟hasūlā), and purslane (rijla). Whatever vegetables you choose, boil them in water first then chop them and put them in a vessel. Next, add fine-tasting, sweet drained yogurt (s͟hīrāz ṭayyib ʿad͟hb). Add enough to cover the vegetables. Mixing the yogurt with ground mustard seeds and zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) will make it even more delicious. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A cold dish of chard (bāridat silq) by ʿAllūn:[/b]\nTake chard, boil the leaves (waraq), and press out their extra moisture. Pound the leaves with fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb), rue, and a handful of boiled fava beans. When the mixture becomes smooth, add salt, coriander seeds, black pepper, cassia, galangal, and cumin, all pounded. \n\tTake the white head of fresh onion and the green stalks, too. Fresh onion is the best for this dish. Chop it, and fry it in a pan using sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) then add the chard mixture. After you fry them together, spread them on a platter. Sprinkle some chopped rue on the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Truffles (kamʾa):[/b]\nTruffles can be cooked in two delicious ways: mukabbaba mamlūla (cut up into pieces and buried and baked in hot ashes), eaten with coarse salt and black pepper. The other is kamʾa mamlūla (whole truffles buried and baked in hot ashes). These are peeled while still hot, put in a bowl, and bruised with a fihr. They are given a sprinkle of salt and a little black pepper then mixed and eaten. \n\tAl-Dihqān used to wash and peel the truffles and put them in an earthenware pot with a narrow top. If this is not available, substitute it with a new kūz (cup-like vessel with handles). He used to pour on them sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) enough to cover them. Then he would add salt or murrī, as needed, dried or fresh thyme, and river mint (būtanaj nahrī). He would then seal the pot with mud and put it in the tannūr fire for about an hour. When done, it is taken out and served. It will be delicious, God willing. \n\tTruffles are very nice, they can be prepared in many wonderful ways such as baking them whole (s͟hawī) or cutting them up into pieces and grilling them (kabāb). They may be incorporated in all kinds of cooked dishes and used with other ingredients to stuff roasted kids and sheep. They may be cooked with ʿujaj (omelets) or prepared as maqluwwāt (fried) with onion, spices, and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). They may be also be fried as Būrān with olive oil, black pepper, and murrī. It is absolutely wonderful. \n\tThey can also be skewered and grilled as kardanāj (on a rotating spit) or buried in hot ashes (i.e. mamlūl). They may be prepared as muraqqaqāt (pounded and shaped into thin patties). When prepared like this, coriander and cassia are added to the pounded truffles, then the mix is flattened into thin discs, fried in oil, and arranged on a platter. Boiled beans (lūbya maslūqa) are shaped by pressing them by hand into small balls and arranged between the truffle patties then the dish i
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a cold dish of beans (bāridat al-lūbyā):[/b]\nBoil the beans and press out their moisture. Put them in a bowl and pour sweetened mustard (k͟hardal muḥallā) and equal amounts of sweet vinegar (k͟hall ʿad͟hb) and sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Sprinkle a generous amount of ground walnut on it, garnish it with chopped parsley and rue, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another bārida of beans:[/b]\nBoil the beans and press out their moisture. Put them on a platter and pour on them sumac juice, juice of unripe sour grapes (māʾ ḥiṣrim), or lemon juice. You can also sprinkle ground sumac on them. Chop rue on the dish, drizzle it with olive oil , and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bārida of purslane by Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nSoak purslane until it is wet then wash it very well. Put it in a clean pot, add an equal amount of chopped fresh onion (baṣal raṭb), a bunch of cilantro, and fresh rue. Add olive oil, the same amount as that of purslane. Pour a handful (kaff) of water and cook it until done. \n\tAdd pleasant-tasting vinegar (k͟hall ṭayyib), just enough to make it taste good, and a similar amount of fine-tasting murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Of the dry spices, add coriander seeds, black pepper, cassia, ginger, spikenard, cloves and caraway, all ground. \n\tLet the pot simmer for a while (sāʿa, one hour) and when the time comes to put it away from the fire, sprinkle it with a small amount of grape wine. Take the pot away from the fire and ladle the food into dishes. Chop rue on it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Preparing qunnābirī (water moss):[/b]\nPick the tender tips of qunnābirī and spread them in a shaded place for three days until they wilt. Grind sweet salt free of bitterness. Put the qunnābirī in a bowl, sprinkle the salt on it, and rub it into the leaves until you see some juice oozing out of them. At this point, press out the liquid and discard it and put the qunnābirī in a big earthenware jar (ḥubb) in layers. Sprinkle each layer with a mixture of ground salt and a good amount of bruised coriander seeds to allow their flavor to penetrate into the vegetable. Set the jar aside \n\tWhenever you want to eat it, take out the amount you need and put it on a platter. Pour on it vinegar and olive oil and eat it. This is the Christians’ mamqūr dish eaten during Lent. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Preparing simulated rabīt͟hā without rabīt͟hā (shrimp):[/b]\nPick over shelled lentil and finely grind it. Add enough salt to it, and pour water, enough to cover it. Set it aside for a day and a night. \n\tTo serve it, smear some of it on ruqāq (thin and flat bread) with olive oil and thyme. Nobody would guess it is not rabīt͟hā. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ṣaḥnāt (small fish relish) without using fish:[/b]\nTake newly cropped habbat k͟haḍra (green terebinth berries) and pound them until all the seeds (bajam) are completely crushed and they have the consistency of damāg͟h (brain i.e. mushy) . \n\tFinely chop radish, and pound it with the terebinth. Pound into mixture some thyme and salt, as much as needed. Put the mixture in an earthenware jar (jarra) and store it away. Use it whenever needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making milk (laban) without udders (ḍarʿ):[/b]\nPeel off the dark skin of a whole shelled coconut. Chop the nut finely with a knife and put it in a vessel of thin glass (ināʾ qawārīr laṭīf). Pour water on it and rub it with the hand thoroughly until it tastes like milk. \n\tPress down the coconut very hard into a strainer. The resulting liquid will be similar to thick and rich milk. Put it in a container, cover it, and set it aside for a while in a warm place, as you do when you make yogurt. It will develop a sourish taste like yogurt. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making libaʾ without milk:[/b]\nTake s͟hahdānaj (hemp seeds) and finely grind them. Add water to them, and press and mash the mixture well. Then strain it in a fine sieve (munk͟hul s͟haʿr). Strain again through a fine piece of cloth (k͟hirqa raqīqa). \n\tPut the liquid in a pot, cover it, and cook it on a low-heat fire until it thickens. Cool it down to prevent the liquid from further evaporating, which might cause it to scorch. When you take it out of the pot nobody would guess it is not real libaʾ. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Omelet (bujja) without eggs:[/b]\nBoil chickpeas until they become as mushy as bone marrow (muk͟h). Boil some onion and pound it with the chickpeas. Add to the mixture, a small amount of olive oil, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), coriander seeds, black pepper, and māʾ al-ṣamg͟h (gum Arabic dissolved in water). Spread this mixture in a frying pan and cook it with some olive oil until it is done, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kāmak͟h without milk, can be consumed the day it is made:[/b]\nGrind and sift kabk (dry ring cookies), and grind zabīb (raisins) after removing the seeds. \n\tTake spikenard, cloves, and cumin, ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) each. Also take 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) cassia, 4 mit͟hqāls (18 grams) cloves, and 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) black pepper. Pound and sift all these spices. \n\tMix all the ingredients with honey, vinegar, and some murrī (liquid fermented sauce). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for s͟hīrāz (drained yogurt) without milk:[/b]\nRemove the seeds from citron pulp. Pound skinned almonds and add them to the citron pulp. If you like, add to the mixture rue, parsley, and nigella seeds (s͟hūnīz). It will come out like s͟hīrāz. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ṭabāhija (braised dish) of shrimp:[/b]\nClean the shrimp, boil them, and take them out of the water. Gently press out moisture or just be patient and wait until they drain. \n\tPut the shrimp in a pot with chopped onion and fry them in olive oil. Add some dry spices (abāzīr yābisa). When dish is done, sprinkle it lightly (yunaḍḍaḥ) with vinegar, scatter some chopped rue on it, and serve it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for g͟hāmiḍ:[/b]\nClean and boil the shrimp. Arrange them on a silver platter and pour sumac juice and sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) on them to submerge the shrimp then serve the dish. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A shrimp recipe for mag͟hmūma (potpie):[/b]\nClean and boil the shrimp. Put them in a pot along with onion sliced crosswise like dirhams (coins). If you are using carrot and eggplant, then slice them the same way. \n\tArrange the shrimp and vegetables in layers in a pot sprinkling each layer with some hot dry spices (abāzīr yābisa ḥirrīfa). Pour on them vinegar, olive oil, and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Cover them with a piece of flat bread (rag͟hīf) and cook the pot until it is done then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sanbūsaj (filled pastries) of shrimp:[/b]\nClean and boil the shrimp. Pound them with a knife along with boiled taro root (qulqās) if in season and you wish to use it. Sprinkle on the shrimp a small amount of the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and the juice extracted from sliced onion. Sprinkle, as well ground dry spices (abāzīr yābisa) and aromatic spices and herbs (afāwī). Add murrī (liquid fermented sauce). If you like it tart, add sumac juice. \n\tWrap mixture in thin sheets of bread (ruqāq) and make them into sanbūsaj. Fry them in sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and serve them. They are scrumptious. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Shrimp prepared as mamqūr (preserved in vinegar):[/b]\nClean and boil the shrimp then arrange them in a wide-mouthed jar in layers alternating with a mixture of salt, coriander seeds, and chopped parsley. Pour vinegar to submerge them and store the jar away. \n\tWhen needed, take some out and put them on a platter. They are tasty served like this. Alternatively, you might take them out of the vinegar, fry them in fine-tasting olive oil, and pour on them the vinegar they were soused in, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Shrimp prepared as maṣūṣ (cooked in vinegar):[/b]\nClean and boil the shrimp. Put them in a pot and add to them chopped parsley and equal amounts of cilantro and rue. Add vinegar and cook them until they are done. Ladle them into a bowl and serve. Saffron may be used in this dish if desired. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Harīsa recipe (porridge) by ʿAbdūn:[/b]\nCook rice in water until it is almost done. Add boiled leeks that have been shredded into thread-like strings. Add liquid of cooked qurṭum (safflower seeds), and continue simmering until porridge thickens and resembles harīsa. It is a wonderful dish. You might also substitute the dasam (animal grease) with ground sesame seeds and ground almonds. It will come out delicious, too. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making maḍīra (white stew cooked with sour milk):[/b]\nTake flour, whip it with vinegar, and put the mixture in a pot. Instead of meat, use skinned sprouted fava beans (bāqillī manbūt). Cook it the same way you cook maḍīra until it thickens then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟hall wa zayt (vinegar and olive oil):[/b]\nPrepare a deep platter. \n\tIn a big cup (qadaḥ), put 3 raṭls (6 cups) wine vinegar, a piece of ice, and water. Stir the mixture until ice dissolves. Add to the mixture, a lump of sugar, a bit of salt, and dry well-leavened white kabk. Stir the mixture with a spoon. Take the kabk out, put it on the platter, and pour the remaining liquid in the cup over it. \n\tPour olive oil over it, and chop on it pulp of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), fresh thyme leaves, pungent (ḥirrīf) fresh basil (bād͟hārūj), and a little salt. \n\tServe the dish, God willing, with hot roasted pullets. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe by Ibn ʿAlyūn:[/b]\nTake a crusty round bread made with fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Make slashes on the top crust with a knife, pour on it some fresh juice of sour unripe grapes, and chill with ice. When the bread is saturated, flip it on the other side and do the same thing. Put the bread on a big platter. \n\tTake 20 almonds, skinned and ground, mix them with fresh juice of sour grapes, and add olive oil to them. Pour the mixture all over the bread. \n\tSpread on the bread, finely shredded breasts of roasted pullets, chopped pulp of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), and basil (bād͟hārūj). Chill the bread with ice. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe:[/b]\nCut round bread made with fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) into small pieces. Pour on it a mixture of vinegar colored with saffron, a lump of sugar, cassia, asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), and pounded dried thyme. Shred breast of roasted chicken on it, pour some olive oil, and set it aside to let the bread absorb the moisture. \n\tSpread on the bread pulp of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), and basil (bād͟harūj), all chopped. Give it a sprinkle of salt and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Nabatean k͟hall wa zayt (vinegar and oil):[/b]\nPut wine vinegar in a vessel and add what equals half of its amount ground sugar. Stir in a little salt. \n\tIn another container, cut bread into pieces, pour water on it, set it aside for a while (sāʿa, one hour) and then drain it. Chop on the bread some pulp of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), a small amount of the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), sharp cheese (jubn ḥirrīf), naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), tarragon, parsley, thyme, and basil (bād͟harūj). Mix well. \n\tPour enough of the vinegar-sugar mixture all over the bread to submerge it. Drizzle as well 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) all over the bread. \n\tArrange on top of the bread some small and smooth cucumbers sliced like dirhams (coins). Spread on top some crushed ice. Using your fingertips, sprinkle the dish (yuras͟h) with rose water syrup (jullāb) mixed with a small amount of vinegar. \n\tIt will be a fabulous dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for māʾ wa milḥ of game meat (laḥm al-waḥs͟h) by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nTake the best parts of game meat such as the top back (sanām) and navel (surra). Cut the meat into big chunks and put it in a pot. Pour water on it and let it boil until it becomes firm. Take the meat out and put it in cold water. Discard water in which it boiled. \n\tDrain the meat pieces very well and return them to the pot. Pour water and sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). Add as well whole and chopped onions, sticks of galangal and cassia, a bunch of dill, and a handful of salt. Let the meat cook, and when it is done, add dry spices such as ground coriander seeds, black pepper, cumin, and ginger. Put them while the meat is still in the pot. \n\tTo serve, pour the broth into a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya kabīra) and arrange meat pieces in it. Garnish the dish with whatever varieties of large sausages (maḥās͟hī) you wish. Chop some rue on it and present it with sauce (ṣibāg͟h) recipe at end of chapter, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for māʾ wa milḥ cooked K͟hurāsānī way:[/b]\nTake big chunks of rump (uṣūl al-afk͟hād͟h) and tenderloin (bis͟ht). It may be from game meat or sheep. Boil the meat chunks in a big pot then discard the water. Cut up the meat into smaller pieces. \n\tReturn the meat to the pot and add 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), sweet salt, galangal, cassia, ginger, dill, chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), and whole skinned onions. Add water to the pot and let it boil. \n\tAdd to the pot, qibba (omasum tripe) which has been stuffed with pounded meat and other ingredients. Continue boiling until the tripe is completely cooked. \n\tTake the cooked meat out of the pot, put it on k͟hiwān (low board or table), and cut it into suitable portions. Arrange them in a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya) taking care not to crowd its edges with meat. Do not use any of the meat broth. Next, put the qibba in the middle, cut it open, and sprinkle it with ground cassia. With your cupped hand, sprinkle it lightly with a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Give it a sprinkle of pungent, white mustard sauce. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for qibba (stuffed omasum tripe):[/b]\nPound together tender meat, the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), and cilantro. Sprinkle dried and pounded coriander seeds, black pepper, and cassia on them. Add to the mixture, a small amount of chopped tender leek leaves (kurrāt͟h baql) and a small amount of rice. \n\tFill the omasum tripe (qibba) very well with the stuffing, and sew it closed with twigs of k͟hilāf (willow). If you like, add to the filling finely minced liver. \n\tWhen stuffed tripe is ready add it to the pot in which māʾ wa malḥ is cooking. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Māʾ wa milḥ cooked with innards (buṭūn) by Abū Samīn:[/b]\nTake whatever you may from buṭūn of kids only. Scrape them clean and wash them thoroughly using salt and parsley. Wrap the pieces around tallow of kidneys and caul fat (t͟harb), press out their moisture, and put them in a pot. Pour enough water to cover them. Add sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), a little bit of salt, and just one piece of galangal. \n\tLet the pot simmer until the meat pieces are cooked. Take them out of the pot and arrange them in a bowl (g͟huḍāra). Immediately, dust the dish with ground cassia and sprinkle it with onion juice. It is fantastic (g͟hāya min al-g͟hāyāt). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Māʾ wa milḥ of gazelle meat (laḥm g͟hazāl):[/b]\nCut gazelle meat into big chunks. Put them in a pot and add to them a lot of salt, soaked chickpeas, galangal, and cassia. Add as well sprigs of dill (ʿīdān s͟habat), black pepper, round onions, and ½ usukurruja (¼ cup) olive oil. Pour enough water to cover the ingredients in the pot and let it cook until the meat is done. \n\tBreak barāzīd͟haj bread into small pieces in a bowl, and ladle on it the meat and its broth. Pour on the dish some liquid mustard (māʾ k͟hardal) and sour juice of unripe grapes (māʾ ḥiṣrim) then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sauce (ṣibāg͟h) served with māʾ wa milḥ:[/b]\nTake 1 part ground walnut; 1 part ground almonds; 3 parts liquid of ground zabīb (raisins), which have been steeped in vinegar; 2 parts of mustard sauce made with raw seeds (k͟hardal maʿmūl fujj); and 1 part aged murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Add as well ½ part sugar, and ½ part good quality rose water if you wish. Beat together all these ingredients. \n\tTo use, pour sauce on the māʾ wa milḥ dish after you sprinkle some ground cassia on it. Alternatively, you may serve it separately as a condiment (ṣibāg͟h) in a small bowl (uskurruja). \n\tʿAbdullāh bin Ṭāhir composed these verses on māʾ wa milḥ: \n[i]Māʾ wa milḥ has a distinguished taste of its own. It far surpasses maḍīra and sikbāja dishes.\nChoice cuts of loins of wild ass in it and sundry pieces of game meat, lean and fatty.\nPut in a bowl with meat of wild calf surrounded, with francolin interspersed,\nAnd in the midst a stuffed tripe sits. Better than any sikbāja and zirbāja dishes.\nIt comforts my heart to see it with sauce furnished. Most nourishing for the tired and the famished.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]The sikbāj recipe, Bidʿa made for al-Amīn:[/b]\nTake delicious beef cuts such as bāṭina (innards), sanām (top back), quṣayrā (lower neck), bawāṭin al-afk͟hād͟h (inner thighs), and matn (shoulder). \n\tTake all the innards—ʿirq (diaphragm, skirt steak), dawwāra (small intestines), mibʿar (large intestines), rummāna (omasum tripe), and banāt al-laban (coiled part of small intestines). However, use none of the liver and spleen. \n\tAll the aforementioned meats are to be washed thoroughly several times in salted water and parsley. Put them in a big pot that has been fumigated with aloe wood. Pour undiluted vinegar to cover them all and some additional water. Add 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), a little salt, a bunch of rue, a bunch of parsley, and another of cilantro. \n\tWhen the pot comes to a boil, take a skinned kid (maslūk͟h), cut it up into big chunks, and add it to the pot. \n\tWhen the pot boils twice, take a whole lamb that has been scalded and cleaned, (samīṭ) and add it to the pot. Let it lie on its chest, with the fore and hind legs tucked underneath it (bārik kneeling position). Add as well 3 excellent quality chickens (dajāj fāyiq), 5 plump young fowls (firāk͟h), and 5 pullets (farārīj). Add them one after the other. Then choose some small birds such as quails (sammān) and sparrows (ʿaṣāfīr), and add as many of these as the pot can hold. \n\tWhen all the meats are cooked, add a handful of salt and a handful of ground coriander seeds. Add as well eggplant that has been peeled and boiled in vinegar in a separate pot along with carrots and onion. Finally after you stop feeding the fire, add 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) saffron if it can take that much. Otherwise, use half this amount. Then keep the pot on the remaining heat and wait until it settles (tahdaʾ) and stops bubbling. \n\tWhen the pot reaches this stage, take the deepest, largest, and widest bowl available. Put in
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sikbāj:[/b]\nTake choice cuts of beef such as bāṭina (innards), sanām (top back), quṣayrā (lower neck), or the inner thighs (bawāṭin al-afk͟hād͟h), and shoulders (matn). Take all the innards such as ʿurūq (diaphragm, skirt steaks), dawwāra (small intestines), mibʿar (large intestines), rummāna (omasum), banāt al-laban (the coiled part of small intestines). \n\tPut all these meats in a soapstone pot (burma) after you wash them and cut them into equal parts and boil them in wine vinegar and water. When they are almost done, take them out and put them on a plate. \n\tChoose some excellent plump chickens, clean them, and put them in the pot with a fresh batch of wine vinegar, return the almostcooked meat, and let them cook. \n\tWhen the chicken is done, add 5 dirhams (15 grams) coriander seeds, 1 dirham (3 grams) ginger, 3 dirhams (9 grams) saffron, and 2 dirhams (6 grams) each of black pepper, parsley, and rue. \n\tCut bread into s͟hawābīr (triangles). Ladle enough broth for the bread to sop it. Arrange the meat and chicken in an organized manner. Garnish it with bazmāward (slices of rolled sandwiches), ṭardīn (thin meat patties), laqāniq (sausages of small intestines), maḥās͟hī (very large sausages of lower intestines), and mabāʿir (sausages of large intestines). Scatter pieces of chopped cheese all over it and serve it with mustard, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sikbāj with musk (misk) by al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nTake the best of innards (buṭūn) and cut them as you wish. Put them in a clean pot and let them boil. Take them out of the pot before they are fully cooked and spread them on a tray. \n\tNow take other meat, cut it into pieces, put it in a pot, and let it cook. When the meat comes to a boil, take it out and spread it on a tray. Let it cool. \n\tTake good quality wine vinegar and pour it into a pot. Add a small amount of water so that the dish does not taste too sour. If the vinegar is weak, then do not dilute it. When it comes to a boil, add the meat to it. Wash the set aside innards and add them to the pot, as well. \n\tAdd watercress (jirjīr), parsley, onion, and a little salt. Add the onion tied (marbūṭ) in a bundle. Add as well coriander seeds, black pepper, and cumin, all ground. \n\tWhen the meat is almost done, take it out. Strain the broth using a clean, tightly woven piece of fabric (k͟hirqa safīqa) to get rid of all spice particles. Return the strained broth to the pot along with the meat. Let it cook until the meat is done. Then add to the pot saffron, and 1 qīrāṭ (¼ gram) musk. If the stew comes out a little too sour, then add as much sugar as needed to balance its taste. \n\tCut the bread into pieces in a bowl and ladle the broth on it. Arrange the meat as you do in the rest of sikbāj dishes. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mulabbaqa (soft t͟harīda saturated in fat):[/b]\nTake pith of bread which has been baked in the tannūr and pith of bread baked in the brick oven (aqrāṣ al-furn). Let the pith be a little dry and stale. Crush it between the fingers and sift it in a sieve. Put it in a pot and pour on it fat from the sikbāj stew (dasam). Start the fire underneath the pot and slowly add a small amount of sesame oil (s͟hayraj). However, if there is enough of the sikbāj fat in it, there is no need to add the extra sesame oil. \n\tAdd to the pot, a bit of sugar, cassia, spikenard, ginger, and saffron, all ground. \n\tBoil some of the sikbāj broth, and pour it on the breadcrumbs in the pot. Keep on stirring until the mixture is saturated and thickened. \n\tLadle the bread into a bowl, and arrange the meat pieces around it along with the stuffed sausages. Garnish it with herbs and vegetables, scatter some chopped rue and parsley all over it, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for rice porridge (harīsat al-aruzz):[/b]\nWash fat meat and put it in a pot. Pour water on it and add some salt. Let it cook until meat disintegrates and falls off the bones. Put the pot off the heat. Take meat out of the pot and pound it in a mortar and pestle (hāwan) if it is still chunky. \n\tNext, pick over white rice and wash it three times. Pour strained milk on the meat broth and bring it to a boil. Add the rice and continue cooking until it is done. Return the pounded meat and keep on stirring until rice grains are crushed. Pour into it butter (zubd), clarified butter (samn), a mixture of equal parts of rendered fat (duhn maslūʾ) and sesame oil (s͟hayraj), or milk (laban). \n\tBeat the mixture continuously until it is completely crushed. Keep on stirring and beating until it looks like nāṭif thick and chewy nougat and meat looks like threads integrated into the rice. \n\tServe the porridge with a bowlful (uskurruja) of murrī (liquid fermented sauce), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for harīsa made with bread:[/b]\nTake three fatty chickens, which you scald, clean, and grill. While the chickens are grilling, put underneath them a container to receive all the fat drippings. \n\tShred the meat of the breasts into thin threads and put it in a clean pot. Pour on it ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil or sesame oil and add enough water to cover the shredded chicken. Let the pot cook until most of the moisture evaporates. Add sifted pith of white fine bread (k͟hubz samīd͟h) it. \n\tNow, let there be a vessel filled with milk (laban ḥalīb) next to you. Pour the contents of the container that received the chicken drippings into the pot. Keep on cooking and stirring it, adding of the milk besides you whenever needed to replenish the evaporated liquid. Continue doing this until the porridge becomes thick in consistency, thicker than the usual harīsa made with wheat. \n\tLadle the porridge into a bowl and serve it with Nabatean murrī, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Harīsa with tripe (kurūs͟h) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nWash and scald the tripe, cut it into pieces, and wash it repeatedly until it is very clean. Boil it the way you boil the meat then shred it into thin threads, the thinnest you can get them. \n\tReturn the shredded tripe to the pot and pour enough milk to cover it. Add cassia and galangal, a piece each. Add as well melted chicken fat and ground rice. Stir the porridge until it thickens. Season it with enough salt and moisten it with kidney tallow, which has been rendered in a frying pan. \n\tLadle the porridge into a big serving bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and sprinkle it with a small amount of ground cassia. Eat it with murrī (liquid fermented sauce), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Harīsa kānūniyya (cooked on a brazier), can be eaten at the place where it is cooked. Abū Samīn used to make it for al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nShred finely roasted chicken breasts. Boil together milk and ground rice until cooked. Add the shredded chicken to the pot and beat the mixture very well. Beat into it strained melted chicken fat. Add pure salt as needed and continue beating the porridge. \n\tLadle it into a bowl and serve it with murrī (liquid fermented sauce), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for harīsa kānūniyya (cooked on a brazier):[/b]\nCombine in a clean pot, meat and hulled and crushed wheat after washing both of them. Add water to pot, and put it on the daykadān (trivet), as you do when you put pots in the tannūr. Continue cooking until all the ingredients fall apart (yataharraʾ). Beat the porridge while the pot is still cooking on the trivet until it is thick. Alternatively, you may cook the meat and wheat separately then combine them. You may pound the meat in a stone mortar (ḥajar) after cooking it, mix it with the wheat then beat them together. Alternatively, half the amount of grains used may be wheat and the other half rice. Whether the rice used is whole or ground, it will certainly enhance the flavor of the milk which is added after the grains and meat are cooked, as in the above recipe. The most delicious fats used in making this porridge are butter and rendered fat of ducks and chicken. Indeed, it will make it comparable to the food of notables (ṭabām al-surāt). Equally delicious will be making it with chicken breasts and bread pith. Moreover, it can be made with chicken breasts, rice, milk, and sugar. This is called muhallabiyya. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟hayṭiyya (porridge with threadlike meat-shreds):[/b]\nChoose fatty meat from the ribs (aḍlāb), rump (abjāz), and sheep’s tail (alya). Cut them into smaller pieces and put them in a clean pot. Add 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) fine-tasting olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and pour enough water to cover the meat. Add a stick of cassia and a piece of galangal and let the pot boil until meat is almost done. Add hulled wheat that has been cracked and boiled separately, and let the pot boil once or twice. Add rice that has been washed repeatedly and dried in a piece of cloth. Do not stir the pot at this point. \n\tWhen the pot gets dry, replenish the liquid with milk, and let it cook under slow fire. Keep on replenishing the milk as needed, and continue cooking under low heat until enough milk is added, and the porridge is fully cooked. Add salt and stir the pot gently. \n\tFor best results, at the early stage of cooking the porridge keep on skimming the froth from the surface whenever it shows up to ensure a porridge clean of any undesirable particles of scum. \n\tLadle the porridge into a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and put a small bowl (auskurruja) of murrī in the middle, God willing. \n\tAbū al-ʿAbbās al-Adīb recited to me this poem on harīsa: \n[i]The most delicious food one may ever eat when April the arrival of summer heralds,\nAnd when kids and lamb are at their best, is harīsa made by niswān (women).\nWith skilled hands, tastiest harīsa they make, birds and lamb combining.\nFats and oils are added to pot, and meat and tail fat and tallow.\nThen geese and quails and fair wheat and grass pea follow.\nNext, milk and rice, which the miller perfectly ground,\nAnd salt and galangal. It wearied the hands that beat and stirred it.\nLike the shining constellations in the sky, it puts all other dishes to shame,\nAs it comes carried by the slave boys, embraced by bowl and tray,\nAbove it is a bamboo vault, which roof and walls
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for aruzziyya sād͟haja (simple rice porridge) by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nClean lamb (laḥm ḥaml) and put it in a pot. Add a few drops of olive oil, a stick of cassia, a piece of galangal, and a handful of salt, or as needed. Add water and cook the pot until meat is done. While cooking you need to remove the scum as it comes up so that nothing remains of it. \n\tNow take the rice, wash it several times until it is clean and then put it in the center of the pot, and cook it under a slow fire (nār layyina). Add the milk gradually and as needed until the porridge is thickened and fully cooked. Let it settle for a while and ladle it into a clean ṣaḥfa (big, wide, shallow bowl). Serve it with a small bowl (uskurruja) of murrī (liquid fermented sauce) put in the center of the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Simple aruzziyya with milk by al-Mutawakkil:[/b]\nPut clean milk in a clean pot and let it slightly boil with cassia and galangal sticks. Discard the cassia and galangal and add rice, which has been picked over and washed very well. Let it cook until completely done. Then stir the porridge vigorously to let the rice disintegrate into a mush. Add salt as needed. \n\tContinue cooking, adding milk whenever it gets dry. Keep on doing this until the porridge thickens and absorbs enough milk and cannot take in any more. Let it simmer and thicken on slow-burning coals (jamr hādī). \n\tIf you wish, add what equals a quarter of its amount white sugar, the way the Persians used to do. If you choose to add the sugar, then add with it fresh and sweet clarified butter. Do this gradually until the porridge takes enough of the butter and thickens. When it is no longer boiling, take it off the heat and ladle it into a bowl, God willing. \n\tAl-Ḥāfiẓ recited to me these lines on aruzziyya. He imitates (yubāriḍ) a poem Ibn al-Mahdī composed on s͟haljamiyya (turnip stew), \n[i]What a wonderful aruzziyya, cooked to perfection, like a full moon in the middle of the sky.\nPurer than the doubly condensed snow that the winds and dew tinted.\nAs white as a large pure pearl spread in a bowl.\nIt dazzles the eyes with its sheen. Behold moonlight even before the evening is seen.\nThe sugar on its sides, like lustrous light projected from the skies.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for rice with milk (aruzz bi-laban) by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nWash the rice and let it soak in milk overnight. Put water in a ṭinjīr (large copper pot) or a regular pot (qidr), according to your estimate, the amount should be enough to cover the rice or a little less. Add fat to water. It can be clarified butter from cows milk, almond oil, or fresh sesame oil. Let the pot boil once. \n\tAdd the soaked rice and a suitable amount of honey. Wait until it is almost cooked then start adding milk gradually until rice is fully cooked and it has absorbed all the milk. Take the pot away from the fire. \n\tIt would be even more delicious if you substitute honey with ground white sugar. Besides, you need to soak the rice in fresh milk that has just been milked. Soaking the rice overnight in milk can only be done in cold weather. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Aruzziyya by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake chunks of lean rump and chunks of sheep’s tail fat. Slice them thinly and smoke them until meat looks brown (aḥmar, literally red). Heat some olive oil in a pot and fry the meat slices in it until done. Sprinkle them with a little salt and water, but avoid using murrī (liquid fermented sauce) lest it should discolor the dish. \n\tTake a big pot, fill it up to its half with milk, , and bring it to a boil. Add galangal and cinnamon, a stick each. Add salt as needed. \n\tNow take some rice, wash it very well, and add it to the milk. When it is done and thickened, add the prepared meat slices with the oil in which it was fried. \n\tStir the rice very well and serve it, God willing. \n\tHere is a poem by Ibrāhīm on this dish: \n[i]Aruzza with milk of any blemishes free.\nMade simple with one kind of grains, drowned in fat.\nHow marvelous is the meat in it, with fat almost as much as the meat.\nThe meat slices like fresh dates, moist and tender. How pretty in the huge bowl it looks.\nA closer regard will make you think it is the full moon but blemish free.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]ﺕﺎﺜﻠﺜﳌﺍ ﺕﺎﻴﻄﻨﳊﺍ ﻞﻤﻋ ﰲ:[/b]\nCook lean and fatty meat with hulled wheat (qamḥ maqs͟hūr) and water until the grains are cooked. However, do not let it get to the point where the wheat falls apart and gets mushy. Add bruised (mas͟hdūk͟h) pieces of cassia and galangal to the pot. \n\tYou may substitute white wheat with green wheat (qamḥ ak͟hḍar farīk). You may pour into it some milk. In fact, you can use milk with the wheat we mentioned first, add as much as it needs. If wished, you can sweeten the dish with sugar, but not much. [b]Another recipe for t͟hulāt͟hiyya:[/b]\nDo it the same way as above but you need to make sure that you do use the cassia and galangal here. For this dish use rice, lentil, and white beans. Let the lentil be the least amount added of the grains and legumes. If wished, add bruised chickpeas (ḥimmaṣ marḍūḍ). Let the amount be equal to that of lentil. \n\tAfter you ladle it into a platter, pour over it some heated fat (duhn maqlū), and arrange around it thin flat breads (ruqāq). Let some be spread flat (mans͟hūr), and others rolled up (malfūf). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another t͟hulāt͟hiyya made with rice and cooked in the tannūr (aruzziyya tannūriyya):[/b]\nIt can be made with rice only, with or without browned onion slices. It can also be made with red or white beans. It should be of medium consistency, thick but still have some liquid (maraq) in it, and the grains themselves should not stick to each other. It is also cooked with extremities (aṭrāf). \n\tThis dish is to be further cooked in the tannūr with a whole kid or fat lamb suspended above it and roasted. Instead of a whole lamb, a whole side of ribs (janb) or a whole chicken may be used. You can cover the dish with ruqāqa (thin flat bread) and you may spread some ʿuṣbān all over the top so that their fat may melt down into the cooking dish. \n\tWhen all liquid is absorbed and the suspended meat is roasted, serve this dry dish (nās͟hif) in a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and arrange the ʿuṣbān around it. As for the roasted sides, slice through each two ribs and spread them around the dish. You may serve the roasted meat separately and not in the ṭayfūriyya itself, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]ﺕﺎﻴﺒﻧﺮﻜﻟﺍﻭ ﺕﺎﺧﺎﻧﺎﺒﺳﻻﺍ ﻞﻤﻋ ﰲ:[/b]\nIsbanāk͟hiyyāt (spinach dishes) and kurunbiyyāt (cabbage dishes) are cooked the same way. The only difference is the vegetable used. Whichever vegetable you choose, start by cleaning it of any unwanted weeds, and cutting off and discarding roots and stalks. Boil it in water until almost cooked, take it out, and put it in cold water. \n\tNow cut medium-size pieces of meat taken from aṭrāf al-mulḥāʾ (from the backbone area), the first few ribs (awāʾil al-aḍlāʿ), and some fatty cuts of meat. Put them in a clean pot and add to them chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), a few drops of sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), and galangal and cassia, a stick each. Sweat the meat until all moisture evaporates. Then pour water over it, enough to cover, and let it boil,. Skim the froth and impurities as they come up. \n\tWhen meat is cooked, wash for it some rice, and add it to the pot along with salt as needed, and a little black pepper. Add the vegetables, let the pot cook for a short while then serve the dish. \n\tIf you like, add to the pot while still cooking whole carrots. Take them out when cooking is done, slice them into rounds like darāhim (coins), and arrange them on the ladled out dish. Serve it with murrī, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for s͟haljamiyya (turnip dish) by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nChoose fatty pieces of meat, large and small intestines, and skirt steak (ʿirq al-kars͟h). Clean them and cook them with some white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and water. \n\tWhen meat is almost done, add turnip cut into large pieces, and skinned whole onions. When turnip and onion are cooked, take them out of the pot and crush them into fine mush in a stone mortar along with ¼ ūqiyya (7½ grams) coriander seeds, ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) cumin, and 3 dirhams (9 grams) black pepper, all ground. Return the turnip mix into the pot, let it simmer gently on the fire, and serve it. \n\tYou may cook the dish with gourd and onion when turnip is not in season. You just cook them, crush them, and add the spices. This will be a good substitute for turnips, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another s͟haljamiyya recipe also by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nCut the meat into pieces, as big as a fist each, and let it be marbled meat (laḥm mujazzaʿ). Clean it and put it in a pot with chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), bruised chickpeas, and galangal and cinnamon, a stick each. Add as well, chopped cilantro, salt, olive oil, and water enough to cover the meat. Let the pot cook until meat is almost done. \n\tPeel whole turnips and boil them in hot water in another pot. Take them out and let them cool down. Slice some of the turnips into rounds, and set them aside. Mash the rest of the turnips in a stone mortar with coriander seeds, ground skinned almonds, and a small amount of soaked chickpeas. Return the crushed turnip mixture into the pot. \n\tSoak some rice and set it aside. \n\tPound lean meat and the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) in a stone mortar. Add to the meat, a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce), coriander seeds, black pepper, cassia, and cumin all ground. Shape the meat into balls (yukabbab), and take them closer to the cooking pot. When it starts boiling, add the meatballs, and stir. When they are almost done, add to the pot some milk, and continue cooking until everything in it is fully cooked. \n\tAdd the set-aside turnip slices and soaked rice to the pot. Continue cooking until everything is fully cooked. Season the pot with ground cassia, black pepper, and spikenard then put it away from heat. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another s͟haljamiyya by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake breasts of chicken or any other birds, slice them thinly, and put them in a pot with a lot of fat. Pour enough water to cover the meat, bring the pot to a boil, and skim the froth. Add chickpeas, olive oil, and chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). When meat is done, sprinkle black pepper, and cumin on it. \n\tBoil some turnips then mash them very well and strain them in a sieve. Add them to the pot. \n\tTake skinned almonds and pound them in a stone mortar very well along with a piece of cheese. Break 5 eggs and add the egg whites only to the almond mixture. Continue pounding until mixture is soft. Add it to the pot of turnips. \n\tIf you have used milk in cooking the turnips, add a little spikenard. Let the pot simmer gently in its own heat until it stops bubbling. Serve the dish with mustard. \n\tIbn al-Mahdī composed a poem on this dish. It is the same poem which al-Ḥāfiẓ imitated (bāraḍa) in his “Aruzziyya”: \n[i]A deep bowl of s͟haljamiyya did strike me with its luster.\nDispersed on it are dirhams of turnip, which the payday overseer will not muster.\nLike a splendid full moon, decked with the stars of the night.\nIt looks as if of silver ‘tis made, cast in light.\nHaving had its fill of milk, it now looks as if wearing a mask so bright.\nIf fasting believers should see it, they will indeed, every single evening hurry up to it.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for Isḥāqiyya:[/b]\nChoose the fattest meat you can get from the lower loins, sides, and ribs. Cut them into small chunks, wash them, and put them in a clean pot.
