Add 2 dirhams (1 teaspoon) olive oil, a stick of galangal, and a stick of cassia. Add as well 1 dirham (3 grams) white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) chopped. \n\tSweat the meat until all moisture evaporates. After that, pour enough water to cover it by half. When the meat is half done, add white beans that have been gleaned of all red or black ones. The meat and the beans should both be done at the same time. \n\tAdd rice to the pot. The amount should be one and half times more than the beans. Add milk enough to cover the contents of the pot. Replenish the milk whenever you notice the pot is drying out. Do this until the dish has enough milk and thickens. While the pot is cooking, keep stirring it frequently and watching it lest it should scorch. \n\tFinally, pour into the pot 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) rendered fat of sheep’s tail and stir it. Add salt as needed. Remove the fire from underneath the pot and wait until it is no longer simmering and bubbling. Ladle it into bowls and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for niḥrīriyya (the crafty dish):[/b]\nThis dish is done exactly like the previous one except that you substitute the beans with lentils that have been picked over, skinned, and pulverized. Add washed rice, the amount of which is one and a half times more than the lentils, or whatever you think is suitable. \n\tPrepare the dish as you did with the other one above, but make sure to use the rendered fat and the murrī (liquid fermented sauce). When you serve it, everybody would believe it to be jullubāniyya (dish of grass pea). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for d͟hājibrija, Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī made for al-Muʿtaṣim:[/b]\nTake 3 raṭls (3 pounds) of scalded (masmūṭ) lamb, and put it in a pot. Pour on it 3 ūqiyyas (1/3 cup) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Add a piece of galangal, 1 raṭl (1 pound) whole skinned onions, 2 dirhams (6 grams) andarānī salt, and whatever the palm and the fingers can hold of chopped cilantro. Add water enough to cover all the ingredients by four fingers’ width. \n\tLet the pot boil until the onions are almost done, then take them out and set them aside. \n\tPour into the pot 1 raṭl (2 cups) wine vinegar and give it a stir. Let the meat cook until it is done or almost done. Add some seasonal vegetables (baql al-zamān). They can be a bunch of leeks (kurrāt͟h) and carrots in winter, or eggplant and gourd in the summer. Cover the pot, and continue cooking. \n\tNow crush the set aside onion with 5 dirhams (15 grams) coriander eeds, ½ dirham (1½ grams) black pepper, and 5 dirhams (15 grams) caraway seeds. Put mixture in a bowl and pour on it, 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and a small amount of the stew liquid. Stir mixture very well, return it to the simmering pot, and continue cooking. \n\tWhen stew is done, put the pot away from the fire immediately while it is still boiling hot. Add a small amount of chopped cilantro and cover it with the lid. When it stops simmering and bubbling, ladle the stew and serve it, God willing. \n\tI recited a poem Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī composed on this dish: \n[i]The cook approached with a bowl, as round as the rising sun,\nFilled with zībrāja, well done and clean, by an expert dexterously ladled.\nSkillfully decked with what it needs, like a necklace a goldsmith threaded with gems.\nPearls of skinned onion alternating with emerald gourd, immaculate and pure.\nDelicate carrots in it, too, like sheets of the purest gold of girdles.\nColored with saffron, easily mistaken 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Zīrbāja (delicate bird stew) by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nTake some pullets, scald them to remove feathers, and clean them. Put them in a pot and pour fresh water, zayt anfāq (olive oil of unripe olives), bruised and soaked chickpeas, mustard seeds, salt, and onion. \n\tWhen pot boils, add vinegar, leeks (kurrāt͟h), and cilantro. Continue cooking until meat is done. Cut the heat from the pot, let it rest then color the stew with saffron. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]White zīrbāja (delicate bird stew) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nChoose a plump chicken, disjoint and clean it, and put it in a clean pot. Pour on it ½ raṭl (1 cup) fresh water, ½ ūqiyya (1 tablespoon) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), and a small amount of chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). \n\tBring the pot to a boil then pour on it ½ raṭl (1 cup) strained white vinegar. Add 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) white sugar, 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) skinned almonds, and 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) rose water. In a piece of thin fabric, tie whole black peppercorns, cassia, and ginger. This is done so that the spices do not discolor the stew. \n\tLet the pot simmer for a little while until stew thickens. After you set it aside to rest, ladle it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Green zīrbāja (delicate bird stew) by Abū Samīn:[/b]\nChoose meat from below the ribs and cut it into medium pieces. Scald and clean a chicken; discard the head, neck, and entrails; and quarter it. Put both meats in a clean pot and pour on them water and rose water, enough to cover the meat. Add as well whole skinned onions. Light a slow fire (nār layyina) underneath the pot and let it cook. \n\tNow take fresh parsley, a sprig of rue, and a handful of shelled pistachio. Crush them all together thoroughly and add them to the pot along with a little salt or māʾ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid fermented sauce). Add as well coriander seeds, black pepper, and cassia, all ground. \n\tWipe clean the inner sides of the pot to remove all particles that might have stuck to the sides while cooking and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Zīrbāja (delicate bird stew) with quince (safarjal) by Ibn al-Mahdī. He used to call it muṣliḥat al-maʿida (the stomach fixer) and burmat al-maʿida (soapstone pot of the stomach):[/b]\n\n\tDisjoint plump pullets and put them in a clean pot along with a piece of galangal, a handful of skinned soaked chickpeas, 1 raṭl (1 pound) whole skinned onions, and a little salt. Pour water enough to cover the meat and add 3 ūqiyyas (1/3 cup) olive oil. Let the pot cook on fire until onions are done. Take out all onions and discard them. \n\tPour into the pot ¼ raṭl (½ cup) vinegar and let it boil until vinegar is cooked. Add ½ raṭl (1 cup) quince juice freshly pressed. Add as well ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) coriander seeds, ½ dirham (1½ grams) black pepper, ½ dirham (1½ grams) spikenard, 3 dirhams (9 grams) cumin, and 20 dirhams (2 ounces) breadcrumbs. Put the pot away from heat and wipe clean the inner sides of the pot. Wait until it rests and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Zīrbāja k͟hamīriyya (delicate bird stew made with bread yeast) of young pigeons by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nChoose 4 young plump pigeons, old enough to fly (nawāhiḍ). Split them in halves and wash them thoroughly. Put them in a pot along with a handful of skinned soaked chickpeas, a little salt, ½ raṭl (½ pound) chopped onion, , a bunch of chopped cilantro, ½ raṭl (1 cup) fresh sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt raṭb ʿad͟hb), and enough water to cover the birds. Let the pot cook until meat is half done. \n\tPour into the pot, 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) good quality wine vinegar, ground coriander seeds, and ¼ raṭl (½ cup) murrī (liquid fermented sauce), let it be whitish in hue. \n\tNow take dough yeast (k͟hamīr) made of samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), the size of two walnuts. The yeast should have been fermenting for days. Mix and blend it (yumras) with 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) nabīd͟h rayḥānī. Mix with it black pepper, dār fulful (long pepper), cassia, and ginger, ½ dirham (1½ grams) each. Add as well 2 dirhams (6 grams) cumin. Beat all these ingredients very well together and add them to the pot. \n\tContinue cooking until the fermented dough is done. Put the pot away from heat and cover it tightly with a lid or something to prevent any steam from escaping the pot until the time you need to serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]White zīrbāja (delicate bird stew) with quince by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nDisjoint two chickens and put them in a pot. Add to them chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and bruised chickpeas. \n\tIn another pot, cook quince in water and take it out when it is cooked. Crush it and press it through a sieve. \n\tAdd to the cooking pot, black pepper, coriander seeds, cassia, a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and vinegar. Add as well the mashed quince along with finely chopped naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) and tarragon. \n\tYou can ladle the dish after you let the pot boil first then simmer and rest. You should have prepared as well small and big sausages, all cooked and ready. To serve the dish, ladle the stew on broken pieces of bread put in a bowl and arrange the sausages around it. \n\tIf the stew turns out to be too sour for your taste, fix it with a little sugar. However, you need to add it at the point when you add the quince and while the pot is still boiling, that is, before you let it simmer and rest (qabla taskīnihā). Serve it as described earlier, God willing. \n\tHere is a poem by al-Ḥāfiẓ on zīrbāja (delicate bird stew): \n[i] Zīrbāja is a unique dish, which of all the living creatures only the smartest relish.\nLanguishing in yellow, like flowers and sprouting grass in spring,\nHaving had its fill of saffron crushed. Free of flaws and blemish.\nIt comes in a bowl of silver shining white, as if from the light of the moon stealing.\nApproaching thus brightly colored, all you see is silver with gold stuffed.\nChicks are in it and almonds, sugar, saffron, and vinegar lusciously sweet,\nWith rose water and spices. Then fire and fuel took care of it and cooked.\nIf wished, plump chicken instead you use, and it will in the pot a wonder be.\nOnly a deft hand, cordial and generous, surpassing others, can cook this dish.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe of ḥummāḍiyya (stew soured with citron pulp) by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nCut meat into medium-size pieces. Put it in a pot, and pour on it water enough to cover it. Add chopped onion and cilantro, zayt anfāq (olive oil from unripe olives), crushed chickpeas, and 1 dirham (3 grams) salt. Bring pot to a boil. \n\tWhen meat is done, add chunks of citron pulp (ḥummāḍ al-utruj) or pulp of utruj bred with lemon (laymū). The amount of citron is to be the same as that of the meat. \n\tContinue cooking. If the stew turns out to be too sour, balance the taste with juice of sweet pomegranate and a lump of sugar. Season the pot with black pepper, coriander, and ginger. \n\tWhen the stew is cooked (laḥaqat), prepare t͟harīd for it of broken pieces of bread in a bowl, pour the stew over it, and arrange the meat pieces around it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ḥummāḍiyya (stew soured with citron pulp) by ʿIbāda:[/b]\nTake pullets or 2 young fowls and scald them, clean them, and disjoint them. Put them in a clean soapstone pot (burma) and add to them a handful of bruised and skinned chickpeas, a piece of galangal, and a stick of cinnamon. Pour water enough to cover the birds and start cooking the pot. As soon as the pot comes to boil, start skimming the froth as it comes up using a ladle until nothing remains. \n\tAdd a handful of chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and continue cooking. When meat is almost done, add coriander seeds and black pepper, as needed. Cover the pot with the lid and continue cooking until birds are cooked. \n\tAdd 1 uskurruja (½ cup) chunks of citron pulp, no need to press the juice out. Make sure to remove pips and peel. Add as well ground cassia, as much as the tips of three fingers could hold. \n\tLet the pot cook for about an hour or until citron pulp falls apart. Pour into the pot one ladleful juice of sour unripe grapes and sprinkle on it 10 almonds that have been skinned and ground. Let the pot rest for a while, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Rummāniyya (stew soured with pomegranate) of Ītāk͟h:[/b]\nQuarter a plump and tender chicken, wash it, and put it in a pot along with 1 dirham (3 grams) salt. Start the fire under the pot. When all liquid evaporates, add to the pot juice of pounded round onion, as well as soaked skinned chickpeas, and galangal and cassia, a stick each. \n\tPour olive oil into the pot and stir-fry (ḥarrik qalyan) the chicken. Add a little water and continue cooking the chicken under a slowburning fire so that it does not burn. \n\tWhen the liquid evaporates, pour on the chicken 1½ raṭls (3 cups) juice of red and sour pomegranate. Skim as needed, sprinkle it with a little ground cassia, and chopped rue, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Rummāniyya (stew soured with pomegranate) by ʿAjīb al-Mutawakkilī:[/b]\nCut to pieces one chicken and 2 pullets, wash them, and put them in a pot along with chopped onion and ½ uskurruja (½ cup) water. Pour olive oil on them and bring the pot to a boil. Then pour juice of 2 sour pomegranates. The third pomegranate may either be sweet or sour. Continue simmering. \n\tAdd to the pot, a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce), black pepper, coriander seeds, caraway seeds, and cloves. Continue simmering the pot until meat is done and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ḥummāḍiyya (stew soured with citron pulp) Ibrāhīmiyya:[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (4 pounds) of fatty meat from slaughtered kid, cut it into chunks  and set it aside. \n\tTake about 1 raṭl (1 pound) of boneless lean meat from its thighs, or use its kis͟htamāzija (tenderloin) and a small amount of its tallow or fat tail, or whatever you wish. Pound the meat in a stone mortar and cook it in a pot on burning coals until it is done. Sprinkle the meat with a sour liquid such as lemon juice, wine vinegar, sumac juice, or citron pulp. Continue cooking the meat until all moisture evaporates. Take the pot away from the fire. Make sanbūsaj (filled pastries) using this meat for the filling and stiff dough, which you have kneaded very well. Set the filled pastries aside. \n\tAlternatively, you can fry the pounded meat in oil and mix it with maṣl (dried yogurt whey), cilantro, and coriander seeds. Make sanbūsaj using this meat mixture and the prepared stiff dough. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Here is a recipe for isfīd͟hbāj speckled with truffles (murammala bi kamʾa):[/b]\nCut meat into small pieces, wash it, and put it in a pot. Add soaked chickpeas, zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil), galangal and cassia, a piece each, chopped onion, chopped fresh herbs, and a little salt. \n\tPour some water into the pot and let it boil, skimming the froth as it comes up. Add black truffles, chopped into small pieces like the meat. However, you should cut the truffles before you do the meat. If truffles are not available, substitute with carrots or gourd, also chopped like the meat. Add them to the pot along with black pepper, coriander seeds, Kirmānī cumin, and a small amount of cheese and ground cassia. \n\tGarnish the top with many poached eggs, and allow the stew to settle and rest for a while. Ladle and serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Green isfīd͟hbāja by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (4 pounds) meat of a sheep in its third year (t͟hanī), and cut it up into bite-size pieces (luqma luqma). Put the meat in a pot with a piece of cassia, 1 raṭl (1 pound) chopped onion, 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) olive oil (zayt), salt as needed, and water enough to cover the meat. \n\tPlace the pot on nāfik͟h nafsihi or kānūn ʿajlān. When meat is half done, add to the pot, 4 pieces of cheese, each weighing 5 dirhams (15 grams). When meat is almost done, add to the stew ½ raṭl (1 cup) juice of cilantro and parsley. Add as well, a handful of ground coriander seeds, 1 dirham (3 grams) black pepper, and ½ dirham (1½ grams) cassia. \n\tLet the pot simmer in the remaining heat then take it away from the stove and serve it, God willing. \n\tIbrāhīm bin al-Mahdī composed these lines on the dish: \n[i]What a splendid green dish Qamar cooked. Amazingly beautiful, free of flaws.\nPut in midst of a bright silver platter with eggs on top, a show-stopping scene!\nGreen emerald embossed in silver, surrounded with eyes cast in gold.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for white baqliyya (vegetable dish) by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nTake tender meat and chop on it the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Pound both with two knives until they resembles bone marrow (muk͟h) in consistency. Put the meat in a pot and add soaked chickpeas, zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil), galangal, cassia, water as needed, and salt. Start cooking the pot. \n\tBoil together roots of chard (uṣūl al-silq) and white leek bulbs (uṣūl al-kurrāt͟h). The amount of both should be equal to that of meat. Pound them with a knife and add them to the cooking pot along with coriander seeds, cumin, cheese cut to pieces, and pitted and chopped olives. Stir the pot to mix the ingredients. \n\tBreak 4 eggs on the meat mix. Pound another piece of cheese with skinned almonds and mix them with the egg white. This will help the dish to set. Take the pot away from the fire, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Baqliyya (vegetable dish) with livers (kubūd) and gizzards (qawāniṣ) by him, too al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nBoil chicken livers and gizzards until they are almost done and all moisture evaporates. \n\tTake another pot and put in it chicken fat and sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Add chopped onion, pounded coriander seeds, soaked and pounded chickpeas, a piece of cassia, and a small amount of water. Put the pot on the burning coals, and fry the onion and all other ingredients until they are done. Add the cooked livers and gizzards to the pot. \n\tTake a suitable amount of mulūk͟hiyya (Jew’s mallow) and chard leaves (silq), boil them, press out extra moisture, and crush them with ½ dirham (1½ grams) black pepper, 7 dirhams (21 grams) coriander seeds, 1 dirham (3 grams) ground cassia, and 5 dirhams (15 grams) grated sharp cheese. Crush the mixture until it resembles bone marrow (muk͟h). Add it to the pot, and stir it to blend with the ingredients. Let the pot come to a good boil. \n\tTake 10 egg yolks and beat them thoroughly with a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Pour the egg yolk into the pot and stir it so that the egg mixes with the rest of the ingredients. \n\tNow take 10 egg whites and beat them with a small amount of murrī and ground cassia. Pour it all over the dish, but do not stir it. \n\tWhen the egg white sets, turn the dish over onto a big wide bowl (qaṣʿa). Serve it with sanbūsaj (pastries) filled with pounded meat and fried in oil. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Broth of chickpeas (māʾ ḥimmaṣ) by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nTake ½ raṭl (½ pound) chickpeas and soak them in water until they puff. \n\tPut in a clean pot, 2 disjointed plump pullets, and 3 dirhams (9 grams) whole cumin seeds tied in a piece of linen cloth, and enough salt. Pour on these the chickpeas liquid in which they were soaked and add half the amount of the soaked chickpeas. \n\tSet the pot on the fire and let it cook until the meat is half done. Add 1 raṭl (1 pound) small whole onions and 7 pieces of aged sharp cheese, each piece weighs 1 dirham (3 grams). \n\tWhen the two pullets and the onions are done, add to the pot 1 dirham (3 grams) black pepper. Break on them 7 eggs, and leave them undisturbed so that they look like cows eyes (ʿuyūn al-baqar). Put the pot away from the heat and let the eggs set in the remaining heat and steam of the pot. \n\tBreak white bread into pieces in a bowl and pour broth all over the bread enough to saturate it. Distribute the pullet pieces and onions over the sopped bread, but do not put any of the chickpeas. Pour about ½ raṭl (1 cup) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb) all over the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for broth of chickpeas (māʾ ḥimmaṣ):[/b]\nTake 4 plump pullets, about 1 raṭl (1 pound) onion, a suitable amount of salt, and 3 sprigs (aʿwād) of dill. Also, prepare 3 dirhams (9 grams) whole cumin seeds and a stick of galangal put in a bundle of linen cloth. Put all these ingredients in a pot and pour on them 1/3 raṭl ( 2/3 cup) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb), 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) zayt rikābī (olive oil extracted from unripe olives). Pour also the water in which chickpeas have been soaking until puffed along with the soaked chickpeas. Cook the pot until all ingredients are done. \n\tTake the crusts (ḥurūf) of k͟hubz jardaq (thick and coarse round bread), break them into somewhat large pieces, and put them in a clean pot. Pour on them most of the broth and oil of the cooked pullets, and let bread cook on low heat until it sops up all the broth. Empty the contents of the bread pot into a wide big bowl (qaṣʿa). Spread all over the bread, the pullet pieces, the onions, and a small amount of the chickpeas, and serve the dish, God willing.

Thread 3 whole cloves of garlic into a toothpick (k͟hilāl) and throw it into the pot. \n\tNow take 3 small and smooth cucumbers (k͟hiyār) and peel them. Discard their stalks and chop the leaves when you chop the cucumbers. Add them all to the pot along with one fresh or dried sprig of būtanaj (mint). Add as well a little black pepper and pounded cassia. Crumble between your fingers a small amount of dried ṣaʿtar bustānī (cultivated thyme) and add it to the pot. Let the pot cook until done. The final stew should be moderately sour (muʿtadilat al-mazāza). \n\tNow take a small amount of almonds, skin and crush them in a mortar and pestle (hāwan) then add them to the pot. \n\tIf you choose to use sour pomegranate juice instead of sour grape juice, then cook the meat with the pomegranate juice and when the meat is done take it out of the pot. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Bustāniyya (cooked with orchard produce) from the copy of Abū Samīn:[/b]\nWash small and sour plums and put them in a wet kerchief (mindīl) to hydrate them if using the dried variety. If fresh ones are used, just add to them some water, press and mash them then strain the liquid. \n\tCut chicken breasts into finger-like strips and add to them whatever you wish of other meats. Put them in a pot, add the strained juice of cherries, and let them boil together. \n\tSeason the pot with black pepper, māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid of fermented sauce), olive oil (zayt), some spices, a small amount of sugar, wine vinegar, and 5 walnuts that have been shelled and crushed. \n\tWhen meat is cooked, break some eggs on it and let them set with the steam of the pot, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mis͟hmis͟hiyya (apricot stew):[/b]\nClean and wash a plump chicken. Disjoint it and put it aside. Choose ripe apricots, which are yellow and sour. Put them in a pot with some water and bring them to a boil. Press and mash them with the water they were boiled in, and strain them into a bowl. \n\tNow go back to the chicken, put it in a clean pot and add the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), cilantro, and rue all chopped. Add as well a piece of galangal, a stick of cassia, and whole pieces of ginger. \n\tLight the fire underneath the pot and let it cook. Then sprinkle the pot with onion juice and add enough of the strained apricot liquid to submerge the chicken. Season the pot with coriander seeds, black pepper, and cassia, all ground. \n\tLet the pot simmer until chicken is cooked and serve it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kis͟hkiyya from the copy of Muḥammad bin Hārūn:[/b]\nWash 3 ratls (3 pounds) meat and put it in a pot. Add ½ raṭl (½ pound) chopped onion, ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) fresh herbs, a handful of chickpeas, 1 piece galangal, and ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil (zayt). Pour water enough to submerge the ingredients in the pot. \n\tLet the pot cook until meat is almost done. Add any of the seasonal green vegetables and a little chard. \n\tWhen everything in the pot is cooked, add 3 pieces (ruaūs heads) of sour kis͟hk, and ½ raṭl (½ pound) kis͟hk of Albū-Saḥar, Mawṣilī, or Bābakī. Pound them into fine powder and dissolve them in 1 raṭl (2 cups) māʾ ḥiṣrim (juice of unripe sour grapes). Add it to the cooking pot. \n\tWhen kis͟hk is done, add 2 dirhams (6 grams) cumin and an equal amount of cassia. Add a handful of finely chopped onion. Do not stir the pot. When the onion cooks and falls apart (yataharraʾ), add to the pot 2 dānaqs (1 gram) cloves and a similar amount of spikenard (sunbul). \n\tStop fueling the fire, let the pot simmer and rest on the remaining heat then take it down, God willing. \n\tThis is how to make basic kis͟hkiyya and it can substitute for all other kinds. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Delicious Adasiyya (lentil dish):[/b]\nWash and pick over hulled lentil and cook it until it falls apart and becomes mushy. Cook with it round onion (baṣal mudawwar), olive oil (zayt), and salt. Add some vinegar. \n\tYou have the option of adding to it sugar and saffron. Alternatively, if you do not like to use saffron or onion, put bruised garlic cloves and a dusting of cumin in the pot after adding the vinegar. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ʿAdasiyya:[/b]\nCook meat with chopped onion and olive oil (zayt). When the pot comes to a boil, remove the froth and add hulled lentils. Cook it until it becomes mushy (yataharraʾ). Then pour on it vinegar, and season it with coriander seeds and cumin. Add garlic, too. \n\tIf wished, use pounded cheese with it. You may color it yellow with saffron and add stalks of chard (aḍlāb silq). In this case, however, use neither cheese nor garlic. Add some sugar to it if liked. Moreover, the meat in this muṣaffara (yellowed with saffron) can be finely shredded and pounded like harīsa, and whole chunks of cheese with its rind may be added to the pot. When serving the dish, ladle it into a bowl, and put the cheese pieces in the middle. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe using large unhulled lentils (badas jalīl g͟hayr maqs͟hūr):[/b]\nPick over the lentils, wash them, and cook them with round onion (baṣal mudawwar) and cheese. Also add chard—root, stalks, and hearts (tender leaves in the center). Break eggs on them, but leave them whole. \n\tThe dish is seasoned with coriander seeds, cumin, and a little cassia and galangal. Besides, you need to add to the pot before the dish is fully cooked a lot of dill and fūdanaj, which is fulayyā (mint). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe:[/b]\nCook meat with chopped onion and oil. Add bruised whole pieces of galangal and cassia (ṣaḥīḥ mas͟hdūk͟h). Remove the scum, and add to the pot whole lentil that has been picked over and washed. When it is almost done, add pieces of cheese and olives. Season the pot with cumin, coriander, galangal, and black pepper. \n\tIf wished, break some eggs on it while still in the pot. You also have the option of adding to the ingredients, stalks of chard and sprigs of fūdanaj, which is fulayyā (mint). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for lūbyāyiyya (bean dish):[/b]\nChoose meat cuts from the shoulders, the lower neck (quṣayrā), fore and hind legs, and alya (sheep’s tail fat). Cut them into nice chunks, and put them in a pot after you have washed them. Add chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), a little oil, and a piece of cassia. Pour water enough to cover the meat. \n\tWhen the pot comes to several boils, add red beans (lūbya ḥamrā), which have been picked over and washed. Let the pot cook until the dish is done. \n\tRender some sheep’s tail fat and add it to the pot along with the needed amount of salt. \n\tLadle it into a bowl and drizzle it with some extra rendered sheep’s tail fat. Serve the dish with mustard, God willing. \n\tIf you like to use white beans (lūbya bayḍā), then go ahead and do so, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for white beans (lūbya bayḍā):[/b]\nBoil the beans and lightly smash them (yus͟hddak͟h). Pour on them vinegar, salt, mustard, and olive oil (zayt). Chop on them parsley, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), and rue. \n\tIt would be even more delicious if you use murrī (liquid fermented sauce) instead of salt. \n\tThe beans can also be made with just vinegar, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and olive oil (zayt). Then, the herbs mentioned earlier are chopped on them, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for red bean dish (lūbyāyiyya ḥamrā):[/b]\nBoil the beans but do not smash them. Mix them with some of the broth in which they boiled along with murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and olive oil (zayt). \n\tChop a little rue and scatter it on the beans. Arrange on the dish fried and boiled salted dried fish. Additionally, boil some eggs and slice them lengthwise. They will taste so good with the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making ṭafs͟hīl of Ṣāliḥ bin ʿAlī:[/b]\nTake a portion (juza) of lentil, a portion of beans, a portion of chickpeas, a portion of mung beans, and a portion of rice. Let the amount of rice be the least of all other grains used. Wash them, soak them in water, and set them aside. \n\tChoose fatty meat and fatty jerked meat (qadīd). Wash them, put them in a clean pot, and pour water enough to cover the meat and a little bit more. Cook the pot until meat is half done. Add boiled chard roots and chard stalks. When the pot comes to a boil, add the soaked pulses along with aged cheese. Pour on it vinegar, mustard, and olive oil (zayt), and add coriander seeds, cumin seeds, and black pepper, all pounded. Stir the pot, and let it cook until done. Then rub and mix (ʿarraka) some white bread with zayt anfāq (olive oil from unripe olives), put it in a bowl, ladle the dish all over it, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]White ṭafs͟hīla:[/b]\nTake 8 raṭls (8 pounds) of marbled meat (laḥm mujazzaʿ) and cut it into slices and set it aside. \n\tTake a suitable amount of soaked chickpeas and double its amount of soaked white beans (lūbya bayḍāʾ). Rub off the skins of both beans with the fingers, put them in a pot, and bring them to a boil. Take some hulled lentils and boil them lightly in another pot. Also, boil a good amount of chard stalks (quḍbān al-silq). \n\tAfter you wash the sliced meat, put it in a big pot along with 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) onions, which you keep whole. Mix 1 raṭl (2 cups) sour vinegar, which has been whitened with flour, with 4 raṭls (8 cups) water. Pour this mixture on the meat and onions. Put the pot on the fire and let it cook until meat is half done. \n\tTake the meat and onions out of the pot. Put the meat first in a stone mortar, pound it very well—let it be even finer than sausage meat—and take it out of the mortar. Do the same thing with the onions. Pound also the stalks of chard as well as the boiled chickpeas, beans, and lentil. \n\tWhen you are done pounding all the ingredients, return them all to the stone mortar, and add coriander seeds, black pepper, fennel seeds (rāzyānaj), and 2 dirhams (6 grams) garlic. Mix and pound them together. \n\tNow take some sour white vinegar and beat it with 2 dirhams (6 grams) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Put it, along with the pounded meat mixture, in the pot in which the meat was cooked . The pot should still have in it the broth of the cooked meat. Add to it 1 raṭl (2 cups) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). \n\tReturn the pot to the burning coals and keep on stirring, never relaxing, until the mixture becomes as smooth as well-done harīsa (wheat porridge). Put the pot away from heat and cover it until needed. \n\tWhen you serve it, everybody would think it is harīsa. You may serve the dish with mustard foam, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Nārbāj (pomegranate stew) by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nCut meat into pieces and disjoint some pullets. Wash them all and put them in a pot, which already has boiling water in it, enough to cover the meat. Add soaked and bruised chickpeas, chopped cilantro, zayt anfāq (olive oil from unripe olives), and salt. \n\tWhen the pot boils, add pomegranate seeds and zabīb (raisins), both whole. When it is done cooking, sprinkle on it some murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and pounded black pepper and galangal. Wait until the pot simmers and rests then serve it, God willing. \n\tFollowing the same recipe: \n\tPound the raisins and mix them with a little vinegar. Press the mixture and strain it with a sieve. Do the same thing with the pomegranate seeds. Pour the juices on the cooking meat in the pot. Apart from this, the dish is done the same way, so you need to know this. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]An unusual (ẓarīfa) nārbāja by Isḥāq bin Ibrāhīm al-Mawṣilī:[/b]\nCut meat into medium-size pieces and put it in a clean pot. Add a lump (ḥaṣāt) of salt, the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), and garlic pounded with coriander seeds. Pour into the pot water enough to cover the meat. \n\tNow take two handfuls of fresh almonds (lawz raṭb) , the freshest you can get, and crush them thoroughly until they have the consistency of ointment (marham). Add them to the pot and cook it. \n\tWhen meat is done, add to the pot 1 uskurruja (½ cup) wine vinegar. Wipe the inside of the pot and let it simmer and rest on the remaining heat of the fire. \n\tIt is an unusual dish. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Summāqiyya stew called Hārūniyya:[/b]\nTake some choice pieces of meat, cut them nicely, wash them thoroughly, and put them in a pot. Pour sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), and a little salt, about 1 dirham (3 grams). Add a bunch of chopped shallots (kurrāt͟h al-ʿaṣal), then fry the ingredients briefly. \n\tPour māʾ al-summāq (strained sumac juice) into the pot. Add enough to cover the meat by four fingers’ width. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]To make māʾ al-summāq (sumac juice):[/b]\nyou can leave sumac berries soaking in water to heat and mellow in the sun. Alternatively, you may pour hot water on them. However, you need to know that sumac spoils if you boil it with water on the stove. The juice is then strained and sumac berries are discarded. \n\tSo, after pouring the sumac liquid add to the pot whatever is available of seasonal vegetables (baql al-zamān), a handful of pounded walnuts, and another handful of shelled whole pieces of walnut. Season the pot with coriander seeds, black pepper, cassia, and ground galangal. \n\tPrepare t͟harīda (broken pieces of bread in a big bowl), sprinkle on it some pounded walnut, and ladle the stew all over the bread. Arrange the meat as previously described in similar meat dishes. Sprinkle the dish with more pounded walnuts and chopped naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Sour milk stew (maḍīra) from the copy of Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake sour milk (laban), proportionate with the amount of meat used, and let it be medium sour. If it is too sour, let two thirds of it be sour milk and one third milk (ḥalīb). Bring the sour milk to a gentle boil under low heat. Then take it away and cover it for an hour so that the whey separates and comes up to the top. Remove the whey and set it aside. \n\tChoose meat cuts from the shoulders and the lower neck (quṣayrā), and cut it into nice small pieces. Wash it and boil it lightly (salqa k͟hafīfa) if you are in a hurry. Take the meat out of the pot, submerge it in cold water, and set it aside to drain. \n\tWhen the meat is fully drained, put it in the pot that has the sour-milk, and start a low-heat fire underneath it. When it comes to a couple of boils, add peeled and chopped eggplant, gourd, and round onions (baṣal mudawwar) after you soak them in brine for an hour. When the pot comes to a boil, add a bunch of naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) do not chop it. When the stew thickens, sprinkle it repeatedly with the set-aside whey. Wipe around the inside of the pot and let it simmer on the embers. \n\tSeason the pot with nothing else but cumin. Discard the mint you put earlier and replace it with fresh mint so that the stew is not discolored. If you do not mind the stew developing a darkish hue, use coriander seeds in addition to cumin. When in season, use asparagus (hilyawn) as well. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Maḍīra by al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nTake sour milk and meat and use them as directed above. Let the milk be fresh and not too acid. However, when you add ḥawāyij, add with them 1 raṭl (2 cups) juice of sour grapes, in three batches. Then add spices put together in a bundle of linen cloth. These spices are coriander, cumin, cassia, and galangal, all bruised. \n\tWhen the sour milk stew thickens, sprinkle it with a small amount of the reserved whey. Wipe around the pot from the inside and let it simmer on the embers. \n\tIt you like, pour on it rendered fat of sheep tail, melted chicken fat, or butter. You have the option of using purslane (baqla hamqāʾ) instead of asparagus. Qaṭaf (orach) may replace ḥawāyij (vegetables), mentioned in the previous recipe. \n\tWhen the pot is done cooking, let it simmer gently on the remaining heat so that the fat rises to the surface then serve it. \n\tAbū al-Ḥusayn recited to me a poem on maḍīra: \n[i]Maḍīra, among all other dishes, the full moon resembles.\nShining on top of the tables, like light illuminating the dark.\nLike the crescent moon beaming through the clouds.\nPale upon a platter it looks for fear of being devoured.\nAbū Hurayra admired it when among other dishes it came,\nAnd his love for it overruled his passion to fast.\nSeeing that eating it would benefit him, he hastened to it.\nRefrained he would have, for sure, from rivaling the immaculate Imām,\nHad it not been maḍīra, the healer of man’s maladies.\nTo gratify one’s desire, having it is no sin deemed.\nUnanimously acclaimed delicious, exotic, and most wonderful of all dishes.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for maṣliyya by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake meat from a small lamb and cut it into strips like fingers. Put the meat in a pot after you wash it thoroughly. Pour on it sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), a piece of galangal, and a stick of cassia. Add as well, chopped cilantro and onion. Cook the meat until done. \n\tLightly sprinkle the meat with black pepper, coriander seeds, and cumin, all ground. Add chard, which has been boiled separately. \n\tPound maṣl first and then add it to the pot. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another maṣliyya by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nTake marbled meat from the ribs and dice it. Put it in a clean pot after washing it very well. Pour water enough to cover the meat and add chopped onion. \n\tWhen the pot comes to a boil, add ground walnuts and ground maṣl (dried yogurt whey). Add as well, a small amount of diced eggplant. \n\tBring the pot to a boil and add spices like coriander seeds and black pepper. When the pot boils with the spices, take it off the fire right away lest it should scorch (tatas͟hyyaṭ). The final dish should have only 2 ladlefuls of liquid remaining in it. \n\tLadle the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Simple maṣliyya made for al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nTake meat with ribs and boil it until it firms up. Take it out and slice it along the ribs into thin long strips. Put the meat in a clean pot with bruised chickpeas, a lot of chopped onion, cassia, and galangal. \n\tNow take chard roots, same amount as that of onion, and cut them into thin long slices as you did with the meat. Boil chard in another pot and set it aside. When the meat is cooked, take a handful of pulverized almonds, beat them with the whites of 20 eggs, and set them aside. \n\tPound maṣl (dried yogurt whey) very well, and spread it on top of the meat in the pot along with the set aside boiled chard. Take 1 raṭl (2 cups) sour yogurt (laban ḥāmiḍ) and add it to the pot. Now, take the set-aside almond-egg white mixture and pour it all over the dish. Let the pot simmer until the eggs set. Wait until it settles and rests then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another maṣliyya recipe:[/b]\nWash fatty meat and cut into small thin pieces. Put it in a pot along with chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and pounded chickpeas previously soaked and skinned. Add as well sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb) and salt. Bring the pot to a boil until meat is almost done. \n\tNow take maṣl ṭarī (fresh yogurt whey), mash it with 5 egg whites, and add it to the pot. \n\tCut boiled chard stalks into strips and add them to the pot. \n\tWhen the meat is done, season it with black pepper, coriander, a little cumin, and 3 cloves of garlic. Allow the pot to settle and rest then ladle it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for maʿs͟hūqa:[/b]\nCut boneless meat into small pieces, the way you usually do with qaliyya (fried meat dish). Wash it very well. Take a suitable amount of tallow and add a little olive oil (zayt) to it. You need to use pounded tallow so that it does not leave any sediments. Put the tallow-oil mix in a clean pot and let it melt on the fire. Add the meat to it after you boil it in a separate pot. \n\tWhen meat fries, add a little sour juice of grapes. If this is not available, use instead, strained sumac juice, mixed with finely pulverized almonds. Let the pot cook until you see that the raṭl (2 cups) of the juice of sour unripe grapes you have added to the pot has evaporated and meat has browned. If you want to use a little vinegar and honey with the juice of sour unripe grapes, then you need to add them at the same time you add the grape juice. \n\tSeason the pot with coriander seeds, a little black pepper, galangal, cassia, and cumin, all pounded. Let the black pepper and the galangal be ½ dirham (1½ grams), each. Use a similar amount of salt. Add as well just a tiny little bit of macerated saffron (rāʾiḥat zaʿfarān). \n\tGet skinned almonds ready. Pulverize part of it, dissolve it in a little rose water and stir it into the pot. Coarsely grind the rest of the almonds and mix them with breadcrumbs so that you spread them all over the meat in the pot later. \n\tRub the sides of the pot with some rue leaves after you have added the almonds with rose water and stirred the pot. Insert several sprigs of rue in the pot and let the sauce absorb their flavor then discard them. Now, spread the almond-crumb mixture all over the meat, and do not stir the pot. \n\tThere should be very little liquid remaining in the pot, equal to the amount of ṣibāg͟h (sauces and dips) or murrī (liquid fermented sauce) usually served with dishes. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for narjisiyya:[/b]\nCut into small pieces meat of kid, lamb, or pullets. Make it almost as fine as pounded meat. Put it in a pot, and mix with it cilantro, white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), olive oil (zayt), salt, and a small amount of water. Let it cook. When meat is done, add skinned fava beans and cook them together. Add to the cooking pot, some coriander seeds, black pepper, and chopped fresh truffles after boiling them. \n\tBreak 5 eggs on top of the meat mixture and leave them whole like cow’s eyes (ʿuyūn al-baqar). Let the eggs set then serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for bas͟hīqa of birds by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nTake pullets, plump chicken, or any other kind of birds. Scald them, disjoint them, and wash them clean. Put them in a pot in which you have poured water just enough to cook them. Let them boil and skim the froth. When they are done, add cilantro, the white part of one fresh onion, and a stick of galangal. \n\tPound thoroughly, ½ raṭl (½ pound) fresh walnuts. Mix them with 1 raṭl (2 cups) juice of unripe grapes and strain them. Add the strained liquid to the pot and let it boil until the liquid stops foaming (taskun rag͟hwatuhu). Add ground black pepper, cassia, galangal, and cumin, just enough to give a slight whiff of their aromas. \n\tIf you like to use rak͟hbīn (dried buttermilk), then dissolve it with the juice of sour unripe grapes. Besides, you can substitute the walnuts with pistachio. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for bas͟hīqa by Ibn al-Mahdī, cooked with olive oil (zayt):[/b]\nDisjoint a bird like ḥubārā (bustard), a duck, or a chicken. Clean the pieces and wash them then put them in a pot with olive oil (zayt), chickpeas, salt, and chopped onion and cilantro. Bring the pot to a boil, pour in it some water, and let it cook. \n\tPound thoroughly meat from leg of lamb along with onion, cilantro, coriander seeds, a little black pepper, and cassia. When bird meat is cooked, add the pounded meat to the pot. Pound together almond, walnut, and pistachio, mix them with sour grape juice, and add them to the pot. \n\tYou may add spinach or sarmaq (orach) as well. You also have the option of adding rak͟hbīn (dried buttermilk) dissolved in some sour grape juice. \n\tIbn al-Mahdī describes narjisiyya (meat dish with sunny-side-up eggs) in this poem: \n[i]You who asked me about the most delicious food, you indeed have asked a man in the know.\nTake, my dearest friend, meat with ribs, thighs, and more of the tal-low.\nChop the fatty tender meat and wash it with water pure.\nThen put it in the pan on fire and with spices fry it in oil.\nWhen meat is browned, ‘tis time to chop on it onion round.\nGreen fresh onion as well, and rue and coriander.\nNext give the dish murrī and ginger and black pepper, too, but sparingly do.\nAugment it with asparagus and break on it eyes of eggs.\nLike the luminous stars of the celestial spheres, or narcissus flowers round.\nGive it a sprinkle of chopped rue and insert a few erect sprigs of it, too.\nServe it in its pan draped or in a basket of willow sticks.\nThen God you praise and may you eat this delectable dish salubriously.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Nibāṭiyya by Isḥāq bin Ibrāhīm a-Mawṣilī:[/b]\nChoose two plump chickens. Clean and disjoint them and put them in a pot. Add chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb), soaked and bruised chickpeas, and a stick of cassia. Let the pot cook for a short while. Pour on it water, enough to cover the chicken. Bring it to a boil twice. \n\tAdd a large piece of cheese and the needed amount of salt to the pot. Of the spices, add coriander seeds, black pepper, cassia, galangal, spikenard, cloves, nutmeg, dār fulful (long pepper), and ginger, all pounded. \n\tWhen the pot comes to one or two boils after putting the spices, add three handfuls of iṭriya made from white dough (ʿajīn abyaḍ). Pour 10 dirhams (2 tablespoons) rose water and let the pot simmer on slow fire until the noodles are cooked. Shell 5 boiled eggs and add them to the pot. Wait until it stops bubbling and rests. \n\tLadle the dish into a bowl. Take out the cheese and the eggs, cut them to pieces, and arrange them around the meat. \n\tYou may add a handful of rice and smoked strips of meat while pot is cooking. That would be a good thing to do, delicious and scrumptious (lad͟hīd͟h ṭayyib), God willing. \n\tHere is a poem Isḥāq al-Mawṣilī wrote on this dish: \n[i]Nibāṭiyya with chicken, as pure as ivory it looks.\nEating it on a cold winter day is far more beneficial than eating sikbāja.\nSwaying like the waves is the fat swimming on its face,\nLike a luminous full moon shining through its lofty mansion.\nThe eggs are stars twinkling from a distance through the dark.\nThe egg yolk, sitting in the midst of its white, as beautiful as pure k͟halūq put in glass.\nThe cheese bits showing through are like beaded pearls set on a crown.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Narjisiyya būniyya:[/b]\nSlice the meat and chop it to pieces, but do not make them too small. Use some tallow with it, too. Cook the meat with the green stalks of fresh onion (k͟huḍrat baṣal), and kurrāt͟h Nabaṭī (tender-leaf leeks), leave them whole. Spread the stalks on top of the meat. \n\tSeason the meat with salt, olive oil (zayt), a bruised piece of cassia and another of galangal. Add as well coriander seeds and a small amount of cumin if wished. \n\tBreak eggs on the spread meat, enough to cover the whole face of the frying pan, which, by the way, should be of stone. Let the eggs look like eyes sunny-side up. \n\tPut the pan as it is on a reed tray (ṭabaq k͟hayzurān) and insert a sprig of rue in the midst of the yolk of each egg. Drape the pan with a big thin bread (ruqāqa) making a hole in the middle as big as the circumference of the pan. This is to hide the blackness of the outside of the pan when it is presented at the table. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for narjisiyya:[/b]\nThis is done the same way as above, using cheese cut into pieces and sprouted fava beans instead of meat. \n\tBreak the eggs on the cooked cheese and fava beans. Then using a daks͟hāb, break the surface of the yolks and let them run into each other. Cover the pan to allow eggs to set. \n\tTo serve it, carefully arrange the cheese pieces so that they show through the eggs. Garnish it with laqāniq (sausages), sanbūsaj (filled pastries), and fried thin bread cut into pieces (ruqāq maqlū). It is delicious served with cooked young fowls and pullets, no need for red meat (luḥūm majmūʿa). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a tasty mag͟hmūma by Isḥāq bin Ibrāhīm al-Mawṣilī:[/b]\nTake some fatty meat and cut it into thin slices, the thinnest you can get them. Take some round onions (baṣal mudawwar) and slice them thinly crosswise into discs like dirhams (coins). \n\tNow prepare a clean pot of soapstone (burma). Spread its bottom with a layer of the prepared meat; sprinkle it with black pepper, coriander, and caraway; and spread a layer of the onion slices. Put another layer of the sliced meat and fat, sprinkle it with spices and salt then another layer of onion. \n\tCover the layered meat and vegetables with a round of bread (rag͟hīf). Cook the pot on a slow-burning fire until meat is cooked. Invert the pot onto a wide and big bowl (g͟haḍāra) and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for mag͟hmūma:[/b]\nChoose 2 plump pullets, wash them then disjoint them. Put them in a pot and add to them 2 dirhams (6 grams) coriander seeds. Add ground black pepper, galangal, and ginger, ¼ dirham (¾ gram) each. As for cassia, use 1 dirham (3 grams). \n\tMix 2/3 raṭl (11/3 cups) vinegar, 1 raṭl (2 cups) onion juice (mā al-baṣal), 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) cilantro, and ½ raṭl (1 cup) olive oil (zayt). Pour this mixture into the pot and cover the ingredients with a disc of bread. \n\tPut the pot on the glowing coals (jamr) and let it cook until done. Take the pot away from heat and set aside to let it settle. \n\tIf you cut the pullets’ meat into thin slices before cooking it, the dish will come out even more delicious, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for mag͟hmūma, K͟hurāsānī style:[/b]\nSlice crosswise round onions (baṣal mudawwar) like dirhams (coins). Cut the meat into thin slices and wash it clean. \n\tStart by pouring a suitable amount of olive oil (zayt) into the pot then spread a layer of meat followed by a layer of onion. \n\tIn a bowl, mix 2 ladlefuls of sour vinegar and a similar amount of māʾ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid of fermented sauce). Add coriander seeds, black pepper, cumin, and caraway. Pour this mixture into the pot. Cover the ingredients with a disc of bread and let the pot cook until done, undisturbed (lā yuḥarrak). \n\tInvert the pot onto a big wide bowl (g͟haḍāra) and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mag͟hmūma from the copy of Abū Samīn:[/b]\nClean and disjoint 2 Kaskarī pullets. Put them in a pot and sprinkle on them a small amount of coriander seeds, about 1 dirham (3 grams). Add as well black pepper, long pepper (dār fulful), galangal, and ground ginger, 1 dānaq (½ gram), each. Sprinkle ½ dirham (1½ grams) cassia. \n\tMix ½ raṭl (1 cup) vinegar, a similar amount of onion juice, and 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) cilantro juice. Add 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) of murrī Nabaṭī known as al-t͟hānī (the second). Add as well, 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). \n\tPour this mixture into the pot, cover it with a disc of bread, and put it on the glowing coals until meat is done. Take the pot away from the heat and let it settle for a while. \n\tIf you cut the meat of pullets into thick slices before cooking it, the dish will be even more delicious, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mag͟hmūma with asparagus (hilyawn) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nChoose fresh and tender asparagus and boil them lightly. Chop them into fine pieces and set them aside. \n\tTake meat and chop it into fine pieces and put it in a pot. Take some chicken fat along with gizzards and livers. Clean them and put them in the pot. The last to add are the livers because they cook faster. Pour into the pot zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Add bruised chickpeas, crushed salt, white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), cilantro, and leeks, all chopped. \n\tPour water into the pot—enough to partially submerge the ingredients—and let it cook until meat is done. Add the asparagus, pounded walnuts and cheese, pitted olives, coriander seeds, and black pepper. \n\tBreak some eggs into a bowl, season them with black pepper and coriander, beat them very well, and add them to the pot. Do this after you have added the cheese and olives. Pour as well a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Stir the pot and let it cook until all moisture evaporates. \n\tCut out a flat bread to match the circumference of the pot. Using a separate pan, fry the disc in olive oil (zayt) then put it on top of the cooked meat in the pot. Serve the dish on this bread disc (i.e. turned over), God willing. \n\tIn this poem, Ibn al-Mahdī describes mag͟hmūma dish: \n[i]There are those who crave an honest plain dish of grains. I for one would love to have whatever is with vinegar seasoned.\nThere are those who do themselves carelessly harm having of foods that do not the season match.\nI for one unfailingly consume whatever definitely in the heat of summer does my body cool.\nVinegar in dishes brings me joy. Anything else saddens my heart.\nThe complexities of making sikbāja appeal to me, the way intricacies of knowledge men of learning intrigue.\nḤiṣrimiyya I find superbly good for me like ṣilāqa which to the welfare of the entire body tends.\nMaḍīra
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Mulahwaja, used to be made a lot for al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nDice meat and put it in a pot. Pour oil on it. Add onion, cilantro, rue, and leeks, all chopped. Let meat fry until it browns. Add to the pot, coriander seeds, caraway, black pepper, a bit of murrī (liquid fermented sauce), a bit of vinegar, cassia, and galangal. \n\tWhen the dish is done cooking, sprinkle it with a small amount of diluted honey, and present it garnished with chopped cilantro. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another mulahwaja:[/b]\nThinly slice meat of a small lamb, clean it, and put in a pot. Pour olive oil (zayt), bruised chickpeas, cassia, salt, and a small amount of water. Cook meat until it is done. Then pour on it 2 ladlefuls of juice of sour unripe grapes mixed with a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tWhen it is cooked, season it with black pepper, caraway, and 2 dirhams (6 grams) ground spikenard and cloves, each. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another mulahwaja:[/b]\nChoose meat of a fat kid, thinly slice it, and put it in a pot. Add chicken fat, olive oil, a piece of galangal, salt, onion juice, and cilantro juice. Let the pot boil gently then add a mixture of Levantine apple juice (māʾ tuffāḥ S͟hāmī), 2 ladlefuls of extremely sour wine vinegar (k͟hall k͟hamr ḥād͟hiq), and a small amount of bruised chickpeas. \n\tWhen the dish is cooked, season it with black pepper, coriander seeds, caraway seeds, and ½ dirham (1½ grams) ground cloves. \n\tAbū al-Qāsim bin al-Mad͟hbūḥ recited this poem on mulahwaja: \n[i]Abodes may be forlorn, but not so their people, for life can still be good with swords unsheathed.\nThe wild asses were plump, with loins like two big jars flanked as if one of their ancestors an elephant was.\nThey were brought to us for lunch that a cook hurriedly made, and the best food is cooked on the run.\nThe wine was clear, neat, and aged. The soul was generous and the purse was loose.[/i] \n\tAbū ʿUmar al-S͟hayyāl once recited some verses that a Bedouin composed: \n[i]Mulahwajāt with meat of fawns (k͟his͟hf) from sides and cuts of shoulders taken.\nThey fell to my share. I did not stab them while drinking at the stream unawares.\nHere they are by masterly hands resplendently cooked.\nThe dish is like the sun shining out of darkness, luscious and like lovers’ saliva taste.\nMore appealing than the clashing marching armies, or fighting thousands of foes.\nCooked hurriedly in just half a day and here it comes, jiggling with fat like crowded fluffs of clouds.\nMulahwajāt with wine undiluted—these are my healers and rejuvenating tonics.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Baṣaliyya by al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nTake chunks of meat from ribs and thighs and slice them into finger-like strips. Soak the meat in cold water, as this will drain the blood and remove the dirt. Hot water, on the other hand, will lock them in. \n\tTake the meat out of the cold water and put it in a pot with a fresh batch of water along with a lot of pounded tallow. You may add galangal and cassia. \n\tChop onion, the amount needed is to be equal to one third of the meat used. If gourd is in season, then go ahead and use it. However, cut it first into fingerlike strips like you did with the meat. Set onion and gourd aside. When the pot comes to a boil, add the onion and the gourd. \n\tA note: The amount of water you added first should not be much. \n\tContinue cooking the pot until the pot is dry. Add murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and dry spices like black pepper, cassia, coriander, and cumin. Add as well one ladleful of vinegar and a small amount of rue. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Baṣaliyya by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nCut meat into strips and add cilantro, onion, and sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). When meat is done, add black pepper, coriander, and cumin. Chop a small amount of kurrāt͟h al-baql (green and tender leaves of leeks) and add it to the meat. \n\tLet the pot simmer slowly on the remaining heat of the fire then settle for about an hour. Ladle it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Baṣaliyya made for al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nChoose chunks of meat from ribs and thighs and slice them into small pieces like fingers. Soak them in cold water for an hour then take them out after they are cleansed and put them in another batch of water in a pot. Let there be a lot of pounded tallow with it. Add as well, cassia, galangal, and previously bruised and soaked chickpeas. Bring the pot to a boil \n\tFinely chop onion, let it be half the amount of the meat used. If lettuce is in season, then slice the stems crosswise into rounds like dirhams (coin). Add both onion and lettuce to the pot and let it boil until the meat is cooked. Add a small amount of rose water. \n\tAs soon as the liquid in the pot evaporates, add murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and dry spices such as coriander, black pepper, cassia, and cumin. Add as well, a ladleful of sour grape juice and some rue. Take the fire from underneath the pot and let it simmer until the stew thickens over the heat of burning coals (jamr). Put a whole bunch of naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint) in the midst of the pot. When it is done simmering and rests, serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for baṣaliyya:[/b]\nChoose meat from the ribs, rump, and fat from the tail of sheep. Dice the meat, wash it very well, boil it, and take it out of the broth, but reserve the broth. \n\tPut the meat in a pot after it has been boiled. Add chopped cilantro and rue, a stick of cassia, and a piece of galangal. Let the meat cook for a while (sāʿa, one hour) until it releases its juices. Then pour on it fresh water, enough to come up to half the level of the meat in the pot. When meat is cooked, add to the pot a ladleful of rendered and strained chicken fat or kidney tallow (s͟haḥm al-kilā), and fry the meat with some spices (abzār). Then pour on it some of the reserved broth and add three bulbous heads of fresh white onion (bayāḍ baṣal murawwas), their amount needs to be equal to that of the meat used. Cover the pot and let it simmer under slow fire (nār layyina). The broth you add to the pot when you add the onions should not submerge the meat. \n\tNow, when the onions are fully cooked and fall apart (inharā), take the fire away, put instead burning coals (faḥm qawī) under the pot, and let it cook until the stew nicely thickens and becomes like fālūd͟haj (thick pudding) in consistency. \n\tAdd ½ dirham (1½ grams) saffron to the pot. Of the spices, add just a trifle (rāyiḥa) of black pepper; cassia, spikenard, and cloves, about ½ dānaq (¼ gram) of each. Add as well coriander seeds and a few snips (qaḍba) of naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). Add the required amount of salt and leave the pot on the remaining heat until it settles and rests. \n\tIf the stew comes out thin, thicken it by spreading breadcrumbs on top of it. Alternatively, you may use skinned and ground almonds or finely ground walnut. Sprinkle the pot with a bit of rose water and cover it. \n\tServe the dish with peeled small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jazūriyya with meat of a slaughtered camel (laḥm jazūr):[/b]\nTake choice cuts of jazūr (slaughtered camel) and cut it into strips the way you do with meat prepared for qalāya (fried dishes). Do the same thing with the camel’s hump (sanām). \n\tDice some onion, crush it, and set it aside. \n\tWash a pot, put the meat in it, but hold the hump for now. Light the fire underneath it, and let it cook. Do not add binn (fermented sauce of rotted bread) or vinegar to it, just the meat. After it releases its moisture and then evaporates completely, add the crushed onion along with a little salt and the hump. Fry the meat until the hump releases all its fat. \n\tSeason the meat with vinegar, māʾ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid fermented sauce), black pepper, coriander seeds, and caraway seeds. Bring the pot to a boil after which you let it simmer and settle. Ladle the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for jazūriyya:[/b]\nCook it the same way described above, but instead of māʾ kāmak͟h use binn (fermented sauce of rotted bread), a small amount of ground fennel (rāzyānaj), and vinegar. Otherwise, use all the spices mentioned in the above recipe and do whatever is required in the recipe. However, you need to use a bit of saffron for this dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for jazūriyya:[/b]\nCut meat, liver, and hump into finger-like strips. Put them in a soapstone pot (burma) and add chopped cilantro and onion, a little black pepper, salt, olive oil (zayt), and two pulverized lumps of sugar. \n\tLight the fire under the pot and stir the meat until it cooks. Pour on it some water, just enough for the meat to boil in. Keep the fire burning until the pot comes to a boil. Add some pounded chickpeas and stir. When cooking is done, taste the dish and check for salt. If it lacks any, add murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and stir the pot. \n\tAdd chopped onion and let the pot cook until the onion is done. Add as well a bit of black pepper, coriander, and cumin seeds. \n\tWhen meat is done cooking, pour some hot water, chopped cilantro, and rue. Drizzle it with a small amount of clarified butter (samn) and put the pot away from heat, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jazūriyya made with lamb by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (4 pounds) of choice cuts of camel meat, 1 raṭl (1 pound) liver, and 1 raṭl (1 pound) hump. Slice them into very thin strips. Keep the meats separate. \n\tDice 1 raṭl (1 pound) onion and put it in a pot along with the strips of camel meat after you wash it. Pour 2/3 raṭl (11/3 cups) olive oil (zayt), and ½ raṭl (1 cup) water. Add 3 dirhams (9 grams) salt. Bring the pot to a boil and remove the scum. Then cover the pot and let it cook until all moisture evaporates. \n\tUncover the pot, stir it, add the hump strips, and stir the pot continuously until the meat and the hump strips are fried. Then add 1 raṭl (2 cups) good quality vinegar and continue cooking until meat is done. At this point, add the liver strips and stir the pot. \n\tAdd 2 dirhams (6 grams) chopped rue and continue stirring until you start smelling the rue. Keep on sprinkling water on the meat while it is cooking until it becomes tender. Add ½ raṭl (½ pound) onion pounded with ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) cilantro and stir the pot. \n\tNow, pour into the meat ¼ raṭl (½ cup) murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and add black pepper and caraway seeds. Let the pot simmer in the remaining heat until it rests. \n\tIf lamb, liver, and tail fat of sheep are used in making this dish, the tail fat will substitute for the hump fat. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Jazūriyya by ʿIbāda made with lamb:[/b]\nChoose fatty and tender meat, dice it, and put it in a pot after washing it. Pour sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb) on it. Add some salt and a small amount of water. Let it fry until almost done. \n\tAdd chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and small eggplants, which have been sliced crosswise into discs like dirhams (coins), soaked in salted water, and drained. \n\tWhen eggplant is done, pour 2 ladlefuls of vinegar and continue simmering until vinegar cooks. Then, mix aged binn (fermented sauce) with some of the liquid in the pot and return it. Season the pot with coriander and black pepper and let it simmer gently in the remaining heat until it settles. Serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jazūriyya by ʿAbbās ibn al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nCut meat of the slaughtered camel (jazūr), wash it, and put it in a soapstone pot. Add salt, zayt anfāq (oil of unripe olives), whole onions, kurrāt͟h Rūmī (Byzantine leeks), snips (jazra) of kurrāt͟h Fārisī (Persian leeks), and a bunch (bāqa) of cilantro. \n\tWhen the burma (soapstone pot) comes to a boil, skim the froth. As soon as meat is done, take out and discard the onion, Rūmī and Fārisī leeks, and cilantro. \n\tSeason and thicken the sauce with black pepper and ground almonds. Prepare t͟harīda (broken pieces of bread in a bowl) for it and drizzle the bread with some sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Ladle the dish over the bread and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a nice and unusual madqūqa from which three varieties may be made, from the copy of Isḥāq bin al-Kindī:[/b]\nPound meat in a stone mortar until it has the consistency of bone marrow (muk͟h). Boil a small amount of water in a clean pot. Add the pounded meat to it. When it boils, skim off the froth and pour on it excellent quality olive oil (zayt fāyiq), salt, and chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Stir-fry the mixture (yuqlā wa yuḥarrak) then add pounded coriander seeds, black pepper, and soaked chickpeas. Add a fistful of almonds, which have been skinned and pounded to resemble bone marrow. Add as well juice of the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) along with some water and cook the pot until everything is done. \n\tAdd beaten eggs to the pot, put it aside to set (ḥatta yajmud) in the remaining heat of the pot, and serve it. \n\tIf you want the dish to be maṣliyya (cooked with whey), add— at the same time you add the almonds—white whey (maṣl abyaḍ) and a little cumin. Then add beaten eggs and a little cumin after the whey is cooked. Apart from this, the dish is done the same way. \n\tIf you want the dish to be ḥiṣramiyya (cooked with grape sour juice), summāqiyya (cooked with sumac), or laymūniyya (cooked with lemon juice), add—the same time you add the almonds—whichever sour juice you choose, as much as needed. If you like, add naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), sorrel (baqlat al-ḥamḍ), qit͟ht͟hāʾ (ridged and long cucumber), and k͟hiyār (small and smooth cucumber). When all the ingredients are cooked, add to the pot a sprig of rue. Apart from this, it is prepared the same way. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for madqūqa:[/b]\nFinely chop the meat and chop tallow the same way. Take some fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb), onion, and rue, and finely chop them. Then pound them (i.e. the meat and vegetables) with a knife until they resemble ointment in consistency. Sprinkle the mixture with ground cassia, black pepper, and caraway. Add as well māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce), vinegar, and olive oil (zayt). Knead together to mix ingredients. \n\tPut meat mixture in a pot, pour on it some water, and let it come to half a boil. Add to the pot, ½ raṭl (1 cup) dissolved alya (sheep’s tail fat) and whatever you fancy of dried fruits like walnuts, almonds, and pistachios. \n\tBeat 10 eggs in a bowl and pour them all over the meat. Let pot cook, undisturbed until eggs are set. It will look like furniyya. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another mudaqqaqa:[/b]\nTake tender meat from the thigh of a yearling sheep, slice it thinly, and pound it. Add finely chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) or chopped kurrāt͟h al-baql (tender-leaf leeks). Add as well spices such as coriander, cumin, and cassia, all ground. Mix and pound all the ingredients in a stone mortar and shape mixture into balls by oiling your hands with sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Put the meatballs (kubab) in a plate and set them aside. \n\tTake a clean pot, and put in it enough water to cover the meatballs. When water boils, add the meatballs, bring it to a boil and skim the froth. \n\tAdd to the pot, sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), crushed salt, bruised soaked chickpeas, and chopped onion, leeks (kurrāt͟h), and cilantro. Cook the pot until it is almost done. \n\tTake 30 dirhams (3 ounces) almonds, which have been skinned and pounded until they resembled muk͟h (bone marrow). Stir them with some water and add them to the pot. Salt the dish as needed. \n\tBeat 10 eggs and pour them into the pot. Stir vigorously so that the meat balls mingle with the eggs. Give the pot a dusting of coriander and just a trifle of (rāʾiḥa) black pepper and cassia. Stir in ṭalʿ simsimānī. Let the pot simmer in the remaining heat of the fire and settle for about an hour then ladle it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for white omelet (bujja bayḍāʾ) by Abū Samīn:[/b]\nThoroughly wash a frying pan and pour into it 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). Now, take 10 eggs, break them in a g͟haḍāra (green-glazed bowl), and pour into them 3 ūqiyyas ( 1/3 cup) milk. Add a handful of ground pistachio, almond, and walnut, all ground. Beat the mixture very well and pour it into the frying pan. \n\tWhen the bottom side is done, flip it to the other side. Then take it away from the fire. It will taste like busr, remarkably excellent and delicious (g͟hāyat al-jawda wa ’l-ṭība), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]An omelet recipe with pungent green onion (ḥirrīf), also by him:[/b]\nTake 3 bunches of pungent green onion, dice them, and boil them in water until done. After straining them, put them in a frying pan with some oil. Let them fry until they brown. Transfer them to a clean g͟haḍāra (green-glazed bowl). \n\tBeak 10 eggs on the onion, whip mixture very well, and pour it onto a frying pan that already has hot olive oil (zayt) in it. When the bottom side is browned, flip the disc. When it is done, serve it with a small bowl of vinegar, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]An omelet recipe with fava beans (bāqillī):[/b]\nRemove the skins of fresh green fava beans then boil them and fry them in oil. When they are done, prepare them the same way you did with the onions above, that is, whip them in a g͟haḍāra (greenglazed bowl) with eggs then pour them into a frying pan. When one side is done, flip it to the other side. When it is cooked, present it with a small bowl of vinegar, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for flipped omelet (bujja maqlūba) made to resemble furniyya, by al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nPound meat, fresh herbs, and leeks (kurrāt͟h) using two knives until the mix looks like bone marrow (muk͟h). Put it in a frying pan. Pour on it a small amount of olive oil (zayt) and a little salt. Keep on stirring the meat while it releases its moisture then dries up and cooks. Sprinkle it with a bit of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). When it is fully done, add black pepper and coriander. \n\tTake the meat out of the pan, and divide it into three parts: \n\tTo a third of it, add maṣl (dried yogurt whey) and a lot of walnut. To the second third add rak͟hbīn (dried buttermilk) and a lot of pistachio and almonds. To the third part, add isfīd͟hbāj (white stew) made with cheese and ground almond. \n\tAdd a bit of cumin to the part that has cheese; add a little ground spikenard and cloves to the part that has rak͟hbīn; and cassia and caraway to the part that has maṣl. \n\tNow take thin sheets of dough (ruqāq min al-ʿajīn) and make different kinds of sanbūsaj (filled pastries) using the three kinds of fillings mentioned above. Let them be small. \n\tFry the pastries in a pot with a lot of animal fat (dasam) mixed with zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Arrange the fried sanbūsaj in layers in the pot, which you put on a strong fire fueled with a good amount of coal. \n\tBeat eggs enough to cover the layered sanbūsaj and pour it all over them. Now, let the pot cook on slow burning coals (faḥm layyin) or in a smoldering tannūr (hādia). When the eggs are set, take the pot out and set it aside until it cools down a little. When you turn it over, it will come out looking like a browned furniyya. It is the best (aḥsan s͟haya). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]An omelet recipe with truffles (kamʾa):[/b]\nPound the meat with two knives until it looks like bone marrow (muk͟h). Take the truffles and do the same thing with them. \n\tPut meat and truffles in a pot with a lot of zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) and animal fat (dasam). Stir the pot until meat and truffles are cooked. Season them with murrī (liquid fermented sauce), black pepper, and cassia. Take them out of the pan and put them in a g͟haḍāra (green-glazed bowl). For each raṭl (1 pound) of meat and truffles, use 5 eggs. \n\tTake a frying pan, 1 small span (fitr) wide, with good high sides, and pour duhn like sesame oil or olive oil (zayt) in it. Put it on slow burning coals and when the oil gets hot, beat the eggs with the prepared meat and truffles and gently pour mixture into the pan. Stir the egg mixture frequently so that it absorbs the fat. \n\tIt would be better if you remove the fire and let the eggs cook and set gently and slowly in the remaining heat. Better still, you may flip the omelet so that it cooks on both sides. Alternatively, you may just let it be scrambled into big lumps. \n\tLet its sauce (ṣibāg͟h) be raisin wine mixed with honey. This will be the best thing to have with it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]White omelet made with starch (nas͟hā):[/b]\nBeat together eggs whites and starch. Mix in almonds, pistachio, and milk. Cook the mixture and when it is done, drizzle on it some murrī (liquid fermented sauce), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another omelet made with sparrows (ʿaṣāfīr):[/b]\nClean the sparrows and fry them in oil and a little salt until they brown. Take 10 eggs, and beat them with a little black pepper and chopped cilantro. Pour the egg mixture on the sparrows, fry them until they are done, and serve them, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another white omelet:[/b]\nChop cilantro, leeks, and onion, and fry them with a little olive oil. Pour on them a ladleful of murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and another of vinegar. \n\tBreak 10 eggs in a g͟haḍāra (green-glazed bowl) and sprinkle them with black pepper and rue leaves. Add eggs to the pan, and beat the mixture in the pot. When done invert the omelet into a bowl. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another omelet recipe:[/b]\nTake some eggs and separate the whites from the yolks. Add a little honey to the whites, beat them together, and add to them chopped rue, tarragon, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), and bad͟harūj (basil). Beat this mixture well, put it in a pot, and light fire underneath it until it sets and thickens (yanbaqid). Sprinkle it with a little cumin, cassia, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and olive oil. \n\tTurn the egg white disc onto a platter and spread it on the layer of egg yolk you have separated, sweetened with sugar, and cooked until thickened and set. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for anjud͟hāniyya (dish cooked with asafetida leaves) by Yaḥya bin K͟hālid al-Barmakī:[/b]\nCut meat into thin slices (yus͟harraḥ) and chop onion and fresh herbs. Put them in a pot and add to them excellent quality olive oil (zayt fāyiq). When the pot boils and the meat browns, add black pepper, cumin, caraway seeds, and a little murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tAdd to the pot, crushed dried asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān), as much as needed. Break eggs on the meat and let it simmer (haddihā) for as long as it needs, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Anjud͟hāniyya recipe by Ibn ʿUmar:[/b]\nChop meat the way you do with qalāyā (fried dishes) and set it aside. Take tallow (s͟haḥm), chop it fine, and fry it. When it melts, take out the sediments and add to the pot, chopped fresh herbs, onion, and the set-aside meat. \n\tWhen everything is fried, take as much as you need of dried asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān) and add it to the pot. Add as well cassia, black pepper, caraway, a small amount of vinegar, and māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce). Sprinkle the meat with a small amount of water, let it simmer for a while then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for anjud͟hāniyya:[/b]\nChop meat, wash it, and put it in a clean pot. Add a little salt and olive oil. Light fire underneath it until it browns. Pound onion and cilantro, add them to the meat, and stir the pot. \n\tAdd to the meat, vinegar, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), a small amount of water, black pepper, coriander, cumin, and a small amount of dried asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān). Break eggs on the meat mixture allow eggs to set in the remaining heat, and serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Māʾ wa milḥ (meat cooked in water and salt) recipe for the lak͟hs͟ha dish:[/b]\nTake meat from the shoulders, hump, navel, and thighs, wash it very well, and boil it for a short while (ṣalqa k͟hafīfa). Take the meat out of the pot and discard the water in which it was boiled. Next, return the meat to the pot, pour fresh water on it, and season it with salt, a stick of cassia, a stick of galangal, but hold the onion. \n\tBring the pot to a boil and add some dill to it. Continue cooking until meat is done then add dried spices such as coriander, black pepper, and cassia, all pounded. \n\tTake the meat out of the pot and put it in another pot with a small amount of the broth so that it does not get cold. Set it aside. \n\tNow, go to the stiff dough you have prepared and flatten it into thin sheets with a rolling pin, as you do when you make jarmāzaj bread. Cut the dough into long strips and cut each strip into triangles (s͟hawābīr). Throw them into the boiling broth and let them cook. Check the salt of the broth and add more if needed. \n\tScoop out the cooked dough with a ladle made of willow twigs (ʿīdān k͟hiāf) and put them in the middle of a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya). If needed, pour on them some of the ṣibāg͟h (dipping sauce). Arrange the meat all over it and around the sides. Serve the dish with its dipping sauce. [b]A recipe for the dipping sauce (ṣibāg͟h):[/b]\nTake 2 parts of maṣl (dried whey), 1 part ground walnut, and 1 part bruised garlic. Put them all in a pot and pour on them broth of māʾ wa milḥ from the recipe above. Put enough to cover the ingredients and more. \n\tBring the pot to a boil and add 7 heated pebbles.
