Ladle the sauce into a clean platter (jām) and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for rak͟hbīniyya (dish with dried buttermilk), quite aromatic (ʿarfa) by Ibn al-Shiṭranjī:[/b]\nChoose some fatty choice cuts of meat and chop them into cubes. Put it in a clean pot with chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and tender-leaf leeks (kurrāt͟h al-baql). Fry them with a little oil. Then add a fistful of bruised chickpeas, a stick of cassia, and a stick of galangal. \n\tAdd some water to the pot and bring it to a boil, skim the froth, and add a variety of dried fruits such as walnut, almond, pistachio, and hazelnut. \n\tWhen the meat is cooked, dissolve dried buttermilk (rak͟hbīn) in a small amount of the meat broth, and add it to the pot. You also add whatever is available of maḥās͟hī (large stuffed sausages), as well as a handful of salt, black pepper, ground cassia, coriander, cumin, and caraway. \n\tWhen everything is cooked and pot is done simmering, break 10 eggs into the stew to poach in the remaining heat. When you serve it, garnish it with the eggs, maḥās͟hī (big sausages), laqāniq (small sausages), ṭardīn (thin meat patties), fresh vegetables, and other similar things, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Rak͟hbīniyya (dish with dried buttermilk) by Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nTake some pullets and other kinds of fatty meat and poultry. Disjoint the meat and put it in a pot. Add chopped fresh herbs and onion, a piece of galangal, salt, olive oil, and a small amount of water. Let the meat fry well after moisture has evaporated and add 2/3 raṭl (1 1/3 cups) sour grape juice. Bring it to a boil and add ground spices such as coriander, cumin, and cassia. \n\tDissolve a small amount of rak͟hbīn (dried buttermilk) in some juice of sour grapes and add it to the pot. When the dish is cooked and the pot stops simmering in the remaining heat, serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for rak͟hbīniyya (dish with dried buttermilk) made by Naẓīf for al-Muqtadirī:[/b]\nCut meat into medium-size pieces, clean it, and put it in a pot along with soaked bruised chickpeas, olive oil, salt, and a piece of galangal. Bring the pot to a boil and add to it juice of onion, leek, cilantro, and rue. Dissolve rak͟hbīn in some liquid and add it to the pot with whole leaves of watercress (jirjīr). \n\tWhen the meat is done, add to the pot ground spices such as coriander, just a trifle of black pepper, and ginger. Add as well shelled walnut and cassia. \n\tWhen the pot stops bubbling and simmering in the remaining heat of the fire, serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for t͟harīda S͟hāmiyya (of the Levant):[/b]\nTake lamb and chicken. Alternatively, use young fowls (firāk͟h) or any other similar birds instead of chicken. You also have the option of using either lamb or poultry. Cut the meat into medium pieces and clean them. Remove and discard the entrails of the chicken and discard the heads and the necks. \n\tPut the meat in a clean pot. Add the strained liquid of truffles, which have been washed and soaked in water overnight. Put enough of the liquid to cover the meat. If truffles are not available, boil some honey until it turns black then pour on it a small amount of māʿ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid fermented sauce), and add it to the pot with a little chickpeas and salt. Light fire under the pot. \n\tTie into one bundle, fresh rue, leeks—either Rūmī or Nabaṭī—and cilantro. Add this bouquet (bāqa) to the pot. Then add ground spices such as coriander, cumin, caraway, and black pepper. Continue cooking the pot until meat is done. \n\tBreak fine bread into pieces in a big bowl and add enough of the broth to submerge it. Put the meat pieces all over the bread and garnish the dish by arranging small sausages and ṭardīn (thin meat patties) all around it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another t͟harīda recipe:[/b]\nTake intestines (ʿuṣbān) from the belly of a kid or a yearling. Take also some of its ribs and other cuts. Wash them thoroughly. \n\tPour water into a clean pot. The amount should be enough to submerge the meat. Bring it to a boil then add the meat, the intestines, and the ribs, along with the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Let the fire underneath the pot be slow. Add fresh rue, some skinned chickpeas, and truffles. \n\tMake dough the night before. Bake the bread in the morning after the dough has soured, which is a good thing, by the way, because you need sour bread for this dish. \n\tCrush well together, onion, coriander, and cumin until the mixture has the consistency of bone marrow (muk͟h). Add it to the pot to thicken the broth. Also add ʿāʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce), black pepper, and coriander. Next, sprinkle the broth lightly with a bit of vinegar— you should barely smell it (tas͟hummuhu s͟hamman). Add some fresh thyme. If this is not available then use dried thyme. \n\tLet the pot cook until the meat is done. Break into pieces the already baked bread, put it in a big wide bowl, and ladle the broth all over the bread to submerge it. Garnish the top with the meat pieces, intestines, and ṭardīn (thin meat patties), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another t͟harīda:[/b]\nChoose fatty meat, cut it into small pieces, and put it in a pot along with soaked chickpeas, whole onions, salt, and some water. Light the fire underneath the pot and let it cook until meat is done. This will come out as isfīd͟hbāj (white stew). \n\tDivide k͟hubz al-māʾ (water bread) into quarters. Arrange the pieces in a qaṣʿa (wide bowl big enough for 10 people), and pour some clarified butter (samn) or fresh butter (zubd) all over them. Do this when the bread has just been taken out of the tannūr and still piping hot. \n\tLadle the broth over the bread, put as much as needed to saturate the bread. Pound some sugar and sprinkle it on the bread before you ladle the broth. Arrange meat pieces all around the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for t͟harīda called al-ʿawharānī (the tricky one):[/b]\nChoose choice cuts of lamb, cut them into medium-size pieces, and put them in a clean pot. Add a little salt, soaked chickpeas, and enough water to submerge the ingredients. Light the fire underneath the pot and let it cook until meat is done. \n\tPour into the pot ½ uskurruja (¼ cup) vinegar. Stir a small amount of soured yeast (k͟hamīr muḥammaḍ) with a little fat and add it to the pot along with a pinch of ground black pepper. \n\tBread used for this dish is dried white bread (yābis ḥuwwārī). Put the broken bread pieces in a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and ladle the meat broth all over it. Drizzle it with clarified butter, give it a dusting of black pepper, and serve it. \n\tCaveat: Do not ladle the broth over the bread until the moment you are ready to serve the dish. The dry bread will spoil if it sits in the broth for too long, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another t͟harīda, exotic (g͟harība):[/b]\nPound together, pomegranate seeds, zabīb (raisins), and some water. Press the juice through a strainer down into a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra) and pour it into a clean pot. Add soaked chickpeas and cilantro. \n\tWash meat pieces and add them to the pot along with chopped onion. Let the pot cook until meat is done. \n\tMake soft dough (ʿajīn raqīq). Put some clarified butter into a washed soapstone pot (burma) and put the prepared dough in it. Cover the pot and bake it in the tannūr until bread is done. Take it out of the pot, lightly strike it with your hand (uḍrubhā) to break it a little and put it in a bowl. Ladle the broth and the meat all over the bread. Give it a dusting of Sulaymānī sugar and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another t͟harīda recipe:[/b]\nBoil milk in a clean soapstone pot and add whole heads of small onions. Keep on stirring the pot until it comes to a boil then add boiled fatty meat cut into small pieces. Stir in soaked chickpeas, onion, and coriander seeds. Season it with some of the aforementioned spices in previous recipes. \n\tPut broken pieces of bread in a bowl and ladle the broth and meat all over it. Give the dish a dusting of sugar and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Levantine t͟harīda, which some Christians cook:[/b]\nCut meat into medium-size pieces and put it in a clean pot. Add chopped cilantro, rue, salt, onion, coriander seeds, and black pepper. Also add cassia and galangal, a piece each. \n\tNow take some smoked slices of meat and put them in the pot along with a handful of sprouted fava beans (bāqillī manbūt), chard stalks (aḍlāb silq), and a big chunk of cheese. Let the pot boil then season it again with the same dry spices you used earlier in the recipe. The dish’s flavor totally depends on enhancing it with this second round of seasoning. \n\tWhen the meat is done, break 5 eggs into the pot, leave them whole so that they look like the stars (kawākib). Using a knife, cut good quality bread into bite-size pieces, and put them in a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya). Moisten the bread with some melted butter, and ladle the broth all over it. Arrange the meat pieces and chard stalks around the t͟harīd and garnish it with the poached eggs and the cheese after you cut it into smaller pieces. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for delicious mulabbaqa (bread softened and enriched with fat), made with laban rāyib:[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (8 cups) sour yogurt (laban rāyib ḥāmiḍ) and thicken it in a pot on the fire, the way you do with mad͟hīra. Add 1 mann (2 pounds) white Sulaymānī sugar, and keep on stirring the pot for a while (sāʿa, an hour). \n\tSprinkle into the pot sifted crumbled pith of white bread, which has been rubbed and moistened with sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). Add as needed. Keep on stirring the pot for about an hour until mixture resembles mulabbaqāt in consistency. \n\tLadle the mulabbaqa into a qaṣʿa (wide bowl big enough for 10 people) and arrange around it meat of sikbāj (stew soured with vinegar) or meat of any other varieties of yellow and sour stews. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another t͟harīda also by him:[/b]\nBoil milk in a pot. Add fatty meat cut into medium-size pieces, soaked chickpeas, chard, cilantro, and afwāh al-ṭīb. When meat is cooked, take it out of the pot along with the chard and chickpeas, and put them in another pot with some of the broth, and set them aside. \n\tLightly knead the remaining broth in the pot with pounded bread, which has previously been dried in the tannūr. Let this mixture be thicker in consistency than k͟hiṭmī, but thinner than dough prepared for furrānī bread. Add to the bread mixture some clarified butter (samn) to moisten it. Let it cook then cool it down. \n\tLadle the cooked bread into qaṣʿa (wide bowl big enough for 10 people) as you usually do . Arrange the meat around it, give it a dusting of white sugar, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for white t͟harīda by al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nTake a disjointed chicken, kid meat, or mutton. Wash it and put it in a pot. Add soaked chickpeas, zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil), galangal and cassia, a piece of each, and a small amount of salt. \n\tBring the pot to a boil and remove the scum. Strain into it some milk and add round onions and boiled carrots. When the pot comes to a good boil, stir into it ground skinned almonds, which have been whipped with 5 eggs and wine vinegar. Season the pot with coriander and a small amount of black pepper and cumin. Let the pot simmer for a while then put it away from heat and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for t͟harīda ʿIrāqiyya (Iraqi style):[/b]\nChoose fatty meat and cut it into pieces suitable for serving with the t͟harīd. Put the meat in a pot and pour enough water to submerge it. Add as well a little salt, vinegar, and a small amount of chopped onion. Light the fire underneath the pot and bring it to a boil. \n\tSprinkle some milk into the pot and add whole onions. Of spices, add black pepper, caraway, and coriander seeds, all tied in a bundle of linen cloth. Add to the pot sprigs of fresh rue and parsley tied together in a bundle and let it cook until meat is done. \n\tIn another pot, put skinned and ground almonds. Add to them enough of the meat broth through a sieve. Stir the mixture and let it boil. Next, strain into it the rest of the meat broth, or if too much is left, add what you estimate to be enough to saturate the bread you are planning to use for the t͟harīd directions for bread given below. Add sugar to taste. Set aside the cooked meat pieces \n\tTake a roasted or a boiled chicken, shred its meat into fine threads, and add it to the almond-broth mix. \n\tNow take rag͟hīf furnī (brick oven bread) made with fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), crumble it, pass it through a sieve (g͟hirbāl), and add it to the almond broth. \n\tTake as well, tannūr bread made with māssa (low-gluten wheat) or samīd͟h flour. Crumble it and pass it through a sieve used for sifting k͟hus͟hkār (whole-wheat flour). Toss the breadcrumbs into the pot of almond-broth, light a weak fire underneath it, and let it cook. Stir it constantly and feed it with the fat skimmed from the pot, or use clarified butter. \n\tLadle the bread into a big wide bowl, arrange the meat pieces all around it, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for qaliyya by al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nCut meat into thin slices. Heat some oil in a pot, put the meat slices in it, and sprinkle them with some salted water. When meat is cooked, add coriander, cumin, and a trifle of black pepper (rāʾiḥat fulful). \n\tWhen the meat absorbs enough salt, take some of the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and crush it with skinned and ground almonds. Sprinkle the meat first with some wine vinegar then spread the crushed onion and almonds all over the meat. Do not stir the pot to keep this layer visible, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Levantine fried dish (qaliyya S͟hāmiyya) by al-Muʿtaṣim:[/b]\nChoose lamb with good strong ribs and divide it into portions, crosswise. Put it in a pot along with shoulder meat, cut into bite-size pieces; and a similar amount of sheep’s tail fat (alya). Sprinkle meat with sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and light the fire underneath the pot. \n\tBoil chickpeas and set them aside. \n\tWhen the meat starts frying, add a little chopped onion and sprinkle it with salted water. When it is partially cooked, add the boiled chickpeas along with coriander, caraway, a bit of black pepper, and cassia, all ground. \n\tBeat 10 eggs in a bowl with a small amount of spices and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). When meat is fully cooked, add the beaten egg mixture. Stir the pot until mixture fries. If wished, sprinkle the dish with wine vinegar. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for Levantine qaliyya:[/b]\nTake shoulder meat from a slaughtered sheep in its third year (t͟hanī) and cut the lean chunks into pieces, the size of a dice (nard) each. Do the same thing with the alya (sheep’s tail fat). Wash the meat, bring it to one boil, take it out of the pot, and set it aside. \n\tTake carrots—double the amount of meat—and cut them into portions, as big as walnuts. Boil them in the meat broth remaining in the pot until almost done then take them out. You can also boil them with some soaked chickpeas. Spread carrot pieces on a tray made of k͟hilāf wood (willow) to drain them. \n\tPut a frying pan on the fire and pour into it sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) or fresh sesame oil (s͟hayraj ṭarī). Fry the drained carrots and chickpeas until they brown then take them out of the pan and set them aside. \n\tPut the remaining oil in a soapstone pot and add the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), coriander, cumin, caraway, ground cassia, 1½ dānaq (¾ gram) black pepper, and saffron. Add the boiled meat and fry it with the spices. When it is fully cooked, add a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and a similar amount of the meat broth. Put the pot away from the heat and stir into it the fried carrots and chickpeas if used. Ladle it into a platter and serve it. \n\tYou may turn the dish into mamqūr (soused with vinegar) by adding vinegar along with the murrī, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Qaliyya recipe from Madāʾin (madāyiniyya):[/b]\nCut into long strips meat from shoulders and ribs. Put it in a soapstone pot with a little salt, and olive oil. Fry the meat. When it browns, sprinkle it with a mixture of water and ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) ground walnuts. \n\tWhen all moisture evaporates and meat is cooked, add more fat, and chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Season it with ground coriander. Add as well ground caraway, cumin, and cassia, the amount of all these taken together should be equal to that of coriander. Also add a tiny bit of saffron (rāʾiḥat zaʿfarān). \n\tLet the pot simmer with the remaining heat. When it settles, add murrī (liquid fermented sauce), sprinkle it with bruised walnut, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another qaliyya, yellow:[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (4 pounds) of fatty lamb. Keep the fat on the ribs. Cut the ribs and the shoulder meat into two-finger wide strips. Wash them and put them in a pot and add olive oil, salt, and white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). \n\tFry the meat, pour on it 1 raṭl (2 cups) water, and let it cook until it is done and all moisture has evaporated. When the meat starts to fry in the pot’s fat, add dry spices and let it fry well until it browns. \n\tNow, mix 1 raṭl (2 cups) vinegar with ½ dirham (1½ grams) saffron and stir it into the pot along with chopped rue and parsley. When the pot boils, stop fuelling the fire and let it simmer in the remaining heat until it settles. Ladle the dish onto a platter and serve it with all kinds of fresh herbs (baql). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for black qaliyya:[/b]\nChoose tender lean meat and plump alya (sheep’s tail fat) and cut them into small pieces, the size of a hazelnut each. Half boil the meat and alya then ladle them out and set them aside. Also ladle out all the broth and set it aside. \n\tPut olive oil in the pot first then spread the alya pieces on it followed by the meat pieces. Let the meat fry in the fat until it cooks and browns. Add coriander, cumin, caraway, and cassia, all ground. \n\tNow mix murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and the reserved broth. Let a third of it be murrī and two-thirds broth, or adjust the amounts to suit your taste. Pour this mixture over the meat, stop fuelling the fire (taqṭaʿ al-nār), and let the pot simmer in the remaining heat until it settles. Serve it with peeled k͟hiyār (smooth and small cucumber). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Qaliyya made with onion:[/b]\nCut fatty meat into small pieces and put it in a soapstone frying pan (maqlā birām). Stir into it a similar amount of chopped onion, chopped alya (sheep’s tail fat), sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb), and 1 raṭl (2 cups) water. \n\tCook the meat until it is done. Sprinkle it with dry spices and continue frying until it browns (yaḥmarr) and drowns (yag͟hraq) in its own oil. When it is thoroughly cooked, sprinkle it with a little salted water. Wait until it simmers and settles in the remaining heat then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Qaliyya with eggplant (bād͟hinjān) and gourd (qarʿ), quite tasty:[/b]\nCut fatty and tender meat into small pieces and put it in a pot which already has boiling water in it, enough to submerge the meat. Add as well chopped gourd and peeled small eggplants. Let all the ingredients boil together. Take out the gourd before it is fully cooked, but leave the eggplant until it is fully done. If you take it out before it is done and let it get cold, it will toughen and will never really cook well. \n\tTake the meat out of the pot and ladle the broth out from the bottom of the pot and set it aside. Pour into the pot some duhn and sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib), along with chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and ground dry spices. Return the meat and let it fry until it browns. Add the gourd and fry it with it until it is cooked. Stir in the eggplant and continue frying, adding more fat. \n\tMix murrī (liquid fermented sauce) with saffron, cassia, and the set aside meat broth, the amount of which should be equal to that of murrī. Pour the mix into the pot. Now, stop feeding the fire and let the pot simmer in the remaining heat and settle (iqṭab al-nār wa haddihā). \n\tYou have the option of making it sour by replacing the murrī with vinegar and cumin. Ladle the dish and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for black qaliyya by al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nPound good quality sumac, boil some water, and pour it on the sumac to let it macerate for an hour or so. Strain the sumac juice. You may repeat the process of soaking and straining to get more juice, thus you do not waste any of it. However, do not use any of the subsequent strained liquids for this dish. \n\tFinely grind ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) almonds and mix it with the first batch of the strained sumac juice (al-fum al-awwal). Set this aside \n\tCut 3 raṭls (3 pounds) meat of fat lamb into small thin slices. Wash it and put it in a pot that already has 1 raṭl (2 cups) of water boiling in it. Add sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and ½ raṭl (½ pound) dissolved chicken fat. Feed the fire underneath it and let it cook until meat is done. Season it with ground coriander, cumin, caraway, cassia, dried naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). Add chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), and pour the reserved sumac-almond mixture. \n\tLet the pot cook until moisture evaporates and meat develops a blackish hue. Do not let it burn and dry out. The dish should still have some moisture in it. Pound a lump of sugar and sprinkle it over the meat. Wait until the pot settles and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A succulent fry (qaliyya raṭba) by al-Ṣūlī:[/b]\nChoose meat from the fore legs of a yearling sheep (ḥawlī). Dice it along with some alya (sheep’s tail fat). Boil the meat in a pot \n\tPeel stems of large heads of lettuce and cut them into walnut-size pieces. Add these to the meat cooking in the pot along with soaked chickpeas. Do it the same way you did with the gourd. \n\tWhen ingredients in the pot are almost done, take them out. Keep the broth aside after straining it and let the meat, chickpeas, and lettuce stems drain. \n\tPut plenty of fat in the pot. Add galangal (k͟hūlanj), 3 round onions (baṣal mudawwar) chopped, and some spices. Return the meat to the pot along with the chickpeas and lettuce stem pieces. Fry the meat until it browns, season it again with spices, and pour on it equal amounts of murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and vinegar. If you use lemon juice (māʾ laymū) instead of vinegar, it would be even more delicious. \n\tSprinkle the meat with a small amount of the meat broth that has been stirred with ½ dirham (1½ grams) saffron. Scatter on the meat a fistful of picked over zabīb (raisins) or sugar. Let the pot simmer in the remaining heat until it settles and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a fried dish called ‘qaliyyat Um Ḥakīm’:[/b]\nChoose red meat from kis͟htamāzaj (tenderloin), the front shoulder, and sheep’s tail fat (alya). Chop them all into small pieces and wash them. Boil water in a clean pot, enough to reach just below the meat. Cook the meat in it then take it out and set it aside. \n\tPour olive oil into a clean frying pan, add the tail fat first, and let it fry until all solids dissolve. Add the meat to it with chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and fry the meat until it browns. Sprinkle it with ground coriander, caraway, cassia, spikenard, and a small amount of cloves. \n\tSpread the meat evenly in the frying pan, and break 10 eggs on it. Do not disturb the eggs and wait until they set (lā tuḥarrikhu). They will look like cow’s eyes (ʿuyūn al-baqar). Give it a dusting of crushed salt and present it with wine vinegar and herbs (baql) or peeled k͟hiyār (small and smooth cucumber), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for qaliyya with truffles (kamʾa):[/b]\nTake thin slices of fatty meat and truffles sliced into rounds like dirhams (coins). Boil them until done then take them out of the pot and set them aside with a small amount of the meat broth. \n\tSet up a frying pan with a concave bottom on the fire. Fry the meat, two to three slices at a time then fry the truffles, like you do with sanbūsaj (filled pastries). Put the fried meat and truffles on a plate (ṣaḥn). \n\tPut some of the oil you used for frying the meat and truffles in a pot, and fry in it chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Season it with black pepper, coriander, caraway, cumin, and a tiny amount of crushed asafetida leaves (anjud͟hān). Pour on it some murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and vinegar, and what equals both of them of the broth. When mixture comes to a boil, pour it all over the meat and truffles on the plate. If you like, toss the dish with some mustard sauce (k͟hardal maʿmūl), and chop on it some rue. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another qaliyya, called al-Madīniyya:[/b]\nTake 3 raṭls (3 pounds) ribs of lamb, separate them into individual ribs, and cut them into a little shorter than finger-length pieces. Put them in a pot, and pour on them 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) water. Cook them on the fire, stirring them constantly. You may need to replenish the water so they do not dry out. Then add ½ raṭl (1 cup) sour vinegar. \n\tWhen meat is done and all moisture has evaporated, spice it with what the fingers can hold of coriander, 2 dirhams (6 grams) black pepper, and 2 dirhams (6 grams) caraway seeds. Also add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) murrī (liquid fermented sauce) mixed with saffron and cassia, ½ dirham (1½ grams) each. \n\tLet the pot simmer in the remaining heat of the embers (jamr). Sprinkle on it 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) nabīd͟h rayḥānī (sweet smelling wine) and wipe the inner sides of the pot with another ūqiyya of the wine. Cover the pot and let it settle, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for kus͟htābiyya cooked in its own juice, from the copy of Ibn ʿUmar:[/b]\nCut meat into thin slices, wash it thoroughly, and put it in a pot. Add 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil), a bit of salt, and a sprig of rue. Set the pot on the fire (yunṣab) on a trivet and cover it so that the meat releases all its moisture. Season it with black pepper, coriander, a bit if cassia, and a small amount of māʾ kāmak͟h (murrī, liquid fermented sauce). Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another kus͟htābiyya dish from the copy of Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nCut meat into very thin slices and put it in a pot. Let the meat be lamb (laḥm ḥaml). Add chicken fat or oil and 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) onion juice, and let it fry. Sprinkle the meat while frying with lemon juice mixed with an equal amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tWhen the meat is done, season it with coriander, cumin, and a bit of black pepper. Ladle it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another kus͟htābiyya recipe cooked with juice of sour unripe grapes:[/b]\nSlice the meat, wash it and put it in a soapstone pot. Add bruised chickpeas and chopped cilantro. Add as well a piece of galangal and 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). \n\tWhen meat is cooked, season it with ground coriander, cumin, and cassia. Ladle the dish. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for kus͟htābiyya seasoned (maftūqa) with vinegar:[/b]\nCut marbled meat (laḥm mujazzaʿ) into thin slices and put it in a soapstone pot. Add some vinegar to the meat and let it cook until done. \n\tSprinkle it with juice of sour unripe grapes, season it with ground spices, and sprinkle it with a small amount of maṭbūk͟h (cooked wine). (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Kus͟htābiyya recipe by Ibn ʿUmar:[/b]\nCut tender meat into very thin slices and marinate it in some murrī for about an hour. Take the meat out, sprinkle it with lots of ground coriander, cumin, caraway, and a bit of black pepper. Fry the meat in fat and sprinkle it with maṭbūk͟h (cooked wine) and water. When meat is done, chop some cilantro and rue on it then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for kus͟htābiyya kabadiyya (made with liver) by al-Hādī:[/b]\nSlice the liver, wash it in cold water, and marinate it in vinegar for an hour. Then wash it to get rid of vinegar and put it in a pot with 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) olive oil and a similar amount of duhn. Fry the liver until it firms up then sprinkle it with Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Stir the pot until liver is cooked. \n\tSeason the dish with spices such as coriander, cumin, and caraway and a bit of black pepper. Chop rue on it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for kus͟htābiyya by al-Hādī, too:[/b]\nCut tender meat into small pieces, as small as a chickpea each. Wash the meat and put it in a pot. Submerge it in olive oil and rendered sheep’s tail fat or chicken fat. Fry the meat and stir in a small amount of rue, cilantro, onion juice, and soaked and skinned chickpeas. Sprinkle it with a bit of murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and wine vinegar. \n\tWhen meat is done, pour on it a small amount of sakanjabīn al-k͟hall (syrup of vinegar and honey). Season it with coriander and black pepper. After you ladle it into a plate, sprinkle it with some rose water and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another kus͟htābiyya called qaranfuliyya (cooked with cloves) by Ḥāmid:[/b]\nChoose tenderloins and any other tender cuts of lamb. Cut the meat into very thin slices, put them in a clean green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra), and keep them submerged in brine from the time of morning prayers dawn until the forenoon (ḍaḥwa). \n\tDiscard the bran and wash the meat until it looks white. Put it in a clean pot and add a stick of cassia, a piece of galangal, and 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). Cook the pot on low-heat fire (nār hādiya). You will not need to add any water because the meat will release a lot of moisture. \n\tWhen the pot boils twice (g͟halyatayn), add a handful of soaked and bruised chickpeas. Add as well 20 dirhams (¼ cup) onion juice, 3 dirhams (9 grams) salt, a whole sprig of rue, and 20 dirhams (¼ cup) distilled water of cloves (māʾ qaranlful muṣabbad). \n\tWhen the meat is done, moisten it with a cup (qadaḥ) of aromatic sweet wine (s͟harāb ʿaṭir ḥilū) and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṭabāhija by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nCut meat into slices and wash it thoroughly. Boil ½ raṭl (1 cup) water in a pot add the meat to it along with sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and a little salt. Then add peeled and chopped eggplant and round onions. \n\tWhen meat is done and moisture has evaporated, sprinkle on it half a ladleful of māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce) and, if wished, half a ladleful of vinegar. Now, take some ground spices such as coriander, caraway, cassia, and cumin. Sprinkle a little bit of each on the meat. Stir the pot for a while (sāʿa, an hour) then wash the inner sides of the pot with a ladleful of water and add two sprigs of rue. Let the pot simmer in the remaining heat for a while (sāʿa, an hour) until it settles then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṭabāhija with fresh cheese (jubn raṭb):[/b]\nCut meat into thin slices, wash it, and put it in a pot. Pour plenty of olive oil and add a bit of salt. Set the pot on a trivet (yunṣab) on the fire, and let it boil until all moisture evaporates. Sprinkle the meat with a little black pepper and anjud͟hān (dried asafetida leaves). \n\tTake fresh cheese that has been kept in brine for 10 days, wash it to get rid of the salt, and slice and cut it into triangles (s͟hawābīr). Spread the cheese pieces in the pot and let them fry with the meat. \n\tWhisk 10 eggs with māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce) and pour them all over the meat mix. Let the eggs cook until they set then serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṭabāhija from the copy of Yaḥya bin K͟hālid:[/b]\nTake a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra). Pour into it ¼ raṭl (½ cup) Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) good quality honey. Whip them together and strain them in a sieve. Season them with 1 dirham (3 grams) coriander, ½ dirham (1½ grams) cassia, and 2 dānaqs (1 gram) black pepper. \n\tCut 2 raṭls (2 pounds) tender meat into wide thin slices and marinate it in this above sauce (ṣibāg͟h) for an hour. \n\tPlace a pot on the fire and pour 4 ūqiyyas (½ cup) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). Let the oil boil then add the meat with its marinade along with 2 dānaqs (1 gram) crushed salt. Cook the meat until it is done and liquid has evaporated. \n\tLadle the meat into a platter. Garnish it with small amounts of chopped cilantro, rue, and mustard greens (k͟hardal ak͟hḍar) then present it. \n\tYou may make the dish ṭabāhija anjud͟hāniyya by adding to it dried asafetida leaves. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṭabāhija from the copy of ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmar, which Abū Samīn Made for al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nTake slices of meat from a fat kid or a yearling lamb and cut them into finger-like strips. Put them in a pot with a suitable amount of salt. Pour ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil and ¼ raṭl (½ cup) water. Set the pot on the fire and let it cook until all moisture evaporates. \n\tMeanwhile pour into a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra) 1 raṭl (2 cups) wine vinegar. Stir in ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) finely ground walnuts or almonds, and 5 dirhams (15 grams) ground and sifted crumbs of white bread. Whip the mixture very well. Add a small amount of it to the pot, let it evaporate then add a little more, and let it evaporate. Repeat the procedure until you use up all the vinegar mix. \n\tSeason the meat with a bit of black pepper, cumin, and a little coriander. Let the meat fry in its juices and oil then take the pot away from the fire and serve the dish. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṭabāhija made with honey by al-Muʿtaṣim:[/b]\nTake 3 raṭls (3 pounds) meat from a yearling lamb. Let it be red (i.e. lean) and free of any fat. Slice the meat and wash it very well. \n\tBoil 1½ raṭls (3 cups) water and drop in it a bundle of linen cloth containing coriander, cumin, and cassia. Add the meat and let it cook until the pot is almost dry. Discard the spice bundle. Pour into the pot ½ raṭl (1 cup) fresh sesame oil and ¼ raṭl (½ cup) rendered chicken fat. Let the meat cook until it fries in its oil and browns. \n\tAdd to the pot, 1 dānaq (½ gram) ginger and 2 dānaqs (1 gram) saffron, both ground. Pour into it 2 raṭls (2 pounds) boiled and skimmed honey and bring the pot to a boil. \n\tTake 4 ūqiyyas (4 ounces) starch (nas͟hā). Dissolve it in 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) rose water and 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) water. Pour this into the pot and keep stirring until sauce thickens. \n\tTake away the fire from underneath the pot and keep stirring in the remaining heat until the oil separates and comes up (yaqd͟hif duhnahu). Put the pot away from the fire and ladle it into a dish. You should have prepared shelled and bruised walnuts or almonds. Scatter them over the dish and serve it. \n\tYou have the option of substituting the starch with fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). In this case, add the flour before you pour the honey into the pot to let it toast in the fat (i.e. when only meat and oil are left in the pot). Then, add the honey, stir the pot until sauce thickens, and take away the fire from underneath the pot as you did above. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṭabāhija by al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nSlice the meat as thin as possible and wash it. Pound onion in a mortar and pestle to extract its juice. You need to get 15 dirhams (3 tablespoons) of the onion juice. \n\tPut a pot on the fire and pour into it sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and chopped tallow (s͟haḥm). When the tallow fries, add the meat and let it fry in it. Pour the onion juice and let it cook until all the liquid is absorbed. \n\tSeason the meat with coriander, cumin, caraway, black pepper, and ginger, all ground. When the meat fries with the spices, stir into it murrī al-s͟haʿīr (liquid fermented sauce made with barley) mixed with ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) ground almonds or ground sesame seeds. \n\tLet the pot simmer and settle on the burning coals. When the time comes to serve it, sprinkle it with fragrant wine (s͟harāb ʿaṭir) or rose water and garnish it with chopped rue, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṭabāhija, called um al-ṭabāhijāt (the mother of all ṭabāhijāt):[/b]\nSlice 3 raṭls (3 pounds) meat from a yearling lamb, wash it, and put it in a pot. Pour ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil, ¼ raṭl (½ cup) rendered fat of sheep’s tail, and 2 dirhams (6 grams) salt. Sprinkle the meat with about ½ raṭl (1 cup) water. It should be enough to cook the meat and then evaporate. \n\tSo, when the meat is cooked and the pot is dry, add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) murrī ṭarī (freshly made liquid fermented sauce). Sprinkle the meat with black pepper and ginger, 1 dirham (3 grams) each. Also add a suitable amount of coriander, caraway, and cassia. \n\tNow, ladle one third of the cooked meat onto a plate and serve it. It will be a delicious ṭabāhija. To the remaining two thirds, add 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) vinegar. Ladle out the second third onto a plate and serve it. Wait until what was served is eaten then ladle the last third remaining in the pot onto a plate, garnish it with 1 dirham (3 grams) finely chopped rue and serve it. This will be another delicious variation on ṭabāhija. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Ṭabāhija made with young fowls (firāk͟h) and their livers:[/b]\nMix chicken fat with salt. Disjoint plump young fowls, and fry them in the chicken fat. When they are almost cooked, season them with coriander and black pepper. Sprinkle them with Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and stir in some chopped rue and parsley. Serve the dish when fully cooked. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ṭabāhija made with honey:[/b]\nIn a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra), mix to blend (yumāth) ¼ raṭl (½ cup) murrī (liquid fermented sauce) with 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) honey. Strain the mix through a sieve (munk͟hul). Add 1dirham (3 grams) coriander, ½ dirham (1½ grams) black pepper, 2 dānaqs (1 gram) cassia, and 2 dānaqs (1 gram) anjud͟hān (dried asafetida leaves). \n\tSlice 2 raṭls (2 pounds) lamb and marinate it in the above sauce (ṣibāg͟h). Set up a pot (yunṣab) on a trivet on the fire and add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib). When the oil is hot, add the sliced meat with its marinade along with 2 dānaqs (1 gram) crushed salt. \n\tCook the meat until the sauce (ṣibāg͟h) is greatly reduced. Let the pot settle for a while (sāʿa, an hour) then serve the ṭabāhija garnished with chopped cilantro and rue. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for janb mubazzar (spiced side of ribs) by Yaḥya bin K͟hālid al-Barmakī:[/b]\nTake side of ribs of a fat lamb, clean it and remove the spinal cord (nuk͟hāb), nodules (g͟hudad), isfīd͟haj, liver (kabd), spleen (ṭiḥāl), and kidney (kulwa) if any are still attached. \n\tKeep the meat marinated overnight in a mix of vinegar, a handful of salt, and a couple handfuls of ground dry spices—coriander, cumin, black pepper, and cassia. The following morning, take the side of ribs out of its marinade and moisten it with a fresh batch of vinegar and spices. Lower the side of ribs into the heated tannūr, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for spiced side of ribs (janb mubazzar) by him, too:[/b]\nTake a side of ribs of a lamb and boil it in extremely sour vinegar until half done. Take the pot away from the heat and leave the side of ribs in it until it cools down. Then take it out, rub it with the dried spices mentioned earlier, and lower it into the heated tannūr. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for roasting liver with the windpipe (qaṣabat miʿlāq) by Ibn ʿUmar:[/b]\nTake the liver with windpipe and lungs attached to it. Clean them and blow into the pipe to inflate the lungs. Pour into it a mixture of vinegar, olive oil, ground caraway seeds, and 1 dirham (3 grams) salt. Lower it into the heated tannūr, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ʿuṣbān (long strips of meat, wrapped in caul fat, and tied with intestines) by al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nTake livers of kids and sheep and parboil them in water seasoned with thyme and olive oil. Take them out of the water and cut them into fine strips (siyūr riqāq). After you do this, lay flat pieces of caul fat (t͟harb) of kids and lamb after you wash them in hot water so that they open up flat. Spread the liver strips on them and sprinkle them with murrī and olive oil. Put some sprigs of rue and thyme. \n\tRoll the caul fat around the liver strips and tie it with intestines (maṣārīn) that have been turned inside out and washed with salt and parsley and water. Rub the roll with olive oil and lower it into the tannūr. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for janb mubazzar (spiced side of ribs), can be eaten immediately, from the copy of Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nParboil a side of ribs of lamb in good quality sour vinegar. Put the pot away from the fire and leave the side of ribs in the vinegar until it cools down. Take it out of the vinegar and press out all moisture thoroughly. Sprinkle it with ground coriander, cumin, black pepper, and cassia, and lower it into the heated tannūr until it is crisp (yaqubb). \n\tIf wished, after you parboil the side of ribs in vinegar, take it out of the hot vinegar and immediately put it in cold vinegar. When it cools down, season it with the spices and lower it into the tannūr. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for dākibriyān:[/b]\nThis is the name of the dish in Persian. In Arabic, it means s͟hawī al-qidr (pot-roasting). \n\tTake a soapstone pot with high sides, make six holes around the side, and let them be spaced so that each two holes are opposite each other. The holes should be half way between the top of the pot (s͟hiffatuha its lip) and its bottom. Insert three trimmed sticks of willow wood (k͟hilāf) through the holes and let them be long enough to stick out of the pot. This will serve as a rack. Seal the holes from the outside of the pot with dough. \n\tPour water into the pot and let it be just below the sticks. Add a piece of galangal and a stick of cassia. \n\tNow take a piece of a fatty side of ribs of lamb with the shoulder. Clean it, sprinkle it with salt then rub it with olive oil, and put it on the arranged sticks in the pot. Cover the pot and seal it tightly with mud. \n\tLight medium-high fire (nār mutawassiṭa) underneath the pot and let it cook until according to your estimate it is done. Uncover the pot, take out the meat, and set it aside. Add rice and milk to the broth in the pot and cook it the way you do with jūd͟hāb. You may add honey, sugar, saffron, or anything else that is usually added to the jūd͟hābāt, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for roasted meat (s͟hiwāʾ) that resembles halām by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake fresh and dry herbs and spices usually used for making halām and stuff with them a fine and fat kid, which has been cleaned and scalded. Stuff the cavity, and make slits (yus͟harraḥ) under the skin and stuff them with the herb and spice mix. \n\tTake a soapstone pot oblong in shape like a safaṭ, and spread in its bottom some of the ahlām spices. Next, place the prepared kid in the pot and spread the ahlām spices all over it. Submerge it in sour vinegar and let it steep in it for a night and a day. Take the kid out of the vinegar, impale it in a fish-roasting spit (saffūd samak), fasten it with ropes (s͟harīṭ), and lower it into the heated tannūr. Serve it hot, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for an enveloped (mag͟hmūm) kid, stuffed with a chicken:[/b]\nClean and scald a suckling kid (jedī raḍīʿ) and a plump chicken. Rub the chicken with a lot of oil and sprinkle it with salt and black pepper. Wrap it in caul fat and stuff it inside the kid. Wrap the kid with caul fat of a fat lamb. \n\tNow take a large kars͟h (stomach), leave it whole, just make an opening large enough to get the kid into it. Scald it, and wash it with salt and parsley. Stuff the kid inside the stomach, and sew it closed. Put the stuffed tripe in tannūr al-rawwās and let it roast slowly overnight. \n\tPrepare for the dish a dipping sauce of toasted mustard seeds, ground and sweetened with crushed zabīb (raisins), sugar, and other similar ingredients. Serve it with the roasted kid after you remove the caul fat (t͟harb). You will eat the meat, the bones, the skin, and the chicken inside it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for roasting braided ṣafāfīr:[/b]\nTake a tender and fatty tenderloin (bas͟htamāzaj), which weighs around 2 raṭls (2 pounds), keep the long piece whole. Choose also, liver of a weaned camel (faṣīl). Let it be as long as the tenderloin and weigh as much. Take as well, a piece of the camel hump, of similar length and weight. Slice lengthwise each of these pieces into finger-thick strips. Marinate them in a mixture of murrī (liquid fermented sauce), black pepper, sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb), coriander, cumin, and pounded cassia. \n\tNow take a strip of each of the three kinds of meat and pin them together from one end with a toothpick (k͟hilāl). Braid the meat strips as you do with hair and tie the ends so that they do not open up. Repeat with the rest of the meat strips. \n\tSmear the braids with a mix of murrī and olive oil. Skewer them in saffūd or k͟huṭṭāf (hooked rod), which you then suspend in the tannūr and let the meat roast until it is cooked. \n\tBring the braids to the table while still hot, cut them into fist-size pieces (qabḍa), and eat them with the following sauce. [b]The sauce recipe:[/b]\nTake anjud͟hān (dried asafetida leaves), black pepper, and galangal, 3 dirhams (9 grams) each. Take as well, 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) Persian thyme (ṣaʿtar Fārisī). Pound them all, sift them, and stir them into wine vinegar and aged murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tServe this sauce with the roasted meat above. It will be a splendid dish, indeed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for janb mas͟hwī (roasted side of ribs):[/b]\nTake the side of ribs of a small lamb, slash it at several places, and rub it with salt, vinegar, anjud͟hān (dried asafetida leaves), and thyme. Hook it in a kullāb (hooked rod), and lower it into the tannūr, but let it be suspended above a pot with water and ruqāq al-sanbūsaj in it. Let the distance between the meat and the water be about the width of four fingers put together. Seal the opening of the tannūr with mud and let meat roast until it is done. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for a roasted spiced side of ribs (mubazzar) by abū Samīn:[/b]\nClean a side of ribs and remove the spinal cord and any organs attached to it. Wash the meat in salted water, dry it very well and then soak it in sumac juice (māʾ al-summāq), and keep it there until it absorbs the tartness of the juice. \n\tRub the meat with spices, attach it to a hooked skewer, and lower it into the tannūr. When it is done, take it out and serve it hot. \n\tIf you wish, substitute sumac juice with juice of sour unripe grapes (māʾ hiṣrim). \n\tAbū al-Ḥusayn al-Kātib once recited to me this poem: \n[i]For my honored guest I have bread; pure, crisp, and well risen,\nSpread on a tray, easily mistaken for the luminous moon in beauty.\nA side of ribs of lamb as well, bounteous, spiced, vinegared, redolent, and saffroned,\nWhich our excellent cook fixed and infused with spices, salt, and murrī.\nAromatics he freely tossed and kept it overnight thus. At crack of dawn he resumed.\nHe lighted the tannūr for it. After it was done flaring with flames and sparks,\nHe lowered the meat, sealed the tannūr, and left it for an hour waiting,\nUntil, to his estimate, the meat by then was surely off the bones falling.\nHe took it out and a dust of coriander gave it: Ethereal, glowing with saffron.\nLooking like busr dates, fresh and crisp and ripe.\nHe thus hastened to us with it. The best alike, whether you tell or show it.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for a Kid Stuffed with Truffles (kamʾa):[/b]\nChoose a fine fat kid, remove its entrails and make from them small and thin ʿaṣābīn. Let the cook detach the thigh meat of the kid from under the skin taking care not to tear the skin or spoil it in anyway. Now, separate the meat from the bones—from the inner side of the thigh—starting with the lowest part of the rump all the way down to the trotters. Do the same thing with the fore legs. Keep the bones intact and do not disjoint them. \n\tTake the meat you have already separated from the bones, discard any blood vessels (ʿurūq) and nodules (g͟hudad), and slice it thinly. [b]Filling the belly:[/b]\nPut in a pot, a third of the sliced meat along with the prepared ʿaṣābīn, and pour on them ¼ raṭl (½ cup) olive oil. Add ½ raṭl (½ pound) chopped onion, 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) chopped cilantro, ½ raṭl (1 cup) wine vinegar, 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) Nabatean murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and ½ raṭl (1 cup) water. Let the mixture boil for a short while and then add ½ mit͟hqāl (2¼ grams) saffron, 3 dirhams (9 grams) coriander, and 1 dirham (3 grams) cassia. Add as well black pepper, ginger, long pepper (dār fulful), spikenard, and galangal, ½ dirham (1½ grams) each. \n\tPut the pot away from heat and wait until it settles. Add chopped truffles, the amount of which should be equal to that of the ʿaṣābīn used. Also add jarādiq (thick round bread), equal in amount to the sliced meat used. Stir to mix the ingredients then set the pot aside to cool down. Now, put the meat mixture in a new and washed strainer made of rush stems (g͟hirbāl asal). The reason why you need to wait for meat to cool down before draining it in this kind of strainer is because hot meat picks up the smell of the rush wood easily, which would spoil it. Leave the meat mixture in the strainer until all moisture drains. \n\tPut the meat in a big bowl (qaṣʿa), sprinkle it with a littl
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sliced meat (s͟harāyiḥ) roasted in the tannūr:[/b]\nSlice meat into long strips and put it in a big bowl (qaṣʿa). Add salt, olive oil, juice of cilantro, and ¼ dirham (¾ gram) ground anjud͟hān (asafetida leaves). Let the meat marinate in this sauce until it absorbs its flavors. Coat the meat slices with olive oil, thread them through a skewer (saffūd), and lower it into the tannūr. \n\tIn a small bowl (uskurruja) mix vinegar, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), anjud͟hān (asafetida leaves), and caraway. Serve this dipping sauce with the meat, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for roasted udder (ḍarʿ mas͟hwī) by Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nTake a big udder, wash it from the outside, and slash it at places where libaʾ (first milk after delivery) would not squirt out of them. \n\tMix milk and murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and coat the udder with the mix (taṭlīhi). Next, coat it with olive oil, sprinkle it with a little cassia and ginger, and lower it into the tannūr. \n\tWhen it is roasted, take it out, slice it nicely, and serve it with mustard, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for janb mubazzar (spiced side of ribs) by Abū Samīn:[/b]\nChoose a fatty side of ribs and marinade it in a mixture of 1 raṭl (2 cups) vinegar, 1 raṭl (1 pound) pomegranate seeds, and ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) zabīb (raisins). Let the side of ribs steep from the evening until the following morning. \n\tTake it out, and spice it with black pepper, coriander, 1 dānaq (½ gram) pounded anjud͟hān (asafetida leaves), and pounded cassia. Coat the meat liberally with olive oil and salt then lower it into a low-heat tannūr (layyin al-ḥarāra), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for roasted s͟harāyiḥ (sliced meat):[/b]\nPour strained thick vinegar into a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra). Add zabīb (raisins), pomegranate seeds, and two to three cloves of garlic crushed with coriander seeds. Let the meat slices steep in this mixture for two hours. \n\tTake out the meat slices and press on them the strained pomegranate seeds, which have been steeping in vinegar. . Set the meat slices aside for an hour and roast them in the tannūr. \n\tEat the meat with vinegar seasoned with anjud͟hān (asafetida leaves) and cumin. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jerked meat (qadīd):[/b]\nTake antelope meat (luḥūm ẓibā) or any other tender variety, cut it into thin and long slices, macerate them in salted vinegar until they absorb the flavor then drape them on a rope. \n\tThe meat slices can be roasted in the tannūr if they still have some moisture in them. They will come out as regular roasted meat slices (s͟harāyiḥ) or even better as they will be brittle and light and crumble in the mouth when eaten. \n\tThey can also be fried but they need to be sprinkled with a little water while frying. This will be similar to fried meat dishes (qalāyā). \n\tIf you like, wind the meat slices while still fresh around reeds or sticks of willow wood (k͟hilāf). When they dry out on the sticks, put them in a slow burning tannūr, where they will further dry and roast a little. Serve them in a bowl (ṭayfūriyya) along with small discs of bread, which can be fried (aqrās maqluwwa) or rolled out thinly and baked (ruqāq mak͟hbūz). You may smear thin bread with binn (fermented sauce) or ṭaḥīn al-simsim (tahini) then cut it into slices. \n\tThese foods can be offered as naql for those who drink wine. Small sausages (laqāniq) may be offered as naql, too. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for kard͟habāj by Ibn ʿUmar:[/b]\nTake some plump Kaskarī pullets or any other fatty birds, clean them, insert them in the roasting spit, and rotate them above the burning coals. When they are almost done, make holes in their breasts, and put in them māʾ kāmak͟h (liquid fermented sauce). Continue rotating. \n\tMix olive oil with crushed salt and brush the pullets with it, using a feather. Do this as long as the pullets are rotating. When they are done and browned, pour on them a bit of māʾ kāmak͟h and rotate them. Then take them out of the spit and serve them with a dipping sauce (ṣibāg͟h), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another kard͟habāj recipe by Ibn Dihqāna:[/b]\nClean some plump pullets, insert them in a roasting spit, and rotate them on the burning coals. \n\tPrepare thin batter, a little thinner than that of qaṭāyif. When the pullets start dripping their juices, coat them with this batter using three or four feathers tied together. Do this while the pullets are rotating. Continue doing this until the batter sets on the birds then dries and cracks. When this happens, start brushing the pullets with a mixture of murrī (liquid fermented sauce), olive oil, and black pepper. Keep on doing this until the pullets are done. They will come out scrumptiously tender and juicy (rak͟hṣa ṭayyiba jiddan), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for delicious kard͟habāj that Abū al-Ṭayyib, Chamberlain of Muanis al-Muẓaffar, gave to his master Muanis as a gift on a hot summer day:[/b]\nChoose big and plump pullets, scald them to remove feathers, clean them, and fumigate them (yubak͟hk͟har) with moistened aloe wood (ʿūd nayʾ). Brush them with olive oil and almond oil then submerge them in a mixture of murrī (liquid fermented sauce) stirred with rose water, black pepper, and cassia. \n\tInsert the pullets into the roasting spit and rotate them on the fire until they brown and almost fall off the bones. Put them whole in sauce (ṣibāg͟h) made by mixing sour juice of unripe grapes, thyme, basil (bād͟harūj), parsley, and a bit of good quality anjud͟hān (dried asafetida leaves). Finally, crush on them some ice. It is a refreshing summer dish. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for delicious tannūriyya of chicken potpie:[/b]\nBoil one chicken (dajāja), pullets (farrūj) , or two young fowls in salt and water. \n\tTake a frying pan and pour tallow and oil into it. Spread bread dough in it to line bottom and sides. Now, take the boiled chicken, pullets, or the two plump fowls and remove the cavity wall. Spread the birds flat on the dough in the pan. \n\tMix finely chopped cilantro and onion with spikenard, cloves, cassia, and black pepper. Pour on them wine vinegar and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). If you prefer, use juice of zabīb (raisins) and pomegranate seeds, instead. Add 1 uskurruja (½ cup) clarified butter or sweet olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) and 5 eggs. Mix thoroughly all these ingredients and pour them all over the chicken. \n\tRoll out another piece of dough into a disc for a crust, cover the chicken with it, and seal together the edges of the dough. Lower the pan into the heated tannūr until it is cooked, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for tannūriyya cooked with beans (lūbyā):[/b]\nSoak skinned beans overnight. If you are using beans with skins on, then bruise them to split them into halves before soaking them. Then after soaking them wash them very well to get rid of all the skins. Take a similar quantity of good quality rice, wash it very well, and mix it with the beans. \n\tFor each 2 raṭls (2 pounds) of bean-rice mixture, use 10 raṭls (20 cups) of milk. Put them in a pot and add to them meat chopped into small pieces. Alternatively, you may use gizzards (qawāniṣ) or meat of a suckling kid (jedī raḍīʿ). Also add a small amount of white murrī (liquid fermented sauce), a piece of galangal, and a piece of cassia. \n\tCook the pot on slow burning coals while you wait for the tannūr to heat up and for flames subside. As soon as the oven is ready, put the pot in the center of the tannūr floor. Scald and clean a whole fatty kid or lamb and suspend it over the pot. Sprinkle the suspended meat with salted water and seal the tannūr with mud, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Jūd͟hāba by al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nTake a whole bread made with the finest samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), let its weight be 1 raṭl (1 pound). Cut it into morsel-size pieces, which you then soak in water in a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra) for about an hour. When bread pieces are saturated and puffed (rabā), put them in a jūd͟hābadān. Pour on them 1 raṭl (1 pound) honey, 2 raṭls (2 pounds) ṭabarzad sugar, and 1 raṭl (2 cups) water. There should be enough to cover the bread and a little bit more. Mix in aromatic spices and saffron, too. \n\tPut the pan in the bottom center of a hot tannūr, suspend a plump chicken over the pan, and let it roast until done, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba of apricot (mis͟hmis͟h) from the copy of al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nChoose sweet and fully ripe apricots and remove the pits. In a clean jūd͟hābadān layer the apricots alternately with a layer of sugar until the pan is full. However, before doing this, you should have lined the bottom of the casserole with a thin round of bread (ruqāqa), and after you finish you need to cover the apricots with another thin round of bread (ruqāqa). \n\tIf you wish, add a little bit of saffron and drench the apricots and sugar in rose water. Put the casserole in a hot tannūr, suspend a fine plump chicken above it, and let it roast, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba of bananas (mawz) by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nPeel the bananas and set them aside. Spread a ruqāqa (thin round of bread) in the pan (jūd͟hābadān) and spread a layer of bananas over it. Sprinkle the banana layer with pure sugar, and spread another ruqāqa all over it. Repeat the layering of banana, sugar, and ruqāqa until the pan is full. Pour enough rose water to drench the layered ingredients, put the pan in a hot tannūr, suspend a fine chicken over it, and let it roast God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another jūd͟hāba recipe by Ibn al-Mahdī:[/b]\nScrape the pith (lubāb) from crusts of fine white bread (samīd͟h naqī), which may be k͟hubz al-furn (brick-oven bread) or tannūr bread. Crumble the pith very well. \n\tGrind skinned almonds, moisten them with water, and add them to the breadcrumbs. Add finely ground pure sugar, as well. \n\tTake a wide pan with low sides jūd͟hābadān, big enough to accommodate a small ruqāqiyya (flat and thin bread). Melt in it some chicken fat or use fresh sesame oil (s͟hayraj) and heat it on the fire. Then take the pot away from the fire and line the bottom with a ruqāqa (flat thin bread). Spread the crumb-almond-sugar mix all over it and pour 2 raṭls (4 cups) milk. Sprinkle the surface with rose water and cover it with another ruqāqa bread. Put the casserole in the hot tannūr, suspend a chicken above it until it is done, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another jūd͟hāba recipe:[/b]\nUse k͟hubz al-māʾ (soft and not so thin bread) or k͟hubz kazmazaj (dry and thin ruqāq bread). Take a jūd͟hābadān pan, wash it, and stack whole breads in it until it is full. Pour on them enough water to drench them. \n\tPush the glowing embers to the sides of the tannūr and close the bottom vent (ʿayn al-tannūr) while baking. Put the pan in the middle of the tannūr and suspend on it a fatty side of ribs (janb) or a fine plump chicken. \n\tWhen you take out the roasted meat from the tannūr, the jūd͟hāba will come out looking like furniyya. Turn it over onto a big serving bowl (ṭayfūriyya), sprinkle it with sugar, and serve it with the meat, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for cooked jūd͟hāba (maṭbūk͟ha):[/b]\nChoose a thick round bread (jardaqa g͟halīẓa) made with samīd͟h or ḥuwwārā flour and set it aside. \n\tCut lean meat into small pieces and put it in a soapstone pot (burma). Add a small amount of clarified butter (samn) and honey. Stir in black pepper, cassia, and cloves, all pounded. Let the meat cook on open fire before you put it in the tannūr. \n\tWhen the meat is cooked, pour on it some milk mixed with 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), and cook the pot until mixture thickens. \n\tFill the jardaqa (bread) with the meat mixture and put it in the same soapstone pot. Pour on it milk and clarified butter (samn) and break on it some eggs, which you need to stir a little so that they mix with the other ingredients. \n\tPut the pot in the heated tannūr and suspend above it a fatty side of ribs (janb) or a fine plump chicken. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba made with melon (biṭṭīk͟h):[/b]\nChoose the sweetest you can get of sweet melon (biṭṭīk͟h ḥilū), cut it into wedges and peel it by slicing off half its thickness (i.e. using the sweetest part of the melon only). Cut the melon into smaller pieces, put it in a clean pot, and let it cook on slow fire. Stir it until it thickens then, transfer it to a g͟haḍāra (green-glazed earthenware bowl) and add ½ raṭl (½ pound) honey, ½ raṭl (½ pound) sugar, and 10 eggs. \n\tTransfer the melon mix into the pan after you put chicken fat in it. Place the pan in the tannūr and suspend a fine plump chicken above it. Let it roast until it is done then serve it with the melon jūd͟hāba, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another jūd͟hāba with qaṭāyif (sweet filled crepes):[/b]\nChoose lawzīnaj (filled pastries similar to baklawa) or qaṭāyif maḥs͟huwwa (filled crepes). Spread a layer of these pastries in a pot followed by a layer of chopped chicken fat. Repeat the layering. \n\tBeat eggs with 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) honey, 1 raṭl (1 pound) pounded sugar, and ½ raṭl (1 cup) milk, and pour the mixture all over the layered pastries in the pot. Drench the pot with sesame oil or zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). This will prevent the dish from sticking to the pot when baked. \n\tPut the pan in the tannūr, and suspend plump chickens above it. The chickens should be unsalted so that salt does not drip into the pot underneath it while baking. When the chickens are done, take the jūd͟hāba pan out of the tannūr, salt the chickens, and return them to the oven for a short while to allow them to absorb the salt. \n\tTurn the jūd͟hāba over onto a wide serving bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and serve it with the chicken, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Jūd͟hāba made with mulberry (tūt) by al-Mahdī:[/b]\nBreak 10 eggs into a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra) and add to them ½ raṭl (1 cup) juice of black mulberry, and 1 raṭl (1 pound) ground white sugar. Beat them together. \n\tMelt for it 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) chicken fat in a pan and spread in it one karmāzaj bread (thin and dry bread). Pour the sweet mix all over it, put it in the heated tannūr and suspend a plump chicken above it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba zabadiyya (like sea foam) made for al-Muʿtaṣim:[/b]\nWhip together in a bowl, 20 egg whites, ½ raṭl (1 cup) milk, and ½ raṭl (½ pound) pounded and sifted white sugar. \n\tRender kidney tallow in a pan, line it with a ruqāqa (flat thin bread), and pour the sweet mix into the pot. The pot has to bake in a slowburning tannūr. Suspend a chicken above it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba Nabaṭiyya:[/b]\nCut into small pieces a thin karmāzaja (dry thin bread), put it in a bowl, and pour on it 2½ raṭls (5 cups) milk. Break on it 10 eggs and add 1 raṭl (1 pound) pounded sugar. Beat the mixture well. \n\tRender 3 ūqiyyas (3 ounces) kidney tallow in a pan and discard any sediments remaining. Spread a ruqāqa (thin round bread) in the bottom of the pan after you take it away from the fire. Pour into it the sweet mix. Put the pan in the tannūr and suspend above it a fatty side of ribs (janb). \n\tInstead of karmāzaj bread, you can use bread pith (lubāb al-k͟hubz). It would be even more delicious, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba made with a duck (baṭṭa) by Abū Samīn:[/b]\nPick over sweet red raisins (zabīb aḥmar). Let them soak overnight then mash and cook them until they fall apart. Strain the juice over ruqāq (thin breads) stacked in a jūd͟habadān pan, and mix it with some pounded sugar in the jūd͟habadāna itself. Put the pan in the tannūr and suspend on it a fat duck or a fatty side of ribs (janb).

Put the pan in the tannūr and suspend a duck over it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba with zabīb (raisins):[/b]\nPick over zabīb and pound it in a mortar and pestle (hāwan). Macerate the pounded raisins in water. Strain the juice on thin breads stacked in a jūd͟habadān pot and stir into it some pounded sugar. Suspend a fat kid over it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jūd͟hāba with qaṭāyif (crepes):[/b]\nLine a pan with a layer of qatāyif followed by a layer of dates, which are fresh, ripe, and moist (ruṭab barīq). (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Jūd͟hāba of truffles (kamʾa) that looks like furniyya:[/b]\nChoose tender cuts of meat and chop on them some fresh herbs, leeks (kurrāt͟h), and onion. Give them a sprinkle of salt. Put the mixture on a hard wooden board (miksār) and pound it with a cleaver (sāṭūr). Season it with ground black pepper, coriander, cumin, and murrī (liquid fermented sauce). \n\tPeel truffles and pound them with a knife, as you did with the meat. Season the truffles with spices, put them in a bowl, break on them 10 eggs, and mix well. \n\tSmear the jūd͟hāba pan with pounded tallow or line it with a sheet of caul fat (t͟harb). Cover the layered ingredients with a ruqāqa (round and thin bread) to enclose it. \n\tPut the pan in a slow-burning tannūr and suspend above it a side of ribs (janb), chicken, pullets, a chunk of tallow, or a chunk of sheep’s tail fat. Let the meat roast until it is done and take out the pan. The jūd͟hāba will look like furniyya. Serve it with the roasted meat, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a beautiful jūd͟hāba (malīḥa), called jullābiyya (made with rose water syrup):[/b]\nBreak into pieces the crusts of fine white bread (rag͟hīf samīd͟h) and put them aside. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe with measurements for fālūd͟haj al-k͟hulafāʾ (pudding of the caliphs):[/b]\nTake as much as you wish of good quality white honey (ʿasal abyaḍ). Pour it into a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Light a slow fire underneath it, bring it to a boil, skim the froth , and strain it with a rāwūq. Return the honey to the ṭanjīr after you put in it fresh sesame oil, half the amount of honey used. \n\tIn a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra), dissolve starch (nas͟hā) in cold water, rose water, and camphor. The amount of the starch should be fifth or sixth the amount by weight of honey used. The amount of the liquid should be the same as the weight of the starch used. \n\tWhen honey and sesame oil come to a boil, pour the dissolved starch and stir the pot all the time until the mixture thickens and the oil separates and comes up. \n\tYou need to keep on stirring the pot with the isṭām (paddle-like iron spatula) so that the pudding does not stick to the pot. It is also important to taste the starch before using it to make sure it has not soured. \n\tYou have the option of making the pudding yellow by adding some saffron to the starch liquid before using it. You can also toast as much as you like of skinned almonds, leave them whole or break them into pieces, and stir them into the cooking pot. \n\tSo, when the pudding thickens and the oil separates and comes up, put the pot away from the fire. Spread the pudding on a sturdy platter (jām) that has been greased with oil of pistachio or almond. Take some sukkar al-ublūj (refined white sugar), crush it with musk, sprinkle it all over the dessert, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for chewy fālūd͟haj, fit for royalty (mulūkiyya):[/b]\nPut 3 raṭls (3 pounds) honey in a clean ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and light the fire under it. When it comes to a boil, skim its froth and pour on it ½ raṭl (1 cup) olive oil, s͟hayraj (sesame oil), or fresh clarified butter (samn). Let it cook on a low-heat fire until it comes to several good full boils. \n\tFinely pound 1/3 raṭl (5 ounces) sweet starch in a mortar and taste it lest it should be sour. Add water, rose water, and crushed camphor or musk, and knead them together. Do not let it be too thin in consistency. In fact, it will be better if it is rather thick. Add ½ dirham (1½ grams) saffron to it and stir it into the pot. \n\tKeep stirring the pot from the moment you put it on the fire until you take it away from it. Do not neglect this for the secret of good fālūd͟haj is good quality honey and starch, and constant stirring (ḍarʿ). \n\tWhen the pudding starts to thicken, gradually feed it with more and more fat , beating all the time until fat starts to separate from the pudding and comes up. Now, start removing the fat as it comes up while you beat the pudding. Do this until fālūd͟haj develops the desired color and thickness. Remove all the remaining separated fat and put the pot away from the fire. \n\tLadle (and spread) the pudding on a platter, God willing. \n\tIf you want to make it extremely chewy in consistency (muʿallaka s͟hadīdan jiddan), use more honey and less starch, thicken the pudding as mentioned above, and let it cook much longer. It will come out very chewy, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Fālūd͟haj made for ʿĪsā bin Jaʿfar:[/b]\nTake as much as you wish of excellent quality honey, put it in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), bring it to a boil and skim its froth. \n\tNow add starch dissolved in water (māʾ al-nas͟hāstaj). For each raṭl (1 pound) of honey, use 1 uskurruja (½ cup) of the dissolved starch. Before adding it to the honey color the dissolved starch with saffron or māʾ bustān abrawīz. Let the starch solution be thick. \n\tLight a slow fire underneath the pot. Let the pudding cook on low heat, beating with the iṣṭām (paddle-like iron spatula). When the pudding begins to thicken, start feeding it gradually with fresh good quality clarified butter or fresh sesame oil. \n\tYou keep on feeding the pudding with fat after you have put a sufficient amount of the dissolved sweet starch. Continue cooking it until it thickens and separates from its oil. Put the pot away from the fire and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fālūd͟haj made with rice (aruzz):[/b]\nWash picked over good quality rice in hot water and drain it. Pound the rice as fine as possible and sift it using waqqāya (silken or linen veil) or a piece of silken cloth. \n\tIf you want to use only rice in making the pudding, then use ½ raṭl (½ pound) rice flour for each 2 raṭls (2 pounds) of honey. \n\tSo when ready, put honey in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) bring it to a boil and skim its froth. Next, pour on the honey what equals half its weight of fresh sesame oil (s͟hayraj) and boil it. \n\tDissolve rice flour, amount as needed, in a little water, rose water, and 1 qīrāṭ (¼ gram) ground camphor. Remove the separated fat, put the pot away from the fire, spread the pudding on a platter, and sprinkle it with ṭabarzad sugar (crushed white cane sugar), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fālūd͟haj made with rice (aruzz):[/b]\nChoose Levantine rice (ruzz S͟hāmī) or Yemenite (Zabīdī). These are the best and whitest rice varieties available. Sheep milk is the best for it. Let the rice soak in milk for three nights and days. However, you need to renew the milk twice a day once during the day and once during the night by draining the rice and soaking it in a fresh batch of milk. This is to prevent it from changing and developing a sour taste. After that, wash it thoroughly in milk. \n\tYou also have the option of soaking the rice in milk during the night, drain it in the morning and let it dry out during the day, and repeat this procedure until three nights of soaking are completed. This would be good, too, God willing. \n\tNow, to make the pudding you have the option of crushing the rice while still damp after straining it from the milk until it becomes as soft as bone marrow, or you may let it dry and then grind and sift it. \n\tMix the rice with one third of its weight good quality starch free of any sourness.
