(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muʿallaka (chewy pudding) by al-Amīn, called al-Amīn’s showcase (muʿarraḍa):[/b]\nTake one part bruised skinned almonds, two parts pure ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), and one part honey. \n\tBring honey to a boil and skim its froth. Cook sugar in another pot until it dissolves and comes to a boil and remove its froth. \n\tMix honey with sugar and let them cook on medium fire. Add the almonds and stir the pot until mixture is condensed. When it is fully cooked, stir into it a small amount of rose water mixed with crushed musk or camphor. Do this just once (fum wāḥid). Take the pot away from the fire, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fālūd͟haj made without starch by Ḥāmid:[/b]\nPut 1 raṭl (1 pound) honey in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), bring it to a boil on the fire, and skim the froth. Put the pot away from the heat and set it aside until it cools down. \n\tUsing a knife, beat 15 egg yolks—do not put any of the egg whites— and stir them into the cooled honey. Put the pot back to the fire, add ¼ raṭl (½ cup) good quality fresh sesame oil, and let it cook on low-heat fire. Stir the pot constantly until it has the consistency of fālūd͟haj. Add skinned almonds. \n\tIf you want to have it thicker, then cook it longer stirring all the time. Otherwise, you may take it away from the fire and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fālūd͟haj made with melon (biṭṭīk͟h):[/b]\nChoose 5 very sweet melons, cut them into wedges. Slice off the rind but do not slice it thinly to ensure that you keep only the sweet section of the melon. \n\tPress and crush the pulp by hand. Strain it into a big bowl using a wide sieve of hair (munk͟hul s͟haʿr) to get rid of all lumps and hard particles. \n\tMix ½ raṭl (½ pound) starch with ½ dirham (1½ grams) crushed saffron, and stir them into 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) water. Put 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and strain into it the starch mixture. Add as well the strained melon. \n\tLight slow fire underneath the pot and cook the mixture stirring all the time until it thickens. Start feeding it with fat and continue cooking constantly stirring until it is done and the fat has separated from the pudding. Remove the fat and put the pot away from heat. Spread the pudding on a platter. If you prefer it to be sweeter, add a little sugar to the melon when you mash it and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for  fālūd͟haj , condensed and chewy (maʿqūda muʿallaka):[/b]\nPut in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), one part honey and one third of its weight fresh almond oil or sesame oil. Bring them to a boil, remove the froth, and start stirring the mixture vigorously on low heat until it almost thickens. \n\tMix 1 uskurruja (½ cup) sweet starch free of any sourness with 3 uskurrujas (1½ cups) water. Add saffron or māʾ bustān abrawīz. Strain the starch solution using a piece of fine cloth (k͟hirqa raqīqa) and take the amount you need for the pudding. The starch in its dry form before dissolving it in water should weigh 1/6 of the weight of the honey used for the pudding. \n\tNow, pour the starch solution into the pot and continue cooking on medium heat. Stir the pot constantly until the mixture greatly thickens and its oil starts to separate. Remove the oil as it separates and comes up until two thirds of it is gone. \n\tPut the pot away from the fire and spread the pudding on a platter (jām) that has been greased with pistachio oil. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for white k͟habīṣ:[/b]\nTake cane sugar (sukkar al-find͟h). Put it in a pot and dissolve it with some water on the fire. Remove any impurities with egg whites. Let it boil on the fire until it develops the consistency of thick syrup then pour on it half its weight of fat (duhn). It can be sesame oil, clarified butter, or fresh zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil). \n\tPrepare a quarter of the sugar weight sweet starch (i.e. free of sourness). Knead it with water and thin it with rose water and camphor. When the syrup (jullāb) comes to a boil with the fat , add the starch solution (māʾ al-nas͟hā). Let mixture cook while constantly stirring until its fat separates and comes up (qad͟hafa duhnahu). Take the pot away from heat. \n\tSprinkle on it a small amount of ground and sifted lubb al-ublūj al-naqī, and beat it into the k͟habīṣ mixture. When dessert cools down, you will see the benefit of adding the sugar. \n\tSpread the k͟habīṣ on a platter and sprinkle on it pounded sugar perfumed with musk (misk). \n\tMake triangles of sugar candy and color them. Color skinned almonds red, yellow, and green. Prepare shelled pistachio, too. \n\tOrder some nāṭif ʿasal bala al-mismār (pulled honey taffy) to be made for you. While it is still hot and malleable, make it into strings (yusalsal). Twist them like ropes (yuḍfar), shape them into a dome, and put it in the middle of the k͟habīṣ spread on the platter. Arrange in decorative patterns on this dome all the dyed almonds and pistachios you have prepared. Also, arrange the rest of the decorations dyed triangles of sugar candy all around the dome, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟habīṣa recipe by al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nPut 3 raṭls (3 pounds) good quality honey in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), light the fire underneath it, bring it to a boil, and skim the froth. \n\tStir 2/3 dirhams (2 grams) saffron in a small amount of rose water, and pour it into the pot to color the honey. \n\tYou should have prepared 1 raṭl (1 pound) skinned and ground almonds. Mix them with a an equal amount of refined pounded sugar and sprinkle them with rose water. Add this mixture to the pot and stir constantly. \n\tNow, pour into the pot 1 raṭl (2 cups) fresh sesame oil. When it begins to boil, sprinkle it with ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) samīd͟h ḥuwārā flour. Keep stirring the pot constantly until mixture thickens. Put the pot away from the heat and continue stirring the pot until it cools down. \n\tSpread the dessert on a flat glass platter (jām zujāj mabsūṭ), sprinkle it with powdered sugar (daqīq al-sukkar) and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ g͟harīb (exotic):[/b]\nTake 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey. Also take 2 raṭls (4 cups) milk of cow, sheep, or goat, and dissolve in it ½ raṭl (½ pound) starch. \n\tBoil the honey, remove its froth , and add the starch liquid. Let the pot cook on low fire until mixture thickens (yanbaqid) stirring all the time. \n\tAdd fat (duhn), it can be walnut oil, which is the best for it, or enhanced sesame oil (s͟hayraj ṭayyib), or butter (zubd). Keep stirring the pot and do not slacken. \n\tTo test for doneness, dip a twig into the pot. If the mixture sticks to it, put the pot away from the fire at once, otherwise the mixture will soon burn and develop a burning stench (tadk͟hīn). \n\tEmpty the pudding into 4 bowls, one big, and three small ones after you have greased them with walnut oil so that the pudding will not stick to them. Spread a ruqāqa (flat thin bread) in a ṭayfūriyya (big wide bowl), turn the big bowl over onto the middle section of the bread, and space the smaller ones around it. Dot the k͟habīṣ mounds with drops of saffron steeped in some water, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ ṭarīf (unusual) by Salīm al-Ḥalāwī:[/b]\nMoisten starch with water, amount of which depends on how much starch is being used. Knead mixture, put it in a bowl, cover it with a piece of cloth, and set it aside for an hour. \n\tPut fresh sesame oil in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). After the oil heats up, put the pot away from the fire, strain the oil, return it to the pot, and bring it to a boil again. Add the dissolved starch after you stir it and taste it to make sure it has not developed a sour taste. \n\tCook the pot on low heat, stirring constantly. Do not let it burn. Check for doneness by tasting a small amount. If it does not stick to your mouth, then it is cooked. \n\tNow start adding pounded and sifted sugar by sprinkling it bit by bit. Though quantity depends on how sweet you want the pudding to be, the extra amount of sugar added will help give it a moist texture. Keep on stirring. \n\tWhen k͟habīṣ is done, spread it on a platter, sprinkle it with pounded and sifted ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), and garnish it with skinned almonds and shelled pistachio. You may color them red and yellow and use them. Make nāṭif al-mismār of honey (pulled taffy). While it is still hot and malleable, form it into strings and shape them into a dome in the middle of the k͟habīṣ, as we described earlier in the first recipe. Make a ṣawmaʿa (minaret-like shape) in the middle of the dome so that it looks like a building. If you further decorate the dome by adding more candy strings in different colors, it will look even prettier, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe:[/b]\nGrind skinned almonds, let them be as fine as flour, and sift them through a fine-mesh sieve (munk͟hul ṣafīq). Put almond flour in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and pour on it a small amount of rose water. Add water, the same amount by weight as that of the almonds. Add as well pounded and sifted sugar, three times the amount of the almonds. Pour walnut oil. Start a slow fire underneath the pot and let it cook, stirring constantly until it is done (i.e. becomes thick). \n\tIf you want the pudding yellow, add saffron steeped in water while it is still cooking in the pot. It is quite unusual (ṭarīf jiddan) and delicious. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ of poppy seeds (k͟has͟hk͟hās͟h):[/b]\nPrepare 1 raṭl (1 pound) fresh sesame oil (s͟hayraj) or any other fat that tastes good in desserts (halāwa), ½ raṭl (½ pound) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), and 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey and sugar. \n\tPut the fat in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and add the flour to it. Light low-heat fire underneath the pot and fold and stir the flour until it is fried. \n\tStir in the honey. Crush and sift the sugar and then add it by sprinkling it into the pot while you are constantly stirring. \n\tWhen the mixture thickens (yanbaqid), stir into it a little saffron steeped in rose water, as well as 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) pounded white poppy seeds, which you add by sprinkling bit by bit. \n\tYou should keep on stirring the pot from start to end. When the pudding thickens and separates from its oil, take the pot away from heat. Let it cool down, sprinkle it with pounded sugar, stir it, and flatten it on a platter. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟habīṣa Maʾmūniyya:[/b]\nTake 1 raṭl (1 pound) ground skinned almonds and a similar amount of fat. Put them in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). \n\tIn another ṭanjīr, put 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) sugar and 1 raṭl (1 pound) honey. Pour 1 raṭl (2 cups) rose water on them, and boil the mixture. \n\tStart cooking the pot that has almonds and fat in it on low heat, and keep cooking until almonds are browned. Sprinkle on mixture two handfuls of fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) bit by bit, until flour is toasted. \n\tPour the boiled syrup on the almond mixture. Steep 2 dirhams (6 grams) saffron in a small amount of water and stir it into the pudding. Continue stirring until it thickens and separates from its fat. Take the pot away from the fire, spread the pudding on a platter, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for dry and white k͟habīṣ by him, too al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nSkin 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) almonds. Split them into halves and cut each half lengthwise into 4 slivers. Set them aside to dry. \n\tBoil 3 raṭls (3 pounds) honey in a ṭanjīr, skim the froth, and continue cooking until it thickens. Put the pot away from the fire and stir it until it cools down. Add whites of 7 eggs and stir the mixture on low heat until it cooks and turns white. It should thicken and look like nāṭif (nougat). To test whether it is thick enough dip the tip of a toothpick (k͟hilāl) in the mixture then strike it on your fingernail. If it does not stick, it is done. \n\tWhen fully cooked, put the pot away from the fire and stir into it the prepared almonds. Using a rolling pin (s͟hawbaq), flatten mixture on a wooden board (k͟hiwān) or a slab of marble (ruk͟hāma) and roll it up like a bazmāward. When the roll is cold and firm enough, cut it crosswise into slices, as you do with bazmāward. Arrange the pieces on a platter, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟habīṣa muwallada (non-Arab) by Ḥāmid:[/b]\nTake a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and put in it 2 raṭls (2 pounds) sugar and 1 raṭl (1 pound) honey. Add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) water. Let the pot cook on low fire and skim the froth. Steep ½ dirham (1½ grams) saffron in rose water, add it to the pot, and cook it for a little bit longer. \n\tEmpty the syrup into a container and put it aside. Wipe the pot and put in it 1¼ raṭls (2 ½ cups) sesame oil. \n\tTake pounded and sifted crumbs of kabk (dry sweet cookies), starch, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), and rice flour (daqīq al-aruzz), 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) each. Mix them and dissolve them in water. \n\tWhen the oil in the pot is hot enough, add the starch mixture and keep stirring until it thickens. Pour the prepared syrup and continue stirring, lightly and quickly (k͟hafīfan sarīʿan) until it throws up (qad͟hafa) its oil. Put the pot away from heat, spread the dessert on a platter, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ murmal by Isḥāq bin Ibrāhīm al-Mawṣilī:[/b]\nHeat 1 raṭl (2 cups) fresh sesame oil, butter, or fresh and sweet olive oil in a clean ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Add ½ raṭl (½ pound) samīd͟h al-ḥuwwārā, and cook it in the oil. Stir vigorously all the time and do not slacken to prevent the flour from burning. When flour is evenly toasted (taḥammaṣa), add ¼ raṭl (½ cup) water to moisten the mixture, and stir it. \n\tTake 2 raṭls (2 pounds) pounded clean and refined sugar and sprinkle it gradually on the mixture in the pot, stirring constantly until pudding thickens and its oil separates. \n\tImmediately take the pot away from the heat and put it on the floor to cool down. Sprinkle a platter with Sulaymānī sugar (crushed hard sugar-candy), spread the k͟habīṣ over it, sprinkle its surface with white pounded sugar, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣa murmala by Isḥāq bin Ibrāhīm al-Mawṣilī:[/b]\nPrepare ½ raṭl (½ pound) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). \n\tTake a clean ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and put in it ½ raṭl (1 cup) zayt mag͟hsūl (washed olive oil) with a pinch of salt. Add the flour as soon as the oil heats. It should be enough to make the oil look dry. Stir the pot vigorously—do not neglect this—until the flour toasts and browns a little (yaḥmarr). \n\tPound three handfuls of ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), add it to the pot along with a small amount of water. Cook and stir the pot until the mixture looks dry (yans͟haf). The cooking fire should be gentle. \n\tAdd Sulaymānī sugar (crushed hard sugar-candy) to the pot, enough to sweeten it, and stir. Take the pot away from the fire and set it on the floor to cool down. \n\tSprinkle Sulaymānī sugar on a platter, spread the k͟habīṣ on it, and sprinkle the top with pounded white sugar, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟habīṣ raṭb (moist) by Abū al-Muʿalla al-Ḥalawānī:[/b]\nTake ½ raṭl (½ pound) sifted fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) and fry it in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), which already contains ¼ raṭl (½ cup) fresh sesame oil or fresh sweet and mellow olive oil (zayt ʿad͟hb). Let the flour fry until it develops a golden hue (yaṣfarr). Put the pot away from the fire. Empty the flour into a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra) and set it aside to cool down. \n\tReturn the ṭanjīr to the fire, wipe it, and pour into it 2 raṭls (2 pounds) refined honey, which has already been boiled and its froth skimmed. When it is heated, sprinkle on it the cooked flour, using your hand, until you finish the whole amount stirring constantly. When the mixture thickens, add more honey and a little rose water, and stir constantly until the mixture looks smooth and well blended. \n\tFeed the mixture with ½ raṭl (1 cup) sesame oil and stir the pudding until its oil separates. Cut the heat from underneath the pot and sprinkle it with a little rose water and camphor. It will still have some moisture in it. Put the pot on the floor and continue stirring it for a while (sāʿa, an hour) until it looses its heat. \n\tSpread the pudding on a platter sprinkled with pounded sugar and drench its surface generously with pounded sugar. Garnish it with skinned almonds, colored red and yellow, and serve it. It is quite delicious, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟habīṣ al-jazar (carrots):[/b]\nChoose fresh, tender, and sweet carrots. Peel them and thinly slice them crosswise. For each raṭl (1 pound) of honey, use 3 raṭls (3 pounds) of theses carrots. \n\tBoil the honey and remove its froth. Pound the carrot in a stone mortar. \n\tSet a clean ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) on a trivet on the fire, and put in it the skimmed honey and carrots. Cook the mixture on medium fire until the carrots falls apart. \n\tAdd walnut oil to the pot. For each raṭl (1 pound) of honey used, add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) oil. Pistachio oil will be the best for it, but you can also use fresh oil of almond or sesame. Add the oil before the honey starts to thicken. However, you do not need to stir the pot. You only scrape the bottom gently when mixture starts to thicken to prevent it from sticking to it. To check for doneness, use a stick or a spoon to see whether the pudding is thick enough or not yet. \n\tWhen pudding becomes thick, put the pot down, and spread the dessert on a copper platter (jām nuḥās). Set it aside to cool down before serving. It will be firm and delicious.trivet on the fire, and put in it the skimmed honey and carrots. Cook the mixture on medium fire until the carrots falls apart. Add walnut oil to the pot. For each raṭl (1 pound) of honey used, add 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) oil. Pistachio oil will be the best for it, but you can also use fresh oil of almond or sesame. Add the oil before the honey starts to thicken. However, you do not need to stir the pot. You only scrape the bottom gently when mixture starts to thicken to prevent it from sticking to it. To check for doneness, use a stick or a spoon to see whether the pudding is thick enough or not yet. When pudding becomes thick, put the pot down, and spread the dessert on a copper platter (jām nuḥās). Set it aside to cool down before serving. It will be firm and delicious. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ of carrots (jazar) and dates (tamr):[/b]\nTake as much as you like of similar amounts of sweet and tender carrots, milk, and dates. Put them in a clean soapstone pot, which you lower into a tannūr heated with medium fire. Close the bottom vent (rawwāj) but leave a finger-wide opening. \n\tLet the pot simmer until the ingredients fall apart. Take it out, and add ground walnuts and ½ dirham (1½ grams) ground spikenard and ginger. Beat the mixture very well. \n\tIf the pudding turns out to be too sweet and thin, add breadcrumbs. If it turns out perfect—sweet and thick enough—add fresh sesame oil and ladle it with its oil into platters. If it turns out deficient in sugar and too thin in consistency, beat the mixture and return the pot to the tannūr until it thickens. When pudding is done, drench it in sesame oil and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ of carrots:[/b]\nPut as much as you like of milk in a soapstone pot (burma). Do not use a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Light low-heat fire underneath it and let it cook stirring constantly so that it does not scorch. \n\tBoil carrots, and cut them into fingers. Add them to the milk with a little oil, spikenard, cloves, cassia, ginger, and nutmeg, all pounded and sifted. \n\tStir the pot very well, let it cook until it is done then break 5 eggs on it. Do not stir the pot. Serve the pudding when the eggs are set. If you like it sweet, add honey as much as you like when you put the spices in the pot, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ of apples (tuffāḥ), marvelously delicious (ṭayyib ʿajīb):[/b]\nTake as much as you like of good quality, fully ripe apples. Levantine Lebanese apples (S͟hāmī Labnānī) are a good choice. \n\tPeel the apples, cut them in halves, and core them. Spread the apple pieces to dry on a piece of kisāʾ (coarse cloth) or a ḥaṣīr in a sunny place, until they are as dry as kabk (dry sweet cookies). Pound or crush the apples, sift them in a wide-mesh sieve if possible, and store them away. Make a big quantity so that it will be ready whenever you need to use it. \n\tTo make the pudding, take 30 dirhams (3 ounces) ground apples, and mix it with a similar amount of good quality, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). \n\tExtract the oil of skinned almonds and pistachio, 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) of each. \n\tTake a clean ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and put in it 1/3 raṭl (5 ounces) butter. Light the fire under the pot. When the butter sizzles, add the apple-flour mixture to it little by little, stirring the pot vigorously with isṭām (paddle-like iron spatula). \n\tAdd to the pot, 1 mann (2 pounds) refined sugar dissolved in water, or 1 mann (2 pounds) honey, which has been heated and skimmed of its froth. Stir the pot vigorously. \n\tAdd to the mixture as much as it takes of the prepared almond and pistachio oils. When the pudding thickens, perfume it with rose water and crushed musk (misk). Put the pot away from heat, sprinkle it with pounded sugar, and stir it constantly until it cools down. \n\tSpread the pudding on a platter, sprinkle it with sugar granules to give it a sandy look, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ of k͟has͟hk͟hās͟h (poppy seeds):[/b]\nPrepare ½ raṭl (1 cup) almond oil, 1 raṭl (1 pound) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), and 1 raṭl (1 pound) ground and sifted sugar. \n\tPut the oil in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and add 2 dirhams (6 grams) saffron. Light a low-heat fire underneath it. When the oil is hot enough, sprinkle on it the flour bit by bit, and continue cooking and stirring until flour fries. \n\tSprinkle the flour with ½ raṭl (1 cup) rose water and stir the pot until mixture is cooked. Sprinkle it with 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) white poppy seeds. Then take the pot away from the fire and let it cool down. Add the pounded sugar to it, mix it well, and spread it on a platter, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fresh ripe dates (ruṭab) when not in Season:[/b]\nChoose qasb (dry dates) that are still soft and fleshy (layyin al-laḥm) and soak them overnight in milk. Take them out of the milk and put them in ʿasal mād͟hī (smooth, thin, and white honey). Nobody will suspect that these are not fresh dates. If you replace the date-stones with skinned almonds, they will be even more delicious. \n\tThe best way to eat ruṭab (ripe dates with a nice crunch) and tamr (fully ripe, sweet and soft dates) is to put them on a platter and scatter broken pieces of ice all over them. They will be scrumptious chilled this way. Likewise, s͟hahd (honey with its wax) can be eaten chilled by putting crushed ice around its dish. Al-Maʾmūn used to do this with tamr and ruṭab, and any other sweet foods. Al-Wāt͟hiq used to have his qaṭāyif (filled crepes) always served chilled with ice. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣa by al-Muktafī:[/b]\nFinely pound ½ raṭl (½ pound) skinned almonds and set them aside. \n\tDissolve 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) refined sugar in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and skim its froth. Pour on it ½ raṭl (1 cup) almond oil and stir the pot. Pound and sift ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) k͟hubz al-nāṭif al-samīd͟h, which has been fried in fresh sesame oil. Add it to the dissolved sugar in the pot. Add as well, the ground almonds. \n\tNever stop stirring the pot. You should have all these ingredients ready for you so that you add them one after the other. Keep on stirring until the mixture thickens. Put the pot away from the heat, stir the pudding constantly until it cools down then spread it on a platter. \n\tWhile the pudding is still in the ṭanjīr pot, you need to sprinkle it with crushed perfumed sugar (sukkar muṭayyab) and rose water. If you wish to color it yellow, add a little saffron steeped in water while it is still in the pot. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A tried and tested recipe (mujarraba) for delicious Ītāk͟hiyya pudding:[/b]\nTake shelled walnuts, peel the thin skins, and pound them finely. Take a similar amount of skinned almonds and pound them as fine. Take a kūz of refined sugar and pound it. The sugar amount should be twice as much as walnuts and almonds combined. Mix all three ingredients and set them aside. \n\tPut a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) on the fire. Pour into it fresh sesame oil, the amount of which is third of the mixed dry ingredients above, that is, half the amount of the sugar used. When the oil heats up, sprinkle on it fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), half the amount of the sesame oil used. When it fries, pour into the pot honey, an equal amount to the sesame oil used. Keep on stirring the pot. \n\tDissolve 5 dirhams (15 grams) starch in water and rose water, 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) each. This amount is enough for 2 raṭls (2 pounds) of sugar and 2 raṭls (2 pounds) of honey used in the recipe. Keep stirring the pot. Next, add the walnut-almond-sugar mixture (al-muk͟hallaṭ), and stir. \n\tThus you keep stirring the pot continuously, adding ingredients one after the other until the pudding thickens. Put the pot away from the fire, and keep on stirring until it cools down. Spread the pudding on a platter, sprinkle it with ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) pounded sugar, and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for candy (ḥalwā) made like fish aspic (qarīṣ):[/b]\nToast skinned almonds but do not let them change color or burn. Pound them thoroughly. Pound a similar amount of refined white sugar, mix the two, and sprinkle them with rose water. Add enough of the rose water to combine the almonds and sugar into very stiff dough. Scent the mixture with camphor (kāfūr). \n\tTake molds made of jujube wood (k͟has͟hab al-ʿunnāb) carved into figures of fish. Fill them with the almond mixture, set them aside to dry out, and unmold them onto a platter, leaving a space between the fishes. \n\tPut in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) honey, which has already been boiled and skimmed of its froth. The amount should be enough to submerge the fishes arranged on the platter. Add sugar as well, fifth the amount of honey. Pour into it saffron that has been steeped in rose water, use enough to give the syrup a saturated red (mus͟habbaʿ al-ḥumra). Put the pot on the burning coals (jamr) and stir it until syrup thickens. Carefully and slowly pour it all around the sides of the platter. Let it be lukewarm (fātir) and not hot so that it does not spoil the shape of the fishes. Allow the dessert to cool down. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟habīṣ, dry and crumbly (yābis maftūt):[/b]\nTake ½ raṭl (½ pound) shelled pistachios and put them in hot water to remove their thin skins. Toast the pistachios to dry them (yujaffaf taḥmīṣan) but do not let them change in color. Finely grind them. \n\tPound 1 raṭl (1 pound) refined sugar into fine powder. Put it in a bowl and sprinkle it with a little rose water and camphor. Fold into it the pounded pistachio and mix until ingredients combine and become one mass. \n\tShape the mixture into discs or make them look like dates, sanbūsaj (filled pastries), cucumber, and melon. You can also use molds. Set them aside to dry on ṭabaq asal (tray made of rush stems) and serve them, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for uncooked k͟habīṣ (bi-g͟hayr nār):[/b]\nFinely grind 1 raṭl (1 pound) skinned almonds. Shell two fresh coconuts, pound them until they release their oil, and mix them with the almonds. \n\tPound 3 raṭls (3 pounds) sugar and sift it in a fine-meshed hairsieve (munk͟hul s͟haʿr). Set aside about ¼ raṭl (¼ pound) of it. Add the rest to the almond-coconut mixture, in addition to ½ dirham (1½ grams) ground saffron. Mix very well to moisten the ingredients. Next, pour on them ½ raṭl (1 cup) almond oil and keep mixing until they are moist enough to gather in one mass. \n\tSpread the mix on a platter and sprinkle the reserved ¼ raṭl sugar on it, the way you do with cooked moist k͟habīṣ as in the previous chapters. Decorate the top with colored almonds and serve the dessert, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟habīṣ recipe made with futūt (breadcrumbs):[/b]\nTake bread made with fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), milk, and sesame oil. It needs to be dried in the tannūr. Alternatively, you may use good quality kabk (dry cookies) baked and completely dried in the furn (brick oven). Or you may use thin breads (ruqāq) made with samīd͟h flour and sesame oil, and dried in the tannūr. Whatever you use, take 3 raṭls (3 pounds) of the dried bread, pound it and set it aside in a big bowl (qaṣʿa) or a wooden plate (ṭabaq k͟halanj). \n\tNow take clean dates (tamr), which have been recently dried (tamr \n\tḥadīt͟h). You may choose any of these varieties: barnī, ṭabarzad, azād͟h, or maʿqilī. Remove the stones and the skins of the dates. \n\tHeat 1 raṭl (2 cups) fresh and enhanced sesame oil (s͟hayraj ṭarī ṭayyib) in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and add 4 raṭls (4 pounds) of the pitted dates (tamr mufallas). Stir the pot. As soon as the dates are heated through, put the pot away from the fire, and add the 3 raṭls (3 pounds) of bread that was crushed to fine crumbs. Knead the mixture while it is still hot. Keep on kneading until it cools down then shape it into discs (aqrāṣ). \n\tPrepare a bowl of rose water mixed with crushed camphor. As you make the discs, sprinkle them with rose water, stack them in a container, and stash them away until needed. \n\tThis is the way to make al-hays (ﺲﻴﻬﻟﺍ), which high-class people (al-k͟hawāṣ) take with them as part of their provisions for their pilgrimage to Mecca. These are the basic amounts (hād͟hā biyāruhu). If you want to make more, multiply the amounts (ḍābifhu), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for basīsa (crumbled pie) from the copy of Ibn al-Mahdī, absolutely delicious:[/b]\nMix 3 raṭls (3 pounds) good quality, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), 6 eggs, a piece of yeast—size of an almond (lawzat k͟hamīr), and a small amount of fat. Knead them into stiff dough, which you put aside for an hour to allow the yeast to move in it (i.e. to rise). \n\tDivide dough into two parts. Roll out one of the portions and make it big enough to line the frying pan (maqlā) you are using. When you spread the dough in the pan, press its edges upwards so that it lines the raised side of the pan, too like a pie. \n\tIn this lined pan, spread 1 1/3 raṭls (1 1/3 pounds) honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Also add ½ raṭl (1 cup) fresh clarified butter of sheep (g͟hanamī). \n\tRoll out the other dough portion. Make it as big as the frying pan with an additional thinner border to set on the edge of the first layer. \n\tDrizzle a little sesame oil or butter over the filling, moisten the edges of the dough with some water, and cover the filling with the prepared crust. Seal the edges completely. There should be no cracks or holes in the dough to prevent any seeping of the filling while baking. Wipe the top crust with water then with some sesame oil. \n\tLower the pan into the tannūr after you have just finished baking your batch of bread, or bake it in a brick oven (furn), or tannūr k͟habbāz al-Ruṣāfī. Keep the tannūr covered while baking. \n\tWhen the pastry is done baking and you take it out, you will see that it has developed a golden hue (tawarrada), an unmistakable sign of doneness. \n\tRemove the pie from the pan and put it in a big bowl or plate. Set it aside until it loses some of its heat. Crumble the pastry with your hands until it looks like t͟harīda. Sprinkle it with pounded sugar and eat it. It is truly excellent and delicious, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for delectable s͟haḥmiyya (pastry with tallow), from the copy of al-Mahdī:[/b]\nTake the best you can get of tallow (s͟haḥm) surrounding the goat’s kidneys, trim it of the blood vessels (ʿurūq), chop it fine, and pound it in a mortar (hāwan). \n\tMix one part of the pounded tallow with two parts good quality, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Rub the two and mix them with your hands until they develop dough-like consistency. \n\tAdd 1 uskurruja (½ cup) water and a bit of salt. Rub the mixture together until it becomes doughy in texture—rather on the stiff side. Shape it into a disc, the same size of the maqlā (frying pan) used. Dust the pan with a little flour then spread the disc of dough on it. \n\tBreak 1 or 2 eggs in a bowl and whip it with your hand until it mixes well. Score the spread disc of dough lengthwise and crosswise with a knife, but do not go all the way down. Rub over the surface of the pastry and its scores with the egg whip. \n\tNext, lower the pan into a low-heat tannūr (sākin layyin) and cover the oven, which should not be hot because the pastry will cook and brown with the low heat. When it is almost done, smear your hand with the whipped egg in the bowl and rub it over the pastry so that it browns well. Do this several times. \n\tWhen baking is done take the pan out of the tannūr, remove the pastry from it, and put it in a big wide bowl (qaṣʿa). Pour about 2 uskurrujas (1 cup) honey all over it. Rescore the pastry. Go all the way down this time so that the pastry absorbs the honey. Sprinkle it with pounded Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), dust it with a bit of black pepper, and serve it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for s͟haḥmiyyat al-k͟hawāṣ (pastry with tallow for the elite):[/b]\nMake dough using 3 raṭls (3 pounds) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), yeast, water, and a bit of salt and knead it well. Take whites of 20 eggs and knead them into the dough, which will develop a soft consistency. Put it aside for an hour to ferment. You should have kneaded the dough with some yeast. \n\tPound kidney fat until it resembles bone marrow in consistency. Smear with it the inside of a soapstone pot with high sides. Use up all the tallow you have. Pour into the pot as well, ¼ raṭl (½ cup) sesame oil. Pour the prepared dough into the pot and lower it into the tannūr after you have just finished baking your bread. Cover the tannūr. \n\tWhen, according to your estimate, the eggs are cooked and the dough has firmed up, take a reed stick (ʿūd nus͟hs͟hāb) and pierce with it the cake at several places. Let the holes go all way down to the bottom of the pot. Return the cake to the tannūr to continue baking. You need to reinsert the stick into the same holes after a while the same way you did to make sure the holes stay open. \n\tWhen the cake is fully baked, take it out of the tannūr, and fill the holes with whatever you fancy of pounded dried fruits such as walnut, hazelnuts, almonds, pistachios, pine nuts, soft dried dates (tamr), and qasb (hard and brittle dried dates). However, they all need to be pounded first. Keep some holes empty. \n\tTake honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth, and pour it all over the furniyya while it is still hot and in the pot. Shake the pot gently with your hands to let the honey get into the sides of the cake and its empty holes. Return the pot to the tannūr briefly (laḥẓa a second) then take it out of the oven. Turn the cake over onto a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya) and dust it with pounded sugar. Turn it over again to let its top side be up. Drizzle it with 1 ūqiyya 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muhallabiyya (milk pudding with eggs):[/b]\nTake 1 raṭl (1 pound) walnuts and almonds altogether and finely pound them. Put them aside \n\tBreak 30 eggs into a big bowl (ṣuḥfa), add to them 2 raṭls (2 pounds) refined pounded sugar and the ground nuts. Beat mixture until well blended and set it aside. \n\tTake a clean pot and pour into it 10 raṭls (20 cups) fresh milk that has just been drawn and is still warm. Light a fire underneath it and boil it down to 5 raṭls (10 cups). Add the egg mixture to it and stir it briskly and constantly until it thickens. At this stage, you can further sweeten the custard with some honey. You should never stop stirring the pudding until it thickens and pot is taken away from the fire. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muhallabiyya (milk pudding) with iṭriya (dry noodles):[/b]\nTake iṭriya noodles, pick them over, and put them in a pot that already has boiling milk in it. Stir the pot with the handle of the ladle so that the noodles do not break, and keep on cooking. When mixture begins to thicken, add 2 raṭls (2 pounds) sugar or honey, and stir the pot carefully lest you should mash the mixture. Pour on it 1/3 raṭl (2/3 cup) butter or fresh sesame oil. \n\tWhen it is fully cooked, take the burning coals (jamr) from underneath the pot, wait until the pot settles then serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muhallabiyya (milk pudding) with iṭriya (dry noodles):[/b]\nMix milk and ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar) in a pot and boil them for an hour until the mixture thickens. Beat 30 eggs in a bowl, pour them into the pot, and add walnuts or almonds. Serve the pudding as soon as it is cooked. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muhallabiyya (milk pudding with rice) from the copy of al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nWash the rice at night and put it in a new piece of cloth to drain and dry. In the following morning, crush the rice into fine powder like flour. \n\tFor each 10 raṭls (20 cups) of milk, use 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) of rice flour. \n\tPut warm milk in a pot and bring it to a boil. Sprinkle the rice flour on the milk the way you do with flour, stirring all the time. Let the pot cook on medium heat until rice is cooked. Pour on it walnut oil or fresh clarified butter. If pudding comes out thick, add more milk as needed. \n\tWhen it is finished cooking, sprinkle it with pounded ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar). If you prefer the pudding white, keep it as it is. If you prefer it yellow, add some saffron. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muhallabiyya (milk pudding with rice and chicken) from the copy of al-Wāt͟hiq:[/b]\nClean and disjoint an excellent chicken, put it in a pot that already has 1 raṭl (2 cups) water boiling in it. Let the pot boil until all moisture evaporates and chicken fries in its oil. Season it with a little coriander, cumin, cassia, and saffron and set it aside. Pour into a pot 7 raṭls (14 cups) milk of sheep or goat and boil it. Prepare 1 raṭl (1 pound) washed good quality rice and add it to the boiling milk along with the chicken. Light medium fire underneath the pot and let it cook. \n\tWhen the rice is almost done, pour into the pot 2½ raṭls (2½ pounds) honey, and stir it gently so that you do not break the rice grains because the beauty of the dish is when the rice grains show through the honey. \n\tStop the fire underneath it (taqṭaʿ al-nār) and perfume it with rose water and saffron, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe of s͟haḥmiyya (pastry with tallow) ʿAbbāsiyya:[/b]\nTake k͟hubz samīd͟h (bread made with samīd͟h flour) or k͟hubz furrānī (thick bread baked in a brick oven), and soak it in milk. Let the milk cover the bread. \n\tCrush ½ raṭl (½ pound) sugar. You may use more or less depending on how much bread you are using. Add it to the soaked bread. \n\tTake a clean pot with low sides. Put in it 1 raṭl (1 pound) tallow and ½ raṭl (1 cup) olive oil (zayt). Cook the pot until tallow dissolves. \n\tPress and mash (umrus) the bread-milk-sugar mix and have it ready. \n\tLine the pot with a ruqāqa (large and thin bread). It should be much bigger than the circumference of the pan Spread the bread mixture in the lined pot and overlap the ruqāq bread edges all over the filling to cover it completely and nothing of the filling seeps out. \n\tReturn the pot to slow burning coals. When the filling is cooked and set, take the pot away from the fire, turn it upside down onto a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya), and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for s͟haḥmiyya (pastry with tallow) ʿAbbāsiyya:[/b]\nMake dough with good quality, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) yeast, and water. Take shelled nuts such as almonds, pistachio, hazelnut, and pine nut. Finely chop them with a knife. Knead the nuts well into the dough and put it aside for almost an hour. You should avoid (iyyāka) letting it fully ferment. Otherwise, it will get sour and spoil. \n\tSet a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) on a trivet on the fire. Pour as much as you wish of fresh clarified butter or walnut oil. \n\tShape your dough into furrānī. You should avoid (iyyāka) letting it be too stiff, otherwise it will not come out right. \n\tWhen the oil starts sizzling (nas͟hs͟ha) in the pot, put one disc, and let it fry until it is golden brown. Take it out and put another disc. Repeat this until you finish all the portions. \n\tClean the ṭanjīr of the remaining fat, pour fine honey, and let it boil until it becomes thick but thinner than nāṭif (nougat). Chop what is left of the almond, pistachio, hazelnut, pine nut, and coconut. Add them to the thickened honey and stir the pot well. \n\tTrickle this syrup over the fried discs and store them away in wicker baskets. You can take them with you wherever you travel for they will never change, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for lawzīnaj from the copy of al-Muʿtaṣim:[/b]\nTake lawzīnaj sheets made by pouring the batter on the ṭābaq (large flat pan). Cover the sheets after they cool down so that they stay malleable. \n\tTake equal parts of shelled pistachios and skinned almonds, and finely grind them. Grind ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), the amount of which should be equal to that of the nuts. Mix the sugar with the nuts and sprinkle them with rose water in which a few cloves were steeped overnight. Add more sugar if needed. \n\tStuff lawzīnaj sheets with the nut filling, cut them into smaller pieces, and arrange them in a small delicate platter. Pour on them fresh almond oil, and sprinkle pounded ṭabarzad sugar on, and in between, the rows of the pieces. You also have the option of perfuming the lawzīnaj with mastic (maṣṭakā) and musk (misk). It is fabulous (g͟hāya min al-g͟hāyāt). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sumptuous drenched lawzīnaj, usually made for kings when traveling:[/b]\nTake as much as you need of shelled and skinned almonds and shelled walnuts. Take sugar as well, the amount of which should be equal to both of them. Pound each of the three ingredients separately. Then combine them and bind them with rose water. Mix in, as well, 1 ḥabba (1/12 gram) musk (misk), 2 ḥabbas ( 1/6 gram) ambergris (ʿanbar), and mastic (maṣṭakā) all crushed. Of the latter, use just enough for its flavor to be discernable in the filling. \n\tNow take some walnuts and almonds, other than the amounts mentioned at the beginning of the recipe. Extract their oil, put it in a glass bottle (zujāja), and set it aside. \n\tTake malleable lawzīnaj sheets and fill them with the nut mix. Stuff the pieces very well. Cut them into smaller pieces, the size of which you decide to your fancy. Take a clean barniyya (widemouthed jar), either green-glazed (g͟haḍār) or glass (zujāj), and pack it with the lawzīnaj pieces until it is almost full. Pour on them the oil you extracted. Put enough to drench them (yug͟harraq). You can use them when traveling or at home. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Dry lawzīnaj (almond brittle) cooked on the fire:[/b]\nTake 2 raṭls (2 pounds) skinned almonds. You need to taste them lest some should turn out to be bitter. Grind them finely and set them aside. Pound 4 raṭls (4 pounds) refined sugar and set aside ½ raṭl of it. \n\tTake a wide ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) or a wide nuqra (big copper pot), and pour 2/3 raṭl (1 1/3 cups) water into whatever pot you choose to use. Add the sugar to it and start a medium fire underneath it. Bring it to a boil until it foams. Then sprinkle it with water mixed with egg white and stir it. Skim the froth with the coagulated egg white to which all impurities in the syrup have adhered Repeat this (i.e. spraying the syrup with egg-white wash) whenever you see that foam is getting black until the syrup is cleansed and purified. \n\tStir the syrup for a while until it thickens and is almost stiff. Sprinkle it with rose water to which you have added some aromatics (ṭīb) such as musk and camphor. Add the set aside ground almonds, mix well, and put the pot away from the heat. \n\tBeat the mixture with a daks͟hāb (stirring wooden utensil) or a piece of wood (k͟has͟haba)—the way you do when you make sukkar Sulaymānī (hard sugar-candy)—until syrup looks white and starts to crystallize (yanbut). \n\tSprinkle some of the reserved ground sugar on a plate. Take a chunk of the sugar mass from the pot, put it on the plate, and knead into it crushed camphor (kāfūr) and musk (misk). Shape it into a ball—size of a fist—and roll it under your palm making it look like a qat͟ht͟hāya (ribbed long cucumber). Cut it crosswise into finger-long pieces or whatever size you fancy. Arrange them on a platter the way you do with qaṭāyif (crepes). Set them aside to cool down and serve them. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Zalābiya recipe made for al-Maʾmūn:[/b]\nPrepare 2 raṭls (2 pounds) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Put ½ raṭl (1 cup) fat in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and heat it under low fire. When the oil boils, sprinkle it with the flour and stir the pot until it toasts (yataḥammaṣ). Pour on it 2 raṭls (4 cups) water, and constantly stir the pot until it releases its fat. Put the pot away from the fire and stir the pot until mixture cooks and develops a firm consistency. \n\tForm dough into smooth balls (yukarhak). Shape each karhaka (ball) into fingers, rings, or discs, the way you do with sukkar Sulaymānī (hard sugar-candy). \n\tNext, take 1 raṭl (1 pound), or as much as you need, of honey, which has been cooked and skimmed of its froth. Sprinkle on it ½ raṭl (1 cup) rose water mixed with some aromatics (ṭīb) such as musk and camphor. Put the pot on the burning coals until it comes to a boil. Take it away from the heat and set it aside. \n\tGrind and sift one raṭl (1 pound) ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar) and set it aside. \n\tPour 1 raṭl (2 cups) fat into an iron frying pan or a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Start frying the dough pieces that have been shaped like sukkar Sulaymānī, and fry them the way you do with zalābiya. The best fat to use for frying is fresh and enhanced clarified butter (samn ṭarī ṭayyib). \n\tThe moment you take the fried pieces out of the pan, dip them immediately and while still hot in the heated honey. Keep them there until they absorb enough of the syrup. Take them out and arrange them on a platter. Then sprinkle the sifted sugar all over them and between the pieces. Do the same thing with the rest and serve them. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for zalābiya mus͟habbaka (latticed fritters) called Wāt͟hiqiyya:[/b]\nMake soft dough using ½ raṭl (½ pound) good quality, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), yeast, and water. Then hold the filled shell from its rim with the right hand—above the frying pan—and let the batter run through the hole into the hot fat, simultaneously moving your hand in circles to make the lattice form. You can make them like discs (mudawwar), balls (mukabbab), or squares (murabbaʿ). (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for unlatticed zalābiya (g͟hayr mus͟habbaka):[/b]\nPut in a pot, fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) and finetasting fat (duhn ṭayyib) such as butter or sesame oil. Fry them in sesame oil (s͟hayraj), olive oil (zayt), or clarified butter (samn). \n\tYou may have them with honey, or murrī (liquid fermented sauce) and harīsa (porridge), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another zalābiya recipe:[/b]\nTake starch and add milk to it, enough to moisten it. Beat the two together very well and add to them a small amount of borax (būraq) and salt. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for exotic (g͟harīb) k͟hus͟hkanānaj Wāt͟hiqī by Abū Samīn:[/b]\nGrind 3 raṭls (3 pounds) refined sugar and sift it in a fine-mesh sieve (munk͟hul ṣafīq). Add 1½ raṭls (1½ pounds) fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Mix them well. Add ¼ raṭl (½ cup) sesame oil and knead mixture the way you usually do with flour dough. \n\tPut the mixture in a mortar (hāwan) and pound it to crush ingredients into each other and help them bind. \n\tTake a small bowl (uskurruja), the smallest you have, or anything similar in shape such as a wooden or brass huqqa (bowl) with a rounded base and a wide rim. Stuff the bowl tightly with some of the sugarflour mixture and turn it over onto a k͟hiwān (wide low table). Do this with the rest of the mixture. \n\tPrepare a large level pan with low sides and arrange the molded pieces, leaving a space between them. \n\tLower the pan into a slow-burning tannūr. Let cookies bake until they are golden brown. Take the pan out and take the cookies out of the pan with a thin spatula (isṭām raqīq). You carefully slide the spatula underneath each cookie and transfer it to a clean platter. Arrange the pieces in one layer (yuṣaff), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for k͟hus͟hkanānaj called Abū Isḥāqī muʿarraj (shaped like crescents):[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (4 pounds) fresh (ṭarī) almonds, taste them for bitterness, shell them then dry them in a big copper pot (nuqra nuḥās) set on the fire. Crumble the pith on a plate and dry it. Finely crush it with some camphor and musk then mix them well. Knead it with ¼ raṭl (4 ounces) fresh yeast dissolved in water, and 2½ raṭls (5 cups) fresh sesame oil. Mix them all together then knead and press and rub the dough vigorously. Keep on doing this while gradually feeding it with water, 5 dirhams (1 tablespoon) at a time until it is thoroughly kneaded. The final dough should be on the stiff side. \n\tDivide the dough into portions, whether small or big is up to you. Take a portion of the dough, roll it out on a k͟hiwān (wooden low table) with a rolling pin. Let it look like a tongue, wide in the middle and tapered towards both ends. Spoon some of the filling and spread it on part of the dough, leaving the borders free of the filling. Fold the dough on the filling lengthwise. Press out air so that the dough and the filling become like one solid mass. If any air remains inside, the cookie will tear and crack (yatas͟haqqaq) while baking in the tannūr. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]K͟hus͟hkanānaj of fried qaṭāyif (crepes) by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nPound 2 raṭls (2 pounds) sugar and 1 raṭl (1 pound) skinned almonds. \n\tBake qaṭāyif crepes shaped round like mirrors (marāyā), the size is up to you. Crush some aromatics (ṭīb such as musk and camphor) in the filling, and fill each crepe disc with some of it. Fold each crepe in half and shape it like k͟hus͟hkanānaj half a moons after you stick the sides together by applying some of the qaṭāyif batter around the edge. Press around the edge with the fingernail (yuẓaffar), or do whatever you can to seal it closed to prevent filling from seeping out while frying. \n\tHeat almond oil or sesame oil in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and fry qaṭāyif in it until they are golden brown (yaḥmarr). Take them out and put them in honey, which has been boiled and skimmed and mixed with an equal amount of thick sugar syrup (qiwām qawī), and perfumed with musk and mastic. \n\tWhen qaṭāyif pieces absorb enough syrup, take them out, arrange them on a platter, and sprinkle them with white sugar. Let them cool down and serve them, God willing. \n\tAbū Jaʿfar Muhammad bin al-Ḥusayn recited to me these verses describing the pastries: \n[i]K͟hus͟hkanān skillfully contrived.
