(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making crepe batter (ʿajīn al-qaṭāyif):[/b]\nTake 2 Baghdadi raṭls (2 pounds) of sifted fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Also take ¼ Baghdadi raṭl (4 ounces) fresh yeast made of ḥuwwārā or samīd͟h flour. Dissolve the yeast in water and remove any lumps. Add 3 dirhams (9 grams) salt, and 1 dirham (3 grams) būraq al-ʿajīn (baking borax), both should be crushed and sifted. \n\tAdd the dissolved yeast along with some water to the flour, and knead the mixture well until it becomes smooth and free of any lumps. In consistency, it should be soft enough to the point if you were to pour some of it on a marble (ruk͟hām), it spreads. \n\tSet the dough aside to ferment and put a mark for the height of the dough on kayl al-daqīq (container for bulk measurements) that you put next to the bowl. The batter is done fermenting when it puffs and rises about a finger’s width above the marked line. \n\tHeat a clean marble slab on the fire. When it is hot enough, ladle some of the fermented batter, and pour it onto the marble, the size is up to you. When it is done, take it away, and examine the back. If it looks too brown, reduce the fire. \n\tWhenever you bake five pieces, wipe the marble with a piece of cloth. When you are done baking, cover the crepes with a clean damp cloth for about an hour and fill them with whatever you wish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Qatāyif made for Harūn al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nChoose ripe fresh walnuts whose shells can easily be rubbed off (jawz ak͟hḍar farik bālig͟h), and peel off their thin skins. Chop walnut with a knife, the way you chop fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb). Take a similar amount of ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), pound it, and mix it with the walnut. Sprinkle the mix with rose water of Jūr (māʾ ward Jūrī), and mix and bind the mixture (yulatt) with almond oil. \n\tUse this walnut mix to fill qaṭāyif crepes recipe above. Let each piece be as small as a morsel (luqma). Arrange them on a platter in attractively organized layers (yunaḍḍad) and pour freshly extracted almond oil on them. Sprinkle pounded sugar over and between the layers. Put the platter in a big wide bowl (ṭayfūriyya) filled with ice, and present it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for pretty (ẓarīfa) qaṭāyif by Ibrāhīm bin al-Mahdī:[/b]\nChoose the tender innermost part (qalb) of fresh jummār, for it tastes exactly like newly dried walnuts (jawz ḥadīt͟h). Finely chop it along with skinned fresh walnuts. Mix the two. Add a similar amount of crushed ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar). Mix and bind (yulatt) them with rose water and a little oil of almond and walnut. \n\tFill small qaṭāyif crepes with the mix and roll them. Each filled piece should not be bigger than a morsel (luqma). Arrange them on a platter in nicely organized layers (yunaḍḍad) and pour newly extracted almond oil on them. Sprinkle pounded ṭabarzad (white cane sugar) over and between the layers and serve them, God willing. \n\tAbū al-Fatḥ Maḥmūd bin al-Ḥusayn al-Kātib recited to me some verses of his own on qaṭāyif: \n[i]I have for friends when hunger strikes, qaṭāyif like piles of books stacked.\nThey resemble honeycombs—with holes and white—when closely seen.\nSwimming in almond oil, disgorged after they had their fill of it.\nWith glistening bubbles, back and forth, rose water sways.\nRolled and aligned like purest of arrows, their sight the smittenhearted rejoice.\nMore delicious than they are is seeing them plundered, for man’s joy lies in what is most hankered.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for qaṭāyif, tasty and pretty:[/b]\nYou can make the crepes small or long and wide. After you fill them, you need to trim their edges with a knife so that they all have a uniform shape and size. Thus, they can be arranged on the platter in an attractive way. \n\tYou may make the crepes huge then divide each into three or four pieces. They can even be a yard wide each. \n\tMix and bind finely ground almond or walnut, sugar, and a little bit of rose water—just enough to bind the dry ingredients. Too much rose water will make sugar melt and cause the filling to be too thin in consistency (yariqq). \n\tFill the qaṭāyif crepes, roll them, and arrange them on a platter in nicely organized layers (yunaḍḍad). Pour almond oil on the pieces if they are filled with walnut, and walnut oil if they are filled with almond. Drench the pieces with ground ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar). \n\tYou may whip the oil with thick rose water syrup and drown the pieces with it. After qaṭāyif pieces have their fill of the syrup, the surplus will settle in the bottom of the plate, like sauce (maraq). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ḥalāqīm (cannolis) used for decorating desserts:[/b]\nTake as much as you like of dough made with pure fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free). Rub it very well with olive or sesame oil. \n\tPrepare some yard-long reeds (qaṣab), scrape their outer layers, and clean them. Wrap the prepared dough around them, cut them into finger-long pieces, and make decorative impressions on them with pincers (minqās͟h). Then color them red, yellow, green, and blue, using the dyes mentioned at the beginning of the book, where it is explained how to produce them Chapter 3. \n\tPut the finished reeds in the tannūr. When baked, remove the reeds, which will leave you with pastry tubes (anābīb mujawwafa). Fill them with a mixture of pounded walnut and sugar. Dip both ends of the reeds in thick and sticky sugar syrup. Sprinkle the ends with chips of Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy) colored with the dyes mentioned above. They will look like a vivid orchard (bustān), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for cookies (aqrāṣ) used to decorate desserts:[/b]\nTake excellent dough made of fine white four and rub it with sesame oil. Roll it out with a rolling pin and cut it out into rounds using cookie cutters (qawālīb). They should all be the same size, neither smaller nor bigger. Prick them with a feather in a decorative manner (yurrayyas͟h) and fry them in sesame oil. Take them out of the oil and set them aside. \n\tMelt bees’ honey in a pot, boil it until it thickens considerably, and add a bit of saffron to give it a reddish hue. Daub the faces of the cookies with this honey then sprinkle them with coarsely crushed sugar that has been dyed with the colors mentioned above. Press the sugar onto the cookies with your hand. \n\tUse these cookies in any way you like to decorate whatever you choose of desserts, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for plain white cookies (aqrāṣ) used as ornamentations:[/b]\nTake some of the dough mentioned above and roll it into a thin sheet (ruqāq). Cut out cookies shaped as rounds (mudawwar), squares (murabbaʿ), crescent-like (muʿarraj), triangles (s͟hawābīr), or whatever you like. Fry them in hot sesame oil and take them out. Do not color them. Leave them white and let them dry out in the air. \n\tWhen their oil is all absorbed and they are fully dry, take some Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), pound it, sift it, and lightly sprinkle (d͟harartuhu) the cookies with it. Press the sugar onto the cookies so that it adheres to them. \n\tUse these cookies to decorate whatever you like of desserts and however you wish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for stuffed cookies (ḥalwā maḥs͟huwwa), delicious and unusual (ṭarīfa):[/b]\nTake equal amounts of almond, pistachio, and hazelnut. Shell them, finely pound them, and add an equal amount of sugar. Mix and moisten the ingredients with rose water in which you have dissolved a lump of musk. \n\tMake dough with pure fine smīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free), milk, sesame oil, and yeast. When the dough ferments, flatten portions into small discs, using a rolling pin. Line a concave mold (qālab) carved with decorative shapes (ṣuwar al-tamāt͟hīl) with a flattened disc, and fill the cavity with some of the sugar-nut mixture. Put another flattened disc on the filling, and seal the edges. Take the cookie out of the mold, and repeat with the rest of the dough. \n\tBake the cookies by sticking them to the inner wall of the tannūr. Alternatively, you can arrange them in a shallow copper pan with a handle similar to that of the bucket (saṭl). Lower the pan into the tannūr and cover its upper opening with a lid for a short while to create moisture then remove it. When the cookies are done, take them out and serve them while still hot. \n\tYou also have the choice to put some fat in the pan before lowering it into the tannūr. When you take the cookies out of the oven and while still hot, dip them in ʿasal muṭaffa, which has been skimmed and scented with aromatic spices (muṭayyab). Let the cookies absorb the syrup then take them out, and arrange them on a platter. Sprinkle them with sugar and serve them. This variety (hād͟hā al-fann) is called rag͟hūnīn raṭb mulūkī (royal moist cookies), so know this, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for nāṭif Ḥarrānī:[/b]\nTake ʿasal muṭaffa, which has been skimmed of its froth and put it in a round copper pot (qidr nuhās) or a round ṭanjīr (copper or brass pot). Add ¼ raṭl (½ cup) water and beat the honey while cooking for about an hour. Set the pot aside until it cools down. \n\tVigorously beat egg whites into the honey until mixture is blended. For each 10 raṭls (10 pounds) of honey, use 10 egg whites. \n\tReturn the pot to the fire and continue beating the mixture lest the egg should burn, and keep on stirring and so that honey whitens. When nāṭif thicken, season it with cassia, black pepper, cloves, and spikenard (sunbul al-ṭīb). Add as well whatever you like of dried fruits such as almond, pistachio, hazelnut, walnut, coconut, pine nut, hulled sesame, or hemp seeds (bazr al-qinnab). You have the option of combining all these nuts or not using anything at all to make it plain (sād͟haj). \n\tThree hours are needed to beat the nougat until it becomes satisfactorily thick, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for nāṭif called k͟hus͟hkafarūs (dry candy):[/b]\nTake 4 raṭls (4 pounds) white sugar, finely grind it, and put it in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Add 1 raṭl (2 cups) water. Bring the pot to a boil and remove the froth with egg whites. Light low-heat fire underneath the pot and let it cook until it thickens. Add to the syrup, 1/3 raṭl (5 ounces) good quality, fine ḥuwwārā flour (bran-free) and cook and beat the mixture until it thickens. \n\tSpread the pudding on a board (k͟hiwān) that has been greased with oil of almond, walnut, or clarified butter. Make the pudding sheet as thin or as thick as you want it to be. Cut it out into squares or triangles and serve it. \n\tIf you want the candy yellow, add some saffron to it while still cooking. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another nāṭif, used to be made for al-Maʾmūn whenever he was on the road. It keeps for a long time:[/b]\nUse newly dried almonds and avoid the old ones. Pound them until their oil oozes. Set the oil and the ground almonds aside, separately. Also take newly-dried walnuts and pound them until they have the consistency of bone marrow (muk͟hk͟h), but not to the point where their oil separates. \n\tMake honey nāṭif and set it aside. \n\tTake fine samīd͟h flour (high in starch and bran free) and make it into dough. It can be dough of furrānī (bread baked in a brick oven) or that of k͟hubz al-māʾ (flat plain bread baked in the tannūr). Flatten the dough into very thin sheets (yuraqq) and bake them on the ṭābaq (large flat pan). \n\tSpread the nāṭif on a sheet of bread while it is still hot. Sprinkle it with ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar) and the pounded almonds and walnuts. Cover it with another layer of bread. With clean clippers, cut the filled bread into smaller portions, two-finger wide squares. \n\tPut strained honey in a pot and immerse the pieces in it, one by one. Layer the pieces as you take them out of the honey in barānī (wide-mouthed green-glazed jars), sprinkling each layer with pounded sugar. When you are done layering, pour on the pieces the almond oil you set aside. \n\tTake them with you as provisions wherever you travel. They will stay as long as you wish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another nāṭif recipe called al-Wāt͟hiqī, made with honey and red sugar. Exquisite:[/b]\nPut in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) honey and red sugar, a pound each. Pour on them a small amount of rose water and let the mixture boil until the sugar melts. Skim off the froth as it comes up. \n\tWhen syrup is almost thick and before it becomes too sticky, add 2 dirhams (6 grams) saffron, and 1 raṭl (1 pound) shelled and picked over walnut. Stir the syrup very well then pour it onto a greased slab of marble or a board and flatten it. Break it into pieces and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another nāṭif recipe, called lualuaī (like pearls):[/b]\nPut 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) that has been securely mounted on the stove (muʿallā). Let it boil very well and remove the froth as it appears. \n\tWhen honey is well thickened, add as much as it takes of hulled sesame seeds. Continue stirring the mixture until it becomes one mass. \n\tPour it onto a greased marble slab, and spread it evenly. Break candy into pieces and use it as needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another kind of nāṭif:[/b]\nPour white bees’ honey into a round pot and add a lot of water or rose water. When it comes to a boil, skim the froth, and beat the syrup vigorously to mix it well. \n\tPut the pot away, wait until it cools down, and beat egg whites into it. Continue beating until they combine. Return the pot to the fire and keep on stirring and beating until mixture thickens and looks white. \n\tAdd 2 dirhams (6 grams) mastic and 2 dirhams (6 grams) afāwīh (aromatic spices). Finally, mix in broken pieces of dry ʿafzīnaj (walnut brittle), use as much as the syrup can take. Stir the pot to incorporate them into the syrup, God willing. Abū al-Ḥusayn recited to me verses of his own on nāṭif: \n[i]After the meal, the cook brought in nāṭif, luminous as silver or marble necks.\nDrenched in smooth honey with a soul of its own, surging with waves that flow and surcease.\nLike solid silver it looks, but soft and sweet as lips it tastes.\nSo welcome in bosom, heart, and belly, like safety when between the ribs of the frightened nests.\nHow lovely in hue, taste, and sight, sweeter still than the stealthy touch of a gazelle.\nWith almonds and walnuts doubly stuffed, and with pistachio shelled between the layers tucked.\nWith an assortment of dried fruits filled, like spring flowers most beautifully arranged.\nBreak it, and the inside even surpasses how it looks when on a platter displayed.\nWhat the honey, what the musk and ambergris, what the mastic, crushed and mixed!\nWhat the eyes of the eater see is a moon in hands of maids resplendent.\nOn a platter, it shines with blooms like those of trees on rugs luscious and green.\nThis is the sweet that pleasures my heart and my craves fulfills. Anything else previously offered by hands of slaves was made.[/i] 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muzawwara of gourd (qarʿ) cooked for people with fevers, from the copy of Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake a fresh and tender gourd, peel it well, and discard the fibrous inside and all the seeds. Cut it into chunks (fuṣūs), and put it in a clean pot. Add chopped white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), a bit of fine salt, and a piece of cassia. Pour into it a suitable amount of oil of hulled sesame. Add as well 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) pounded chard, 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) fresh water (māʾ ṭayyib), and coriander seeds and cassia, both ground. \n\tWhen the stew is cooked, thicken it with some pith of bread (lubāb al-k͟hubz), and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muzawwara recipe, good for fevers and people suffering from excess of yellow bile (aṣḥāb al-ṣafrāʾ), from the same copy:[/b]\nTake a clean gourd, peel it, and discard the inside seeds. Dice it and put it in a pot. Pour on it a small amount of fresh and good quality sesame oil, a small amount of fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb) rue, and a pinch of salt. \n\tWhen the stew is done, sprinkle it with a little rose water and coriander seeds only. Sprinkle it lightly with sour juice of unripe grapes (māʾ ḥiṣrim). Add as well a bit of white sugar, enough to balance its sweet and sour taste (mazāza). Thicken the stew with some crumbled pith of k͟hubz maʿrūk (bread with a chewy texture). Ladle it into a bowl and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muzawwara of zīrbāj (delicate stew) for people suffering from excess in yellow bile (aṣḥāb al-ṣafrāʾ):[/b]\nDice the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal) and fry it in almond oil with fresh herbs. Take whichever is available of lettuce stems (uṣūl al-k͟hass) or gourd. Cut them into big pieces, add them to the onion, and fry them until they are all golden brown (yaḥmarr). Sprinkle them with a small amount of wine vinegar. Add as well a bit of saffron and a piece of cassia and serve it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Chard stew for people with fevers:[/b]\nBoil chard, take it out of the pot and press out its moisture. Pound it into paste in a mortar and set it aside. \n\tPut in a clean pot, the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), cilantro, and rue, all chopped. Pour on them 1 raṭl (2 cups) fresh water (māʾ ʿad͟hb), 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) sesame oil, and a piece of cassia. When water starts boiling, add the chard to the pot. If there is not enough liquid in the stew, add another raṭl (2 cups) of water. When the onion is cooked, season the pot with pleasant-tasting salt (milḥ ṭayyib). Taste the stew, adjust the seasoning then thicken it with pith of bread, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another muzawwara recipe of chard (silq):[/b]\nDice the onion, and put it in a pot with slightly bruised chickpeas, and a little salt. Boil them in water until they are cooked. Add oil of almond or sesame, a few stalks of chard (aẓlāb al-silq), a suitable amount of skinned almond, and a little vinegar. Also add coriander seeds, cumin, a piece of Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), and enough of pith of fine k͟hubz maʿrūk (bread with a chewy texture) to thicken the stew. \n\tStir the pot and take it away from the fire. Ladle it and let the sick person eat it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muzawwara of gourd (qarʿ) for the sick (ʿalīl):[/b]\nPeel gourd, cut it into pieces, and boil it. When it is almost done, add some laban (milk/yogurt), salt, cumin, and black pepper. It is recommended for people with fevers, (ḥumma), dizziness (dawarān), and diarrhea (al-mas͟hī), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another stew recommended for people suffering from pleurisy (barsām):[/b]\nTake the tender tips (aṭrāf) of cilantro sprigs, parsley, and dill, as well as sesame oil and water. Make stew with them. When it is done, add a small amount of fennel seeds (rāzyānaj) and nānk͟hawāh seeds (ajowan). It will cure people with dry (phlegm-free) pleurisy, with God’s permission. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe good for pleurisy and ailments in liver and abdomen (ḥas͟hā):[/b]\nCombine in a pot, water, salt, dill, and ground pistachio. Boil the mixture Eat the solids and have its liquid for soup (taḥsū maraqahu). It is beneficial for pleurisy, liver ailments, and fever, with God’s permission. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for the same conditions:[/b]\nCook together, gourd, onion, lentil, water, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and cumin. Eat the solids and have the liquid for soup, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for the same conditions:[/b]\nTake a fresh and tender green gourd, smear it with mud, and put it in the fire. When it is cooked, remove the peel, and discard the inside seeds with the fibers surrounding them (laḥā). Cut the gourd into small pieces. Drench them in murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and eat them. \n\tGourd is soft (layyin). It agrees with people with hot temperaments and sick people can have it to satisfy their hunger. Indeed, it is recommended for any sicknesses provoked by heat, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another stew recipe:[/b]\nWash liver and discard its gall bladder (marāra). Cook it in oil and water and season it with ginger, long pepper (dār fulful), salt, and some parsley. Let it cook until it is done. The stew should be thin in consistency. Let the sick person have it like soup. It is good for hemorrhoid (bāsūra), indigestion (baṭan), and weakness in the stomach (riqqat al-maʿida). Besides, it strengthens the body and stimulates the appetite, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muzawwara of gourd (qarʿ), beneficial to feverish people:[/b]\nTake a gourd, peel it, discard the inside, and dice it. Boil it in a pot with sour juice of unripe grapes, a piece of galangal, 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) almond or sesame oil, a bit of salt, and diced white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). \n\tWhen stew is done, season it with coriander and cassia and thicken it with pounded dried pith of bread (lubāb al-k͟hubz). Offer it to the sick person with a spoon (milʿaqa). \n\tIt is good for people with fevers, especially those triggered by surfeit of yellow bile (ḥumma ṣafrāʾ). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for muzawwara of gourd (qarʿ) for people with fevers and those suffering from excess in hot properties (aṣḥāb al-ḥarārāt):[/b]\nChoose a tender green gourd, peel it, and discard the inside including the seeds. Chop it, boil it until cooked, and pound it in a mortar until it resembles bone marrow in consistency (muk͟h). Set it aside. \n\tNow take a clean pot and put in it 1 dirham (3 grams) diced white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), a piece of cassia, 2 ūqiyyas (¼ cup) oil of almond or sesame, a small amount of chopped fresh herbs (abzār ruṭb), and 1 raṭl (1 pound) of the prepared gourd. Pour on it juice of unripe sour grapes and fresh water, ½ raṭl (1 cup) each. \n\tWhen the onion is cooked, add to the pot, 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) skinned and ground almonds, 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), 1 dirham (3 grams) salt, 2 dirhams (6 grams) ground coriander seeds, and 2 dirhams (6 grams) bread pith mixed with 5 dirhams (1 tablespoon) rose water. \n\tThe final stew should be medium in consistency, neither too thin nor condensed. Offer the stew to the sick person with a spoon. It is good for feverish people and those suffering from excess in hot properties, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A vegetable dish (baqla) for people with fevers and acute diarrhea (ik͟htilāf al-mas͟hī):[/b]\nChoose a tender gourd, peel it, and cook it. When it is almost done, take it out, pound it, mash it, strain it to get a smooth consistency free of lumps, and return it to the pot. \n\tAdd what equals half its amount of milk. Add as well a small amount of the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), salt, black pepper and cumin, all crushed. Thicken the dish with pith of saljan (kabk), and add a small amount of almond or walnut oil. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another stew recipe for similar conditions:[/b]\nPut milk in a pot. When it boils, add chard that has been boiled, pounded, and mixed with chopped onion. Also add cilantro, a bit of salt, black pepper, coriander seeds, and cumin. Stir the pot. \n\tWhen stew is cooked, add k͟hat͟ht͟hāra (thickening agent) to it, such as a ladleful of fine crushed bread that has been rubbed with oil of almond or sesame, and serve it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Muzawwara of chard for people suffering from excess in yellow bile (aṣḥāb al-ṣafrāʾ):[/b]\nBoil chard stalks (aḍlāb al-silq) then take them out and put them in cold water. Press out their moisture and put them in a green-glazed bowl (g͟haḍāra). Dredge the chard with a handful of sifted sumac. You may stir the sumac so that the chard absorbs its tartness. Season the dish (yuṭayyab) with a small amount of olive oil (zayt), sesame oil (duhn s͟hayraj), or almond oil (duhn al-lawz). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for meat juice (māʾ al-laḥm) good for people suffering from chest pain, coughs (suʿāl), and shortness of breath (buhr):[/b]\nChoose tender lamb, preferably from the upper thigh (uṣūl al-afk͟hād͟h), shoulders (mutūn), and tenderloins (bas͟htamāzijāt). These are the most nourishing cuts of the meat and the strongest in properties. \n\tCut the meat into very thin slices, put it in a pot, and without adding water let it cook on the fire. Whenever it releases some moisture, take it, strain it, put it in a small bowl (uskurruja), and sprinkle it with a bit of ground cassia. \n\tServe this meat juice to whoever needs it. It will sustain the stomach (yuqawwī al-maʿida). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for meat juice (māʾ al-laḥm), good for the same conditions:[/b]\nTake cuts of meat from the shoulders, tenderloins, and upper thighs. Cut them into thin slices, and put them in a pot. Add neither salt nor water, and light slow-burning fire underneath it. Whenever the meat releases its juices, take it all out, and repeat doing this until the meat is completely dry. Add a bit of salt to the accumulated meat juice. If you want to increase its hot properties, add some Chinese ginger (zanjabīl Ṣīnī). If you want to decrease its hot properties, add some aniseeds (anīsūn). Let the sick person drink it. \n\tThis meat juice is good for people with consumption (sull) and those suffering from excess in hot or cold properties (aṣḥāb al-ḥarārāt wa ’l-burūdāt). It also agrees with people whose bodies are naturally prone to cold or hot properties (ajsām bārida wa ajsām ḥārra), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for nārbāj (pomegranate stew) good for diarrhea (ik͟htilāf al-baṭn) caused by abrasive bowel disorders (saḥj), from the copy of Yuḥannā bin Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake as many as you can get of larks (qanābir), clean them, discard the entrails, and wash them. Put them in a pot, pour on them some zayt anfāq (olive oil made from unripe olives). Add as well, the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), and a piece of galangal. \n\tPound together raisins and pomegranate seeds, mix them with water, and add them to the pot. \n\tStart the fire underneath the pot and let it cook until meat is done. Season the pot with coriander seeds, black pepper, and cassia. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for lark stew (marqat qanābir) for people with colic (qawlanj), from the copy of Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nClean larks thoroughly, put them in a pot, pour on them water, and drizzle them with a small amount of olive oil (zayt). Add as well salt and the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Boil the pot until meat is done then season it with these spices. \n\tThe sick person should have the liquid only. He should eat nothing of its meat. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for chicken juice (mā al-laḥm min al-dajāj) beneficial to people with ulcers (qurūḥ) in their bowels:[/b]\nTake a plump chicken and slaughter it. Do not scald it to remove the feathers, but strip off its skin, instead. Take its breast and fat, slice them thinly, and put them in a pot. Start a slow fire underneath the pot, and let it cook until it releases its moisture. \n\tTake the released juice and fat, season it with a bit salt, and let the ailing person have it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A stew recipe recommended in cases of ik͟htilāf al-ag͟hrās (frequent bowel movements due to taking laxatives):[/b]\nTake meat from a partridge (ḥajal) and larks (qanābir), wash it, and put it in a clean pot. Add a drop of olive oil (zayt), 1 dirham (3 grams) white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal), and a piece of galangal. Pour a bowl of strained sumac juice, and a bowl of strained juice of raisins and pomegranate mixed together. Add enough to submerge the meat. \n\tWhen meat it done, strain it with a sieve (munk͟hul), and discard the bones. Thicken the stew with pith of bread or saljan (kabk), and pounded almonds. \n\tLet the sick person have it like soup (ḥasū). It is very beneficial, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for maṣūṣ (meat cooked in vinegar) for phlegmatic diarrhea (ishāl al-balg͟ham):[/b]\nBoil chicken, larks (qanābir), and sparrows (ʿaṣāfīr). Stuff their cavities with a mix of parsley, rue, and naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint); as well as seeds of anise, caraway, cumin, and coriander, all fried. Add to these, nānk͟hawāh (ajowan) and thyme. \n\tBoil the birds again in vinegar that has been left overnight to steep in thyme, cumin, cassia, and black pepper then strained. \n\tIt is good and very effective, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another maṣūṣ recipe recommended for diarrhea caused by excess in yellow bile (ishāl al-ṣafrāʾ):[/b]\nCombine toasted pomegranate seeds, sumac, myrtle berries (ḥabb al-ās), and toasted coriander seeds. Pound them all and stuff with them the birds’ cavities mentioned in the previous recipe. Cook the birds in vinegar of myrtle berries, sour juice of unripe grapes, and sour pomegranate juice. It is beneficial, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another maṣūṣ for the same condition:[/b]\nTake naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), parsley, rue, fresh thyme, and nammām (cultivated oregano), and cook them with pullets, larks, partridge, or sparrows. The liquid they are to be cooked in is sour juice of unripe grapes that has been infused with parsley, mint, fresh and dried thyme and strained. Add to the liquid, black pepper, caraway, cumin, anise, and toasted milḥ andarānī (good quality translucent rock salt), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe, recommended for the same condition, tried and effective (mujarraba):[/b]\nTake al-baqla al-ḥāmiḍa, stems of purslane (rijla), and cilantro. Cook them with young fowls (firāk͟h) in sour juice of unripe grapes. Add to the liquid, sour pomegranate juice, coriander seeds, juice of citron pulp (ḥummāḍ al-utruj), and citron leaves, with God’s permission. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another maṣūṣ recipe used for the same ailment, from the copy Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nPut together parsley, naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint), fresh and dried thyme, cilantro, rue, and a small amount of the white part of fresh onion (bayāḍ baṣal). Add as well, a few citron leaves and a few tender and fresh myrtle leaves with their berries if available. Put all these on a board, and pound them with a knife. Sprinkle on them salt, coriander seeds, and black pepper. Continue pounding the mixture until the ingredients mix well. \n\tSprinkle them with juice of sumac, juice of sour unripe grapes, and juice of pomegranate that has been pressed with its white pith (s͟haḥm) and peel. Put as much as needed. Mix all these ingredients together, and stuff the cavities of cleaned birds mentioned in above recipes with them. \n\tBoil the birds in vinegar until they cook and absorb the flavors of the spices. Serve the dish, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for almond soup (ḥasū al-lawz):[/b]\nWash a pot, fill it with clean water, and put it on the fire. Add white sugar, half the amount of water used. Add as well finely ground almonds, the amount of which is equal to that of sugar. When the soup is cooked, add crushed dried bread pith, and almond oil. When you ladle it, the soup should be moist and runny (raṭba) in consistency. It will do the sick person good, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fava-beans broth (māʾ bāqillī), good for soothing pain of a sore throat and hoarseness of the voice (baḥḥa) caused by having a cold:[/b]\nTake sprouted fava beans (bāqillī manbūt) and boil them with the skin until they fall apart. Take 1 raṭl (2 cups) of the beans broth, dissolve in it 1/3 raṭl (10 ounces) fānīd͟h s͟hajarī, and sip it (yuḥsā). It is quite beneficial, God willing. After that, eat the beans themselves unsalted, for they are also good, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Stew recipe (marqa), recommended for coughs:[/b]\nCook together, gourd, onion, lentil, water, murrī (liquid fermented sauce), and cumin. Sip the broth (yuḥsā) and eat the vegetables. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another stew, recommended for the same condition:[/b]\nPeel fava beans, pound them, and cook them with water until stew is done and thickened (rabā). Season it with ground caraway and a bit of salt. It can be eaten hot or cold. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe, good for coughs:[/b]\nTake sweet and sour pomegranate, parsley, dill, onion, and sesame oil. Cook them all together and season them with a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Sip the broth (yuḥsā) and eat the vegetables. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A stew recipe good for coughs, from the copy of Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake fresh fish and cook it well. Add pounded walnut and boil them together. Sip the broth (yuḥsā), for it is healing, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for stew of kis͟hk, recommended for coughs, tightness of the chest (ḥaṣar), and pleurisy (barsām), a tried-and-true cure (mujarraba):[/b]\nCook the kis͟hk in water, and season it with ginger, long pepper (dār fulful), and cumin. Add a small amount of clarified butter of sheep. \n\tLet the stew be thin in consistency so that the sick person can sip it (yaḥsū). It will ease the tightness of the chest, coughs, and pleurisy, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for curing coughs, asthma (rabū), and wheezing (ṣufār), from the same copy Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake one part of each of the following: cassia, long pepper, ginger, kat͟hīrā (gum of tragacanth tree), kernels (lubāb) of cottonseeds, lubān d͟hakar (white frankincense), condensed licorice juice (rubb al-sūs), gum Arabic, and nānk͟hawāh (ajowan). \n\tPound the spices and sift them. Add honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth, and mix them into paste. Store it in a green-glazed earthenware jar (burma k͟haḍrāʾ) or glass jars (qawārīr). \n\tTake a lump, size of a hazelnut, of the paste twice daily—first thing in the morning and before you sleep. It is a tried-and-true cure. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another cough medicine from the same copy Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake 5 mit͟hqāls (22½ grams) fānīd͟h s͟hajarī (sugar-candy), 5 mit͟hqāls (22½ grams) kundur d͟hakar (excellent-quality frankincense), 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) afyūn (opium). \n\tPound the ingredients separately. Knead them into paste by adding some cold water to them. Set mixture aside for a short while then form it into small balls (banādiq), the size of the stone of the fruit of the medlar-tree (nabq), each. \n\tPut one piece under the tongue once a day. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another cough medicine, quite effective, from the same copy:[/b]\nTake one part of each of the following: seeds of marū (sweet-smelling herb of the mint family), seeds of s͟hāhasfaram (variety of mint, smells like thyme), bazr qaṭṭūna (fleawort), and kat͟hīrā (gum of tragacanth tree). \n\tPick the ingredients over and put them in a glass (qadaḥ). Pour on them a small amount of water and whip the mixture. Stir in oil of violet (banafsaj) or narcissus (narjis). Drink it first thing in the morning. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ḥarīra (silk-smooth soup) recommended for coughs and chest pain, from the same copy Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nTake strained broth of fava beans and throw into it a suitable amount of fānīd͟h (chewy sugar-candy). Dissolve starch in water, strain it, and add it to the broth. Let the soup cook into a soft and smooth consistency (layyin rak͟hū). Add oil of sesame or almonds. When it is done, ladle it into a bowl, and let the sick person have it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another ḥarīra (silk-smooth soup) for people suffering from excess in hot properties (aṣḥāb al-ḥarārāt):[/b]\nPut ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar) in a pot and pour water on it, enough to cover it or even less. Let it boil, strain it, and skim the froth. \n\tRub starch between your fingers very well to break down lumps and sift it in a fine sieve (munk͟hul s͟haʿr). Add it to the pot and cook the mixture until the soup becomes soft and smooth (layyin rak͟hū). Add oil of almond or oil of unhulled sesame (duhn al-ḥal) and let the soup absorb it. Ladle it into a bowl (g͟haḍāra), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ḥasū (smooth soup), good for chest pain and coughs, from the same copy Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nPour the needed amount of water into a clean pot. Add sugar, half the amount of water used. Drizzle into the pot a few drops of fat. When it comes to a good boil, add 2 dānaqs (1 gram) black pepper, 1 dirham (3 grams) coriander seeds, 1 dirham (3 grams) gum Arabic, 1 dirham (3 grams) lubān d͟hakar (excellent-quality frankincense), and 2 dirhams (6 grams) flour of fava beans. \n\tLet the pot come to a boil then add some fine ḥuwwārā flour (branfree) to thicken its broth. When it boils and develops a smooth and moist consistency, add almond oil, or oil of unhulled sesame seeds (duhn al-ḥal). Let the sick person have it. It is a tried-and-true cure. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Stew recipe for upset stomachs and indigestion, from the same copy Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nStart with unhusked rice, dry toast it in a frying pan and remove whatever is shelled of its husk. Then boil the rice with pomegranate seeds and water. When it is done, add a piece of long pepper (dār fulful), a small piece of ginger, salt, and cumin, all ground. \n\tContinue boiling until everything is cooked. Let the final stew be thin so that the sick person can sip it (yaḥsū). It is good for indigestion (fasād al-maʿida) and for those whose food lingers in the stomach undigested. It purges flatulence and softens and improves the bowels. It is quite healthy (ṣāliḥ) and easy to digest (marī), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for stew of pomegranate seeds and dry toasted rice (aruzz maqlū), good for liver, fevers, and pain in the upper gate of the stomach (wajaʿ al-fuʾād):[/b]\nPut in a pot, pomegranate seeds, dry toasted shelled rice (aruzz muqas͟hs͟har maqlū), sesame seeds, long pepper, ginger, cumin, and salt. Add water to the pot and let it cook. The stew should be thin in consistency so that the sick person can sip it (yaḥsū). \n\tIt is recommended for the liver, fever, gall (marār), wind in the ureters (ḥālibayn) and the sides (al-janb). It relieves pain in the upper gate of the stomach (fuʾād), strengthens the body, cures and sustains the stomach. It is a tried-and-true cure. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another stew, good for gastric ailments and painful joints:[/b]\nCook together in water, cumin, dill, and 3 crabs (saraṭān). When the stew is done, sprinkle it with ground walnut, and eat it. It is good for all the ailments we mentioned, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another stew recipe, recommended for a person suffering from gastric ailments (mabṭūn):[/b]\nPound cumin and put it in a qaṣʿa (big, wide plate). Add to it a few cloves of garlic and pound them together. Sprinkle them with a little hot water, olive oil (zayt), and sumac. Eat this paste with the meal. \n\tIn the following morning, eat ḥurf (seeds of pepper grass) and bazr qaṭṭūna (fleawort) mixed with some water and olive oil (zayt). This will restrain bowel movements and relieve gastric pain. \n\tAlternatively, you can wash unhusked rice and let it dry in a shaded place for a short while. Boil it, remove its husk then crush the grains. Next, cook it with cumin, a bit of coriander seeds, a small lump of salt, and a small amount of clarified butter (samn) or olive oil (zayt). Eat the solids and sip the liquid. Add a generous amount of black pepper to the stew. This is a proven cure. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another stew recipe for gastric ailments:[/b]\nCut off both ends of leeks (kurrāt͟h) and chop the remaining part (i.e. stalks). Pour water enough to submerge them. Let them cook until all moisture evaporates and leeks cook and turn yellow. \n\tMince the leaks, break on them 3 eggs, and add a small amount of murrī (liquid fermented sauce). Briefly cook the ingredients and mix them gently. Serve the dish when the eggs are slightly set. It is very good for gastric ailments, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe, good for pleurisy (barsām):[/b]\nMix clarified butter of cow’s milk with sesame oil. Rub this on the head of the patient, and wrap it with a bandage. This is good for severe cases of pleurisy. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe a poultice used when pleurisy affects the head:[/b]\nMix flour of barley and wheat and knead them together with some water until they resemble bread dough. Make it into a ball (qurṣ), which you then flatten and smear with hot oil of violet (banafsaj). \n\tYou need to have two discs drenched in the oil and ready to use. You put one under the back of the patient’s head (qaḥf al-raʾs) and when it cools down, replace it with a hot one. Repeat this procedure three times. Do it twice daily—once in the morning, and once at bedtime. Moreover, use violet oil to induce sneezing (tasʿīṭ). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for barley broth (māʾ al-s͟haʿīr) from the copy of Ibn Māsawayh:[/b]\nWhen you want to make this broth for the patient, take new or old barley with the husk and wash it clean after you pick it over. Soak it for a whole hour (sāʿa ṣāliḥa, a good hour), drain it then cover it with a thick cloth overnight. \n\tIn the following day, pound the barley in a stone mortar (ḥajar) or brass mortar (hāwan). You can also use a hand mill (mijas͟hs͟ha) to bruise it. Then winnow it (yunassaf to get rid of husk), pick it over, and put it in a clean pot. \n\tFor each kayl (measure) of barley, add 14 kayls (measures) of water. Start a slow fire of coals underneath the pot and let it simmer slowly until two thirds of the liquid evaporate and it develops a slightly thick consistency. Let the patient drink (yusqā) the drained broth, with or without sugar. It is beneficial. \n\tBarley broth can also be made by putting the prepared barley and water in a pot. Put this pot in another pot that has water in it. Light the fire underneath it and cook it as described above, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe good for people with jaundice (yaraqān):[/b]\nWash the fish thoroughly in juice of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār). Stuff it with cucumber and sprinkle it with a bit of salt and olive oil. Bake it and let the sick person eat it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another fish recipe:[/b]\nTake uks͟hūt͟h (dodder), pulp of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), sprigs of rue, a small amount of parsley, and fresh leeks. Chop them all into fine pieces. Stuff the cavity of a fish with this mixture and bake it or cook it in vinegar or any other liquid. It is a tried-and-true cure, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A medicinal recipe for jaundice that men can use (yastaʿmiluhu al-rijāl):[/b]\nMix equal amounts of sticks of gum-lac (luk), ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), dried dodder (uks͟hūt͟h), and dried peel of yellow cucumber (k͟hiyār aṣfar). Grind them all and knead them with pure honey. Let the man sick with jaundice have it with juice of rue (māʾ sad͟hāb). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for jaundice women can use:[/b]\nIf the afflicted person is a woman, pregnant or breast-feeding, let her have what we prescribed above with fresh juice of small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), or juice of endive (hindibāʾ). It will do her good, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another one for jaundice:[/b]\nTake leeks (kurrāt͟h) and eat it with boiled fish, especially s͟habbūṭ (carp). It is beneficial, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for ibmāl al-fuqqāʿ, which ʿAbdullāh al-Sharābī used in making Ḥarrāniyya for al-Muʿtaḍid:[/b]\nChoose good quality newly-harvested white barley. The best would be barley that was harvested two or three months ago. Wash it thoroughly to get rid of the husk, dirt, and stones that might be in it. After that, let it soak for a day and a night 24 hours. \n\tDrain the barley the following day and spread it on a clean reed mat (bāriyya) put in a shaded place. Sprinkle the barley with water whenever it looks dry until it sprouts and becomes thick and entangled like green fenugreek (hulba). At this point, stop sprinkling it with water and leave it until it dries out. Then grind the sprouts with the grain shells and use whatever amount you need of it to make beer. \n\tThe resulting ground barley is called daqīq al-s͟haʿīr (ground malted barley). It is used in making fuqāb. \n\tBarley sprouted during the coldest days of the year will grow faster, and yield better results, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fuqqāʿ made with k͟hubz samīd͟h:[/b]\nTake daqīq al-s͟haʿīr (ground, malted barley, recipe above) and put it in a vessel. For each 50 kūz ṣag͟hīr (beer glasses) you are making, use 3 raṭls (3 pounds) of the malted barley. \n\tBoil water, enough for making 50 beer glasses, and pour it on the malted barley. Stir and mix until only barley shells remain. Set it aside to cool down then strain it and take the amount enough for making 50 beer glasses. Add a suitable amount of andarānī salt (pure and white rock salt) so that the beer will be neither too salty nor bland. The best way to judge is for the beer-maker to taste it. Set the liquid aside until it settles and looks like clear water. This clear water will be referred to in the recipes as māʾ al-s͟haʿīr ‘barley water’. \n\tNow take k͟hubz samīd͟h, and for each 50 beer glasses, use 2½ breads. Remove the crust, and put the pith in a sieve set on a big glass (qadaḥ). Pour some of the strained barley water on the pith and keep on mashing and rubbing it in the strainer, adding barley water as needed until nothing of the pith remains in the sieve. \n\tPut the sieve right above the barley water vessel and let the mashed pith you have in the glass pass through the sieve into the barley water. \n\tFor each 20 beer glasses of barley water, add 1½ ūqiyyas (1½ ounces) Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), and 1 dānaq (½ gram) sukk or musk. Therefore, for making 50 beer glasses, you will be adding 3¼ ūqiyyas (3¼ ounces) Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), and 2½ dānaqs (1¼ grams) sukk or musk. \n\tPour the prepared brew into big decanters (kīzān) in which beer has recently been brewed (ṭariyya). Any ḥubb (big earthenware jar), ināʾ (container), and kīzān (decanters) used in making fuqqāʿ need to be used for 10 days only. They have to be replaced to prevent fermentation. (Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fuqqāʿ al-aruzz (rice beer):[/b]\nIn all its varieties, rice beer is done the same way bread beer is done previous recipe. You only substitute bread with rice. \n\tFor each 20 beer glasses (kūz) of barley water (māʾ al-s͟haʿīr) details in previous recipe, use 1 beer glass of jaʿfarī rice. Wash the rice thoroughly, finely grind it, add it to the strained barley water, and whip the mixture. \n\tIncrease the amount of sugar specified in the bread beer recipe above . Add ½ ūqiyya (½ ounce) more to the 1 ½ ūqiyyas (1½ ounces) of Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy) we specified for each 20 beer glasses. \n\tAdd to the liquid the same amounts of sukk and all the other ingredients we mentioned in the bread beer above, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fuqqā al-lawz (almond beer):[/b]\nSubstitute rice used in recipe above with almonds. For each 20 kūz of barley water, use 1 kūz of skinned almonds. Grind them as you did with rice and add them to the barley water. Prepare the drink as described in the bread beer, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for fuqqāʿQaras͟hī, flavored with spices:[/b]\nYou make it exactly as we described in the bread beer up to the point where we say, “until it settles and looks like clear water.” \n\tNow, to each 50 beer glasses (kūz) of barley water add 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) black pepper, 2 dirhams (6 grams) cassia, 2 dirhams (6 grams) spikenard and cloves, and two nutmegs. Add as well mace (basbāsa), black cardamom (qāqulla), chestnut (kistāna), and long pepper (dār fulful), use 2 dānaqs (1 gram) of each. Crush all these spices until they are as smooth as bone marrow (muk͟h), and add them to the strained barley water. Whip the mixture with the hand and set it aside to let it settle and become clear. \n\tAdd 2 dānaqs (1 gram) sukk misk, and 1/3 raṭl (5 ounces) Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy) for each 50 beer glasses (kūz) of barley liquid. Flavor it with rue, tarragon, and naʿnaʿ (cultivated mint). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Fuqqāʿ al-ʿasal (honey beer):[/b]\nTake good quality honey and for each part of honey, use 4 parts water. Honey if thick might take more than four parts of water. \n\tTake equal amounts of black pepper, long pepper, cloves, ginger, cassia, Ceylon cinnamon (qarfa), spikenard, and a small amount of black cardamom (qāqulla). Grind them all very well, and mix with them a handful of millet flour (jāwars͟h). \n\tGet the beer-brewing containers (kīzān) ready and for each kūz make two covers of leather. \n\tNow, fill these containers with honey, which has been whipped in hot water ratios mentioned above, and add what your nail can hold of the ground spices. Put sprigs of rue in each container, and cover and tie their heads, but not too tightly to allow some of the gases to escape. \n\tPrepare a hole in the ground for them, line its bottom with pieces of felt (labda), and stack the containers one above the other in it. Cover them with felt and leave them there for two days. Drink of the beer on the third day, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another honey beer:[/b]\nMix honey with hot water and add cassia, spikenard, cloves, and black pepper. Add ½ qisṭ (1½ cups) of the barley water recipe in bread beer above, and put mixture in the containers (kīzān). Add some sprigs of rue to the brew then cover the containers, turn them upside down, and leave them like this overnight, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another honey beer recipe:[/b]\nBoil water and mix it with honey, using five parts of water for each part of honey. While water is still hot, whip the mixture with the hand very well. Add to it a small amount of wine dregs (durdī nabīd͟h) and set it aside for a day to sour (qaraṣa). \n\tNow, add to the honey liquid, a similar amount of barley water (māʾ al-s͟haʿīr) recipe in bread beer above. Flavor it with Ceylon cinnamon (qarfa), spikenard, saffron, and a few sprigs of rue. Pour it into bottles (qawārīr), which you set aside overnight.
