(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for making k͟hamr (intoxicating wine) from raisins:[/b]\nFor each 10 raṭls (10 pounds) of raisins, use 22 raṭls (22 pints) of soft water (māʾ ḥilū sweet). Follow the instructions we give in making al-s͟hamsī wine (fermented in the heat of the sun) last recipe in this chapter. Use the same ingredients required except for faṭṭāra (fermented dough used as wine yeast), which you replace with honey. For each jar (jarra) of wine, use 3 ūqiyyas (3 ounces) honey. \n\tWhisk the mixture with miḍrab (whisk) and stow the jars away in a sunny place, as we mention. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for plain honey wine (s͟harāb muʿassal sād͟haj):[/b]\nTake 10 raṭls (10 pounds) good quality bees’ honey and 20 raṭls (40 pints) river water, which you collect at the time of the river rising tide (madd). Whip them together and boil the mixture until one third of it evaporates. Add 1½ ūqiyyas (1½ ounces) saffron. \n\tEmpty the liquid into large flagons (qarrābāt). Leave the vessels in the sun for 40 days after which you can store them and use the wine as needed. In color and taste, it will be exactly like S͟hīrāzī. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A delicious drink (s͟harāb ṭayyib) from the recipe of Abū Yazīd al-Madīnī:[/b]\nPrepare 20 raṭls (20 pounds) honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth, and 60 raṭls (60 pints) water. Also prepare nutmeg, cloves, black cardamom (qāqulla), zurnubād (zedoary), and fennel, 6 mit͟hqāls (a little less than an ounce) each. Use as well, 30 mit͟hqāls (4 ounces) ginger. Grind all these spices, sift them, and put them in a loosely tied bundle of thin cloth. \n\tPut honey, water, and the spice bundle in a pot. Let them cook on low heat until all the water evaporates and only honey remains. Put the pot away from the fire. Add 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) saffron and 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) musk, each crushed separately. \n\tPour the drink into a glass jar (qārūra) and use it. With God’s permission, it is a good cure for cold kidneys, kidney pain (wajaʿ al-k͟hāṣira), and a cold stomach. It also stimulates the appetite and cleanses the stomach. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making cooked raisin wine (nabīd͟h zabībī muʿālaj):[/b]\nTake one measure (kayl) of raisins and 20 measures of water. Soak the raisins in the water overnight. In the following morning, put the pot on the fire and boil it until one third of the liquid evaporates. Crush the raisins, strain their liquid, and return it to the pot. Add 10 raṭls (10 pounds) honey and let liquid boil until sixth of the original amount is reduced and only half of the original amount remains. \n\tIf you prefer it flavored, then go ahead and add some spices to it. It will be wonderful, God willing 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making Egyptian wine (nabīd͟h Miṣrī):[/b]\nTake one part (juza) honey with its wax and froth no need to boil it and skim it and put it in a pot. Stir into it 5 parts water and bring it to a boil until fourth of it is reduced. Set the pot aside to cool down and then pour the liquid into dinān (large earthenware casks) or kīzān (decanters). \n\tSpread grape leaves all over the liquid to cover it but leave a hole to let the fermentation gases escape. \n\tWhen fermentation subsides, seal the wine containers with mud and leave them in the sun for 40 days after which you put them away from the sun. Empty the wine into glass jars (qawārīr), cover their openings with pieces of leather, and stow them away in a shaded place for 4 months after which you can use the wine, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sun-fermented raisin wine (zabīb s͟hamsī), done the Egyptian way (bala raʾī ahl Miṣr):[/b]\nFor each 10 Egyptian raṭls (approx. 7 pounds) of raisins, use 27 raṭls (18 pints) soft water (māʾ ḥilū). Put aside 7 raṭls (approx. 5 pints) of the water mentioned, and soak the raisins in the remaining 20 raṭls (13 pints) in muṭr muzaffat. Any other similar vessels will do. Let the raisins soak for six to seven days. Meanwhile, press and mash them very well with the hands (marasa) twice or thrice a day. \n\tEmpty the raisin mash into a large mājūr (large earthenware tub), press it with your feet, and strain the juice. Next, thoroughly wash the remaining pith with the set-aside 7 raṭls of water until nothing remains to be extracted from it. Strain the liquid and add it to the rest of the juice. \n\tAdd to the raisin juice, 1 fals (3 grams) fresh fennel seeds (s͟hamar g͟harīḍ), 3 fals (9 grams) murratayn ak͟hḍar (fresh wormwood and rosebay), 8 dirhams (24 grams) laurel leaves (waraq rand), and 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) rose buds (zir ward). \n\tIncorporate sugar (yuḥalla) to the must by whipping in 3 raṭls (2 pounds) of faṭṭāra bāl. Empty the must into jars (jirār) and stow them away in a sunny place for two weeks. Adding durdī al-k͟hamra (wine dregs), as well, will make even a better wine. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A non-intoxicating drink (g͟hayr muskir), delicious:[/b]\nPut 5 manns (10 pounds) of fine ṭabarzad (white cane sugar) in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and add 5 manns (20 cups) grape juice. Boil them together then add 100 dirhams (10 ounces) poppy seeds (k͟has͟hk͟hās͟h) and 1 raṭl (2 cups) milk. \n\tWhen mixture comes to a boil, add 5 manns (20 cups) water. Bring it to a boil and put it away from heat. Sprinkle it with rose water, empty it into dasātīj, and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another drink made from sugar, non-intoxicating:[/b]\nTake bowlfuls of refined sugar and dissolve it in half its amount of water. Add a small amount of juice of unripe excellent-quality apples. Let the liquid boil until it is reduced to two thirds of its original amount. Flavor it with ginger and empty it into glass jars (qawārīr). Use it diluted with water, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another drink, for wintertime:[/b]\nTake 10 raṭls (10 pounds) bees’ honey and a similar amount of water . Add juice of white grapes, an equal amount to both of them. \n\tLet the mixture boil and flavor it with a bit of spikenard and cloves. When it is done boiling, empty it into a green-glazed jar (jarra k͟haḍrāʾ) and use it. It is a healthy drink. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making a sour drink (qāriṣ) from camel’s milk (laban al-ibl):[/b]\nTake camel’s milk and pour it into a leather bottle. Put in it a small amount of black raisins (zabīb aswad) and set it aside overnight. \n\tIn the following morning, add to the milk 10 dirhams (1 ounce) black pepper, and 1 dirham (3 grams) galangal. Keep the leather bottle suspended in a cold place and drink of the beverage as needed. You will find it sour and biting to the tongue. It is beneficial, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another drink from sheep’s milk (ḥalīb al-ḍān):[/b]\nDissolve 2 raṭls (2 pounds) sugar in 10 raṭls (20 cups) milk of sheep, no need to boil the mix at this point. Add 20 dirhams (¼ cup) rose water, 5 dirhams (15 grams) crushed mastic, and 1 dirham (3 grams) saffron. \n\tBoil mixture briefly (g͟halya k͟hafīfa), let it cool down, and drink it mixed with sawīq (crushed toasted grains). It is healthy and delicious (nāfiʿ lad͟hīd͟h). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A drink recipe made from cow’s milk (albān al-baqar):[/b]\nTake 20 raṭls (40 cups) cow’s milk and put it in a vessel. Stir in 10 raṭls (10 pounds) refined bees’ honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Put the mix in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), boil it, and add 5 dirhams (15 grams) spikenard (sunbul), 3 lumps of musk, and 5 dirhams (15 grams) mastic (maṣṭakā). \n\tWhen the mixture comes to a vigorous boil, take it away from heat and sprinkle it with 3 dirhams (9 grams) saffron. Set it aside to cool down and use it. It is a wonderful drink (g͟hāya). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making a thirst-quenching, healthy drink (muṭaffī nāfiʿ):[/b]\nPut 20 raṭls (20 pounds) of refined sugar in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Add 100 dirhams (2½ cups) juice of jummār (heart of the date palm) and 2 raṭls (2 pounds) poppy seeds (k͟has͟hk͟hās͟h). \n\tBring mixture to a boil then add 5 raṭls (10 cups) grape juice, 2 raṭls (4 cups) mulberry juice, and ½ dirham (1½ grams) camphor. \n\tBoil mixture well, put it away from heat, empty it into glass jars (qawārīr), and use it. It is a healthy tried-and-true drink. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another drink:[/b]\nDissolve 5 raṭls (5 pounds) white sugar in 100 dirhams (2½ cups) māʾ al-buzūr (strained liquid of boiled seeds). Add 2 dānaqs (1 gram) camphor and 1 raṭl (1 pound) jujubes (ʿunnāb). Let the fruit be whole. \n\tWhen mixture comes to a boil, discard the jujubes. Pour into it juice of Nabatean tūt (white and sweet mulberry), the amount of which should be equal to that of sugar, and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for another drink:[/b]\nDissolve 5 raṭls (5 pounds) refined white sugar in 5 raṭls (10 cups) māʾ qarʿ (strained juice of gourd) and bring them to a boil. Add to the syrup, 100 dirhams (10 ounces) purslane seeds (bazrat baqla) tied in a cloth bundle. \n\tWhen the syrup is done boiling, empty it into containers. To use, dilute the syrup with an equal amount of water. It is a tried and healthy drink. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for wine (nabīd͟h) made from dates (tamr) and dād͟hī:[/b]\nTake 100 raṭls (100 pounds) of good quality dates, which have been newly dried, and put them in a big pot. Add water to submerge them and let them boil until one third of the liquid is gone. Set the pot aside to cool down. Strain the dates then press them in a silk cloth to extract whatever juice remains to yield. \n\tAdd water to the strained date juice to make it watery in consistency and pour it into big earthenware vessels (ḥibāb). Take a stick, fasten a round piece of wood to one of its ends, and use it to stir the juice. Do this for three days. \n\tAdd to the juice, 5 raṭls (5 pounds) of good quality clusters of brownish hop cones (dād͟hī). Add as well 5 raṭls (5 pounds) honey. \n\tSeal the vessels with mud and do not use the wine until three months have passed. This will make fabulous wine. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for wine (nabīd͟h) made from date syrup (dibs) and dād͟hī:[/b]\nTake 50 raṭls (50 pounds) date syrup and put it in a vessel. Pour on it a similar amount of water and put the vessel in a sunny place for 20 days. \n\tTake 5 raṭls (5 pounds) dād͟hī and a similar amount of honey. Put them in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom) and pour on them 10 raṭls (20 cups) water. Boil them and pour them into the prepared date syrup. Whip the mixture for three days after which you seal the vessels with mud. \n\tWhen two months have passed, open up the vessels. The wine will be splendid. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sun-fermented grape juice (baṣīr al-ʿinab al-s͟hamsī):[/b]\nChoose fully ripe juicy grapes and press them in the press (miʿṣara). Let the resulting juice warm up under the sky for three nights. \n\tPrepare pitched (muzaffat) wine vessels. Fumigate them with mastic and moistened aloe wood (ʿūd nayʾ). Empty the juice into the vessels and spread grape leaves all over the juice to cover it leaving a hole in the middle to allow the fermentation gases to escape. Keep the jars like this for 5 days then seal them with mud. Put them in a sunny place for 40 days after which keep them under a shade. \n\tThe longer this wine is allowed to age, the better it gets in aroma, taste, and color, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for grape juice wine:[/b]\nChoose grapes with the most juice and the thinnest skin and press them. Put the juice in pitched vessels (ẓurūf muzaffata). Cover the surface of the juice with grape leaves but leave a hole in the middle so that the fermentation gases escape out of the vessels. Keep them like this for 5 days. Seal the vessels with mud and open them after a whole year has elapsed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for raisin wine (nabīd͟h zabībī):[/b]\nTake 50 raṭls (50 pounds) zabīb (raisins) and put them aside. \n\tTake 30 raṭls (30 pounds) bees’ honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Add half its amount of water. Bring them to a vigorous boil. \n\tAdd the raisins to the boiling liquid as well as 20 raṭls (40 cups) water. Boil the mix then strain it to get rid of the raisin seeds. Flavor it with 5 dirhams (15 grams) saffron, 5 dirhams (15 grams) spikenard, 3 dirhams (9 grams) mastic, and 1 dānaq (½ gram) musk. \n\tEmpty the liquid into glass jars (qawārīr) and stow them away in a shaded place. You can use it after 40 days. It is a wonderful wine. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mead (nabīd͟h ʿasalī) without raisins:[/b]\nPut 50 raṭls (50 pounds) honey in a pot and add 50 raṭls (100 cups) water. Let it boil until one third of the liquid evaporates, which amounts to 33 raṭls. At this point, add to the pot 2 mit͟hqāls (9 grams) saffron and 2 dirhams (6 grams) mastic. Pour into the pot 5 raṭls (10 cups) cold water. \n\tEmpty the liquid into glass jars (qawārīr). Set them aside in a shaded place for 50 days after which you seal them with mud. Use the wine in winter by mixing one part of it with two parts of muskflavored water (nāfābā). It will be a splendid drink. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for sugar wine (s͟harāb al-sukkar) which Abū al-Ḥurr made:[/b]\nTake 12 kūz of ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar), grind it, and put it in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Pour on it 26 raṭls (52 cups) pure water. Boil the dissolved sugar until 11 raṭls (22 cups) of it evaporate. \n\tFumigate qarrābāt (large flagons) with aloe wood and fill them with the cooked sugar. Flavor it with a small amount of musk if it is winter, and camphor in the summer, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A wine recipe (s͟harāb) from chewy candy (fānīd͟h sukkarī, K͟hurāsānī, and S͟hajarī):[/b]\nTake 10 mann (20 pounds) or as much as you need of any of these of candies. Break them into smaller pieces and put them in a huge ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom). Sprinkle them with 1 uskurruja (½ cup) of water. Light low-heat fire under the pot and let it cook until the candy melts. \n\tStrain the melted candy, measure it, and return it to the cauldron with three times of its amount water. Let it boil under a slow fire until it reduces to one third of its original amount or less if you wish. \n\tEmpty the boiled liquid into jars—green-glazed (k͟haḍrāʾ) or glass (zujāj). Flavor it with saffron, spikenard, cloves, cassia, and nutmeg— as you usually do with mead (s͟harāb al-ʿasal). \n\tYou can use the wine after a month. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another sugar wine:[/b]\nTake one part pounded sugar and pour on it five parts water. Boil it until two parts evaporate and three parts remain. While boiling, add some saffron tied in a piece of cloth to color it yellow. But you need to use it sparingly. \n\tAfter boiling the liquid, empty it into a glass jar (qārūra) or a green-glazed one (jarra k͟haḍrāʾ). Tie the mouth of the container, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making gourd drink (s͟harāb al-qarʿ) with sugar:[/b]\nTake 10 raṭls (10 pounds) gourd and gourd seeds. Discard the fibrous pulp (s͟haḥm) around the seeds. Also take 10 raṭls (10 pounds) white Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy). Thoroughly pound each separately. \n\tTake 5 raṭls (5 pounds) ginger conserve (zanjabīl murabba) and 2 raṭls (2 pounds) jalanjabīn (rose petal and honey conserve). Add to these, frankincense (lubān), cassia and spikenard, 30 mit͟hqāls (5¼ ounces) each. Use as well, 40 mit͟hqāls (7 ounces) cloves. Grind them all and sift them. \n\tAdd all these ingredients (adwiya) to 10 raṭls (10 pounds) good qual-ity honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Knead them together and put the paste in a green-glazed jar (jarra k͟haḍrāʾ). Set it aside in a shaded place for a month. \n\tThis drink will be similar in effect to electuaries (juwāris͟hun), which stimulates the appetite and warms up the kidneys. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for carrot drink (s͟harāb al-jazar):[/b]\nWash carrots, cut off their ends, crush them lightly (yuraḍḍak͟h), and put them in a copper pot (qidr nuḥās). For each measure of the carrots used, add seven measures of water. Let pot come to a single boil and strain the carrots. \n\tReturn carrots to the pot and add to them honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. For each raṭl (pound) of honey, use 11 raṭls (11 pounds) carrots. Bring the pot to a boil and let it cook until carrots are completely done. \n\tAdd to the pot, ginger conserve (zanjabīl murabba) and a small amount of water. Put it away from the fire and let it cool down. Then strain the mixture and put the resulting syrup in a pitched jar in which wine has previously been made (jarra muzaffata ḍāriya). Flavor it with the spices usually used with honey wine. Throw into it a few stems of uncrushed saffron and stir in ½ uskurruja (1/4 cup) honey, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for caper drink (s͟harāb al-kabar) made by Ibn al-Muḥibbī:[/b]\nTake as much as you wish of fresh caper branches. Wash them in water once or twice then soak them in a tub (ijjāna) or a bucket (nabbār). Pour brine on them, put as much as needed to submerge them. Put the vessel in the sun for two days or three or more until the capers’ flavor seeps into the liquid. Strain the brine and put it in a copper pot coated with lead (qidr nuḥās murassas). Add a small amount of saffron or dried ginger (zanjabīl yābis). Add as well, walnut, spikenard, and cassia. \n\tLight a low-heat fire underneath the pot, and let it cook slowly until the liquid thickens and darkens. Let it cool down in the pot, strain it, and pour it into glass jars (qawārīr) or whatever vessels you prefer. \n\tWhenever you need to use it, pour as much as required into a glass (qadaḥ), dilute it with enough water, and drink it. It is good for expelling winds (riyāḥ) in the abdomen and the joints. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Carrot drink to warm up the kidneys and invigorate coitus:[/b]\nSlice carrots like darāhim (coins), put them in a pot, and pour on them an equal amount of water. Let them cook until done then strain the liquid and discard the dregs (t͟hafal). \n\tIn a clean pot, combine two parts of the strained carrot juice and one part honey. Boil the mixture until one third of it evaporats. Add a small amount of mace (basbāsa) and nutmeg (jawz bawwa). Set it aside for days then use it. It is a beneficial drink, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for chickpeas drink (s͟harāb al-ḥimmaṣ). It warms up stomach and kidneys, expels dense excretions (fuḍūlg͟halīẓa), and invigorates coitus:[/b]\nTake as much as you want of chickpeas and cook them with water until one third of the liquid evaporates. Transfer them to a clean vessel and add to them a small amount of saffron, black cardamom (qāqulla), cloves, galangal, and ginger. \n\tSeal the vessel with mud, set it aside for days, and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for poppy seeds drink (s͟harāb al-k͟has͟hk͟hās͟h), good for chest pain and persistent coughs:[/b]\nSoak 2 raṭls (2 pounds) poppy seeds in 8 raṭls (16 cups) rain water (māʾ al-maṭar) and spring water (māʾ al-ʿuyūn) for a day and a night. Then cook the poppy seeds with the water they were soaked in until liquid is reduced by half. Strain and press the seeds to extract all the juice from them. \n\tReturn the resulting liquid to the pot and add honey and cooked wine (ṭilā maṭbūk͟h), 36 1 raṭl (2 cups) each. Cook the mixture until it is thickened. Add a small amount of saffron and stow it away to mature and age (yaʿtaq). \n\tWhenever you need it, take a spoonful of it and mix it with māʾ al-kis͟hk (barley broth). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for ṭilā (cooked wine), recommended for pain in liver, chest, lungs, and cold-related aches and pains:[/b]\nTake 12 raṭls (24 cups) spring water and boil it down to half its original amount. Add 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey and cook them together until they boil down to thick syrup. Add a small amount of saffron. \n\tSome physicians add to the water used 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey and 1 raṭl (1 pound) sugar. Then they boil it down to syrup. \n\tStow the syrup away and use it as needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for chard drink (s͟harāb al-silq):[/b]\nPound chard leaves and press out their juice. Put in a pot equal amounts of chard juice and honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Light a slow fire underneath the pot and let it cook down to half its original amount. Add the four spices (al-afāwīh al-arbaʿa) which are spikenard, cloves, cassia, and nutmeg. Empty the drink into glass jars (qawārīr) and use it as needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for apple drink (s͟harāb al-tuffāḥ):[/b]\nChoose sweet and sour apples, pound them, and press out their juice. Mix 4 parts of the apple juice with 1 part honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Add all kinds of aromatic spices (min jamīʿ al-afwāh) to the drink and empty it into a green-glazed jar. \n\tDrink of it as much as you wish whenever you need it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Quince drink (s͟harāb al-safarjal):[/b]\nPound quince and press out its juice. Combine 5 parts of quince juice with 1 part good quality honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Also add 12 parts of ṭilā (cooked grape wine) made by boiling down grape juice to third of its original amount. Stir and mix all these ingredients. \n\tEmpty the drink into a scented clean vessel (muṭayyab) and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for pomegranate drink (s͟harāb al-rummān):[/b]\nCook well together 9 parts pomegranate juice and 1 part honey. Stir into the liquid, ṭilā (cooked grape wine) made by boiling it down to a third of its original amount. Shake the drink (k͟haḍk͟hiḍhu) and empty it into a clean vessel. You may flavor it with a bit of spices. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for plum drink (s͟harāb al-ijjāṣ) with honey:[/b]\nTake as much as you like of unripe plums, remove the pits, pound them, and press out their juice. Take one part of this juice and one part honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Cook them together under a slow fire until mix develops a thick consistency. \n\tYou have the option of replacing honey with ṭabarzad sugar (white cane sugar). A single drink of this mix weighs 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce/2 tablespoons) used diluted with water. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for peach drink (s͟harāb al-k͟hawk͟h):[/b]\nIn a clean pot, put 10 qisṭs (30 cups) juice of peach and 3 qisṭs (4½ pounds) honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. \n\tPrepare a bundle of thin cloth containing saffron, spikenard, cloves, Ceylon cinnamon (qarfa), cassia (dār Ṣīnī) and mastic, ½ dirham (1½ grams) of each, and let them be crushed. Put this bundle in the pot and bring it to a vigorous boil. After you put it away from the heat, strain the liquid, empty it into glass jars (qawārīr) and use it, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Drink of unripe grapes (s͟harāb al-ḥiṣrim) which curbs yellow bile (ṣafrāʾ) and heat (ḥarāra):[/b]\nTake 10 parts juice of unripe grapes and 3 parts honey. Put them in a clean pot. Take saffron, spikenard, Ceylon cinnamon (qarfa), cassia (dār Ṣīnī), white mastic gum (ʿilk al-Rūm), and camphor, a bit of each. Grind them and add them to the pot. \n\tLet the pot boil twice or thrice. Then, take the fire away from underneath the pot to let the drink cool down. Empty the drink into vessels and use it as needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for apple mayʿa made for al-Mutawakkil:[/b]\nTake unripe sour apples and keep them whole. Peel and core them, pound them, and press out their juice. \n\tTake the juice and boil it in a clean pot until it is reduced to half its original amount. Take it away from the fire, let it cool down, and strain it. Set it aside overnight and return it to the pot the following morning. For two parts of the apple juice, add one part honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth, and one part pleasant-tasting ṭilā (cooked grape wine). In a piece of cloth, tie mastic, qāqulla (black cardamom), hāl (green cardamom), and cassia, 3 mit͟hqāls (13½ grams) each, and add it to the pot. \n\tCook the mixture until it becomes like thin honey. Add 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) saffron, 20 ḥabbas (1¼ grams) cloves, one nutmeg— outer skin scraped (muqas͟hs͟har), 3 pieces qaṣab al-d͟harīra (chiretta plant), and 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) ground Indian aloe wood (ʿūd Hindī). \n\tEmpty the syrup into vessels and cover and tie their openings. You can use the syrup after a month. \n\tTo drink it, take 1 ūqiyya (2 tablespoons) of the syrup and dilute it in cold water. It is recommended for g͟has͟hī (fainting fits) and ḍaʿf (debility). It also strengthens the stomach, with God’s permission. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Mayba recipe prepared for al-Muʿtamid:[/b]\nTake 10 raṭls (20 cups) of strained juice of half-boiled (maṭbūk͟h ʿlā al-niṣf) sweet and sour quince. Take also 5 raṭls (10 cups) of each of the following: juice of Levantine apples; honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth; and well aged sweet-smelling cooked wine (maṭbūk͟h ʿatīq rayḥānī). \n\tMix all these ingredients in a pot and cook them under a slow fire, skimming the froth as it comes up. When liquid is reduced to syrup, take the pot away from the fire. \n\tCombine 5 dirhams (15 grams) choice aloe wood (ʿūd muṣṭafā), 3 dirhams (9 grams) sukk (aromatic compound), 4 dirhams (12 grams) saffron, and 5 dirhams (15 grams) mace blades (s͟hag͟hīz basbāsa). Also add spikenard, cloves, nutmeg, aẓfār al-ṭīb, hāl (green cardamom), and qāqulla (black cardamom), 1 dirham (3 grams) each. To these add, 3 dirhams (9 grams) mastic, and 1dirham (3 grams) musk. Put all these spices in a tied bundle of linen cloth and throw it into the prepared syrup. Empty the drink into a vessel and cover it with a lid. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for mayʿa made with vinegar. It may replace the ones given above:[/b]\nTake 5 raṭls (10 cups) juice of half-boiled quince. Combine it in a pot with 2 raṭls (2 pounds) honey and 2 raṭls (4 cups) vinegar. Cook the mixture until it becomes like thin honey. Skim the froth as needed. \n\tPrepare hāl (green cardamom), qāqulla (black cardamom), dār fulful (long pepper), ginger, and cassia, 5 dirhams (15 grams) each. Coarsely grind them and tie them in a bundle made of a clean piece of thin cloth. Throw the bundle into the pot. \n\tEmpty the syrup into a green-glazed jar (jarra k͟haḍrāʾ) or glass jars (qawārīr) and use it as required. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jalanjabīn (rose petal syrup) made with ṭabarzad (white cane sugar):[/b]\nTake one part of red rose petals, which have just been picked and untouched by water. Clip the petals into small pieces with clippers (maqārīḍ) discarding the parts closer to the calyxes. Make sure to discard them all. Take as well 3 parts of crushed ṭabarzad sugar. \n\tPrepare a vessel—green-glazed (ak͟hḍar) or glass (zujāj)—and arrange in it the rose petals and the sugar in layers until you use up all the quantities you have. Press the layers hard, cover the vessel, and put it in an enclosed warm place (ḥār kanīn). Cover it with several layers of clothes and let it warm up. Leave it like this for the rest of the day and the night. \n\tIn the following morning, take the vessel out to the sun and gently stir its contents with a willow stick (ʿūd k͟hilāf) until they mix well. Keep the vessel in the sun for a month or forty days, stirring the mixture two or three times during the day and take it inside during the night. \n\tTake the vessel in and use the syrup. To have a dose of it (s͟harba), dilute 10 dirhams (1 ounce) of the syrup in hot water and drink it first thing in the morning (balā al-rīq), God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for jalanjabīn (rose petal syrup) with honey:[/b]\nClip red rose petals into small pieces with clippers (miqrāḍ) and spread them on a piece of cloth or a tray made of date palm fronds (ṭabaq k͟hūṣ). Set them aside for a day and a night. Then weigh the petals and for each part use three parts honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Gently mix the two and put mixture in a glass container (ināʾ zujāj) or a green-glazed wide-mouthed jar (barniyya k͟haḍrāʾ). Put the container out in the sun for 40 days, stirring the mixture twice or thrice during the day and take it inside during the night. \n\tIf it needs more honey, then add some, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for juwāris͟hun (electuary), which alleviates gripes. It is also recommended for winds (riyīḥ) and flatulence (nafk͟h):[/b]\nCombine equal parts of Ceylon cinnamon (qarfa), spikenard, cubeb (ḥabb al-ʿarūs), dried rose petals, and white cumin (kammūn abyaḍ). Now take ginger, the amount of which should be twice as much as the amount of all the preceding spices combined. Grind the ingredients separately then sift and mix them. \n\tAdd to the spices enough of white honey with its wax (s͟hahd) to bind them into paste, which you then store in a bustūqa (earthenware jar with a narrow neck). \n\tA dose (s͟harba) of this paste will be what equals the size of 2 chickpeas, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for juwāris͟hun raṭb(moist electuary) which invigorates coitus. Not to be given to women:[/b]\nTake sweet Ceylon cinnamon (qarfa ḥulwa), spikenard, cloves, qust baḥrī (sea costus), and ginger, ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) each. Take as well, 3 ūqiyyas (3 ounces) of each of the following: long pepper (dār fulful), ḥaṣwat al-baḥr (sea musk), seeds of watercress (ḥabb al-jirjīr), seeds of Persian leeks (ḥabb kurrāt͟h Fārisī), and carrot seeds (ḥabb al-jazar). \n\tPound all these spices and mix them with honey to bind them into paste. \n\tEat one lump of this paste—the size of an almond—twice a day, in the morning on an empty stomach and at bedtime, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for juwāris͟hun recommended for colds and body aches:[/b]\nTake black myrobalan (ihlīlaj aswad), ginger, white pepper (fulful abyḍ), and black cumin (kammūn aswad). Take equal amounts of these spices after you grind them and sift them except for cumin, which you do not sift. \n\tBind all these spices with honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth, and make it into a thick electuary (laʿūq k͟hāt͟hir). \n\tHave some of it after the meal as a digestive and emollient. A spoonful of it can also be taken in the morning on an empty stomach (balā al-rīq). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Juwāris͟hun recommended for asthma (rabū), labored breathing (nafas), and coughs (suʿāl):[/b]\nGrind separately, dried fenugreek (ḥulba), Persian thyme (ṣaʿtar Fārisī), and rue (sad͟hāb), 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) each. Grind also ½ mit͟hqāl (2¼ grams) jaws͟hīr. Add walnut oil to these ingredients and knead them together. \n\tTake it diluted in māʾ al-kammūn (strained liquid of boiled cumin) for seven consecutive days. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for juwāris͟hun lozenge to restrain bowel movements (yaʿqil al-baṭn):[/b]\nPut in a ṭanjīr (copper cauldron with a rounded bottom), 1 mann (2 pounds) Sulaymānī sugar (hard sugar-candy), 10 ūqiyyas (10 ounces) ginger, 2 dānaqs (1 gram) musk, and a small amount of saffron. \n\tLet the ingredients boil into thick syrup, which you then empty on a board to spread, and cut it into whatever shapes you like. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A Recipe for another juwārishun that benefits the stomach:[/b]\nTake ginger, mastic, black pepper, and spikenard, 6 mit͟hqāls (27 grams) each. Take as well 5 mit͟hqāls (22½ grams) celery seeds (bazr al-karafs) and add to them ifranjamus͟hk and nānk͟hawāh (ajowan), 2 mit͟hqāls (9 grams) each. If ifranjamus͟hk is not available, use sād͟haj (Indian leaf) instead. \n\tGrind and sift all these ingredients and make them into paste by binding them with honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserve of ginger (zanjabīl murabba) beneficial to people with cold humoral properties (amzāj bārida):[/b]\nTake as much as you wish of big pieces of dried ginger. Soak them for three days in aromatic aged wine (s͟harāb) or aged cooked grape wine (ṭilā). Take ginger out of the wine, allow it to dry out, clean it very well, and put it in aged s͟harāb or ṭila. \n\tNow, take saffron, spikenard, black cardamom (qāqulla), black pepper, and long pepper (dār fulful), using eye measurements (bi qadar raʾī al-ʿayn). Grind these spices and sift them. But you grind saffron and add it separately. \n\tNow boil the ginger with the saffron and honey. When the mixture is done, transfer it to a clean container and add the set aside ground spices. Keep on stirring the mixture until the ginger pieces are thoroughly coated with the spices. Stow the container aside for three to five months then use it as needed. \n\tConserve of black halīlaj (myrobalan) is prepared the same way. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Conserving Chinese black myrobalan (tarbiyat halīlaj aswad Ṣīnī):[/b]\nPrepare them as described at the beginning of the recipe above, i.e. soak them in aged wine then put them in rubb al-tamr or dibs (date syrup) for days. Take them out and put them in honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. It will be excellent, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserving citron (tarbiyat al-utruj) from the book of al-Buzūrī:[/b]\nRemove the pulp of utruj (citron), put the peels in a clean vessel, and soak them in salted water for three days. Take them out and soak them in plain water for three days. During these three days replace the water twice a day to get rid of all traces of saltiness. Then take them out. \n\tBoil honey until it thickens and pour it on the peels. Set the mixture aside for four or five days and have a look at it. If you find the honey has thinned in consistency, put the mixture in a pot and boil it once or twice. Then wash the mix by adding water to it and letting it boil to original consistency. Put the mix aside and see if it has thinned again in consistency and repeat the ‘washing’ if needed. The more you ‘wash’ the mix the better it gets. \n\tRepeat the procedure until you see that honey has the same consistency as when you first put it. It is only then that you consider the conserve done. \n\tConserves of gourd, small and smooth cucumber (k͟hiyār), ribbed and long cucumber (qit͟ht͟hāʾ), and shelled and skinned almonds and walnuts, all these are made the same way as above. Indeed, this is the way to prepare whatever needs to be made into conserve. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserving apples (tarbīb al-tuffāh) from the same copy of al-Buzūrī:[/b]\nChoose large and fragrant Lebanese apples, peel and core them, and take 10 raṭls (10 pounds) of these. \n\tTake honey and vinegar, boil them in a pot, and add the prepared apples to them. Let the apples cook gently on slow fire stirring constantly until apples become as mushy as k͟habīṣ (thick pudding). \n\tAdd to the pot, 2 ūqiyyas (2 ounces) cassia, and 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) of each of the following: black pepper, cloves, black cardamom (qāqulla), and mace. Also add ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) spikenard and 3 nutmegs with outer skins scraped (muqas͟hs͟har). However, before adding them to the pot, you need to grind and sift each spice separately then mix them well, and add them to the pot. Besides, the amount of honey and vinegar used should be enough to cover the apples. \n\tFinally, add 1 mit͟hqāl (4½ grams) crushed saffron. Stir the pot until the ingredients mix well and look like k͟habīṣ (thick pudding). \n\tTransfer the conserve into a clean vessel, God willing. Know that pear conserve (tarbīb al-kumat͟hra) is done exactly like apples. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserving quince (tarbīb al-safarjal):[/b]\nQuarter and core quince, put it in a pot with honey, and pour water on it. Let the pot come to a boil then drain the quince, return it to the pot and add honey to it. Do not use water this time. Cook the quince again until it is well done. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserving carrots and radish (tarbīb al-jazar wa ’l-fujl):[/b]\nTake whichever you wish of these two, cut them to pieces, and soak them in salted water for three days. Rinse them in water or vinegar, put them in a vessel, and drench them in honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Add ground ginger and saffron or whatever you wish of the spices. Stir in sugar. \n\tLet the vessel sit in the sun for a whole month. After that, you can use the conserve, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserving busr:[/b]\nChoose dates that are still firm, boil them twice in pure water then remove the pits and the calyxes discard the pits but keep the calyxes. \n\tGrind spikenard, cloves, ginger, cassia, and saffron. Fill the dates with this mix to replace the pits and return the calyxes back to the dates. Put the dates in a glass jar (qārūra) and cover them with honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Set the glass jar aside until date conserve matures. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for conserving citron (tarbīb al-utruj):[/b]\nTake whatever you wish of citron rind and peel it from the outside the outer skin as well as the inside the white inner lining of the peel. Cut the peels as you wish, soak them in salted water for a day and a night, take them out, and soak them in pure water for another day and night. \n\tDrain the peels, put them in a pot, cover them with fresh water, and let them boil lightly. Drain them and set them aside to dry out a little. \n\tLet the peels simmer in hot water for a day and a night, take them out of the water, color them yellow with saffron, put them in a vessel, and submerge them in strained sugar honey (ʿasal maʿmūl), which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Add nutmeg, mace, cloves, cassia, harnuwa, hāl (green cardamom), and mastic (maṣṭakā). \n\tStore the conserve and use it as needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for plain condensed plum juice (rubb al-ijjās):[/b]\nTake as much as you need of ripe black plums, discard their pits, put them in a pot, and pour on them pure water (māʾ ʿad͟hb). For each 2 qafīzes (120 pounds) of plums use 1½ dawraqs (60 cups) of water. The dawraq equals 20 raṭls (40 cups). \n\tCook the plums until the liquid turns red and the fruit falls apart. Press out the juice and discard the dregs (t͟hafal). \n\tReturn the juice to the pot, and boil it until it condenses and becomes like thin honey in consistency. Strain the syrup and store it in a vessel. \n\tA single dose of this (al-s͟harba) weighs 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for condensed walnut juice (rubb al-jawz), recommended for sore throat, colds, and phlegm (balg͟ham):[/b]\nPound fresh green walnuts with the shell and press out the juice discard the dregs. Take as much as you want of the juice and boil it down to half its original amount. \n\tCombine in a pot, 5 parts of the reduced juice and 1 part honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Let the mixture cook on a slow fire until it condenses. Strain it and store it in glass jars (qawārīr). Use it as needed. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another walnut recipe, even more effective than the one above:[/b]\nTake fresh green walnuts and grind them with the shell. Press out the juice and discard the dregs. \n\tCombine in a clean pot, 5 parts of the walnut juice; 3 parts of honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth; and 3 parts sweet ṭilā (cooked grape wine). Add as well, 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) black pepper, ½ ūqiyya (15 grams) cubeb, and 1 ūqiyya (1 ounce) saffron. Boil down the mixture until it thickens then strain it and use it to cure a sore throat, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Rubb recipe for citron (utruj) that checks heat:[/b]\nRemove the white pith (s͟haḥm) and seeds (ḥabb) of citron pulp then pound it and press out its juice. Boil down the juice to fourth of its original amount then strain it and store it in glass jars (qawārīr). Use it as needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making concentrate of citron juice (rubb al-utruj), recommended for all stomach disorders:[/b]\nPound citron pulp, press out its juice, and strain it. Combine 4 parts of the juice with 1 part sukkar ṭabarzad (white cane sugar) or honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Boil mixture down to half its original amount. \n\tAdd to the pot, saffron and nutmeg, 1 mit͟hqāl of each (4½ grams), bruised (marḍūḍ) and tied in a bundle of thin cloth. This amount is enough for 20 raṭls (40 cups) of citron juice. \n\tContinue boiling the juice until it is condensed to thick syrup. Take the pot away from the fire. After it cools down, strain it and use it whenever needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for concentrated quince juice (rubb al-safarjal), good for diarrhea, vomiting, and excessive heat:[/b]\nPeel and core sweet quince. Pound it, press out its juice then boil it on a slow fire until it is reduced to a quarter of its original amount. Take it away from the fire, strain it, and set it aside until all boiling subsides (ḥattā yaskun). Return it to the fire and give it another boil. Store it in glass jars (qawārīr) and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for condensed juice of myrtle berries (rubb al-ās), recommended for hayḍa and diarrhea (istiṭlāq):[/b]\nPound ripe and soft myrtle berries, press out and strain their juice. Boil it in a clean pot until it is reduced to fourth of its original amount. Take the pot away from the fire then strain the concentrate and use it as needed, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making condensed juice of sour unripe grapes (rubb al-ḥiṣrim):[/b]\nCombine in a clean pot, 6 qisṭs (18 cups) juice of unripe grapes and 1 qisṭ (1½ pounds) honey, which has been boiled and skimmed of its froth. Cook the mixture until it thickens then strain it and store it in glass jars (qawārīr). \n\tIf you do not like honey and would rather not use it, substitute it with sukkar ṭabarzad (white cane sugar). A dose of this syrup (al-s͟harba) weighs 10 dirhams (1 ounce). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe of plain condensed pomegranate juice (rubb al-rummān al-sād͟haj):[/b]\nChoose ripe sweet-and-sour pomegranate (rummān muzz) with red seeds. Extract and strain the juice and put it in a clean soapstone pot (qidr birām). Boil it on slow fire until it is reduced to a third of its original amount then strain it and store it in glass jars (qawārīr). 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for us͟hnān (alkali compound) made for al-Ras͟hīd:[/b]\nTake cloves, salīk͟ha (bark similar to cassia), qāqulla (black cardamom), and falanja, one part each. \n\tAlso take what equals one part altogether of mastic, id͟hk͟hir (esparto grass), suʿd (cyperus), and mayʿa yābisa. You also need 3 parts of marjoram (marzanjūs͟h), 5 parts of white clay of Mecca (ṭīn abyaḍ Makkī), and us͟hnān Bāriqī, double or triple the amount of clay. Prepare as well, rice that has been soaked, dried, ground, and sifted. Its amount is similar to that of us͟hnān. \n\tPound each ingredient separately then mix them all, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe for a lesser us͟hnān:[/b]\nFinely grind together equal amounts of alkali (us͟hnān) and white clay (ṭīn abyaḍ). Mix with them, sixth of their amount pounded and sifted esparto grass flowers (id͟hk͟hir), and a fourth of their amount ground and sifted cyperus (suʿd). Mix in, as well, twelfth of their amount grated sandalwood (ṣandal maḥkūk). \n\tPour on the ingredients liquid of camphor (māʾ al-kāfūr), enough to bind ingredients into paste, knead them all into an integrated mass, and use, God willing. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Another recipe for a lesser us͟hnān:[/b]\nPick over white alkali (us͟hnān), pound it, sift it, and set it aside. Take grated white clay (ṭīn abyaḍ), half the amount of alkali used, pound it, sift it, and mix it with the alkali. \n\tTake ground and sifted id͟hk͟hir (esparto grass flowers), a quarter of the amount of the alkali-clay mix, and ground and sifted cyperus (suʿd), as much as the alkali used. \n\tMix all the ingredients with some liquid of camphor (māʾ al-kāfūr), rub them (yufrak) together to make a crumbly mix, and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]Making pure and white maḥlab:[/b]\nSkin, grind, and sift maḥlab kernels. The way to skin them is to lightly pound them, which will break the skins and make removing them easier. \n\tKnead the ground and sifted maḥlab with jasmine oil (duhn zanbaq) of Sābūr. Stick this dough to the inner side of a barniyya (wide-mouthed green-glazed jar). Fumigate the jar with moistened aloe wood (ʿūd nayʾ) several times, Do this by inverting the jar on the mijmara (censer with coals and incense) and fumigating it until the dough surface looks set and dry. Tie the mouth of the jar and stow it away. \n\tTo use maḥlab, take the amount needed, put it in a bowl, and knead it with jasmine oil (duhn al-zanbaq) of Sābūr. Perfume it with balsam oil (duhn balasān), citron oil (duhn utruj), and liquid of camphor (māʾ kāfūr), and use it. 
(Abbasid, VIII–X c.)\n[b]A recipe of royal maḥlab for the elite (maḥlab al-k͟hāṣṣa al-sulṭānī):[/b]\nTake good quality maḥlab kernels, pick them over one by one, remove the skins completely, and pick them over to get rid of all the yellowed and rotten kernels. Grind and sift them with a fine sieve (munk͟hul ṣafīq) and put the grind in a wide-mouthed jar made of glass (barniyya zujāj). Knead it with Persian jasmine oil (zanbaq Fārisī) and fumigate it with good quality aloe wood and camphor. Do the fumigating a hundred times within three days. During this period stir and mix the dough and stick it again to the side of the jar, twice a day. \n\tWhen you are done fumigating, put the dough in a glass (qadaḥ) and mix it with jasmine oil (duhn al-zanbaq) of Sābūr. Add a small amount of oil of Persian roses (duhn ward Fārisī), balsam oil (duhn balasān), citron oil (duhn utruj), good quality liquid of camphor (māʾ kāfūr), and as much as you like of crushed camphor, God willing.

Grind and sift them then knead them with good quality jasmine oil (zanbaq). Stick the dough to the inner side of a wide-mouthed jar (barniyya) and fumigate it with bunk (coffee shreds), qusṭ murr (bitter costus), suʿd (cyperus), mayʿa yābisa (dry resin of the storax tree), saffron, and sandalwood. Pound one nutmeg, mace, cloves, sandalwood, cubeb (kabāba), and black cardamom (qāqulla). Mix all these spices and stir them into the maḥlab dough. \n\tFinally, pour on them liquid of camphor (māʾ kāfūr) and lees of balsam oil (ʿakar al-balasān). \n\tIbrāhīm bin al-Mahdī composed these verses on us͟hnān and maḥlab (hand-washing compounds): \n[i]Crystal us͟hnān vessel etched from outside and within.\nBeasts and birds you see in them, and redolent ūs͟hnān of ʿaīr.\nIt smells of musk slathered on necks, and looks more like pebbles of camphor.\nLike soft, luxuriant, and silken fabric to the touch.\nThe maḥlab cup (qadaḥ) is preeminently placed,\nOverflowing with maḥlab with liquid camphor kneaded,\nOil of moringa beans and gillyflowers, fragrant as if wine.\nMore aromatic than ambergris tucked in breasts, more redolent than princely perfumes.\nIt has a lid perfectly contoured, made of silver, embossed with gold.\nLike the colorful designs on the back of a gazelle’s hand, so young and pure, adorned with dainty bracelets of silver and embroidery.\nAnd yet beware: the eyes are of a bewitching scoundrel, with horns of hair.\nIn his right hand he holds a bar of light—a spoon of gold—splendidly bright,\nStudded with jewels precious.
